rule_summary: Arrange multiple works in a citation alphabetically by author name.
rule_detail: Rule added: ‘Arrange the works alphabetically by author name.’

rule_summary: Follow each author name in a citation with publication dates separated by commas.
rule_detail: Rule added: ‘Follow the name with each date of publication separated by a comma. Arrange the dates chronologically, starting with the earliest date.’

rule_summary: Allow more standard abbreviations for months and days of the week.
rule_detail: Shortened forms for months and days of the week – We allow more contractions for use as standard abbreviations: ‘Tue’ ‘Thur’ ‘Thu’ ‘Jun’ ‘Jul’ ‘Sep’.

rule_summary: Use roman numerals rather than Arabic numerals for World War abbreviations.
rule_detail: There is a rule change for the shortened form. We now recommend using roman numerals not arabic numerals – write ‘WWII’ not ‘WW2’.

rule_summary: Write all centuries with numerals.
rule_detail: Centuries – Write all centuries with numerals (3rd century).

rule_summary: Place time zone initialisms after the time.
rule_detail: The initialisms for time zones now appear after the time (13:45 AEST) not before the time (AEST 13:45).

rule_summary: Use en dashes for particular types of year spans.
rule_detail: Dates and spans – ‘Use en dashes for particular types of year spans’ (H2)

rule_summary: Use words for spans of days and months in body text.
rule_detail: ‘Use words for spans of days and months in body text’ (H2)

rule_summary: Use en dashes for spans of days and months when space is limited.
rule_detail: ‘Use en dashes for spans of days and months when space is limited’ (H2)

rule_summary: Use en dashes for spans of time when space is limited.
rule_detail: ‘Use en dashes for spans of time when space is limited’ (H2)

rule_summary: Follow the manual’s number rules for duration.
rule_detail: ‘Follow the manual’s number rules for duration’ (H2)

rule_summary: Combine dates and times correctly.
rule_detail: ‘How to combine dates and times’ (H2)

rule_summary: Combine dates and times carefully when space is limited.
rule_detail: ‘Combining dates and times when space is limited’ (H3)

rule_summary: Use shortened forms for units of time when space is limited.
rule_detail: ‘Use shortened forms for units of time when space is limited’ (H2)

rule_summary: Meet standards for data systems and information interchange.
rule_detail: ‘Meet standards for data systems and information interchange’ (H2) and associated H3s

rule_summary: Insert a non-breaking space correctly.
rule_detail: ‘Insert a non-breaking space correctly’

rule_summary: Use words instead of symbols to improve accessibility.
rule_detail: ‘Use words instead of symbols to improve accessibility’ (H2) – text added to better explain why words are preferred in general content; additional examples

rule_summary: Use symbols when user research supports their use.
rule_detail: Rules about symbols restructured under new heading ‘Use symbols when user research supports their use’ (H2)

rule_summary: Use code for symbols, not punctuation.
rule_detail: ‘Use code for symbols, not punctuation’ – more symbols added; the terms ‘operators’ and ‘relations’ explained; example changed

rule_summary: Do not use a symbol or a space for ratios.
rule_detail: ‘Don’t use a symbol or a space for ratios’ – section moved higher up for flow; explanatory text added to examples

rule_summary: Use a minus sign for subtraction and negative numbers.
rule_detail: ‘Subtraction and negative numbers’ – new text and additional examples

rule_summary: Use the division rule for narrow no-break spaces and thin spaces.
rule_detail: ‘Division’ – now a stand-alone section; revised with new information about narrow no-break spaces and thin spaces; example algebraic expressions added and italicised as per mathematical style

rule_summary: Use the multiplication dot correctly.
rule_detail: ‘Multiplication’ – now a stand-alone section; revised with new information about the multiplication dot; new examples added for dot and asterisk.

rule_summary: Use the correct style for equations.
rule_detail: ‘Use the correct style for equations’.

rule_summary: Use capitals for most acronyms and initialisms.
rule_detail: ‘Use capitals for most acronyms and initialisms’ – new example

rule_summary: Standardise the style of state and territory governments when they appear as authors in page references.
rule_detail: Changes for consistency: standardise style of state and territory governments that appear as author in page references.

rule_summary: Use the term First Nations people instead of First Nations Australians.
rule_detail: [Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples](/node/179): change from the term ‘First Nations Australians’ to ‘First Nations people’.

rule_summary: Use words to explain why symbols are preferred in general content.
rule_detail: ‘Use words instead of symbols to improve accessibility’ (H2) – text added to better explain why words are preferred in general content; additional examples

rule_summary: Do not cite the Style Manual when you use its guidance to create content.
rule_detail: You don’t need to cite the Style Manual when you use its guidance to create content.

rule_summary: Use the equivalent referencing style for titles mentioned in body text.
rule_detail: A long-held convention is that titles mentioned in body text follow their equivalent referencing style.

rule_summary: Follow the styles shown in the Author–date and Documentary–note systems when referring to the Style Manual.
rule_detail: We recommend that Australian Government writers follow the styles shown in either of the Author–date and Documentary–note systems.

rule_summary: Treat mentions of the Style Manual as the name of a website.
rule_detail: If you mention the Style Manual in your content, treat it as the name of a website.

rule_summary: Use title case for the Style Manual website name.
rule_detail: Follow the capitalisation style of our website – title case – and use italics.

rule_summary: Italicise the Style Manual website name.
rule_detail: Follow the capitalisation style of our website – title case – and use italics.

rule_summary: Introduce the shortened form Style Manual in parentheses at first mention.
rule_detail: Introduce the shortened form ‘Style Manual’ in parentheses at first mention.

rule_summary: Use Style Manual for later mentions after first introducing the shortened form.
rule_detail: Use the shortened form for later mentions.

rule_summary: Treat a Style Manual webpage as part of a larger publication or series.
rule_detail: When you mention a webpage from the Style Manual in your content, treat it as part of a larger publication or series.

rule_summary: Use sentence case for the title of a Style Manual webpage.
rule_detail: Use sentence case and quotation marks.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks for the title of a Style Manual webpage.
rule_detail: Use sentence case and quotation marks.

rule_summary: Cite the Style Manual whenever you paraphrase or quote it.
rule_detail: Always cite the Style Manual when you paraphrase it or quote it in your content.

rule_summary: Hyperlink the name of the website and any webpages you cite.
rule_detail: Please also hyperlink the name of our website and any webpages you cite.

rule_summary: Use an in-text citation and a full reference list citation in Author–date style.
rule_detail: This system comprises an in-text citation and a full citation in the list of references.

rule_summary: Use italics and title case for the name of the website in an Author–date full citation.
rule_detail: For the full citation, use italics and title case for the name of our website.

rule_summary: Follow the website name in an Author–date full citation with the URL.
rule_detail: Follow this with our URL.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks for the title of a Style Manual webpage in Author–date citations.
rule_detail: To cite a Style Manual webpage in Author–date, use: quotation marks for the title of the webpage.

rule_summary: Use sentence case and italics for the publication name in a Style Manual webpage citation.
rule_detail: To cite a Style Manual webpage in Author–date, use: sentence case and italics for the name of the publication.

rule_summary: Follow the title of the website with the word website in a Style Manual webpage citation.
rule_detail: To cite a Style Manual webpage in Author–date, use: title of the website followed by ‘website’.

rule_summary: Use Documentary–note citations for endnotes and footnotes.
rule_detail: Follow the citation rules in ‘Documentary–note’ if you use endnotes or footnotes in your content.

rule_summary: Use the Documentary–note element order shown in the style manual rather than the Author–date order.
rule_detail: The order of some elements differs from the order shown in Author–date.

rule_summary: Use the Style Manual to apply government style to all kinds of content formats.
rule_detail: Use the Style Manual to learn how to apply government style to all kinds of content formats.

rule_summary: Use the Style Manual to write and edit user-focused content.
rule_detail: It tells you how to write and edit user-focused content.

rule_summary: Use guidance on each page to understand how to create government content.
rule_detail:
Guidance on each page helps you understand how to:

- create content for government
- use rules and conventions to create consistent content.

rule_summary: Use guidance on each page to understand how to create consistent content.
rule_detail:
Guidance on each page helps you understand how to:

- create content for government
- use rules and conventions to create consistent content.

rule_summary: Use the manual for external-facing content designed for end-users.
rule_detail: You can use the manual for services and products that are designed for end-users (external-facing content).

rule_summary: Use the manual for internal government content as well.
rule_detail: It’s equally applicable to content for government users (internal-to-government content).

rule_summary: Check whether your organisation's style guide is current and refers to the Style Manual.
rule_detail: Your organisation might have its own style guide. Check if it is current and refers to the Style Manual.

rule_summary: Use the search box in each page header to find guidance.
rule_detail: Use the search box in the header of each page to find the guidance you’re looking for.

rule_summary: Type your search query into the header search box to find relevant content.
rule_detail: Type your search query into the box to find relevant and related content.

rule_summary: Use the 'Guidance' headings to identify topics and rules.
rule_detail: Use the ‘Guidance’ headings at the top of each page to identify topics and rules.

rule_summary: Use each heading as a concise statement of guidance.
rule_detail: Each heading leads to a concise statement of guidance. This is a style rule.

rule_summary: Use examples to illustrate rules.
rule_detail: Rules are illustrated by examples. Find examples in a callout box titled ‘Example’.

rule_summary: Use paired examples to compare what to do and what not to do.
rule_detail: Some examples are presented in pairs to compare what to do and what not to do.

rule_summary: Use paired headings such as 'Write this' and 'Not this' or 'Like this' and 'Not this' for paired examples.
rule_detail:
These example boxes have paired headings like:

- ‘Write this’ and ‘Not this’
- ‘Like this’ and ‘Not this’.

rule_summary: Use paired examples to confirm your understanding of the rule.
rule_detail: Use these paired examples to confirm your understanding of the rule.

rule_summary: Use highlighted content in example boxes to identify where the rule applies.
rule_detail: Highlights in example boxes draw attention to the content the rule applies to. Look for highlights to understand how you should apply the rule in your content.

rule_summary: Use words in square brackets after examples to clarify how the example relates to the rule.
rule_detail: Some examples are followed by words in square brackets. These words clarify how the example relates to the rule.

rule_summary: Treat callouts as additional obligations to consider alongside style.
rule_detail: Some Style Manual guidance is accompanied by additional highlighted information. These callouts mean you have other obligations to consider, as well as style.

rule_summary: Follow accessibility requirements sourced from WCAG.
rule_detail: The Style Manual includes information about accessibility requirements. This information is sourced directly from the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).

rule_summary: Use accessibility callouts to consider which WCAG elements apply to the content you create.
rule_detail: Accessibility callouts explain which elements of WCAG should be considered when creating different types of content. They give practical advice and a link to more information about the criteria for accessibility.

rule_summary: Use the advice to create content that users can understand.
rule_detail: Use the advice to create content that your users can understand.

rule_summary: Add alternative text for all images.
rule_detail:
Add alternative text for all images. For help with writing good alt text: the W3C
[alt text decision tree.](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/decision-tree/) - Write alternative text that describes the information or function of the image. For help to describe images: the W3C/WAI Web accessibility
[images tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/).

rule_summary: Write alternative text that describes the information or function of the image.
rule_detail:
Add alternative text for all images. For help with writing good alt text: the W3C
[alt text decision tree.](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/decision-tree/) - Write alternative text that describes the information or function of the image. For help to describe images: the W3C/WAI Web accessibility
[images tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/images/).

rule_summary: Consider information management obligations when creating Australian Government records.
rule_detail: Information that you create as part of your work for the Australian Government is a record. Records provide evidence of what your organisation has done and why. Information management callouts explain your responsibility to manage and dispose of records.

rule_summary: Comply with the Australian Privacy Principles when handling personal information.
rule_detail: When you handle personal information, you must comply with the [Australian Privacy Principles](https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles). Privacy callouts explain your legal responsibility when collecting, handling and storing personal information.

rule_summary: Consider security classification requirements for Australian Government content.
rule_detail: Australian Government content is subject to security classification assessment under the [Protective Security Policy Framework](https://www.protectivesecurity.gov.au/). Security classification callouts provide resources about applying security classifications and protective markings.

rule_summary: Consider criteria from the Digital Service Standard that might apply to your content.
rule_detail: The Digital Transformation Agency’s [Digital Service Standard](https://www.dta.gov.au/help-and-advice/about-digital-service-standard) is a set of criteria for designing and delivering government services. Digital Service Standards callouts identify criteria from the standard that might apply to your content.

rule_summary: Follow the Style Manual guidance that applies to both digital and print formats.
rule_detail: Most of the guidance in the Style Manual applies to digital and print formats.

rule_summary: Look for guidance under 'Print considerations' when designing content for print.
rule_detail: There are particular things to keep in mind when you design content for print. These things appear as guidance under the heading ‘Print considerations’. The guidance is highlighted so it is easy to find.

rule_summary: Provide clear link text and make sure it looks like a link when publishing Easy Read as a PDF with links.
rule_detail:
Publishing Easy Read as a PDF means it may be read online or printed. When you have links in the material, you need to:

- provide clear link text and make sure it looks like a link
- spell out the URL next to the linked text.

rule_summary: Spell out the URL next to linked text.
rule_detail:
Publishing Easy Read as a PDF means it may be read online or printed. When you have links in the material, you need to:

- provide clear link text and make sure it looks like a link
- spell out the URL next to the linked text.

rule_summary: Treat the digital Style Manual as superseding the cited sources.
rule_detail:
The digital Style Manual supersedes the:

*Style manual for authors, editors and printers*(sixth edition, 2002)- Digital Transformation Agency’s Content Guide.

rule_summary: Use the Style Manual when creating Australian Government content.
rule_detail: Use the Style Manual when creating Australian Government content.

rule_summary: Treat accessibility as a mandatory standard for government agencies.
rule_detail: Accessibility is a mandatory standard for government agencies.

rule_summary: Test content against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines success criteria.
rule_detail: Test your content against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) success criteria.

rule_summary: Commit to improving agency performance against the accessibility standard.
rule_detail: Agencies should commit to improving their performance against the standard.

rule_summary: Use WCAG to guide your agency about accessibility.
rule_detail: Use WCAG to guide your agency about accessibility

rule_summary: Recognise WCAG 2.2 as the current version.
rule_detail: WCAG 2.2 is the current version.

rule_summary: Meet WCAG level AA and aim higher.
rule_detail: Meet WCAG level AA, but aim higher

rule_summary: Include an accessibility statement.
rule_detail: Include an accessibility statement

rule_summary: Include information in an accessibility statement about how WCAG has been addressed.
rule_detail: information about how you’ve addressed WCAG

rule_summary: Include information in an accessibility statement about the technical specifications tested.
rule_detail: information about the technical specifications you’ve tested

rule_summary: Include evidence of a commitment to accessibility in an accessibility statement.
rule_detail: evidence of a commitment to accessibility.

rule_summary: Include a page that explains the extent to which a service or product complies with WCAG.
rule_detail: Include a page on your site that explains the extent your service or product complies with WCAG.

rule_summary: Consider other relevant W3C standards.
rule_detail: You may also need to refer to [other relevant W3C standards](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/).

rule_summary: Check procurement content against AS EN 301 549:2016.
rule_detail: For procurements, check [ Accessibility requirements suitable for public procurement of ICT products and services](https://infostore.saiglobal.com/en-au/standards/as-en-301-549-2016-100620_saig_as_as_211428/) (AS EN 301 549:2016).

rule_summary: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs.
rule_detail: Use WCAG principles to meet user needs

rule_summary: Treat user needs as the basis for applying accessibility principles.
rule_detail: User needs are at the heart of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). When you take user needs into account, applying accessibility principles becomes simpler, though not necessarily easier.

rule_summary: Make content perceivable so any user can perceive it.
rule_detail:
Principle: content is perceivable

Any user can perceive the content.

rule_summary: Provide text alternatives for images.
rule_detail: I can understand any information contained in an image. ([Guideline: text alternatives](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#text-alternatives))

rule_summary: Provide equivalent information for video and audio content.
rule_detail: I can access equivalent information to anything contained in a video or audio file. ([Guideline: time-based media](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#time-based-media))

rule_summary: Allow content presentation to change without losing information or structure.
rule_detail: I can change the content’s presentation without losing information or structure. ([Guideline: adaptable](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#adaptable))

rule_summary: Ensure colour or sound distinctions can be controlled easily.
rule_detail: I can easily control how I see and hear distinctions if colour or sound convey meaning. ([Guideline: distinguishable](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#distinguishable))

rule_summary: Make content operable so any user can operate navigation and interface.
rule_detail:
Principle: content is operable

Any user can operate the navigation and interface.

rule_summary: Ensure content can be operated using only a keyboard.
rule_detail: I can operate the content using only a keyboard. ([Guideline: keyboard accessible](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#keyboard-accessible))

rule_summary: Give users enough time to read and use timed content.
rule_detail: I can control any features that involve timing so I have enough time to read and use the content. ([Guideline: enough time](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#enough-time))

rule_summary: Prevent content from causing seizures or physical reactions.
rule_detail: I can use the content without experiencing a seizure or physical reaction. ([Guideline: seizures and physical reactions](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#seizures-and-physical-reactions))

rule_summary: Make it easy for users to find, navigate and determine their location on the webpage.
rule_detail: I can find and navigate the content and determine where I am on the webpage. ([Guideline: navigable](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#navigable))

rule_summary: Support operation with input methods other than a keyboard.
rule_detail: I can operate the webpage with something other than a keyboard, like a pointer. ([Guideline: input modalities](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#input-modalities))

rule_summary: Make content understandable so any user can understand the information and interface.
rule_detail:
Principle: content is understandable

Any user can understand the information and the interface.

rule_summary: Make text readable, including when it contains unusual words, shortened forms or languages other than English.
rule_detail: I can read and understand text, even if the content includes unusual words and shortened forms,or features languages other than English. ([Guideline: readable](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#readable))

rule_summary: Make webpage behaviour and appearance predictable.
rule_detail: I can predict the webpage’s appearance and how I will operate the content. ([Guideline: predictable](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#predictable))

rule_summary: Help users avoid input mistakes and correct errors.
rule_detail: I can avoid making any mistakes with my inputs, and correct any that I might make. ([Guideline: input assistance](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#input-assistance))

rule_summary: Make content robust so assistive technologies can interpret it.
rule_detail:
Principle: content is robust

Assistive technologies can interpret the content.

rule_summary: Ensure markup supports software and assistive technology access.
rule_detail: I have confidence the markup language supports my use of software and assistive technology to access the content. ([Guideline: compatible](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/#compatible))

rule_summary: Look for accessibility requirements when checking guidance for different topics.
rule_detail: Look for accessibility requirements as you check guidance for different topics.

rule_summary: Treat callout boxes as links between user needs and accessibility actions.
rule_detail: Callout boxes in the Style Manual relate user needs to fundamental actions you can take to ensure content is accessible by design.

rule_summary: Use callouts to include references to WCAG criteria and technical details.
rule_detail: Callouts also include references to WCAG criteria that link to technical details (level A, level AA and level AAA success criteria).

rule_summary: Include links to external accessibility resources when relevant.
rule_detail: The Style Manual also includes links to other external resources about accessibility.

rule_summary: Design products and services so they work for everyone.
rule_detail: Inclusive design means that the products and services we create work for everyone.

rule_summary: Use design for all methods to improve people’s experience of digital content.
rule_detail: This body of knowledge offers practical methods to improve people’s experience of digital content.

rule_summary: Promote the Digital Service Standard methods in line with Style Manual guidance.
rule_detail: The Style Manual promotes some of these methods, in line with the Digital Service Standard, such as: understanding needs through user research, embedding accessibility as a foundation, using consistent and responsive design.

rule_summary: Design for a diverse range of needs.
rule_detail: The goal is inclusive design that meets a diverse range of needs.

rule_summary: Consider user experience in different situations and on different devices.
rule_detail: Inclusive design considers user experience in a range of situations – for example, on different devices and for time-poor users.

rule_summary: Do user research for content.
rule_detail: Do user research

rule_summary: Test content to gain input, views and feedback from users.
rule_detail: As part of your user research, test content to gain: input from the users you’re designing for; views and feedback from a diverse and representative users.

rule_summary: Combine user research with accessibility techniques to design usable content.
rule_detail: Combine your user research with accessibility techniques to design usable content.

rule_summary: Ask what makes content usable.
rule_detail: Ask what makes content usable

rule_summary: Treat usability and accessibility as closely linked.
rule_detail: Usability and accessibility are closely linked.

rule_summary: Recognise accessibility as a foundation for broader user needs.
rule_detail: Accessible content is a foundation to address broader user needs.

rule_summary: Use accessibility as a necessary step to create usable content.
rule_detail: You can think of accessibility as a necessary step to create usable content.

rule_summary: Provide description for content that uses images and cannot otherwise be perceived.
rule_detail: Consider a user who cannot perceive images and the content provides no description, such as alt text. In this situation, visual content is not usable because it is not accessible.

rule_summary: Design content so it does not create barriers to access.
rule_detail: Government content needs to be designed so it does not create barriers to access.

rule_summary: Design content to serve people with diverse abilities and conditions.
rule_detail: When you design content, it needs to serve people with: age-related conditions, changing abilities, disability, health issues, cognitive, neurological and learning disabilities.

rule_summary: Write and design content that matches how users read.
rule_detail: Write and design content that matches how users read. Use short sentences and simple structure.

rule_summary: Use short sentences.
rule_detail: Write and design content that matches how users read. Use short sentences and simple structure.

rule_summary: Use a simple structure.
rule_detail: Write and design content that matches how users read. Use short sentences and simple structure.

rule_summary: Take into account how people read and what makes content easy to read.
rule_detail: To create usable content, take into account how people read and what makes content easy to read.

rule_summary: Increase usability with legible page design.
rule_detail:
You can increase usability with:

- legible page design
- readable language
- comprehensible structure.

rule_summary: Increase usability with readable language.
rule_detail:
You can increase usability with:

- legible page design
- readable language
- comprehensible structure.

rule_summary: Increase usability with comprehensible structure.
rule_detail:
You can increase usability with:

- legible page design
- readable language
- comprehensible structure.

rule_summary: Understand the needs of all users and create content they can access.
rule_detail: You must understand the needs of all users of your service and create content they can access to meet the Digital Service Standard:

rule_summary: Use a clear structure to help people understand the type of content.
rule_detail: To help people understand the type of content, use a clear [structure](/node/75).

rule_summary: Write clear page titles.
rule_detail: - Write clear page titles. This is the first thing a screen reader user will hear and should align with the first heading on the page.

rule_summary: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings.
rule_detail: - Organise content with a clear structure using section headings. Describe the topics or the following section in the heading.

rule_summary: Let users navigate through all content in the intended order.
rule_detail: - Make sure users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they're using. Use the same navigation elements across the service.

rule_summary: Do not rely on colour alone to structure pages.
rule_detail: - Don’t rely on colour alone to structure pages.

rule_summary: Do not rely on sensory characteristics to explain things.
rule_detail: - Don’t rely on sensory characteristics such as shape, size, visual location, orientation or sound to explain things.

rule_summary: Write in plain language.
rule_detail: - Write in plain language. This helps all users and is essential for some.

rule_summary: Aim for a lower secondary education reading level for Level AAA.
rule_detail: - Level AAA requires a lower secondary education reading level, after removal of proper names and titles (year 7 or between 12 and 14 years old).

rule_summary: Avoid or explain unusual words, phrases, idioms and similar forms.
rule_detail: - Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Expand acronyms on first use.
rule_detail: - Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Avoid using double negatives.
rule_detail: - Avoid using double negatives

rule_summary: Use short sentences to help people build reading rhythm.
rule_detail:
Help people build reading rhythm with:

- short sentences
- new
[paragraphs](/node/53) - line breaks.

rule_summary: Use new paragraphs and line breaks to help reading rhythm.
rule_detail:
Help people build reading rhythm with:

- short sentences
- new
[paragraphs](/node/53) - line breaks.

rule_summary: Aim for an average sentence length of 15 words.
rule_detail: For most readers, aim for an average sentence length of 15 words per sentence.

rule_summary: Keep long sentences to no more than 25 words.
rule_detail: Long sentences should have no more than 25 words.

rule_summary: Use paragraphs to help readers find and absorb ideas.
rule_detail: Paragraphs give people a rest before launching into a new idea. They also help people quickly find an idea in the writing.

rule_summary: Use line breaks to package information effectively.
rule_detail: Line breaks also package information. Used well, they are an effective way to keep people focused and interested.

rule_summary: Use line breaks to help people focus on one idea at a time.
rule_detail:
Line breaks are used to:

- help people focus on one idea at a time
- draw attention to a point – this is why a paragraph of one short sentence can be so effective.

rule_summary: Use line breaks to draw attention to a point.
rule_detail:
Line breaks are used to:

- help people focus on one idea at a time
- draw attention to a point – this is why a paragraph of one short sentence can be so effective.

rule_summary: Avoid line breaks that break ideas in the wrong place.
rule_detail:
Poorly used line breaks either:

- break ideas in the wrong place – for example, by creating too many short lines
- let ideas run together – for example, by creating long lines.

rule_summary: Avoid line breaks that let ideas run together.
rule_detail:
Poorly used line breaks either:

- break ideas in the wrong place – for example, by creating too many short lines
- let ideas run together – for example, by creating long lines.

rule_summary: Use changes in rhythm to support comprehension.
rule_detail: Variations need to support comprehension. For example, you can use a change of rhythm for emphasis: to make a point or draw the reader's attention to a certain word.

rule_summary: Use structure, punctuation and parenthetical information to vary rhythm.
rule_detail:
You can vary rhythm using:

- headings, lists and other elements that give
[structure](/node/75) [punctuation marks](/node/119)- parenthetical information – set off using
[brackets](/node/111),[commas](/node/109)or[dashes](/node/199).

rule_summary: Use headings, lists and other structural elements to vary rhythm.
rule_detail:
You can vary rhythm using:

- headings, lists and other elements that give
[structure](/node/75) [punctuation marks](/node/119)- parenthetical information – set off using
[brackets](/node/111),[commas](/node/109)or[dashes](/node/199).

rule_summary: Use parenthetical information set off with brackets, commas or dashes.

rule_summary: Use culturally appropriate and respectful language when writing with, for or about First Nations people.
rule_detail: Use culturally appropriate and respectful language when writing with, for or about First Nations people.

rule_summary: Consult with traditional owners, local elders, community and content experts when writing about sensitive matters like cultures and history.
rule_detail: It’s important to consult with traditional owners, local elders, community and content experts. Consultation is essential when writing about sensitive matters like cultures and history.

rule_summary: Use specific terms, such as the name of a community, before broader terms.
rule_detail: Specific terms, like the name of a community, before using broader terms

rule_summary: Use plurals when speaking about collectives.
rule_detail: plurals when speaking about collectives (peoples, nations, cultures, languages)

rule_summary: Use present tense unless speaking about a past event.
rule_detail: present tense, unless speaking about a past event

rule_summary: Use empowering, strengths-based language.
rule_detail: empowering, strengths-based language

rule_summary: Avoid shorthand terms, including ‘Aborigines’, ‘Islanders’ and ‘ATSI’.
rule_detail: shorthand terms like ‘Aborigines', ‘Islanders’ or acronyms like ‘ATSI’

rule_summary: Avoid using ‘myth’, ‘legend’ or ‘folklore’ for First Nations beliefs.
rule_detail: using terms like ‘myth’, ‘legend’ or ‘folklore’ when referring to the beliefs of First Nations people

rule_summary: Avoid blood quantums and percentage measures such as ‘half-caste’.
rule_detail: blood quantums (for example, ‘half-caste’ or percentage measures)

rule_summary: Avoid ‘us versus them’ language.
rule_detail: ‘us versus them’ or deficit language

rule_summary: Avoid possessive terms such as ‘our’ in references to Aboriginal peoples.
rule_detail: possessive terms such as ‘our’, as in ‘our Aboriginal peoples’

rule_summary: Avoid ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’ because it implies ownership.
rule_detail: ‘Australian Indigenous peoples’, as it also implies ownership, much like ‘our’.

rule_summary: Do not use the past tense to describe First Nations people as if they no longer exist.
rule_detail: This use of past tense continues the historical erasure of First Australians.

rule_summary: Capitalize both Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country.
rule_detail: Always capitalise both.

rule_summary: Use Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country as distinct practices with different requirements and meanings.
rule_detail: Welcome to Country is an important ceremony for many First Australians. An Acknowledgement of Country is a way of showing respect. Both are distinct practices with different requirements and meanings.

rule_summary: Use the specific nation, island or community name when writing about a specific group.
rule_detail: a specific group, use their nation, island or community name

rule_summary: Use a regional term when writing about many Aboriginal nations if it is more appropriate.
rule_detail: many Aboriginal nations, there may be a regional term that is better, such as ‘Murris’ or ‘Kooris’

rule_summary: Use a regional term when writing about many Torres Strait Islander peoples or islands if it is more appropriate.
rule_detail: many Torres Strait Islander peoples or islands, there may be a regional term that is more appropriate, such as Kulkalgal (encompassing the central islands of Masig, Poruma, Warraber and Iama)

rule_summary: Use First Nations people, First Australians or Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples when writing about both groups.
rule_detail: both Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, use terms such as ‘First Nations people’, ‘First Australians’ or ‘Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander peoples’.

rule_summary: Treat ‘Indigenous’ and ‘Aboriginal’ as broad terms imposed without consultation.
rule_detail: ‘Indigenous’ and ‘Aboriginal’ are broad terms imposed on First Australians without consultation. These are not words they chose for themselves.

rule_summary: Use ‘Indigenous Australians’ only when writing generally about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and only when you cannot avoid it.
rule_detail: If you must use it, remember to only do so when writing generally about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

rule_summary: Capitalise the term ‘Indigenous Australians’ and use it in the first instance only.
rule_detail: The term should always appear as ‘Indigenous Australians’ in the first instance, always with a capital ‘I’. Afterward you can use ‘Indigenous’, capitalised, so long as the context is correct and clear. Using ‘Indigenous’ alone is inaccurate.

rule_summary: Do not use ‘Indigenous’ alone to mean First Australians.
rule_detail: Using ‘Indigenous’ alone is inaccurate.

rule_summary: Do not refer to First Nations languages as extinct.
rule_detail: Hundreds of distinct First Nations languages and dialects are alive and spoken today. Never refer to them as ‘extinct’.

rule_summary: Use ‘sleeping’ to describe languages that are being revived.
rule_detail: Many communities are working to revive their languages. The preferred term to describe these languages is ‘sleeping’.

rule_summary: Follow the spellings that local traditional owners, elders or community members use for words from their languages.
rule_detail: Follow the spellings that local traditional owners, elders or community members use for words from their languages.

rule_summary: Do not italicise names or words from First Nations languages.
rule_detail: Do not italicise names or words from First Nations languages. They are Australian languages, not foreign languages.

rule_summary: Refer to age only when it is necessary.
rule_detail: Refer to age only if it is necessary. Use respectful language and consistent style if age is relevant.

rule_summary: Use respectful language and consistent style when age is relevant.
rule_detail: Refer to age only if it is necessary. Use respectful language and consistent style if age is relevant.

rule_summary: Question whether age is relevant before referring to it.
rule_detail: Question whether age is relevant. Avoid referring to a person’s age or an age group if it’s not relevant.

rule_summary: Avoid referring to a person's age or age group when it is not relevant.
rule_detail: Question whether age is relevant. Avoid referring to a person’s age or an age group if it’s not relevant.

rule_summary: Punctuate age references that come before a noun with hyphens.
rule_detail: - When the reference to age comes before a noun, punctuate it with [hyphens](/node/105). - Unless the age reference begins a sentence, use [numerals](/node/198).

rule_summary: Use numerals for age references unless the age reference begins a sentence.
rule_detail: - When the reference to age comes before a noun, punctuate it with [hyphens](/node/105). - Unless the age reference begins a sentence, use [numerals](/node/198).

rule_summary: Avoid characterising age references when it is not strictly relevant.
rule_detail: Avoid characterising age references when it’s not strictly relevant.

rule_summary: Avoid using standalone words like 'old' and 'young' when they may carry bias or unintended subtext.
rule_detail: Standalone words in everyday use, like ‘old’ and ‘young’, can carry bias or unintended subtext. Words that carry stereotypes, for example ‘elderly’, are not acceptable.

rule_summary: Do not use stereotypical age-related words such as 'elderly'.
rule_detail: Standalone words in everyday use, like ‘old’ and ‘young’, can carry bias or unintended subtext. Words that carry stereotypes, for example ‘elderly’, are not acceptable.

rule_summary: Use 'people' with an age reference when the age or age range is relevant to a fact.
rule_detail: When an age or age range is relevant to a fact, you can use the term ‘people’ with the age reference.

rule_summary: Use respectful and inclusive language that talks to the person, not their difference.
rule_detail: Use respectful and inclusive language that talks to the person, not their difference. It’s the law.

rule_summary: Use the term 'older people' for older people.
rule_detail: The term ‘older people’ is acceptable. Don’t use the term ‘old people’. It is disrespectful.

rule_summary: Do not use the term 'old people'.
rule_detail: The term ‘older people’ is acceptable. Don’t use the term ‘old people’. It is disrespectful.

rule_summary: Use 'older people', 'retired people', 'retirees', 'older Australians', 'senior Australians', or 'seniors' as appropriate for context.
rule_detail: - older people - retired people or retirees - older Australians - senior Australians or seniors

rule_summary: Use 'young people' as the most neutral term for young people.
rule_detail: The most neutral term is ‘young people’. ‘Youth’ is a gender-neutral term and is also acceptable.

rule_summary: Use 'youth' as an acceptable gender-neutral term.
rule_detail: The most neutral term is ‘young people’. ‘Youth’ is a gender-neutral term and is also acceptable.

rule_summary: Be careful using the plural 'youths'.
rule_detail: Be careful using the plural ‘youths’. This is often used to refer to male youths only and may carry other connotations.

rule_summary: Avoid using 'junior' or 'juniors' for young people.
rule_detail: - young people - youth - Not this - junior or juniors

rule_summary: Use 'adolescents', 'children', or 'babies' depending on context.
rule_detail: Depending on the context, you can use the words ‘adolescents’, ‘children’ and ‘babies’. ‘Kids’ can be suitable, depending on the [content’s voice and tone](/node/40).

rule_summary: Use 'kids' only when it suits the content's voice and tone.
rule_detail: Depending on the context, you can use the words ‘adolescents’, ‘children’ and ‘babies’. ‘Kids’ can be suitable, depending on the [content’s voice and tone](/node/40).

rule_summary: Refer to students by their level of study rather than by age.
rule_detail: Refer to students by the level of study they are doing, not by their age, unless the age is relevant.

rule_summary: Refer to students by age only when age is relevant.
rule_detail: Refer to students by the level of study they are doing, not by their age, unless the age is relevant.

rule_summary: Use study-level terms such as preschool, high-school, or postgraduate students.
rule_detail: - preschool students - high-school students - postgraduate students

rule_summary: Refer to tertiary students simply as 'students' or as 'PhD candidates' for PhD students.
rule_detail: Tertiary students can be many ages. Refer to them simply as ‘students’ or, in the case of PhD students, as ‘PhD candidates’.

rule_summary: Avoid using 'mature-age student' unless it is relevant.
rule_detail: Avoid using ‘mature-age student’ unless it is relevant to what you are writing.

rule_summary: Use inclusive language that respects cultural and linguistic diversity.
rule_detail: Australians have different cultural backgrounds and speak many languages. Use inclusive language that respects this diversity.

rule_summary: Talk to the person, not their difference.
rule_detail: Speak to the person, not their difference

rule_summary: Use the general term ‘multicultural communities’ for people from different cultural backgrounds.
rule_detail: Use inclusive language. You can use the general term ‘multicultural communities’ to write about people from different cultural backgrounds.

rule_summary: Avoid using the acronym CALD unless writing for a specialist audience.
rule_detail: People writing for government sometimes use the term ‘culturally and linguistically diverse’ (CALD) communities. Avoid using the acronym unless you’re speaking to a specialist audience.

rule_summary: Use respectful and inclusive language that talks to the person, not their difference.
rule_detail: Use respectful and inclusive language that talks to the person, not their difference. In Australia, it’s the law.

rule_summary: Mention people’s cultural affinity or identity only when necessary.
rule_detail: Mention people’s cultural affinity or identity only when you need to.

rule_summary: Avoid words such as ‘ethnic Australians’ or ‘ethnic groups’.
rule_detail: Avoid using words such as ‘ethnic Australians’ or ‘ethnic groups’. This can imply that migrant heritage or migrant status is unusual.

rule_summary: Refer to people living in Australia as Australians.
rule_detail: Refer to people living in Australia as ‘Australians’

rule_summary: Explain what you mean by Australian when context requires it.
rule_detail: Depending on the type of content, you might need to explain what you mean by the term. For example, ‘Australian students’ could refer to all students in Australia including international students.

rule_summary: Mention heritage, cultural or other national identity only if necessary.
rule_detail: Mention heritage, cultural or other national identity only if it’s necessary. Consult guidance on how to refer to [nationalities, peoples and places outside of Australia](/node/133#write_nationalities_peoples_and_places_with_initial_capitals).

rule_summary: Connect a dual identity adjective to Australian with an en dash.
rule_detail: When you specify a dual identity or other heritage as an adjective, connect the reference and the term ‘Australian’ with an [en dash](/node/199).

rule_summary: Use the Japanese–Australian community as the model for a dual-identity adjective.
rule_detail: The Japanese–Australian community takes part in the Summer Festival in Melbourne. [Dual identity expressed as an [adjective](/node/199#join_nouns_with_en_dashes_to_show_equal_relationships)]

rule_summary: Use a noun phrase to express dual identity when appropriate.
rule_detail: Japanese Australians take part in the Summer Festival in Melbourne. [Dual identity expressed as a [noun phrase](/node/144#noun_phrases_function_as_nouns)]

rule_summary: Do not use nationality terms that fail to convey dual identity.
rule_detail: Many Japanese take part in the Summer Festival in Melbourne. [Does not convey dual identity of community or individuals]

rule_summary: Use ‘migrants’, ‘immigrants’ or ‘new arrivals’ for people who have recently arrived in Australia.
rule_detail:
To refer to people who have recently arrived in Australia, use the words:

- ‘migrants’
- ‘immigrants’
- ‘new arrivals’.

rule_summary: Use these terms only for people who have recently arrived and not after citizenship or settlement.
rule_detail: These words don’t say anything about a person’s culture or language: they are neutral. Don’t use these words once people have settled and become Australian citizens. They suggest a temporary or marginal status.

rule_summary: Use the terms ‘given name’ and ‘family name’.
rule_detail: Use the terms ‘given name’ and ‘family name’

rule_summary: Recognise that naming systems vary across cultures.
rule_detail: Many naming systems around the world differ from those used in English-speaking countries.

rule_summary: Place given names before family names in English-speaking contexts.
rule_detail: Given names come before family names in English-speaking countries. In some Asian cultures, people write the family name first.

rule_summary: Do not ask for Christian name, first name, forename or surname.
rule_detail: When you ask people their name, don’t ask for ‘Christian name’, ‘first name’, ‘forename’ or ‘surname’. These terms all take for granted the European conventions and order of names.

rule_summary: Ask for given name and family name instead.
rule_detail:
Instead, ask for their:

- given name
- family name.

rule_summary: Use a preferred name if someone states one instead of their given name.
rule_detail: Some people state a preferred name instead of their given name. This could be different from their legal name, so be clear about which you need.

rule_summary: Treat names with only one name or no given-family split according to their full form.
rule_detail:
Other countries have variations of name order. For example:

- In Indonesia, some people have only one name. They might use this in Australia for both their given name and family name to conform with Western conventions.
- In Myanmar, names are not divided into given and family names. These names keep their full form instead.

rule_detail: Disability does not define people. Neurological differences are a natural part of human diversity. Use inclusive language that respects diversity.

rule_detail: Inclusive language conveys gender equality and is gender neutral.

rule_detail: Respect people’s gender and sexual identity with pronoun choice, job titles and personal titles.

rule_detail: Use gender-neutral language

rule_detail: Use terms that recognise gender equality.

rule_summary: Avoid terms that discriminate on the basis of gender or sexual identity.
rule_detail: Avoid terms that discriminate on the basis of a person’s gender or sexual identity.

rule_summary: Avoid discriminatory terms on the basis of sex, marital or relationship status, pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity, intersex status and breastfeeding status.
rule_detail:
It is unlawful to discriminate against a person under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984. This discrimination relates to their:

- sex
- marital or relationship status
- actual or potential pregnancy
- sexual orientation
- gender identity
- intersex status.

It is also unlawful to discriminate against a person because they are breastfeeding.

rule_summary: Learn the user’s pronouns and, if they are not clear and you cannot ask, choose gender-neutral pronouns.
rule_detail: Learn the user’s pronoun. If it’s not clear and you can’t ask them, choose gender-neutral pronouns.

rule_summary: Use the singular ‘they’ as a gender-neutral pronoun.
rule_detail: The singular ‘they’ is gender-neutral. It avoids specifying a person’s gender.

rule_summary: Use ‘they’ or ‘them’ instead of singular personal pronouns when needed.
rule_detail:
You can use ‘they’ or ‘them’ when you would otherwise use a singular personal pronoun such as:

- ‘he’
- ‘she’
- ‘him’
- ‘her’.

rule_summary: Use ‘themselves’ or ‘themself’ instead of ‘himself’ or ‘herself’ when appropriate.
rule_detail: You can also use ‘themselves’ or ‘themself’ instead of ‘himself’ or ‘herself’. ‘Themself’ is an extension of using ‘they’ for a single person.

rule_summary: Use gender-neutral pronouns for people of unknown gender or people who do not identify as a particular gender.
rule_detail:
The use of gender-neutral pronouns to refer to a person of unknown gender has a long history. Usage now covers people who either:

- don’t wish to identify as a particular gender
- identify as non-binary or gender-fluid.

rule_summary: Avoid using gender-specific pronouns when possible.
rule_detail: There are many ways to avoid using gender-specific pronouns.

rule_summary: Use second-person pronouns, plural pronouns, or no pronoun where these options suit the context.
rule_detail:
You must provide copies of the application to your referees. [Use the second-person pronouns (‘you’ and ‘your’) with direct tone and active voice.]

Candidates must provide copies of the application to their referees. [Use a plural pronoun. The pronoun ‘their’ relates to a plural subject ‘candidates’.]

Every candidate must provide copies of the application to referees. [Leave the pronoun out altogether.]

rule_detail: Avoid using job titles that end in ‘-man’ or ‘-woman’.

rule_detail: You should also avoid job terms that specify women.

rule_summary: Use gender-specific adjectives only when gender is relevant.
rule_detail: Gender is not relevant to a person’s profession or title in general. Use gender-specific adjectives only when gender is relevant. For example, an economic analysis might discuss ‘female-dominated’ or ‘male-dominated’ industries.

rule_summary: Use ‘Ms’ instead of ‘Mrs’ or ‘Miss’ where appropriate.
rule_detail: ‘Ms’ is now widely used instead of ‘Mrs’ or ‘Miss’. It does not disclose marital status.

rule_summary: Use ‘Mx’ when a person indicates that is their preference.
rule_detail: ‘Mx’ refers to non-binary people and those who do not wish to be referred to by their gender. Use ‘Mx’ when a person indicates this is what they prefer, but not otherwise.

rule_summary: Do not ask for a title or gender identity unless the form is designed to collect that information.
rule_detail: Forms and surveys can ask for people to specify gender. Don’t ask for a title or gender identity unless the form is designed to collect this information. For example, a form can ask for a person’s given and family name. It does not need to ask for their preferred title.

rule_summary: Take care in areas where language is changing.
rule_detail: Take care in areas where language is changing.

rule_summary: Follow the rule that people have the right to identify their sexual orientation and gender identity as they choose.
rule_detail: Follow the rule that people have the right to identify their sexual orientation and gender identity as they choose.

rule_summary: Use the listed definitions for gender and sexual diversity terms as guidance for terminology.
rule_detail:
It can help to know the meanings of words people use about gender and sexual diversity. This includes sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics.

- ‘Gender’ is about social and cultural differences and identity. ‘Gender’ and ‘sex’ both mean ‘the state of being male or female’ but are often used in different ways.
- ‘Gender expression’ is the way a person expresses their gender.
- ‘Gender identity’ is about who a person feels themself to be. It refers to the way a person identifies or expresses their masculine or feminine traits.
- ‘Gender-queer’ and ‘non-binary’ refer to people who don’t identify as either male or female. They may identify as both or neither. ‘Gender-fluid’ refers to people who do not identify with a fixed gender.
- ‘Intersex’ refers to people with innate genetic, hormonal or physical sex characteristics that do not conform to medical norms for female or male bodies.
- ‘Sex’ refers to the legal status that was initially determined by sex characteristics observed at birth.
- ‘Sex characteristics’ are a person’s physical sex features, such as their chromosomes, hormones and reproductive organs.
- ‘Sexual orientation’ is a person’s romantic or sexual attraction to another person, such as heterosexual, gay, lesbian or bisexual.
- ‘Sexuality’ includes biological sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, pregnancy and reproduction.
- ‘Transgender’ means people whose gender identity is different from that given to them at birth.

rule_detail: Australians have different cultural backgrounds and speak many languages. Use inclusive language that respects this diversity.

rule_summary: Use inclusive language that conveys gender equality and is gender neutral.
rule_detail: Inclusive language conveys gender equality and is gender neutral. Respect people’s gender and sexual identity with pronoun choice, job titles and personal titles.

rule_summary: Respect people’s gender and sexual identity with pronoun choice, job titles and personal titles.
rule_detail: Inclusive language conveys gender equality and is gender neutral. Respect people’s gender and sexual identity with pronoun choice, job titles and personal titles.

rule_summary: Use inclusive language that respects diversity.
rule_detail: Disability does not define people. Neurological differences are a natural part of human diversity. Use inclusive language that respects diversity.

rule_summary: Design content to be accessible and inclusive.
rule_detail: Help them by designing accessible and inclusive content.

rule_summary: Make content available to everyone.
rule_detail: Government services and products need to be available to everyone.

rule_summary: Create inclusive content.
rule_detail: This means creating inclusive content.

rule_summary: Recognise Australia’s diversity and the diversity of technology Australians use online.
rule_detail:
Inclusive content recognises:

- Australia’s diversity
- the diversity of technology Australians use to engage online.

rule_summary: Accommodate cultural and linguistic diversity among users.
rule_detail:
For example, inclusive content accommodates:

- cultural and linguistic diversity among users
- diversity of abilities among users
- how users interact with technology in different contexts.

rule_summary: Accommodate diversity of abilities among users.
rule_detail:
For example, inclusive content accommodates:

- cultural and linguistic diversity among users
- diversity of abilities among users
- how users interact with technology in different contexts.

rule_summary: Follow accessibility guidance in context.
rule_detail: Follow accessibility guidance in context

rule_summary: Use Style Manual topic guidance to create accessible content.
rule_detail: Style Manual topics give you the guidance you need to follow to create accessible content.

rule_summary: Use Style Manual callouts when specific accessibility requirements or guidance apply.
rule_detail: Where there are specific accessibility requirements or guidance, the Style Manual provides callouts to make it clear what you need to do.

rule_summary: Use contextual guidance in addition to the Style Manual’s general guidance.
rule_detail:
In addition to this contextual guidance, the Style Manual also provides information on:

- designing for accessibility and inclusion
- applying the principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)
- the responsibilities of government agencies.

rule_summary: Design content for equal access.
rule_detail: Design content for equal access.

rule_summary: Help people with ongoing, temporary or situational barriers access the information they need.
rule_detail: People can experience ongoing, temporary or situational barriers to access information they need. Help them by designing accessible and inclusive content.

rule_summary: Treat accessibility as a mandatory standard for government agencies.
rule_detail: Accessibility is a mandatory standard for government agencies. Test your content against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) success criteria. Agencies should commit to improving their performance against the standard.

rule_summary: Test content against WCAG success criteria.
rule_detail: Accessibility is a mandatory standard for government agencies. Test your content against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) success criteria. Agencies should commit to improving their performance against the standard.

rule_summary: Commit to improving performance against the accessibility standard.
rule_detail: Accessibility is a mandatory standard for government agencies. Test your content against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) success criteria. Agencies should commit to improving their performance against the standard.

rule_summary: Take user needs into account when applying accessibility principles.
rule_detail: User needs are at the heart of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). When you take user needs into account, applying accessibility principles becomes simpler, though not necessarily easier.

rule_summary: Apply accessibility principles.
rule_detail: User needs are at the heart of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). When you take user needs into account, applying accessibility principles becomes simpler, though not necessarily easier.

rule_summary: Create products and services that work for everyone.
rule_detail: How we design has a direct influence on what we design. Inclusive design means that the products and services we create work for everyone.

rule_summary: Write content at an Australian Year 7 level for most users.
rule_detail: Literacy can be a barrier to access for Australian users. Writing to an Australian year 7 level makes content usable for most people.

rule_summary: Use short sentences and simple structure.
rule_detail: Write and design content that matches how users read. Use short sentences and simple structure.

rule_summary: Use culturally appropriate and respectful language.
rule_detail: Use language that is culturally appropriate and respectful of the diversity of Australia’s peoples.

rule_summary: Create a blog only if it helps people find and use government services and products.
rule_detail: Create a blog if it will help people find and use government services and products.

rule_summary: Use user research before starting a blog.
rule_detail: Before starting a blog, do [user research](/node/76). Find out if people will use the blog and why.

rule_summary: Use blogs to detail one aspect of a service or product.
rule_detail:
Blogs can support user needs by:

- detailing one aspect of a service or product
- giving information about policy issues
- highlighting innovations, research and best practice
- inviting feedback.

rule_summary: Use blogs to give information about policy issues.
rule_detail:
Blogs can support user needs by:

- detailing one aspect of a service or product
- giving information about policy issues
- highlighting innovations, research and best practice
- inviting feedback.

rule_summary: Use blogs to highlight innovations, research and best practice.

- giving information about policy issues

rule_summary: Use blogs to invite feedback.
rule_detail:
Blogs can support user needs by:

- detailing one aspect of a service or product
- giving information about policy issues
- highlighting innovations, research and best practice
- inviting feedback.

rule_summary: Do not use blogs for essential stand-alone information.
rule_detail: Don’t use blogs for essential information that should be stand-alone content. Don’t duplicate information that’s available elsewhere.

rule_summary: Do not duplicate information that is available elsewhere.
rule_detail: Don’t use blogs for essential information that should be stand-alone content. Don’t duplicate information that’s available elsewhere.

rule_summary: Update a blog regularly.
rule_detail: Update the blog regularly. For example, aim for a new post once a week on the same day. But make sure you have something useful to say.

rule_summary: Aim for a new blog post once a week on the same day.

rule_detail:
A blog post should solve users’ problems or answer their questions. Common places you can find information on these include:

- user research
- search logs
- call centre and shopfront data
- social media
- web analytics
- surveys.

rule_summary: Write a title that helps users understand the post.
rule_detail: Start with a title that helps users understand what the post is about. Include [keywords](/node/72). Avoid clickbait titles.

rule_summary: Include keywords in blog post titles.
rule_detail: Start with a title that helps users understand what the post is about. Include [keywords](/node/72). Avoid clickbait titles.

rule_summary: Avoid clickbait titles.
rule_detail: Start with a title that helps users understand what the post is about. Include [keywords](/node/72). Avoid clickbait titles.

rule_summary: Use headings and short paragraphs to break up blog posts.
rule_detail: Break up your post with headings and short paragraphs. Order headings from most to least important. Cover one main idea per paragraph. Keep paragraphs to a maximum of 2 to 3 sentences so people can read them on mobile devices.

rule_summary: Order headings from most to least important.
rule_detail: Break up your post with headings and short paragraphs. Order headings from most to least important. Cover one main idea per paragraph. Keep paragraphs to a maximum of 2 to 3 sentences so people can read them on mobile devices.

rule_summary: Cover one main idea per paragraph.
rule_detail: Break up your post with headings and short paragraphs. Order headings from most to least important. Cover one main idea per paragraph. Keep paragraphs to a maximum of 2 to 3 sentences so people can read them on mobile devices.

rule_summary: Keep paragraphs to a maximum of 2 to 3 sentences.
rule_detail: Break up your post with headings and short paragraphs. Order headings from most to least important. Cover one main idea per paragraph. Keep paragraphs to a maximum of 2 to 3 sentences so people can read them on mobile devices.

rule_summary: Use a warm and conversational tone in blog posts.
rule_detail: Use a warm and conversational tone in your blog posts. This will help you engage with the people reading the blog.

rule_summary: Write clear page titles that align with the first heading.
rule_detail: Write clear page titles. This is the first thing a screen reader user will hear and should align with the first heading on the page.

rule_summary: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings.
rule_detail: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings. Clearly describe the topics or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Describe the topics or the following section clearly in headings.
rule_detail: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings. Clearly describe the topics or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Ensure users can navigate content in the intended order.
rule_detail: Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they are using. Use the same navigation elements consistently across services.

rule_summary: Use the same navigation elements consistently across services.
rule_detail: Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they are using. Use the same navigation elements consistently across services.

rule_summary: Use images of text only when they are essential.
rule_detail: Use images of text only where it's essential to help convey the information.

rule_summary: Include images in blog posts when they convey meaning or interest.
rule_detail: Include images in blog posts if they convey meaning or interest. Unless images are for decorative purposes, describe the visual information in [alt text](/node/49).

rule_summary: Describe non-decorative images with alt text.
rule_detail: Include images in blog posts if they convey meaning or interest. Unless images are for decorative purposes, describe the visual information in [alt text](/node/49).

rule_summary: Include video or audio only if they meet a user need and are accessible.
rule_detail: Include video or audio if they meet a user need and are accessible.

rule_summary: Use Easy Read to broaden access to information.
rule_detail: Create Easy Read to broaden access

rule_summary: Design Easy Read for people who are not familiar with English or who have low literacy or learning disability.
rule_detail: Easy Read is a way to present information for people who are not familiar with English, or who have low literacy or learning disability.

rule_summary: Research the people who will use the information before you start.
rule_detail: Before starting, make sure you do research with people who will use the information.

rule_summary: Find out how users will access the materials.
rule_detail: Find out how they will access the materials – in print, online or with support from others.

rule_summary: Engage Easy Read experts.
rule_detail: It is best to engage Easy Read experts.

rule_summary: Design your Easy Read materials as a printed handout.
rule_detail: Design your Easy Read materials as a printed handout to be used by people in several scenarios.

rule_summary: Make Easy Read materials available alongside the source material.
rule_detail: Make Easy Read materials available in addition to any source material they are derived from.

rule_summary: Publish Easy Read materials in HTML and accessible PDF at the same time as the source material.
rule_detail: Publish them in HTML and as an accessible PDF at the same time as the source material.

rule_summary: Provide clear link text and make sure it looks like a link.
rule_detail: provide clear link text and make sure it looks like a link

rule_summary: Spell out the URL next to linked text.
rule_detail: spell out the URL next to the linked text.

rule_summary: Use W3C updates on making content usable for people with cognitive and learning disabilities.
rule_detail: Follow W3C updates on making content usable for people with cognitive and learning disabilities.

rule_summary: Make the structure of Easy Read PDFs accessible.
rule_detail: Make the structure of Easy Read PDFs accessible to help people who will need to download them from the website.

rule_summary: Make all government content accessible to people with disability.
rule_detail: Make all government content accessible to people with disability.

rule_summary: Provide timely information.
rule_detail: This includes providing information that is timely, which is part of Australian law under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992

rule_summary: Treat the Easy Read version as a summary of the source material.
rule_detail: Think of the Easy Read version as a summary of the source material.

rule_summary: Include examples throughout to help explain ideas and concepts.
rule_detail: Include examples throughout to help explain ideas and concepts.

rule_summary: Choose images users can relate to and understand.
rule_detail: Ask your Easy Read expert to help you choose images users can relate to and understand.

rule_summary: Use images first to help users derive meaning before they read the text.
rule_detail: Users will be drawn to the images first to derive meaning, before looking at the adjacent text.

rule_summary: Keep Easy Read simple with plain language principles such as simple words and sentences.
rule_detail: Easy Read follows some plain language principles – such as using simple words and sentences – but Easy Read and plain language are different.

rule_summary: Check that content reads at a year 4 to year 6 level.
rule_detail: Check your content reads between a year 4 to year 6 reading level.

rule_summary: Use simple words and grammar.
rule_detail: Use simple words and grammar, but don’t use childish language if the users are adults.

rule_summary: Avoid childish language for adult users.
rule_detail: Use simple words and grammar, but don’t use childish language if the users are adults.

rule_summary: Bold difficult words when you need to use them.
rule_detail: If you need to use a difficult word, write it in bold.

rule_summary: Define difficult words in the next sentence or phrase.
rule_detail: Define the difficult word in the next sentence or phrase.

rule_summary: Include a glossary at the end if you define many words.
rule_detail: If you have defined a lot of words, include a glossary at the end of your document.

rule_summary: Call the glossary a word list.
rule_detail: Call it a word list.

rule_summary: Use questions only in headings for Easy Read.
rule_detail: Only use questions in headings for Easy Read.

rule_summary: Avoid questions in the text.
rule_detail: Questions in the text can make some people anxious.

rule_summary: Follow questions with practical examples when you need information from people.
rule_detail: If you need information from people, follow questions with practical examples so people know how to respond.

rule_summary: Involve people from your target user group as you write, design and test the materials.
rule_detail: Involve people from your target user group as you write, design and test the materials.

rule_summary: Use users' own terms where possible.
rule_detail: They can help you to choose imagery and to use terms they use themselves.

rule_summary: Check the draft with the original author when you finish it.
rule_detail: When you finish the draft, check with the original author to make sure you have the meaning right.

rule_summary: Keep Easy Read brief.
rule_detail: Keep your Easy Read brief.

rule_summary: Divide complex content into a few documents if needed.
rule_detail: This is not always possible for complex information. In that case, think about whether you can divide the content into a few documents.

rule_summary: Check whether dividing the content will meet user needs.
rule_detail: Check if this decision will meet user needs.

rule_summary: Use a standard Easy Read layout.
rule_detail: Follow a standard Easy Read layout

rule_summary: Use a consistent layout and minimum design elements.
rule_detail: Use a consistent layout and minimum design elements so it’s easy for people to use or explain.

rule_summary: Find out whether your agency has an Easy Read publishing template before using a table grid.
rule_detail: Your agency might have an Easy Read publishing template. Find out before using a table grid to format images and text.

rule_summary: Use tables to align images and words only if needed.
rule_detail: Tables help to align images and words. If you use them, follow accessibility requirements for tables.

rule_summary: Code tables using role="presentation" when designing Easy Read material.
rule_detail: When designing the Easy Read material, code tables using the role="presentation" attribute

rule_summary: Use wide margins and plenty of white space.
rule_detail: Use wide margins and plenty of white space to make the text easy to read.

rule_summary: Learn about the user before you design a form.
rule_detail: Understand the user and their needs before you design any kind of form (web-based or print).

rule_summary: Find out the language users can relate to.
rule_detail: Discover the terms and phrases that people use when they talk about the topic. This includes the words they use in search engines.

rule_summary: Develop a question protocol before designing the form.
rule_detail: A ‘question protocol’ is a document that helps you find out what you need to ask the user. It lists: the questions you will ask; why you are collecting information; what you will do with it.

rule_summary: Use a question protocol to challenge unnecessary questions.
rule_detail: A question protocol also gives you a way to challenge and push back against unnecessary questions. Every time we ask a user for information it costs them and your organisation. It takes time and effort for the user to provide it, and for your organisation to manage it.

rule_summary: Record the information management requirements in the question protocol.
rule_detail: Your question protocol becomes a record. So does anything you collect from a form. Records provide evidence of what your organisation has done and why.

rule_summary: Keep one thing per page when prototyping forms.
rule_detail: Putting one thing on each page helps you see everything you need to find out, without guessing about the best way to group it.

rule_summary: Prototype forms with one piece of information, one decision, or one question per page.
rule_detail: Begin prototyping with one thing per page over any number of pages: one piece of information you’re telling a user; one decision the user has to make; one question the user has to answer.

rule_summary: Treat each question as potentially needing more than one field.
rule_detail: Each question might have more than one field. An address is one thing that would use several fields.

rule_summary: Reduce cognitive load by using a single thing on each page.
rule_detail: Having a single thing on each page helps you: reduce the cognitive load for users; save the user’s answers as they move through the form; capture analytics about each question; handle branching questions and loops.

rule_summary: Use user research to decide the order of questions.
rule_detail: Your research with users will help you decide what order to put the questions in. This should include thinking about which topics are more related to each other, or need to be answered by a particular user.

rule_summary: Group questions and create sections only when needed.
rule_detail: This will help you work out if you need to group questions and create sections. You might find that you do not need to group any questions.

rule_summary: Keep testing the structure of questions until the user can complete the tasks smoothly.
rule_detail: Keep prototyping and testing the structure of the questions until the user can: understand what you’re asking them to do; focus on the specific question and its answer; find their way through an unfamiliar process; use the service on a mobile device.

rule_summary: Avoid showing a progress indicator for short forms.
rule_detail: If the form is short (for example, 5 questions or fewer with no branching), the user won’t need a progress indicator. Adding the indicator would be extra work that the user might not even notice.

rule_summary: Avoid using a progress indicator on complex forms.
rule_detail: It’s difficult to design an accurate indicator that shows a user their progress through a complex form. Complex forms can branch. They might have sections that don’t apply to some users and optional questions. This means the user might not move through the form in a predictable way.

rule_summary: Test adding a task list and a check your answers page for complex forms.
rule_detail: If you need to help the user estimate how long it will take to fill in a complex form, test adding: a task list page at the start; a ‘check your answers’ page at the end.

rule_summary: Use task list pages to show tasks and support navigation through a transaction.
rule_detail: Task list pages help users understand the tasks in a transaction and their order. These pages show the user the tasks they have completed and help them to jump to incomplete tasks.

rule_summary: Use a check your answers page to summarise the form and let users review responses.
