rule_detail: A ‘check your answers’ page summarises the sections of a form. The summary shows the user what information they’ve provided. This step can help users go back and change any responses, or confirm that they’re giving the correct information.

rule_summary: Write clear questions and headings.
rule_detail: When you know how to group the questions, you will be able to create the structure.

rule_summary: Organise form content using section headings.
rule_detail: Organise content in the form using section headings. Describe the topic or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Write short active content for forms.
rule_detail: Write short active content for forms, including ‘help text’ and error messages – this is called ‘microcopy’.

rule_summary: Follow the guidance to write clear questions and headings.
rule_detail: Fundamentals: Follow the guidance to write clear questions and headings.

rule_summary: Use familiar words in familiar ways.
rule_detail: Write and design forms starting with plain language. Include the terms that are familiar to users.

rule_summary: Test whether topic terms help users understand and use the form.
rule_detail: Test the form with the terms included. If they help the user understand and use the form, keep them.

rule_summary: Include plain language definitions when users do not understand terms.
rule_detail: If some users don’t understand the terms, include plain language definitions.

rule_summary: Establish the appropriate voice and tone.
rule_detail: Establish the appropriate voice and tone.

rule_summary: Tell users what the form is for and whether they need to fill it in.
rule_detail: Before a user starts a form, they need to know: what the form is for and if they need to fill it in; who can use the form (if they are eligible for the service); what they need to submit the form (for example, tax file number and passport number); if they can ask someone else to fill it in for them; what happens after they submit it and any other stages.

rule_summary: Show the full service process with a task list when the form is part of a multi-stage service.
rule_detail: If the form is part of a service that will involve other stages, show the full service process with a task list. Include information about any other forms the user will need to fill in.

rule_summary: Only ask for information you need and do not mark questions as required.
rule_detail: You must only collect personal information if it is necessary. Collect the least amount needed for the function or activity related to the form. You don’t need to mark questions as ‘required’ because you will only be asking for information that is needed.

rule_summary: Tell people why you are collecting personal information and what privacy rights they have.
rule_detail: Tell people when and why you are collecting their personal information, and what their privacy rights are. Use a collection statement on the form.

rule_summary: Mark questions as optional when you invite users to provide extra information.
rule_detail: Sometimes you need to invite the user to tell you something they think is important and they want us to know (for example, to collect feedback). Mark these questions as ‘optional’.

rule_summary: Comply with the Australian Privacy Principles when handling personal information.
rule_detail: When you handle personal information, you must comply with the Australian Privacy Principles. Personal information is any information that could identify an individual, in any format.

rule_summary: Respect access rights under the Privacy Act 1988 and the Freedom of Information Act 1982.
rule_detail: People have a right to request access to their personal information under the Privacy Act 1988. People also have the right to request access to government-held information under the Freedom of Information Act 1982. This includes personal information collected in a form.

rule_summary: Keep digital forms in a single column.
rule_detail: Don’t use multiple columns in digital forms.

rule_summary: Avoid using a second column in print forms.
rule_detail: Avoid using a second column in print forms.

rule_summary: Keep the same number of columns throughout the form if you use multiple columns.
rule_detail: If you have to use multiple columns, keep the same number throughout the form.

rule_summary: Make columns visually distinct if you use multiple columns.
rule_detail: Make sure the columns are visually different (for example, with a thick line between them).

rule_summary: Use alt text to explain information in images for screen reader users.
rule_detail: Alternative text explains information in images for screen reader users.

rule_summary: Use captions to describe images and help users relate them to surrounding text.
rule_detail: Captions describe images to help users relate them to surrounding text.

rule_summary: Use titles to identify images and number them in long-form content.
rule_detail: Titles identify images and number them in long-form content.

rule_summary: Make sure all users can access the same information.
rule_detail: Give all users access to the same information

rule_summary: Keep image titles distinct from the HTML title attribute.
rule_detail: Titles help identify specific images (for example, ‘Figure 1’) – particularly if they are listed or referenced in other parts of the content. They are different from the HTML title attribute.

rule_summary: Write captions as brief descriptions related to the image.
rule_detail: Captions are brief descriptions related to the image (for example commentary, attributions or quotations).

rule_summary: Write alt text as a short description of the information an image conveys.
rule_detail: Alternative text (alt text) is a short description of the information an image conveys. It’s either available to the user as an HTML attribute or through a document’s accessibility tool. Alt text is not usually visible on the page.

rule_summary: Use an extended description for a complex image when alt text is not enough.
rule_detail: An extended description is alternative text that explains a complex image. It is visible either on the same page or on a separate page. You might write an extended description for a chart or process, for example.

rule_summary: Do not hide information in alt text.
rule_detail: hide information in the alt text, as a user might not see it

rule_summary: Do not repeat in alt text information that users can read in the caption.
rule_detail: repeat information in the alt text that a user would read in the caption

rule_summary: Do not use the longdesc attribute for extended descriptions.
rule_detail: use the <longdesc> attribute for extended descriptions.

rule_summary: Add short alt text for all informative images.
rule_detail: Include short alt text – less than about 100 characters – for all informative images. Decorative images should have null alt text (alt="").

rule_summary: Use null alt text for decorative images.
rule_detail: Include short alt text – less than about 100 characters – for all informative images. Decorative images should have null alt text (alt="").

rule_summary: Write alt text so users can understand what is in the image and why it is there.
rule_detail: Users need images to have alt text for different purposes.

rule_summary: Add alternative text for all images.
rule_detail: Add alternative text for all images. For help with writing good alt text: the W3C alt decision tree. Write alternative text that describes the information or function of the image. For help to describe images: the W3C/WAI Web Accessibility Tutorials - Images.

rule_summary: Describe the information or function of the image in alternative text.
rule_detail: Write alternative text that describes the information or function of the image. For help to describe images: the W3C/WAI Web Accessibility Tutorials - Images.

rule_summary: Add captions for all images unless they are only decorative.
rule_detail: Add captions for all images, unless they are only decorative.

rule_summary: Use captions to acknowledge the creator or copyright holder of images.
rule_detail: Use captions to acknowledge the creator or copyright holder of images in captions. Use your organisation’s referencing style.

rule_summary: Include the HTML figcaption element to associate the caption with the image.
rule_detail: Include the HTML <figcaption> element to associate the caption with the image.

rule_summary: Attribute copyright material when referencing images and text.
rule_detail: When referencing, you must attribute copyright material. This includes images and text.

rule_summary: Write attribution as part of the caption or after the copyright material.
rule_detail: Write the attribution as part of the caption or following the copyright material. Alt text is also licensed under copyright.

rule_summary: Choose alt text, captions and titles based on why you included the image.
rule_detail: The detail you need to include in alt text, captions and titles depends on the reason you have included the image.

rule_summary: Treat decorative images as visual interest only, not as information.
rule_detail: Decorative images add visual interest but not information (for example, the background pattern on a website).

rule_summary: Treat informative images as conveying simple concepts or information.
rule_detail: Informative images convey simple concepts or information (for example, how to open a medication bottle).

rule_summary: Treat functional images as part of interactions rather than as information.
rule_detail: Functional images are part of interactions and don’t convey information (for example, Australian Government branding that links to a home page).

rule_summary: Use empty alt text for decorative images.
rule_detail: Include an empty value, or null text, for alt text if the image is decorative. This is 2 double quotation marks with no space (alt="").

rule_summary: Set decorative images as decorative or background images in documents.
rule_detail: In documents, set images as ‘Decorative image’ or ‘Background image’.

rule_summary: Use surrounding text to support search engines for decorative images.
rule_detail: Include keywords in the surrounding text to support search engines. Don’t create alt text to add keywords.

rule_summary: Do not create alt text to add keywords.
rule_detail: Include keywords in the surrounding text to support search engines. Don’t create alt text to add keywords.

rule_summary: Make alt text for informational images convey the same important information as the image.
rule_detail: Write alt text that conveys the same important information as the image.

rule_summary: Use images only when they help the user complete a task or understand information.
rule_detail:
Add images only if they help the user

Use images if they help users complete their task with your service or product. Images can make it easier for some people to understand information.

rule_summary: Get permission to use copyright material, including images and text.
rule_detail: You must get permission (a licence) to use copyright material. This includes images and text.

rule_summary: Choose images that reflect and support the diversity of Australia’s peoples and cultures.
rule_detail: Choose images that reflect and support the diversity of Australia’s peoples and cultures, especially if you are using images of people.

rule_summary: Keep images simple and use them to support information in the text.
rule_detail: Keep images simple and use them to support information in the text.

rule_summary: Make images accessible, easy to understand, relevant, uncluttered, credible, and stylistically consistent.
rule_detail:
Images must be:

- accessible
- easy to understand
- relevant
- uncluttered
- from a credible source
- consistent in design and style across the content.

rule_summary: Use the same font, typeface, line thickness and colour scheme in all images of the same type.
rule_detail: Use the same font and typeface, line thickness and colour scheme in all images of the same type.

rule_summary: Include decorative images only when they are relevant to the content.
rule_detail: Include decorative images only if they are relevant to the content

rule_summary: Do not use images to fill space.
rule_detail: Don’t use images to fill in space. Decorative images must still be relevant. Use images that relate directly to the content.

rule_summary: Add alt text to all images.
rule_detail: Add alt text to all images.

rule_summary: Include captions for all non-decorative images.
rule_detail: Include captions for all images that are not decorative. Add titles to help users scan content.

rule_summary: Add titles to help users scan content.
rule_detail: Include captions for all images that are not decorative. Add titles to help users scan content.

rule_summary: Include images only if they meet a real user need.
rule_detail: Include images on a page only if they meet a real user need.

rule_summary: Use real text rather than images of text whenever technically possible.
rule_detail: Use real text rather than images of text whenever technically possible. (Logos can be an exception.)

rule_summary: Do not use colour as the only visual means of conveying information in graphs and diagrams.
rule_detail: Make sure that colour is not the only visual means of conveying information in graphs and diagrams. Text labels and patterns can supplement the use of colour. Make sure the contrast is sufficient for all users.

rule_summary: Set image resolution to suit the content.
rule_detail: Image resolution must be appropriate for the content.

rule_summary: Do not embed large image files in content you will publish online.
rule_detail: Don’t embed images with a large file size into content that you will publish online, such as PDFs or webpages. Optimise and compress all image files so it makes it quicker for the user to access the information.

rule_summary: Optimise images for mobile and desktop screens.
rule_detail: Design for mobile devices first. An image will scale to the device people view it on. Check that it’s easy to read on a mobile phone screen and a desktop.

rule_summary: Seek specialist advice to choose the best image file format.
rule_detail: There are many file types for images. Seek specialist advice to optimise an image file as a vector or raster file format.

rule_summary: Use graphs, charts and maps when they explain complex information better than text.
rule_detail: Use graphs, charts and maps if they explain complex information

rule_summary: Do not use graphs, charts or maps when another format better meets the user need.
rule_detail: Don’t use them if another format meets the user need – such as a list, table or tool.

rule_summary: Use line graphs and bar charts to show trends, distributions, comparisons, and processes or relationships.
rule_detail:
Graphs and charts display data, making it easier to understand. They are good for showing:

- trends – such as change over time
- statistical distributions and patterns
- simple comparisons – such as totals for different categories or different rates of change
- processes and relationships – such as an organisational structure or a workflow chart.

rule_summary: Do not add borders or background tints to line graphs and bar charts.
rule_detail: Don’t add borders or background tints.

rule_summary: Use gridlines only where they help people read the data.
rule_detail: Use gridlines only where they help people read the data.

rule_summary: Use tick marks on axes to show data intervals at a glance.
rule_detail: Use ‘tick marks’ on the x- and y-axes to show the scale of data intervals at a glance. Avoid more than 10 tick marks on the y-axis.

rule_summary: Avoid more than 10 tick marks on the y-axis.
rule_detail: Use ‘tick marks’ on the x- and y-axes to show the scale of data intervals at a glance. Avoid more than 10 tick marks on the y-axis.

rule_summary: Keep the y-axis scale consistent across the viewport or page.
rule_detail: Scale the y-axis to be consistent across the viewport or page.

rule_summary: Keep line graphs simple by limiting them to no more than three or four data series.
rule_detail: Keep it simple (for example, include no more than 3 or 4 data series on a line graph).

rule_summary: Do not use colour as the only source of meaning in charts and graphs.
rule_detail: Don’t use colour as the only source of meaning. Try adding dots and dashes to lines and cross hatching to areas.

rule_summary: Add legends to all graphs, charts and maps.
rule_detail: All graphs, charts and maps should have a legend that tells people the meaning of lines, colours and symbols.

rule_summary: Keep legends consistent in position, font, typeface, colours and symbols across related pages.
rule_detail:
Make legends consistent in a webpage or group of webpages dealing with the same topic. Place the legend in the same position (for example, bottom centre, top left or to the right).

Use the same font and typeface, and colours and symbols for the same types of information.

rule_summary: Include a scale bar and a north arrow on maps.
rule_detail: Maps must also have a scale bar and an arrow to show which way is north.

rule_summary: Include all units of measurement.
rule_detail: Include all [units of measurement](/node/147). This helps people understand what the numbers mean.

rule_summary: Label axes, legends, titles and captions as relevant.
rule_detail: Label the x- and y-axes, as well as legends, titles and captions as relevant.

rule_summary: Use appropriate units for the scale and context.
rule_detail: Use appropriate units (for example, millions of dollars for a company balance sheet but thousands of dollars for a household budget).

rule_summary: Use the appropriate number of decimal places on labels.
rule_detail: Use the appropriate number of decimal places on labels (for example, $1,000 – not $1,000.00 – for a scale of zero to $10,000).

rule_summary: Refer to complex images in the body text.
rule_detail: Refer to complex images in the body of the text. It helps people relate the discussion in the text to the information displayed in the image.

rule_summary: Place an image close to the text that mentions it.
rule_detail: Place the image close to where you mention it in the text. For example, a graph must be on the same page and after the paragraph that refers to it.

rule_summary: Refer to images with locator numbers instead of repeating captions in the text.
rule_detail: Don’t repeat the whole [caption of the image](/node/49) in the text. Instead, use a locator number to refer to it, for example ‘Figure 1’.

rule_summary: Do not refer to images using left-right sensory language.
rule_detail: Don’t refer to ‘the photograph on the left’. This sensory language is not accessible for some users.

rule_summary: Include all parts of the periodical when publishing a serial.
rule_detail:
Because each issue is complete in itself, you must include the following:

- title
- year, volume and issue number
- name of the sponsoring body
- name of the publisher or distributor or both
- copyright details
- restrictions on circulation
- International Standard Serial Number (ISSN).

rule_summary: Include the standard article details for each journal article.
rule_detail:
As well as the parts listed for periodicals, it is usual for each article in a journal to have:

- the title and author details
- an abstract
- references as footnotes, endnotes or a list of references
- a document object identifier (DOI)
- extra material useful for the content.

rule_summary: Include key information on the home page of an online periodical.
rule_detail:
The home page should have:

- the periodical’s branding and contact details
- the names of the editors
- the aim of the periodical
- information for authors on how to submit articles
- details on how to subscribe.

rule_summary: Use EPUB for accessible digital periodicals when appropriate.
rule_detail: Consider using EPUB, which is an accessible eBook format that users can read on mobile devices.

rule_summary: Ensure any PDF provided for a strong user need is accessible.
rule_detail: If there is a strong user need to provide a PDF (for example for printing), the document must still be accessible.

rule_summary: Place odd page numbers on the right-hand pages of printed and PDF periodicals.
rule_detail: If the periodical shows page numbers, use odd numbers for the right-hand pages.

rule_summary: Make government content accessible to people with disability.
rule_detail: You must make all government content accessible to people with disability.

rule_summary: Choose a copyright licence for released copyright materials.
rule_detail: You must choose a licence to release copyright materials.

rule_summary: Use an open access licence for government copyright materials if possible.
rule_detail: If you work in government, use an open access licence if you can (for example, [Creative Commons](https://creativecommons.org.au/)).

rule_summary: Follow the government copyright rules in the intellectual property manual.
rule_detail: Read the government copyright rules in the [ Australian Government intellectual property manual](https://www.ag.gov.au/rights-and-protections/publications/australian-government-intellectual-property-manual).

rule_summary: Contribute publications through legal deposit.
rule_detail: Your agency is obliged to contribute publications through legal deposit.

rule_summary: Start each new volume at page 1.
rule_detail: In print and PDF periodicals, start each new volume at page 1.

rule_summary: Number pages continuously across issues within a volume.
rule_detail: Number the pages of the issues so they continue from one issue to the next, throughout the volume.

rule_summary: Include the volume cover information on the outside front cover of the volume.
rule_detail:
If the issue has a cover, it will be removed when the issues are put into volumes:

- Include the title, date of issue, International Standard Serial Number (ISSN) and sponsoring body on the outside front cover of the volume.
- Repeat all of this information, except for the ISSN, on the first page with the rest of the essential information, such as copyright and any restrictions on circulation.

rule_summary: Repeat the volume cover information on the first page, excluding the ISSN.
rule_detail:
If the issue has a cover, it will be removed when the issues are put into volumes:

- Include the title, date of issue, International Standard Serial Number (ISSN) and sponsoring body on the outside front cover of the volume.
- Repeat all of this information, except for the ISSN, on the first page with the rest of the essential information, such as copyright and any restrictions on circulation.

rule_summary: Put publication details on the cover page when a periodical has no separate cover.
rule_detail:
Put the publication details for each issue on the cover page. Include:

- the title
- the publishing date
- the sponsoring body
- the volume and part number (if any).

rule_summary: Add printer, publisher, distributor or agent details on page 2 or the back page.
rule_detail:
Put this extra information on page 2 (with the contents list) or the back page:

- the name of the printer, publisher, distributor or agent
- the editorial address
- subscription rates.

rule_summary: Start each issue without a separate cover at page 1.
rule_detail: Start each issue of a periodical without a separate cover from page 1. Include the title, date and page number at the top or bottom of the page.

rule_summary: Include the title, date and page number at the top or bottom of each page.
rule_detail: Start each issue of a periodical without a separate cover from page 1. Include the title, date and page number at the top or bottom of the page.

rule_summary: Treat government serials as records and manage them accordingly.
rule_detail: Articles, journals and other serials that you create for the Australian Government become records.

rule_summary: Manage and dispose of records in line with information management requirements.
rule_detail: Managing and disposing of records properly is a requirement under the [ Archives Act 1983](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C2004A02796). You must follow your organisation’s information management requirements.

rule_summary: Apply for identifying numbers for your periodical.
rule_detail: Apply for identifying numbers for your periodical

rule_summary: Use separate ISSNs for digital and print versions of a periodical.
rule_detail: ISSNs are a unique way to locate the work. Use separate ISSNs for a digital periodical and a print periodical, even if they look the same.

rule_summary: Publish at least 5 articles before applying for an ISSN for digital-only content.
rule_detail: For digital-only content, you must publish 5 articles before you can apply for an ISSN.

rule_summary: Tell users how to access extra material in both printed and digital periodicals.
rule_detail: Both printed and digital periodicals must tell their users how to access extra material.

rule_summary: Use a hyperlink in online periodicals to provide access to extra material in most cases.
rule_detail: Online periodicals use a hyperlink in most cases.

rule_summary: Explain how to access extra material in printed periodicals when it is not in the appendices.
rule_detail: Printed periodicals need to tell people how to access this material if it is not in the appendices.

rule_summary: Create PDFs only when research shows there is a specific need for them.
rule_detail: Only create PDFs if your research shows there are specific needs for this format.

rule_summary: Make PDF content accessible to everyone who needs it.
rule_detail: Make PDF content accessible to everyone who needs it.

rule_summary: Create webpages by default instead of PDFs.
rule_detail:
Create webpages by default

Create content in HTML pages instead of PDFs.

rule_summary: Configure HTML pages for printing and sharing.
rule_detail: You can configure HTML pages for printing and sharing.

rule_summary: Provide PDF content in another accessible format when you publish a PDF.
rule_detail:
When you publish a PDF:

- provide the content in another format that is accessible
- mark up the PDF with the right tags
- check that assistive technology reads the PDF content in the correct order
- add 'PDF' and file size to
[meaningful link text](/node/193/#link_to_something_only_if_it_helps_meet_the_users_need).

rule_summary: Mark up PDFs with the right tags.
rule_detail:
When you publish a PDF:

- provide the content in another format that is accessible
- mark up the PDF with the right tags
- check that assistive technology reads the PDF content in the correct order
- add 'PDF' and file size to
[meaningful link text](/node/193/#link_to_something_only_if_it_helps_meet_the_users_need).

rule_summary: Check that assistive technology reads PDF content in the correct order.
rule_detail:
When you publish a PDF:

- provide the content in another format that is accessible
- mark up the PDF with the right tags
- check that assistive technology reads the PDF content in the correct order
- add 'PDF' and file size to
[meaningful link text](/node/193/#link_to_something_only_if_it_helps_meet_the_users_need).

rule_summary: Add 'PDF' and file size to meaningful link text for PDF downloads.
rule_detail:
When you publish a PDF:

- provide the content in another format that is accessible
- mark up the PDF with the right tags
- check that assistive technology reads the PDF content in the correct order
- add 'PDF' and file size to
[meaningful link text](/node/193/#link_to_something_only_if_it_helps_meet_the_users_need).

rule_summary: Do research to find why users need a PDF.
rule_detail: Do research to find why users need a PDF

rule_summary: Check whether other document formats meet the user need before using a PDF.
rule_detail: Before using a PDF, check if other document formats will meet the need. An example is the electronic publishing (EPUB) file format. EPUB documents scale to the screen sizes of different mobile devices.

rule_summary: Do not use Microsoft Word if you need to protect a document from changes after sharing it.
rule_detail: Don't use a Microsoft Word document if you need to protect the document from changes after it's shared.

rule_summary: Provide a landing page with a high-level summary when significant barriers prevent another accessible format.
rule_detail:
When there are significant barriers to providing content in another format, at least:

- create a landing page with a high-level summary of the content
- provide a way for people to request an accessible version – for example, an email address.

rule_summary: Provide a way for people to request an accessible version when significant barriers exist.
rule_detail:
When there are significant barriers to providing content in another format, at least:

- create a landing page with a high-level summary of the content
- provide a way for people to request an accessible version – for example, an email address.

rule_summary: Create reports with the required structural parts in the correct order.
rule_detail: Create complete reports with a landing page, preliminary content, body and endmatter. Include other parts if the report needs to be tabled in parliament.

rule_summary: Order report parts according to the conventions that apply to report information.
rule_detail: There are conventions that apply to how the information in reports should appear.

rule_summary: Use a landing page or cover to identify the report and help users decide whether to read it.
rule_detail: Use the landing page or cover to identify the report

rule_summary: Include a title page and preliminary parts in the report as needed.
rule_detail: Include a title page and preliminary parts

rule_summary: Use the same preliminary information in online reports as in printed versions.
rule_detail: Australian Government reports published online should include the same information as a printed version.

rule_summary: Include the required information on the title page.
rule_detail:
A title page should include the following:

- title
- subtitle, if any
- author’s name
- name of the sponsor, if applicable.

rule_summary: Include the specified extra details on the title page when relevant.
rule_detail: It can also have additional details such as the name of a compiler, translator, reviser or illustrator.

rule_summary: Include imprint-page details that do not appear on the title page.
rule_detail:
The reverse title page, or ‘imprint’ page, includes details that don’t appear on the title page, such as:

- copyright notices, including copyright held by others such as photographers and illustrators
- the publisher’s imprint or name and address
- lists of editions and reprints
- list of other volumes in a multi-volume set (this can also be on a separate page)
- identifying numbers and library classification data
- name of others contributing to the document, such as the editor, designer or illustrator.

rule_summary: Make copyright and other report information easy to find wherever imprint-page material appears.
rule_detail: Wherever it features, people should be able to easily find copyright and other information about the report.

rule_summary: Use the reverse title page material somewhere else if necessary in print publications.
rule_detail: You can put information prepared for the reverse title page somewhere else such as the inside front cover or back cover, if you’re not leaving those blank.

rule_summary: Include half-title and reverse half-title pages in printed reports when appropriate.
rule_detail: Printed reports can also have half-title and reverse half-title pages.

rule_summary: Show the main title exactly as it appears on the cover on the half-title page.
rule_detail: Show the main title exactly as it appears on the cover.

rule_summary: Do not show subtitles on the half-title page.
rule_detail: Do not show any subtitles.

rule_summary: Include a series title on the half-title page if the report is part of a series.
rule_detail: Include a series title if the report is part of a series.

rule_summary: Treat the reverse half-title page as optional and use it for supporting front-matter.
rule_detail:
The reverse half-title page is often blank. It can include:

- a list of other works by the same author
- a list of other contributors
- details of the series it is part of
- details of other volumes in the set
- part of an illustration that spills over from the title page.

rule_summary: Number preliminary pages with lower-case roman numerals.
rule_detail: Check the order of the preliminary pages. Number them with lower case roman numerals such as ’i’, ’ii’, ’iii’ and ’iv’.

rule_summary: Apply identifying numbers and classification data to locate the report.
rule_detail:
Identifying numbers are a unique way to locate the work. They include:

- International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs)
- International Standard Serial Numbers (ISSNs), if the report is part of a series.

rule_summary: Include an ISSN only if the report is part of a series.
rule_detail: International Standard Serial Numbers (ISSNs), if the report is part of a series.

rule_summary: Choose an open access licence for government copyright materials if possible.
rule_detail: If you work in government, use an open access licence if you can (for example, [Creative Commons](https://creativecommons.org.au/)).

rule_summary: Include a letter of transmittal when the report requires one.
rule_detail: A letter of transmittal is a message or letter to the person requesting the report. It is often included in annual reports and other reports prepared by committees, commissions and consultants. Sometimes it must be part of a report.

rule_summary: Include the report's purpose and audience in the letter of transmittal.
rule_detail:
The letter of transmittal must include the purpose of the report and who it is for. It must have:

- the signature of the person responsible for the report
- the day, month and year the report was submitted.

rule_summary: Place a foreword in the preliminary content and have it written by someone other than the author.
rule_detail:
A foreword:

- is always in the preliminary content
- is usually written by someone other than the author and often includes their signature
- explains the purpose of the report and why it’s important
- helps a wider audience to relate to the report.

rule_summary: Place a preface in the preliminary content and have it written by the author.
rule_detail:
A preface:

- is always in the preliminary content
- can replace a short introduction
- is written by the author and can include the author's signature
- tells the user why and how the report was prepared
- can include a short list of acknowledgements
- describes changes if it's a new version or update.

rule_summary: Place an introduction in the preliminary content or main body as needed.
rule_detail:
An introduction:

- can be in the preliminary content or main part of the report
- should be in the main part of the report if people will need the content to understand the report – for example, if the introduction includes terms of reference
- is by the author or someone else
- does not include a signature
- can replace a preface to discuss why and how the report was prepared
- includes long lists of acknowledgements
- describes changes if it’s a new version or update.

rule_summary: Use the heading 'Contents' for the contents list.
rule_detail: Use the heading ‘Contents’, not ‘Table of contents’ or ‘List of contents’.

rule_summary: Limit contents structures to no more than three heading levels.
rule_detail: There is rarely a need to use more than 3 levels of headings. Use design elements such as colour or typeface size for complex contents. This can separate the levels of heading and show the structure of the report. Make sure design elements are accessible.

rule_summary: Include a list of images and tables when it helps the user.
rule_detail: Include a list of images and tables if it is helpful to the user.

rule_summary: List images and tables in the prescribed order.
rule_detail:
The order of lists is:

- photographs (only in print)
- figures
- maps (if listed separately)
- tables.

rule_summary: Use a summary for long reports to present key findings, recommendations and conclusions.
rule_detail: For long reports, use a summary to present findings, recommendations and conclusions.

rule_summary: Name the summary to reflect its purpose and do not call it an executive summary.
rule_detail:
Name the summary to show its purpose. For example, you can use ‘Recommendations’ or ‘Summary’
*.* - Don't use ‘Executive summary’. Although this is common, it is not best practice.

rule_summary: Organise the main body of the report into chapters or parts.
rule_detail:
To organise the text in the main body of the report use:

- chapters
- parts for long reports, with chapters in each part.

rule_summary: Give chapters and parts short titles that clearly describe their content.
rule_detail: Both chapters and parts need short titles that tell the user what is in the content.

rule_summary: Number chapter titles consecutively through the report, including across parts.
rule_detail: Use consecutive numbering for chapter titles through the report. If the report contains parts, continue the chapter numbering into each part. For example, ‘Part 2’ might start with ‘Chapter 5’.

rule_summary: Number parts using one of the approved numbering styles.
rule_detail:
There are many ways to number parts:

- Part 1, Part 2
- Part A, Part B
- Part One, Part Two.

rule_summary: Identify the audience, purpose and platforms before designing social media content.
rule_detail: Identify the audience, purpose and platforms and design content for them.

rule_summary: Use social media monitoring tools to track conversations and understand audience concerns.
rule_detail: Use a social media monitoring tool to track conversations online. Find out what people are saying about your topic. Understand their problems and concerns.

rule_summary: Use social media to help users find information, engage, share updates, promote content and events, and build a network.
rule_detail:
You can use social media to:

- help people find information about government services and policy
- encourage people to engage with your agency by commenting and sharing
- share updates on important work
- promote other content, such as blog posts
- promote and encourage participation in events
- build a network of people who are interested in your agency’s work.

rule_summary: Follow your organisation’s social media strategy for anything published on social media.
rule_detail: Anything published on social media should follow your organisation’s social media strategy. Never rely on social media alone to engage with the community.

rule_summary: Do not rely on social media alone to engage with the community.
rule_detail: Anything published on social media should follow your organisation’s social media strategy. Never rely on social media alone to engage with the community.

rule_summary: Approve posts according to your organisation’s social media or communications policy.
rule_detail: Get posts approved according to your organisation’s social media or communications policy.

rule_summary: Ensure Australian Government employees follow the APS social media guidance.
rule_detail: Australian Government employees must follow the [Guidance for Australian Public Service Employees and Agencies](https://www.apsc.gov.au/social-media-guidance-australian-public-service-employees-and-agencies).

rule_summary: Treat content created for Australian Government work as a record.
rule_detail: Content that you create as part of your work for the Australian Government becomes a record. Records provide evidence of what your organisation has done and why.

rule_summary: Follow your organisation’s information management requirements.
rule_detail: Managing and disposing of records properly is a requirement under the [ Archives Act 1983](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C2004A02796). You must follow your organisation’s information management requirements. Visit the National Archives of Australia website for:

rule_summary: Define the audience before you write social media content.
rule_detail: Define the audience before you write

rule_summary: Find out who will engage with your post and why before you start writing.
rule_detail: Find out who will engage with your post and why before you start writing. Each social media platform has a different audience.

rule_summary: Use each platform’s analytics tool to learn about its audience.
rule_detail: Each platform has its own analytics tool to help you learn about them.

rule_summary: Ensure you have capacity to engage with comments and enquiries on your post.
rule_detail: Ensure there's capacity to engage with comments and enquiries on your post.

rule_summary: Prepare content specifically for each relevant platform.
rule_detail: Prepare content specifically for each platform. Check that a social media platform is the best option before you publish.

rule_summary: Check that a social media platform is the best option before publishing.
rule_detail: Prepare content specifically for each platform. Check that a social media platform is the best option before you publish.

rule_summary: Use social media only if it will help users of your services and products or help them understand government.
rule_detail:
- Will it help the people who use your services and products?
- Will it help them understand the people and processes of government?

rule_summary: Make content accessible on any platform you use.
rule_detail: Content needs to be accessible no matter which platform you use, including [video and audio content](/node/42).

rule_summary: Use LinkedIn for professional networking content such as jobs, insights, case studies, training and industry news.
rule_detail:
Business, government and industry use LinkedIn for professional networking. LinkedIn is suitable for publishing:

- job openings and career opportunities
- professional insights
- case studies
- information about training and other opportunities
- industry news.

rule_summary: Use X for current events, news and positive stories.
rule_detail: X is a platform for current content. Use X to tap into current events, news and positive stories.

rule_summary: Keep tweets to 280 characters or less.
rule_detail: The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters. Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence. Most tweets have a key idea and a link to a webpage. Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

rule_summary: Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence for each tweet.
rule_detail: The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters. Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence. Most tweets have a key idea and a link to a webpage. Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

rule_summary: Include a link to a webpage in most tweets.
rule_detail: The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters. Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence. Most tweets have a key idea and a link to a webpage. Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

rule_summary: Do not use internet slang in government tweets.
rule_detail: The maximum length of tweets is 280 characters. Write one idea in a short, attention-grabbing sentence. Most tweets have a key idea and a link to a webpage. Don’t use internet slang in government tweets.

rule_summary: Use keywords in hashtags to help people find and follow topics.
rule_detail: Use keywords in hashtags, which have a # symbol. Hashtags help people find and follow topics of interest. If you are publishing a new topic, try to use an existing or trending hashtag rather than creating a new one.

rule_summary: Use an existing or trending hashtag for a new topic instead of creating a new one.
rule_detail: Use keywords in hashtags, which have a # symbol. Hashtags help people find and follow topics of interest. If you are publishing a new topic, try to use an existing or trending hashtag rather than creating a new one.

rule_summary: Use no more than two hashtags.
rule_detail: You need no more than 2 hashtags. Too many hashtags makes your content difficult to read and less accessible.

rule_summary: Keep hashtags to a maximum of two to maintain readability and accessibility.
rule_detail: You need no more than 2 hashtags. Too many hashtags makes your content difficult to read and less accessible.

rule_summary: Use camel case in compound hashtags.
rule_detail: Use ‘camel case’ for compound hashtags. The first letter of each word in the hashtag starts with a capital letter – for example, #SelfQuarantine.

rule_summary: Address other users with an @ sign before their username.
rule_detail: Address other users with the @ sign before their username. Remember, these tweets are public and visible.

rule_summary: Do not publish technical content on Facebook.
rule_detail: Do not publish technical content on Facebook.

rule_summary: Use Facebook for human interest stories, staff profiles, communities of practice, events and career opportunities.
rule_detail:
Facebook is suitable for publishing:

- human interest stories
- profiles of staff
- information for communities of practice
- events
- career opportunities.

rule_summary: Keep Facebook videos short, interesting and focused on one clear message.
rule_detail: Videos on Facebook should be interesting and as short as possible. They should have only one message that is clear in the first second.

rule_summary: Make Facebook content compelling enough to stop people scrolling.
rule_detail: Facebook content has less than 2 seconds to grab attention before people scroll past it, if they see it at all. Content needs to be compelling so it reaches the people you want to reach.

rule_summary: Keep YouTube videos well produced, titled and framed with a poster image.
rule_detail:
YouTube videos should:

- be well produced
- include a compelling title
- include a poster frame – a still image that acts as a thumbnail for the video.

rule_summary: Use YouTube videos to show, explain, share stories, celebrate case studies or include people in events.
rule_detail:
Most videos on YouTube are between 3 and 12 minutes in length and can:

- show people how to do something
- explain a complex topic
- share human interest stories
- celebrate case studies
- include people in events.

rule_summary: Provide transcripts, captions and audio descriptions for accessible audio-visual content.
rule_detail: Users need transcripts, captions and audio descriptions for accessibility.

rule_summary: Work with experts to record and mix audio.
rule_detail: Work with experts to record and mix audio.

rule_summary: Check branding, copyright and permissions requirements.
rule_detail: Check branding, copyright and permissions requirements.

rule_summary: Include a transcript for people who do not want to watch the video or listen to the audio and for search engine indexing.
rule_detail: a transcript for people who don’t want to watch the video or listen to the audio – and for [search engine indexing](/node/103)

rule_summary: Include closed captions for people who cannot hear the dialogue and other sounds.
rule_detail: closed captions for people who can’t hear the dialogue and other sounds (symbol [CC])

rule_summary: Include an audio description for people who cannot see the video.
rule_detail: an audio description for people who can’t see the video.

rule_summary: Choose a media player that can be operated with a keyboard and mouse, display closed captions, adapt resolutions for low bandwidth, and work in landscape and portrait mode.
rule_detail:
Choose an accessible media player that:

- can be operated with a keyboard and mouse
- can display closed captions
- adapts resolutions to support low bandwidth connections
- works in landscape and portrait mode.

rule_summary: Avoid autoplay for video or animation.
rule_detail: Don’t set video or animation to autoplay.

rule_summary: Avoid flashing more than three times in any one second period.
rule_detail: Do not include anything that flashes more than 3 times in any one second period.

rule_summary: Make video text contrast at least 4.5:1.
rule_detail: Make sure the colour contrast of text in videos is at least 4.5:1.

rule_summary: Normalise audio so each recording has the same volume.
rule_detail: Normalise your audio to make sure each recording has the same volume.

rule_summary: Reduce background sounds to at least 20 decibels below foreground speech content.
rule_detail: Remove background sounds or make sure they are at least 20 decibels lower than the foreground speech content.

rule_summary: Provide equivalent information to anything contained in a video or audio file.
rule_detail: I can access equivalent information to anything contained in a video or audio file.

rule_summary: Let users control how they see and hear distinctions when colour or sound conveys meaning.
rule_detail: I can easily control how I see and hear distinctions if colour or sound convey meaning.

rule_summary: Allow users to operate the content using only a keyboard.
rule_detail: I can operate the content using only a keyboard.

rule_summary: Prevent content from causing seizures or physical reactions.
rule_detail: I can use content without experiencing a seizure or physical reaction.

rule_summary: Include a transcript for audio-visual and audio-only time-based media.
rule_detail: Time-based media (video and audio) must have a transcript so they are accessible to everyone. Transcripts are also important for search engine indexing.

rule_summary: Format transcripts in plain text or simple HTML.
rule_detail: Format the transcript in plain text or simple HTML.

rule_summary: Consider adding headings and time markers to transcripts.
rule_detail: Consider breaking the transcript into headings and adding time markers. This means that people can easily find and play a part of the audio.

rule_summary: Place transcripts on the same page as the content or link to a separate transcript page.
rule_detail: You can place the transcript on the same page as the content. Alternatively, you can also add a link below or beside the content to a page with the transcript.

rule_summary: Include all dialogue and speakers' names in transcripts.
rule_detail: Include all dialogue and the speakers’ names.

rule_summary: Introduce a single speaker by name and omit the name from subsequent dialogue when it is not crucial.
rule_detail: If there is only one speaker, introduce them by name in the transcript. You can then leave out their name with the dialogue, unless it is crucial to the content.

rule_summary: Write non-verbal information in square brackets in transcripts.
rule_detail: Write non-verbal information in square brackets.

rule_summary: End transcripts with 'End of transcript'.
rule_detail: End the transcript with ‘End of transcript’.

rule_summary: Distinguish subtitles from captions by using subtitles only for dialogue and captions for all audio cues.
rule_detail:
Subtitles display only the dialogue and are commonly used for translations.

Captions display any audio in a video, including dialogue and sound cues.

rule_summary: Use either open captions or closed captions as appropriate, noting that closed captions can be toggled by the user.
rule_detail:
Captions can be open captions or closed captions.

Open captions, which the user cannot turn off, are burned onto the video itself. Closed captions can be turned on or off by the user.

rule_summary: Prefer closed captions over subtitles or open captions when possible.
rule_detail: If you have a choice, closed captions are preferable to subtitles or open captions. Some media players also allow for multilingual captions that users can select on demand if they need translations.

rule_summary: Use Australian terms and spelling for an Australian audience.
rule_detail: Use Australian terms and spelling for an Australian audience, regardless of the accent or intention of the speaker. Government agencies might use alternative spellings in video content for some overseas audiences.

rule_summary: Choose video or audio only when users will find it easy to understand and access.
rule_detail: Use video or audio when users find it easy to understand and access

rule_summary: Use time-based media only when it is the best way to deliver a message or tell a story.
rule_detail: Ask whether time-based media (video or audio) is the best way to deliver a message or tell a story.

rule_summary: Check your audience, access method and purpose before deciding on video or audio.
rule_detail: understand who will use it, how they will access it and why

rule_summary: Confirm you have the resources and expertise before creating time-based media.
rule_detail: have (or can you get) the resources and expertise to do it.

rule_summary: Use video or audio when the information suits the format, reaches the intended audience and is accessible to them.
rule_detail:
Use video or audio if it:

- suits the type of information you want to include
- helps you reach most people who need to find that information
- is accessible to those people.

rule_summary: Consider accessibility, flicker, language, environment and timing when creating time-based media.
rule_detail:
If you create video or audio content, be aware of:

- accessibility for time-based media (for example, closed captions)
- the potential effect of flickering and dynamic content on a screen
- language difficulties
- the user’s environment (for example, a workplace where sound disturbs colleagues)
- timing in the content and the time users are likely to spend using the content.

rule_summary: Provide a text alternative for users who cannot rely on captions or audio, are time poor, or need SEO support.
rule_detail:
Provide a text alternative to video and audio for:

- users who cannot reliably read captions or hear audio
- users who have time pressures
- search engine optimisation (SEO).

rule_summary: Do user research before deciding whether video or audio is the right format.
rule_detail: Before deciding if video or audio is the right format, do [user research](/node/76).

rule_summary: Choose text-based content when it is the more feasible and accessible option.
rule_detail: Text-based content is usually a more feasible and accessible option to meet a user need.

rule_summary: Create accessible video and audio with the correct alternative versions.
rule_detail: Create accessible video and audio with the correct alternative versions so everyone can access the information.

rule_summary: Meet AAA success criteria for video when the content is of national importance.
rule_detail: Meet AAA success criteria for video when content is of national importance. For example, for voting or Census participation and access to National Health and Safety information.

rule_summary: Follow the detailed requirements for video and audio.
rule_detail:
Follow the detailed
[requirements for video and audio](/node/41).

rule_summary: Create video when the user needs a quick explanation.
rule_detail: Create video if the user needs a quick explanation

rule_summary: Keep videos short, accessible and focused on information people need quickly.
rule_detail: Video works best when it is short, accessible and shows something people need to know quickly.

rule_summary: Keep online videos to one key message.
rule_detail: Online videos should have one key message.

rule_summary: Limit online videos to no more than one to two minutes, especially for social media.
rule_detail: They should be be no more than one to 2 minutes long, especially if you share the video on social media.

rule_summary: Check your organisation’s policy for the preferred length of longer videos.
rule_detail: Videos covering complex topics and hosted on your organisation’s website can be longer. Check your organisation’s policy for the preferred length of videos.

rule_summary: Break complex or multi-message videos into smaller stand-alone pieces.
rule_detail:
Break the video into smaller, stand-alone pieces if:

- the message is complex
- there is more than one message.

rule_summary: Check video publishing guidelines before choosing a platform.
rule_detail: Once you have chosen a platform, check its video publishing guidelines.

rule_summary: Use the video format preferred by the platform and check accepted file formats.
rule_detail: Video is the preferred format of some [social media platforms](/node/43#design_for_each_relevant_platform). Check which file format the platform accepts.

rule_summary: Add tags or hashtags to help people find video content.
rule_detail: You can add tags or hashtags on any platform to help people find video content.

rule_summary: Use hashtags across several platforms to increase discoverability.
rule_detail: Add hashtags across several platforms to increase the likelihood that people will find the video.

rule_summary: Choose words that users are likely to type into search engines.
rule_detail: Use words that the user is most likely to type into search engines.

rule_summary: Use animation to show complex processes or abstract ideas.
rule_detail: Use animation to show complex processes or abstract ideas.

rule_summary: Make animation work for social media and understandable with or without audio.
rule_detail: Animation works well on social media platforms. People can usually understand them with or without audio.

rule_summary: Give animation a story and a call to action.
rule_detail: As for other types of videos, animation must tell a story. You should include a call to action so users know what they can do next.

rule_summary: Use animated infographics to explain government information and services.
rule_detail: Use animated infographics to show and explain government information and services.

rule_summary: Use professionals to create animation videos.
rule_detail: Use professionals to create animation videos.

rule_summary: Meet minimum colour-contrast requirements when using text or images of text in animation.
rule_detail: When using text or images of text in animation, meet minimum requirements for colour contrast.

rule_summary: Ensure colour is not the only way to convey meaning in animation.
rule_detail: Ensure colour is not the only means of conveying meaning.

rule_summary: Follow the requirements and standards for video and audio.
rule_detail:
Follow the
[requirements and standards for video and audio](/node/41).

rule_summary: Use live action to show people in a real-world environment.
rule_detail: Use live action to show people in a real-world environment.

rule_summary: Keep live-action subjects clearly lit, in focus and unobstructed.
rule_detail:
Ensure that the subject is:

- clearly lit
- in focus
- not obstructed by other features.

rule_summary: Use candid, simple, interesting and original scenes for live action.
rule_detail: Use candid shots and real scenes that are simple, interesting and original.

rule_summary: Make live-action visuals crisp and use natural colours.
rule_detail: Visuals should be crisp and use natural colours.

rule_summary: Avoid distracting clothing, branding and moiré-prone patterns in video.
rule_detail:
People in the video should wear appropriate clothing and avoid:

- offensive slogans or slogans that will distract the viewer
- branding and logos
- fine patterns and stripes, which reduce image quality by creating a ‘moiré’ pattern.

rule_summary: Use the format that helps meet the user’s need.
rule_detail: Use the format that helps meet the user’s need. This could be a form, a blog, an image or another format.

rule_summary: Use clear structures in blog posts.
rule_detail: Blog posts can help users solve common problems. Use clear structures and ensure content is accessible. Moderate comments if you allow them.

rule_summary: Ensure blog content is accessible.
rule_detail: Blog posts can help users solve common problems. Use clear structures and ensure content is accessible. Moderate comments if you allow them.

rule_summary: Moderate comments on blogs if you allow them.
rule_detail: Blog posts can help users solve common problems. Use clear structures and ensure content is accessible. Moderate comments if you allow them.

rule_summary: Combine text with layout and imagery in Easy Read materials.
rule_detail: Easy Read combines text with layout and imagery to simplify and explain information. Users often print Easy Read materials. The standard layout works as a handout.

rule_summary: Use the standard layout as a handout for Easy Read materials.
rule_detail: Easy Read combines text with layout and imagery to simplify and explain information. Users often print Easy Read materials. The standard layout works as a handout.

rule_summary: Write concise letters and emails.
rule_detail: Concise letters and emails tell a recipient what they need to know. Use the right level of formality for the recipient and purpose. Be mindful of people’s privacy.

rule_summary: Use the right level of formality for the recipient and purpose.
rule_detail: Concise letters and emails tell a recipient what they need to know. Use the right level of formality for the recipient and purpose. Be mindful of people’s privacy.

rule_summary: Be mindful of people’s privacy in letters and emails.
rule_detail: Concise letters and emails tell a recipient what they need to know. Use the right level of formality for the recipient and purpose. Be mindful of people’s privacy.

rule_summary: Design digital forms for completion by the user.
rule_detail: This guidance helps you to design digital forms filled in by the user. Most of the guidance also applies to printed forms, but there are some differences noted.

rule_summary: Make images clear and simple.
rule_detail: Images can help users if they are clear and simple. Make sure everyone can access the information that images convey.

rule_summary: Ensure everyone can access the information that images convey.
rule_detail: Images can help users if they are clear and simple. Make sure everyone can access the information that images convey.

rule_summary: Number each issue of a serial and include other publication information.
rule_detail: Journals, magazines and newspapers are known as ‘periodicals’. Periodicals are published at regular intervals, so they are sometimes called ‘serials’. Number each issue of a serial and include other publication information so people can find it.

rule_summary: Create PDFs only when research shows a specific need for the format.
rule_detail: Only create PDFs if your research shows there are specific needs for this format. Make PDF content accessible to everyone who needs it.

rule_summary: Make PDF content accessible to everyone who needs it.
rule_detail: Only create PDFs if your research shows there are specific needs for this format. Make PDF content accessible to everyone who needs it.

rule_summary: Create reports with a landing page, preliminary content, body and endmatter.
rule_detail: Create complete reports with a landing page, preliminary content, body and endmatter. Include other parts if the report needs to be tabled in parliament.

rule_summary: Include other parts if the report needs to be tabled in parliament.
rule_detail: Create complete reports with a landing page, preliminary content, body and endmatter. Include other parts if the report needs to be tabled in parliament.

rule_summary: Identify the audience, purpose and platforms for social media content.
rule_detail: Social media can enhance your engagement with users and stakeholders. Identify the audience, purpose and platforms and design content for them.

rule_summary: Design social media content for the identified audience, purpose and platforms.
rule_detail: Social media can enhance your engagement with users and stakeholders. Identify the audience, purpose and platforms and design content for them.

rule_summary: Make video and audio content accessible if the format meets a user need.
rule_detail: Video and audio are time-based media. Users can choose when and how much they view or listen to. If the format meets a user need, make sure anyone can access the content.

rule_summary: Use italic type sparingly.
rule_detail: Use italic type sparingly as it can affect readability.

rule_summary: Limit italics to the uses described on the page.
rule_detail: Limit italics to the uses described on this page, which link to detailed guidance.

rule_summary: Do not use italics for large blocks of text.
rule_detail: Don’t use italics for: large blocks of text

rule_summary: Do not use italics for material already set apart from the page text.
rule_detail: Don’t use italics for: material that would normally be in italics but is set apart (such as a list of titles under a heading)

rule_summary: Do not use italics for aggregation pages.
rule_detail: Don’t use italics for: aggregation pages (such as a [page listing legislation](https://www.legislation.gov.au/search/status(inforce)/type(principal)/collection(act))).

rule_summary: Use a consistent type style.
rule_detail: Use a consistent type style. For some users, it can be difficult to read the text when presented in a style that is different or unfamiliar. This includes changes to the shapes of letters, as between roman and italic type.

rule_summary: Avoid chunks of italic text.
rule_detail: Avoid chunks of italic text.

rule_summary: Italicise titles of stand-alone works, legal cases and Acts.
rule_detail: Italicise titles of stand-alone works, legal cases and Acts

rule_summary: Do not italicise sacred texts.
rule_detail: Don’t use italics for the titles of sacred texts, such as the Bible or the Koran.

rule_summary: Italicise the titles of specified published works.
rule_detail: Use italics for the [titles of these published works](/node/165#style_and_spell_titles_consistently): books and periodicals; plays; classics; most musical compositions; ballets and operas; films, videos and podcasts; blogs; television and radio programs; artworks.

rule_summary: Set unpublished works in roman type.
rule_detail: Unpublished works are in roman type.

rule_summary: Use reverse italics in titles of published works when a word would otherwise be italicised.
rule_detail: In some titles, there are words that would normally be italicised. To make sure they stand out from the rest of the italicised title, write the words in roman type. This is called ‘reverse italics’.

rule_summary: Italicise primary legislation and legal cases.
rule_detail: Use italics for primary legislation and legal cases but not for delegated legislation or bills. Follow the [guidance for legal material](/node/163).

rule_summary: Avoid italics for foreign words and phrases when an English equivalent exists.
rule_detail: Italics contrast words and phrases that are not in English from surrounding text. Foreign words and phrases should generally be avoided in government writing, unless there is no English equivalent.

rule_summary: Write borrowed words without italics or accent marks.
rule_detail: Standard Australian English can absorb words or phrases from other languages. Write these ‘borrowed’ words without italics or accent marks.

rule_summary: Do not italicise names or words from First Nations languages.
rule_detail: Do not italicise [names or words from First Nations languages](/node/179#style_for_first_australian_languages_needs_to_recognise_continuing_cultures). They are Australian languages, not foreign languages.

rule_summary: Do not italicise Latin shortened forms.
rule_detail: Don’t use italics for Latin shortened forms. The ‘common use’ principle applies to Latin shortened forms (such as ‘etc.’ and ‘i.e.’). Write the full Latin word in italics but not the shortened form.

rule_summary: Use single quotation marks for special meaning instead of italics.
rule_detail: Italics are often used for the first instance of a technical term when it’s defined or introduced for the first time. Instead, to draw attention to words with special meaning, [use single quotation marks](/node/114).

rule_summary: Italicise well-known mathematical theorems and formulas.
rule_detail: Specialist uses of italics include well-known [mathematical theorems and formulas](/node/145).

rule_summary: Avoid blocks of italics where possible.
rule_detail: Remember to avoid blocks of italics wherever possible. Blocks of italics are difficult to read, so consider other formatting and design options.

rule_summary: Italicise the official names of vehicles, excluding any definite article.
rule_detail: Ships, trains, aircraft and other vehicles sometimes have a proper name. The name is in italics excluding any definite article. The brand or type of vehicle is in roman type.

rule_summary: Italicise genus and species in scientific names, but not common names.
rule_detail: Use italics for the genus and species, including any subspecies, but not for the common name.

rule_summary: Italicise the scientific names of infectious organisms.
rule_detail: Write the scientific names of infectious organisms, including some bacteria and fungi, in italics.

rule_summary: Use italics sparingly for emphasis.
rule_detail: Italics, used sparingly, can work for this purpose.

rule_summary: Use italics to stress a word for meaning or emotion.
rule_detail: Sometimes you want to stress a word for meaning or to convey emotion, including a change in tone.

rule_summary: Use italics in quotations only when you mark the change with a note.
rule_detail: If you do this, write ‘emphasis added’ in square brackets following the italicised text. This way, people will know the italics didn’t appear in the original quotation.

rule_summary: Use the note 'emphasis from original' when italics are in the original quotation.
rule_detail: If the italics is part of the original text, write ‘emphasis from original’ in the square brackets following the quotation.

rule_summary: Spell official place names correctly.
rule_detail: Spell official place names correctly.

rule_summary: Use standard shortened forms in addresses.
rule_detail: Use standard shortened forms in addresses.

rule_summary: Check official Australian place names using the Australian Place Names dataset.
rule_detail: You can check the spelling of a place name using the Australian Place Names dataset.

rule_summary: Contact the relevant state or territory naming authority if you are still unsure about a place name.
rule_detail: If still unsure, contact the relevant state or territory naming authority.

rule_summary: Recognise that official place names are generally given under Acts of parliament and associated rules.
rule_detail: Official place names are generally given under Acts of parliament and associated rules.

rule_summary: Understand that place-naming processes differ across states and territories.
rule_detail: Each state and territory has its own legal and administrative processes.

rule_summary: Apply national naming principles to support consistency across Australia.
rule_detail: National principles for naming are intended to provide consistency across the country.

rule_summary: Allow for exceptions to general naming rules where historical and cultural realities require them.
rule_detail: Because of this reality, there may appear to be exceptions to the general rules given in this guide.

rule_summary: Consult relevant communities about conventions for naming and spelling in specific First Nations languages.
rule_detail: Consult directly with relevant communities about conventions for naming and spelling in specific First Nations languages.

rule_summary: Write Australian place names as proper nouns in standard Australian English.
rule_detail: Australian place names are proper nouns, written using standard Australian English.

rule_summary: Use a standard 26-character alphabet in place names.
rule_detail: use a standard 26 character alphabet

rule_summary: Do not use diacritical marks in place names.
rule_detail: don’t use diacritical marks

rule_summary: Do not make place names possessive.
rule_detail: are not possessive

rule_summary: Do not generally use punctuation in place names.
rule_detail: don’t generally have punctuation.

rule_summary: Preserve or adjust spelling and capitalisation when official names are adopted from other languages.
rule_detail: Spelling and capitalisation can change when they’re adopted as an official Australian place name.

rule_summary: Remove accent marks and diacritics from the official spelling.
rule_detail: loses any accent marks or diacritics

rule_summary: Add capitalisation when spelling official names.
rule_detail: adds capitalisation.

rule_summary: Use hyphens and apostrophes only when they are part of the commemorated person's name.
rule_detail: Hyphens and apostrophes can be part of an official name. They appear if they were part of the name of the person commemorated by the place name.

rule_summary: Use a spaced forward slash between the two parts of an official dual name.
rule_detail: When writing official dual names, use a spaced forward slash to separate the 2 parts of the name.

rule_summary: Keep the order of dual names as written in the official name.
rule_detail: The order should be as written in the official name, which you can check in the Australian Place Names dataset.

rule_summary: Capitalise place names.
rule_detail: Words that don’t usually need an initial capital have one when they are part of a place name.

rule_summary: Capitalise the names of roads, streets and other thoroughfares.
rule_detail: The names of roads, streets and other thoroughfares also take an initial capital.

rule_summary: Write generic and plural terms in lower case when styling building and place names.
rule_detail: Names of buildings, structures and public places have initial capitals. Write generic and plural terms in lower case.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for private property names.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the names of private properties.

rule_summary: Spell out the names of Australian states and territories in formal content.
rule_detail: Spell out the names of Australian states and territories in formal content.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms for state and territory names only as adjectives, where space is limited, to avoid repetition, or in addresses.
rule_detail: You can use shortened forms when: the name is used as an adjective; space is limited; the full name would result in repetition; you are writing an address.

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop after shortened state and territory forms.
rule_detail: Don’t use a full stop after the shortened forms. This rule applies to the initialisms (NSW, WA, ACT and NT), abbreviations (Vic and Tas) and the contraction (Qld).

rule_summary: List states and territories in a consistent order that suits the context.
rule_detail: States and territories are generally listed in an order when more than one is mentioned. Other orders might be more suitable for some content. Use the order that fits with context and helps people understand your content.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for commercial terms such as trade marks, brands and business names.
rule_detail:
Use initial capitals for commercial terms

Use initial capitals for trade marks, brands and business names.

rule_summary: Preserve a business’s own unusual spelling, spacing, capitals and lower case letters when writing its name.
rule_detail: An exception to using initial capitals is where the business itself uses an unusual mix of spacing, capitals and lower case letters. In this case, write it the way the business writes it.

rule_summary: Do not capitalise a trade mark or brand at the start of a sentence if it begins with a lower-case letter.
rule_detail: Don’t use an initial capital at the start of sentences when the trade mark or brand starts with a lower case letter.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for the proprietary names of drugs and other chemicals, and lower case for generic names.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the proprietary names of drugs and other chemicals, but lower case for generic names.

rule_summary: Spell trade mark as two words when writing for government.
rule_detail: ‘Trade mark’ is spelled as 2 words in the Trade Marks Act 1995. Use this spelling when writing for government, even though most dictionaries prefer ‘trademark’.

rule_summary: Spell trade mark as two words when using it as a verb, although register a trade mark is better.
rule_detail: You should also spell ‘trade mark’ as 2 words when you use it as a verb, although it’s better to say ‘register a trade mark’.

rule_summary: Use a common word instead of a trade mark or brand name where possible.
rule_detail:
Use a common word for a product if you can

Avoid using trade marks and brand names if possible. Instead use a generic word.

rule_summary: Avoid using registered and trade mark symbols for trade marks if possible.
rule_detail: Avoid using the registered (®) symbol or the trade mark (™) symbol for trade marks if possible.

rule_summary: Use a capital letter for a registered trade mark only when the term is still registered and used for that brand.
rule_detail: If a term is still registered as a trade mark, you should use it only for that brand and use a capital letter. This may vary between different countries.

rule_summary: Do not rely on dictionaries to determine whether a term has trade mark status.
rule_detail: Dictionaries show the way such words are used. Don’t rely on dictionaries to work out if such words have legal status as trade marks.

rule_summary: Use the brand name with a capital letter when a registered trade mark is still registered in Australia.
rule_detail: Find out if a trade mark has been registered in Australia by using Australian trade mark search. If you’re not sure, seek legal advice.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for a brand name when it is still being used as a trade mark, and use the generic lower-case form when it is used generically.
rule_detail:
A product name can change meaning when used in the generic sense

A few words have different meanings when used as a trade mark or used generically.

#### Example

- Band-Aid [A sticking plaster; initial capitals only for that brand]
- bandaid [A word meaning a temporary or makeshift solution to a problem]
- Google [A popular search engine; initial capital only for that brand]
- google [A verb meaning to search on the internet using a search engine]

rule_summary: Write common household names in lower case unless they begin a sentence.
rule_detail: Other brand names have become so widely used that they are no longer associated with a specific product. They have become common household names used in a generic sense. They start with lower case except at the start of a sentence.

rule_summary: Use the correct term and apply consistent capitalisation for government terms.
rule_detail: Use the correct term and follow the rules for capitalising government terms. People find it easier to understand content that has a consistent style.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals only for formal names and titles of government entities and office holders.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals only for the formal names and titles of government entities and office holders. Use lower case for generic references.

rule_summary: Treat specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation as a possible exception.
rule_detail: These are rules for general content. There might be exceptions if you are writing specialist legal content using terms defined in legislation.
