rule_summary: Refer to the national government of Australia as the Australian Government.
rule_detail: Refer to the national government of Australia as the ‘Australian Government’. Use an initial capital for both words only when they occur together.

rule_summary: Use lower case for bench and full bench in general content.
rule_detail: In general content, use lower case for the ‘bench’ and ‘full bench’.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for the Budget to distinguish it from the generic term.
rule_detail: Use an initial capital for ‘the Budget’ to show the difference from the generic reference.

rule_summary: Use lower case for budget when it is an adjective or a plural.
rule_detail: Use lower case for ‘budget’ when it is used as an adjective or as a plural.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for the Cabinet to distinguish it from the generic term.
rule_detail: Always use an initial capital for ‘the Cabinet’ to show the difference from its generic reference.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for Commonwealth.
rule_detail: ‘The Commonwealth of Australia’ is the name of Australia in the Constitution. Use an initial capital for ‘Commonwealth’.

rule_summary: Avoid using Commonwealth government to mean Australian Government.
rule_detail: Do not use the phrase ‘Commonwealth government’ to mean ‘Australian Government’.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for the Crown.
rule_detail: Always use an initial capital for ‘the Crown’ to show the difference from its generic reference.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals only for formal names of departments and agencies.
rule_detail: Use initial capital letters only for the formal names of government departments and agencies. Check the names of departments and agencies in the government online directory.

rule_summary: Use lower case for generic mentions of departments and agencies.
rule_detail: Don’t use capital letters for generic mentions. For example, use: ‘the agency’ instead of ‘the Agency’; ‘the authority’ instead of ‘the Authority’; ‘the commission’ instead of ‘the Commission’; ‘the department’ instead of ‘the Department’.

rule_summary: Use a shortened form of a department or agency name only if the organisation uses it regularly.
rule_detail: Use a shortened form of the name only if the department or agency uses it regularly in their own content.

rule_summary: Use the name published in a source if the organisation has since changed its name.
rule_detail: If you cite a source written by an organisation that has since changed its name, use the name published in the source. This might not be the organisation’s current name.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for the Treasury.
rule_detail: Always use an initial capital for ‘the Treasury’ to show the difference from its generic reference.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for formal names of areas in organisational structures.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the formal names of areas in a department or agency's organisational structure. Don't use initial capitals for generic mentions of parts of the formal names.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for federal only when it is part of a formal name.
rule_detail: Use an initial capital letter for ‘federal’ when it forms part of a formal name. Don’t capitalise it when it is used as an adjective.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for Federation only when referring to Australia’s Federation in 1901.
rule_detail: Use an initial capital for the word ‘federation’ only when referring to Australia’s Federation in 1901.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for government only when it is part of a formal name.
rule_detail: Use an initial capital for the word ‘government’ if it is part of a formal name. Use lower case everywhere else.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for full names of government programs, treaties, protocols and similar agreements.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the full names of: government programs; treaties; protocols and similar agreements.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for specific abbreviations but not for generic references or abbreviations.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for abbreviations that remain specific but not for generic references or abbreviations.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for formal and abbreviated titles of current heads of state.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the formal and abbreviated titles of current heads of state.

rule_summary: Use lower case for generic references to the position of head of state or to previous incumbents.
rule_detail: You do not need to use capitals for generic references to the position or when referring to previous incumbents.

rule_summary: Use government sources to check the titles of legislation.
rule_detail: Use government sources to check the titles of legislation, especially: the Federal Register of Legislation - the Australian Parliament House list of bills and legislation.

rule_summary: Follow the manual’s guidance to use the correct title for legislation.
rule_detail: Follow the guidance in this manual to use the correct title for legislation.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for Act, Ordinance, Regulation and Bill when referring to specific legislation.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for these terms when referring to specific legislation: Act, Ordinance, Regulation, Bill.

rule_summary: Use lower case for generic references to bills, regulations and ordinances.
rule_detail: Use lower case for generic references to bills, regulations and ordinances. Use initial capitals for all references to Acts.

rule_summary: Follow the detailed rules for references to delegated legislation.
rule_detail: Follow detailed rules for references to delegated legislation.

rule_summary: Use official titles for ministers and departmental secretaries.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the official titles of ministers and departmental secretaries. Use lower case for generic references.

rule_summary: Use lower case for generic references to ministers and departmental secretaries.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the official titles of ministers and departmental secretaries. Use lower case for generic references.

rule_summary: Introduce scientific terms and common names when that helps users, while using the correct spelling and style.
rule_detail: Medical terms have specific meanings. Introduce scientific terms and common names if that helps users, but always use the correct spelling and style.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital letter for a medical term only when it is a proper noun, a proper adjective, or a genus name.
rule_detail:
Use an initial capital letter for medical terms only if the term is a proper noun or adjective, or if it is the name of a genus. Otherwise don’t use initial capitals for the names of:

- diseases and viruses
- diagnostic procedures
- syndromes
- anatomical parts.

rule_summary: Use capital letters for acronyms and initialisms of medical terms.
rule_detail: Use capital letters for acronyms and initialisms of medical terms. Spell out the full term in lower case, unless the word or term you’re shortening includes a proper name or a genus name.

rule_summary: Spell out the full medical term in lower case unless the shortened form includes a proper name or genus name.
rule_detail: Use capital letters for acronyms and initialisms of medical terms. Spell out the full term in lower case, unless the word or term you’re shortening includes a proper name or a genus name.

rule_summary: Use the possessive case for diseases named after people who had the disease.
rule_detail:
When referring to an eponym in writing, use the following rules:

- If it is a disease named after people who had the disease, use the possessive case.
- If it is a disease or anatomical part named after the person who discovered, studied or described it, don’t use the possessive case.

rule_summary: Do not use the possessive case for diseases or anatomical parts named after the person who discovered, studied or described them.
rule_detail:
When referring to an eponym in writing, use the following rules:

- If it is a disease named after people who had the disease, use the possessive case.
- If it is a disease or anatomical part named after the person who discovered, studied or described it, don’t use the possessive case.

rule_summary: Do not apply the eponym possessive rule to organisations; use the organisation's own name form.
rule_detail: This rule doesn’t apply to names of organisations dedicated to studying certain diseases or supporting people who are affected by them. Always refer to organisations in the same way as they refer to themselves.

rule_summary: Italicise scientific names of infectious organisms.
rule_detail: Write scientific names of infectious organisms – such as viruses, bacteria and parasites – in italics. Use an initial capital for the name of the genus only.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital only for the genus name in scientific organism names.
rule_detail: Write scientific names of infectious organisms – such as viruses, bacteria and parasites – in italics. Use an initial capital for the name of the genus only.

rule_summary: Use generic drug names where possible and write them in lower case.
rule_detail: Use the generic names of drugs where possible. Write them in lower case.

rule_summary: Put brand names in parentheses after the common drug name and capitalise the brand name.
rule_detail: You can include the brand name in parentheses after the common name. Use initial capitals for brand names. Commercial terms might be trade marked: take care [using product names](/node/89#take_care_using_product_names).

rule_summary: Use inclusive, person-focused language when referring to medical conditions and avoid outdated or stigmatizing terms.
rule_detail:
Refer to medical conditions using clear and inclusive language

The language you use for some medical conditions can change as research and social understanding of the conditions evolve. Be mindful of outdated language that can perpetuate stigma or misunderstandings about the condition.

Refer to peak bodies that study the condition or that provide support and information to people affected by it.

### Example

The term ‘bipolar disorder’ replaces ‘manic depression’, a term that is no longer in use.

When you are writing about people with a medical condition, focus on the person. Use neutral language to describe the condition. Don’t label the person.

rule_summary: Use neutral, person-first wording instead of labeling people by their medical condition.
rule_detail: When you are writing about people with a medical condition, focus on the person. Use neutral language to describe the condition. Don’t label the person.

rule_summary: Place the scientific name in parentheses after the common name, and do not use 'or' between them.
rule_detail: If you’re writing both the scientific and common names for a medical condition, place the scientific name in parentheses. Don’t use ‘or’. This could confuse readers into thinking they are 2 separate medical conditions.

rule_summary: Refer to peoples and places outside Australia based on current information.
rule_detail: Refer to peoples and places outside Australia based on current information. Correct spelling and style avoids causing confusion or offence among users.

rule_summary: Check official sources for country and place names.
rule_detail: Check official sources for country and place names

rule_summary: Use a consistent official country name chosen from trusted references.
rule_detail:
Some countries have several official names. Consult trusted references to decide which name to use, then use it consistently. Helpful references include:

- the
[countries, economies and regions](https://www.dfat.gov.au/geo/pages/countries-and-regions)webpages, on the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade website - the United Nations
[geographical names database](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/geoinfo/geonames/) - the Australian Bureau of Statistics
.*Standard Australian classification of countries*

rule_summary: Use the official name of a country consistently when names change.
rule_detail: The names of countries can change for political reasons. For example, a country might change its name to show independence from a former occupying country.

rule_summary: Capitalize country, state, territory, and province names.
rule_detail:
Spell country names with a capital letter

Use initial capitals for:

- the official name of a country
- any commonly used short forms of the country’s name
- the names of states, territories and provinces.

The definite article ‘the’ isn’t capitalised unless it begins a sentence.

rule_summary: Use a short form of a country name only when it is clear and accurate.
rule_detail:
Shorten a country name only if it is clear to the user

Use a short form of a country’s name only if it’s clear and accurate. Shortened forms can make it easier to read text or tables, illustrations, notes, lists and bibliographies.

rule_summary: Use English versions of country and place names in most content.
rule_detail:
Use English versions of countries and places in most content

English-language content usually uses the English version of a country’s name.

rule_summary: Use preferred non-English official names where applicable.
rule_detail: There are some cases where the preferred official name isn’t in English.

rule_summary: Use established English forms for well-known place names in English-speaking countries.
rule_detail: In English-speaking countries, the convention is to use the established English forms for well-known place names.

rule_summary: Do not capitalise generic uses of place-name words.
rule_detail: When the name is used generically, you don’t need an initial capital.

rule_summary: Capitalize recognised political or geographic region names.
rule_detail:
Check the official status for area and region names

Groups of nations or areas that are recognised as political or geographic regions take initial capitals.

rule_summary: Use lower case for compass-point terms used descriptively rather than as part of a name.
rule_detail: Use lower case if the names of compass points (such as north and south-east) are not part of the name but are used to refer to the geographic area.

rule_summary: Use dictionary guidance to decide whether a semi-official regional name is appropriate.
rule_detail: Some names that aren’t officially recognised become well known and gain a semi-official status. Use a dictionary to help you decide when this is appropriate.

rule_summary: Capitalize nationality, people-group, religion, language-group, and regional identity terms.
rule_detail:
Write nationalities, peoples and places with initial capitals

There’s usually a clear relationship between the name of the country or region and the word used for the nationality. It’s not always obvious though, so check a dictionary to ensure you’re using the correct term.

rule_summary: Follow the guidance for writing non-English personal names.
rule_detail: Follow guidance for writing non-English [ personal names](/node/90).

rule_summary: Capitalize names of certain people groups and related identities.
rule_detail:
Capitalise the names of certain groups.

### Example

- People groups – Hispanic, Sentinelese, Vietnamese Rục, Sámi
- Clans – Clan Campbell (Scottish)
- People from particular regions – Asian, European, Sumatran, Basque
- People who follow particular religions – Jewish, Christian, Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu, Greek Orthodox
- People who speak particular languages – Hokkien-speaking

rule_summary: Use the correct language name when it differs from the country name.
rule_detail:
Check if an official language differs from the country name

The name of a country’s language isn’t always derived from the name of the country.

rule_summary: Apply standard capitalisation rules to most natural phenomena.
rule_detail: Standard rules of capitalisation apply for most natural phenomena

rule_summary: Capitalise proper nouns in natural phenomena terms.
rule_detail: Proper nouns start with a capital letter.

rule_summary: Keep adjectives and common nouns in natural phenomena terms lower case.
rule_detail: Adjectives and common nouns are in lower case.

rule_summary: Do not use italics for natural phenomena terms.
rule_detail: Do not use italics.

rule_summary: Write generic climate and weather terms in lower case.
rule_detail: Write generic terms for climate and weather in lower case. This rule applies to many compound nouns.

rule_summary: Write scientific names for types of clouds in lower case when they are specific terms.
rule_detail: Specific terms usually take lower case. For example, this rule applies to scientific names for types of clouds.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for scientific terms for natural phenomena that combine common nouns into proper nouns.
rule_detail: Scientific terms for natural phenomena can include common nouns that combine to form a proper noun. Use initial capitals when spelling out this kind of scientific term. Common shortened forms are in full capitals. Any non-English names retain the spelling of the original.

rule_summary: Write climate and weather events using their proper names.
rule_detail: Climate and weather events take on proper names

rule_summary: Follow Bureau of Meteorology capitalisation style for named climate and weather events.
rule_detail: There are specific capitalisation rules for climate and weather events. We follow the style recommended by Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology.

rule_summary: Follow the standard capitalisation rules for events not listed on the page.
rule_detail: For events not listed here, follow the standard rules for capitalisation.

rule_summary: Capitalise cyclone names, including the given name and the words immediately before it.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the names of cyclones. Do this for the given name and for the adjectives and common nouns that appear immediately before the given name. The bureau uses ‘Cyclone’, ‘Tropical Cyclone’ and ‘Severe Tropical Cyclone’ as part of the cyclone’s name.

rule_summary: Verify cyclone names against the Bureau of Meteorology website.
rule_detail: Check the name is accurate on the bureau’s website.

rule_summary: Apply the cyclone naming rule to hurricanes and typhoons.
rule_detail: Use the same rule for hurricanes and typhoons. These are different terms for the same natural phenomenon.

rule_summary: Write Cyclone as part of the name unless the context makes the cyclone clear.
rule_detail: Always write ‘Cyclone’ as part of the name unless it is clear from the surrounding text that you are referring to a cyclone.

rule_summary: Capitalize drought names when the name is a formal period.
rule_detail: If the time is a formal period, the name has an initial capital.

rule_summary: Capitalise bushfire names for the adjectival part and any proper noun.
rule_detail: Bushfires take initial capitals for the adjectival part of their name as well as any proper noun. Fires leading to substantial loss of life and property are usually named after the worst day or where they started.

rule_summary: Name major fires after the worst day or place of origin.
rule_detail: Fires leading to substantial loss of life and property are usually named after the worst day or where they started.

rule_summary: Use the year-location-event format for floods, earthquakes and tsunamis.
rule_detail: Use ‘year Location event’ as the naming convention for floods, earthquakes and tsunamis. Only the location (the proper noun) has an initial capital.

rule_summary: Spell and punctuate organisation names correctly.
rule_detail: Spell and punctuate organisation names correctly. This helps people to understand your content.

rule_summary: Write organisation names the way the organisation writes them.
rule_detail: Write the name of the organisation the same way the organisation writes it. This rule applies except in rare cases when the organisation name is in all lower case. Use an initial capital for these names in body text. This helps people identify the name as a proper noun.

rule_summary: Preserve lower-case initial letters and medial capitals in organisation names.
rule_detail: Some names start with a lower case letter but have a medial capital (for example, ‘eBay’). Write the name the same way, including to begin a sentence. A medial capital is enough to identify the name as a proper noun.

rule_summary: Include all punctuation and logograms in organisation names and do not add extra words.
rule_detail: Pay attention to the use of capital letters, punctuation (such as apostrophes) and logograms (such as ‘&’). Make sure to include all words in the name. Don’t add additional words.

rule_summary: Check reliable sources to confirm an organisation's correct name.
rule_detail: The names of organisations can change. The most efficient way to confirm an organisation’s name is to check its website, annual report or letterhead. If this is unsuccessful, there are other reliable services.

rule_summary: Use the government online directory for Australian Government entities.
rule_detail: For Australian Government entities, use the government online directory. Directory entries contain links to departmental pages listing annual reports. Annual reports are a good way to find the former names of departments.

rule_summary: Use specified registers and directories for non-government entities.
rule_detail: For non-government entities, use: the Australian Securities Exchange's listed companies; the Australian Securities and Investments Commission registers.

rule_summary: Use the Australian Business Register ABN lookup and other publications for all entities.
rule_detail: For all entities, use: the Australian Business Register's ABN lookup; a publication that lists organisations such as the Directory of Australian associations or Margaret Gee’s media guide, if your organisation has access.

rule_summary: Use the published name from the source when citing an organisation that has changed its name.
rule_detail: If you cite a source written by an organisation that has since changed its name, use the name that was published in the source. This may be the organisation’s or government department's past name.

rule_summary: Write registered business names in the capitalisation the organisation uses.
rule_detail: Some organisation names appearing on the Australian Business Register have all capitals. Our first rule applies: write the name as the organisation does.

rule_summary: Follow the organisation's preferred capitalisation style.
rule_detail: Check the organisation's website and publications to find how it capitalises its name and follow the organisation's preferred style.

rule_summary: Use an organisation's shortened form only if it regularly uses it.
rule_detail: Use the organisation’s shortened form only if the organisation regularly uses it in its own content.

rule_summary: Spell out a shortened form on first mention unless the organisation is known only by that form.
rule_detail: Spell out the shortened form the first time, unless the organisation’s name is known only by the shortened form.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms such as Ltd, Pty Ltd, Co and Inc as part of a legal name when that is the organisation's name.
rule_detail: Some organisations use shortened forms such as ‘Ltd’, ‘Pty Ltd’, ‘Co’ and ‘Inc’ as part of their legal name. Others use the spelt-out forms.

rule_summary: Do not add a full stop after Co or Inc unless they end a sentence.
rule_detail: Don't add a full stop at the end of ‘Co’ and ‘Inc’ unless they finish a sentence. No full stop is the correct Australian Government style for abbreviations.

rule_summary: Use the full title on first mention and omit optional legal words on later mentions in print documents.
rule_detail: Use the organisation’s full title on first mention in a publication. On subsequent mentions in print documents, you can omit words like ‘proprietary’ and ‘limited’ and the corresponding shortened forms.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for official organisation names and first mentions.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for: all words capitalised in the full, official names of organisations; the first mention of an organisation.

rule_summary: Use lower case for generic terms and for multiple organisations with the same generic name.
rule_detail: Don’t use an initial capital for: generic terms – such as ‘the department’ or ‘the agency’ – even if the organisation being referenced capitalises the generic term in its content - mentions of several organisations with the same generic name.

rule_summary: Use the definite article 'The' in organisation names in emails and letters when it is part of the official name.
rule_detail: Some organisations use the definite article ‘The’ in their name with an initial capital. Use the full name, including ‘The’, in 2 situations: in emails and letters - if the name appears in an alphabetical list (arrange by ‘The’ as the first word in the name).

rule_summary: Use lower case 'the' in body text for organisation names that include the definite article.
rule_detail: Always use lower case ‘the’ in body text. This follows the practice of most organisations.

rule_summary: Omit 'The' from organisation names when the organisation does not use it.
rule_detail: If organisations omit the definite article from their name, don’t use it in emails and letters. In body text, ‘the’ appears before the correct name or isn’t needed at all.

rule_summary: Use a possessive apostrophe in an organisation name only if the official name includes one.
rule_detail: Put a possessive apostrophe in a name if the organisation does

rule_summary: Do not use possessive apostrophes in organisation names unless they are part of the official name.
rule_detail: Use an apostrophe only when it forms part of the official name of an organisation. In all other cases for organisation names, don’t use possessive apostrophes. The apostrophe is disappearing from many organisational names, particularly from those that contain plural nouns ending in ‘s’. In these cases, the plural noun is descriptive rather than possessive.

rule_summary: Treat plural nouns ending in s as descriptive rather than possessive when an organisation drops the apostrophe.
rule_detail: The apostrophe is disappearing from many organisational names, particularly from those that contain plural nouns ending in ‘s’. In these cases, the plural noun is descriptive rather than possessive.

rule_summary: Use a singular verb with organisation names, even when the name looks plural.
rule_detail: Always use a singular verb. This applies even if organisation names end in an ‘s’ and look plural.

rule_summary: Use the form of a personal name that the person uses.
rule_detail: When you write to or about people, always use the form of personal name that the person uses.

rule_summary: Ask the person which name they prefer if possible.
rule_detail: If you can, ask the person which name they prefer.

rule_summary: Use reputable sources to confirm personal names when you cannot ask the person.
rule_detail: Otherwise, consult reputable sources for: Names of people who work within government or in roles related to government, including state and territory governments: Directory.gov.au. Records of names of people closely associated with Australia: The National Archives of Australia. Historical and biographical information: The Australian dictionary of biography and Trove. Information on prominent Australians, search ‘eResources’ such as Who’s who in Australia or Encyclopedia Britannica: National Library of Australia. The accepted form of authors’ names and the names of people being written about: library catalogues.

rule_summary: Use ‘given name’, ‘family name’ and ‘previous names’ instead of culturally or gender-biased terms.
rule_detail: To avoid cultural or gender bias when referring to parts of names, use: ‘given name’ instead of ‘Christian name’; ‘family name’ instead of ‘surname’; ‘previous names’ instead of ‘maiden name’.

rule_summary: Capitalize personal names, initials and nicknames with initial capitals.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for personal names, initials and nicknames.

rule_summary: Capitalize the names of real and fictitious people.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for the names of real and fictitious people.

rule_summary: Write people’s initials unspaced and without full stops.
rule_detail: Capitalise the initials of people’s given names. Write them unspaced and without full stops. Use non-breaking spaces to ensure that initials are not separated from family names.

rule_summary: Use non-breaking spaces so initials stay attached to family names.
rule_detail: Use non-breaking spaces to ensure that initials are not separated from family names.

rule_summary: Put nicknames in quotation marks the first time they appear.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals for nicknames. The first time they appear in your text, place nicknames in quotation marks.

rule_summary: Preserve a person’s chosen lowercase styling for their name.
rule_detail: Be aware that a few people don’t use capitals for their names. This is a deliberate style decision that is part of their personal identity. Examples include bell hooks and kd lang. Use the form the person uses.

rule_summary: Form plural personal names by adding s or es according to spelling.
rule_detail: The plural of any personal name is formed by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’. It depends on the spelling of the personal name.

rule_summary: Add es to names ending in s, x or z to make the plural.
rule_detail: Names ending in ‘s’, ‘x’ and ‘z’ — Add ‘es’.

rule_summary: Keep y and add s for plural names ending in y.
rule_detail: ‘y’ — Keep the ‘y’ and add ‘s’.

rule_summary: Keep i and add s for plural names ending in i.
rule_detail: ‘i’ — Keep the ‘i’ and add ‘s’.

rule_summary: Add s to plural names ending in o.
rule_detail: ‘o’ — Add an ‘s’.

rule_summary: Add s to plural names ending in any other letter.
rule_detail: All other letters — Add an ‘s’.

rule_summary: Use an apostrophe and s for possessive personal names, even when they end in s.
rule_detail: Use an apostrophe and an ‘s’ with personal names, even when they already end in ‘s’.

rule_summary: Use only an apostrophe to make plural personal names possessive.
rule_detail: Plural personal names take just an apostrophe. Simply add an apostrophe to the end of the plural form.

rule_summary: Add apostrophe s to singular names ending in s to show possession.
rule_detail: Singular (one person) | ‘s’ | Add apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) | Jas’s report

rule_summary: Add apostrophe s to singular names ending in any other letter to show possession.
rule_detail: Singular (one person) | Any letter other than ‘s’ | Add apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) | Tui’s signature

rule_summary: Add only an apostrophe to plural names ending in s or es to show possession.
rule_detail: Plural (2 or more people of the same name) | The plural ‘s’ or ‘es’ | Add only an apostrophe (’) without an extra ‘s’ | The Joneses’ responses or the Nasrins’ name tags

rule_summary: Add apostrophe s to the last name of plural people with different names to show possession.
rule_detail: Plural (2 or more people of a different name) | Any letter other than ‘s’ | Add only an apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) on the last name | Aiko and Tashi’s team

rule_summary: Add apostrophe s to the noun for plural personal references using singular pronouns.
rule_detail: Plural (2 or more people using singular pronoun and possessive pronoun with a noun) | Any letter other than ‘s’ | Add only an apostrophe ‘s’ (’s) on the noun | You and your partner’s luggage

rule_summary: Retain hyphens in hyphenated given and family names.
rule_detail: Always retain hyphens when you write given and family names that are hyphenated.

rule_summary: Write all parts of compound family names.
rule_detail: Write all parts of compound family names. Keep the compound when writing a person’s family name.

rule_summary: Write every family name the first time when someone has more than one family name.
rule_detail: Sometimes someone has more than one family name but is only known by one. Write all the names the first time and use the well-known family name after.

rule_summary: Use the same form and spelling that the person uses for non-English names wherever possible.
rule_detail: As far as possible, if you need to write a non-English name, use the same form and spelling as the person uses.

rule_summary: Check personal correspondence or authored works to confirm a non-English name.
rule_detail: Check their personal correspondence or works they have written.

rule_summary: Ask the person how you should address them if possible.
rule_detail: If you can, ask them how you should address them.

rule_summary: Use the most commonly used written form of a non-English name as a last resort.
rule_detail: As a last resort, use the name that is most commonly used in writing about the person.

rule_summary: Italicise genus and species names.
rule_detail: Italicise genus and species names

rule_summary: Set the genus in italics with an initial capital.
rule_detail: - the genus is in italics and takes an initial capital

rule_summary: Set the species in italics and lower case.
rule_detail: - the species is in italics and is lower case.

rule_summary: Italicise subspecies names and varietal names.
rule_detail: Subspecies and the names of varieties are also italicised.

rule_summary: Use a full stop in abbreviations for subspecies and variety.
rule_detail: In these names, abbreviations for the words ‘subspecies’ and ‘variety’ take a full stop. This is an exception to the general rule for abbreviations.

rule_summary: Use the semantic tag em for italicised names in HTML.
rule_detail: Screen readers don’t pronounce italics. Use the semantic tag <em> to provide emphasis for italicised names in HTML.

rule_summary: Write common names in lower case.
rule_detail: Use lower case unless they are also a proper noun, a registered trade mark or in some specialised content such as genetics.

rule_summary: Do not italicise common names.
rule_detail: Do not use italics.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals in common names when they include a proper noun.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals when the name includes a proper noun.

rule_summary: Write plant and animal names that are everyday words in roman type without capitals.
rule_detail: Names that have become everyday words are shown in roman type and don’t need a capital letter.

rule_summary: Write English derivatives of scientific names in roman type without capitals.
rule_detail: This includes English derivatives. These are plant and animal names that came from the scientific classification system and are now in everyday use.

rule_summary: Use lower case for most breed names.
rule_detail: You usually don’t need to use an initial capital for breeds, even if they are derived from a regional name.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for registered cultivars or breeds.
rule_detail: Use an initial capital for names of registered cultivars or breeds. In a sentence, the registered name is sometimes in quotation marks.

rule_summary: Check a dictionary or reputable source to confirm capitalisation for cultivar and breed names.
rule_detail: It’s best to check a dictionary or another reputable source to confirm whether the name has an initial capital. Refer to related guidance on commercial terms.

rule_summary: Use lower case for bird names in generalist Australian Government content unless they contain a proper noun.
rule_detail: In generalist Australian Government content, use lower case for the names of birds unless the name contains a proper noun.

rule_summary: Adapt bird-name capitalisation to specialist content or international conventions when readers will understand it.
rule_detail: This style may vary in some specialist content and content following international conventions. If writing for these, check and use the style that readers will understand.

rule_summary: Use lower case for bird names in lists of common names.
rule_detail: In both generalist and specialist content, use lower case for bird names in a list of common names of plants and animals.

rule_summary: Use italics for gene names.
rule_detail: Use italics for the names of genes.

rule_summary: Use roman type for protein and enzyme names.
rule_detail: Use roman type for the names of proteins (enzymes).

rule_summary: Include the genus and species at first mention of a common name.
rule_detail: For this reason, include the species name in parentheses when you first mention the common name so it is clear which plant or animal you are writing about.

rule_summary: Write the scientific name in parentheses at first mention after the common name.
rule_detail: For this reason, include the species name in parentheses when you first mention the common name so it is clear which plant or animal you are writing about.

rule_summary: Treat common names as potentially ambiguous across regions and species.
rule_detail: The common name of a plant or animal can be a local name for more than one species in different places. Only the scientific name is the definitive name.

rule_summary: Use an abbreviated genus name after the full genus has already been written.
rule_detail: If you have already written the full name of the genus, use a shortened form for later mentions. This is often just the first letter of the genus name, followed by a full stop. This is an exception to the general rule for abbreviations.

rule_summary: Use a two-letter genus abbreviation when several genera share the same initial.
rule_detail: When there are several genera that start with the same letter, include the second letter in the abbreviation.

rule_summary: Use classification hierarchy to determine capitalisation and italics for plant and animal names.
rule_detail:
Plants and animals are classified in a hierarchy from general to specific. The style you use is set by where the name is in the hierarchy:

- Names down to genus level start with capital letters.
- Species names are in lower case.
- Genus and species names are in italics.

rule_summary: Use capital letters for names down to genus level.
rule_detail: - Names down to genus level start with capital letters.

rule_summary: Write species names in lower case.
rule_detail: - Species names are in lower case.

rule_summary: Set all classification names above genus level in roman type with initial capitals.
rule_detail: All classification names above genus level are in roman type and take initial capitals.

rule_summary: Check the spelling of scientific names when you use them.
rule_detail: The scientific names of plants and animals often derive from Latin. Check the spelling when you use them.

rule_summary: Use the standard spelling pattern -ceae for plant family names.
rule_detail: The family names of plants usually end in ‘ceae’.

rule_summary: Use the standard spelling pattern -idae for animal family names.
rule_detail: The family names of animals usually end in ‘idae’.

rule_summary: Italicise the names of individual ships, aircraft and other vehicles and use initial capitals.
rule_detail:
Write the names of individual ships, aircraft and other vehicles:

- in italics
- with initial capitals.

rule_summary: Do not use the definite article for navy ships.
rule_detail: Don't use the definite article for navy ships.

rule_summary: Use the semantic <em> tag to mark italicised vehicle names in HTML.
rule_detail: Screen readers don’t pronounce italics. Use the semantic tag <em> to provide emphasis for italicised names in HTML.

rule_summary: In citations, use roman type for vehicle names when the title is italicised.
rule_detail:
Separate the names of vehicles from titles in citations and reference lists. Separate them according to the type of publication:

- If the title is in italics (such as in book and website titles), use roman type for the name of the vehicle.
- If the title is in roman type (such as a journal article), use italics for the name of the vehicle.

rule_summary: In citations, use italics for vehicle names when the title is in roman type.
rule_detail:
Separate the names of vehicles from titles in citations and reference lists. Separate them according to the type of publication:

- If the title is in italics (such as in book and website titles), use roman type for the name of the vehicle.
- If the title is in roman type (such as a journal article), use italics for the name of the vehicle.

rule_summary: Do not italicise vehicle brands, models or classes.
rule_detail:
Don’t write brands or types of vehicles in italics

Begin the names of the brands, models and classes of vehicles with an initial capital letter but don’t use italics.

rule_summary: Begin vehicle brands, models and classes with an initial capital letter.
rule_detail: Begin the names of the brands, models and classes of vehicles with an initial capital letter but don’t use italics.

rule_summary: Do not italicise or capitalise vehicle types unless the type begins a sentence.
rule_detail: Don’t italicise or capitalise types of ships, aircraft or other vehicles. Use an initial capital for a generic name only if it starts a sentence.

rule_summary: Do not italicise the definite article before a vehicle name unless it is part of the name.
rule_detail: Don’t italicise the definite article (the word ‘the’) before the vehicle’s name unless it is part of the name.

rule_summary: Do not italicise abbreviated parts of a ship’s name.
rule_detail: Don’t put the abbreviated parts of a ship’s name in italics.

rule_summary: Do not italicise a ship’s class name.
rule_detail: Don’t use italics for the ship’s class name.

rule_summary: Refer to vehicles with the pronoun 'it'.
rule_detail: Use the pronoun ‘it’ for ships, aircraft and other vehicles. Do not write ‘she’ when referring to vehicles in government content. Use pronouns that reflect gender-neutral language.

rule_summary: Use capitals for official place names and check their spelling against an authoritative source.
rule_detail: Check official place names and style them correctly. You can check the spelling of an official name using the Australian Place Names dataset.

rule_summary: Capitalize the full names of mountains, rivers, valleys, bays, islands and other topographic features.
rule_detail: The full names of mountains, rivers, valleys, bays, islands and other features always take initial capitals.

rule_summary: Capitalize popular shortened forms or nicknames when they are established names.
rule_detail: Some shortened forms that are popular names or nicknames are also capitalised.

rule_summary: Use lower case for a topographic name when it is used as a generic term in most cases.
rule_detail: In most cases, don’t use initial capitals when you use the name as a generic term.

rule_summary: Use lower case for the generic term when it applies to two or more named places in the same sentence.
rule_detail: When using the same generic term for 2 or more names in the same sentence, use lower case for the generic term.

rule_summary: Keep the capital when a general term is a well-recognised abbreviation that functions as a proper name.
rule_detail: Keep the initial capital when the general term is a well-recognised abbreviation and works as a proper name.

rule_summary: Use lower case for a noun used in a generic sense rather than as part of a proper name.
rule_detail: Don’t use an initial capital if you’re using the noun in a generic sense.

rule_summary: Use the abbreviation Mt consistently and with an initial capital for mountains.
rule_detail: ‘Mt’ is a common and easily recognisable abbreviation for mountains. Use the abbreviation consistently in content and use initial capitals.

rule_summary: Spell out other topographic feature names unless space or repetition makes the abbreviation necessary.
rule_detail: Spell out the names of other topographic features if you can. Use the abbreviated form only where there’s limited space or a lot of repetition, such as in tables and maps.

rule_summary: Use Geoscience Australia's authorised abbreviations for topographic features.
rule_detail: Use Geoscience Australia’s authorised abbreviations.

rule_summary: Do not use apostrophes in possessive topographic names.
rule_detail: Don’t use an apostrophe for topographic terms involving possessives. Official place names are not possessive and do not usually include punctuation.

rule_summary: Form plural topographic names by adding s or es.
rule_detail: The plural of any topographic name is formed simply by adding ‘s’ or ‘es’.

rule_summary: Write compass points in lower case in text and hyphenate compound directions.
rule_detail: In text, write the points of a compass in lower case. Use hyphens for points such as ‘north-east’.

rule_summary: Use compass point initialisms only in tables, illustrations and some specialist works, and write them in capitals with no full stops or hyphens.
rule_detail: You can use initialisms in tables, illustrations and some specialist works. Always use capital letters with no full stops or hyphens.

rule_summary: Check official sources for correct names and terms.
rule_detail: Check official sources for correct names and terms.

rule_summary: Use consistent capitalisation and punctuation.
rule_detail: Use consistent capitalisation and punctuation.

rule_summary: Use numerals for 2 and above in text.
rule_detail:
Use numerals for ‘2’ and above.
- Write the numbers ‘zero’ and ‘one’ in words.

rule_summary: Write zero and one in words in text.
rule_detail: Write the numbers ‘zero’ and ‘one’ in words.

rule_summary: Follow the same numeral-or-word rule in headings and subheadings.
rule_detail: Follow the same rule for writing numbers in [headings and subheadings](/node/51). Apply exceptions to this general rule in specific situations, explained on this page.

rule_summary: Use words for numbers when starting a sentence.
rule_detail:
Use words for numbers when:

- starting a sentence

rule_summary: Use words for numbers when writing a fraction.
rule_detail:
Use words for numbers when:

- writing a fraction

rule_summary: Use words for numbers in proper nouns that include a number written as a word.
rule_detail:
Use words for numbers when:

- writing a proper noun that includes a number written as a word

rule_summary: Use words for numbers in publication titles that include a number written as a word.
rule_detail:
Use words for numbers when:

- writing a publication title that includes a number written as a word

rule_summary: Use words for numbers when quoting a figure of speech.
rule_detail:
Use words for numbers when:

- quoting a figure of speech.

rule_summary: Use words for numbers below 10 in government content that follows journalistic conventions.
rule_detail: In addition, use words for numbers below 10 for government content that follows journalistic conventions (for example, media releases).

rule_summary: Start a sentence with words rather than numerals.
rule_detail: Start sentences with words rather than numerals. If you must use a number at the start of a sentence, write it out in words.

rule_summary: Write numbers at the start of a sentence in words if unavoidable.
rule_detail: If you must use a number at the start of a sentence, write it out in words.

rule_summary: Use words for fractions in general text.
rule_detail: Write words in general text for [fractions](/node/146).

rule_summary: Use fractions when an exact number is not important.
rule_detail:
Use fractions when:

- an exact number is not important
- the user needs only a general idea of the values.

rule_summary: Use fractions when the user only needs a general idea of the values.
rule_detail:
Use fractions when:

- an exact number is not important
- the user needs only a general idea of the values.

rule_summary: Use decimals instead of fractions when the exact number and value is important.
rule_detail: If the exact number and value is important, use decimals instead.

rule_summary: Write numbers as words when they appear in a name or title.
rule_detail: Write numbers as words if this is how they appear in a name or title.

rule_summary: Use words for figures of speech.
rule_detail: Use words for figures of speech.

rule_summary: Use consistent number style throughout a content set or series.
rule_detail: Be consistent. Once your style for numerals or words is settled, use the same style throughout the content or series of publications.

rule_summary: Use numerals in units of measurement.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- in units of measurement

rule_summary: Use numerals for mathematical relationships, equations, ratios and decimals.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- to show mathematical relationships – such as equations and ratios – and for decimals

rule_summary: Use numerals when comparing numbers.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- when you are comparing numbers

rule_summary: Use numerals in tables and charts.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- in tables and charts

rule_summary: Use numerals for dates and times.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- for dates and times

rule_summary: Use numerals in a series of numbers.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- in a series of numbers

rule_summary: Use numerals in specific contexts such as steps, instructions, age and school years.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- in specific contexts – such as steps, instructions, age and school years

rule_summary: Use numerals in scientific content.
rule_detail:
Write all numbers as numerals:

- in scientific content.

rule_summary: Always use numerals to report a measurement.
rule_detail: Always use numerals to report a measurement (unless it is a large rounded number).

rule_summary: Use numerals for mathematical relationships, such as equations and ratios.
rule_detail:
Always use numerals:

- to show mathematical relationships (such as equations and ratios)
- in decimal numbers
- to compare numbers
- in tables, graphs and charts.

rule_summary: Use the correct numbers, words and symbols for currency so people are clear about the amount.
rule_detail: Use the correct numbers, words and symbols for currency so people are clear about the amount.

rule_summary: Write currency amounts with the relevant symbol followed by numerals.
rule_detail: Write amounts using the relevant currency symbol followed by numerals. Don’t put a space between the currency symbol and the numerals.

rule_summary: Write amounts under $1 as either cents or a decimal value.
rule_detail: For an amount less than $1, you can write it either as a whole number of cents or as a decimal value.

rule_summary: Use the letter c after numerals to show cents.
rule_detail: Use the letter ‘c’ for cents after the numerals.

rule_summary: Do not leave a space between numerals and the c for cents.
rule_detail: Don’t add a space between the numerals and the ‘c’

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop after c unless it ends a sentence.
rule_detail: Don’t use a full stop after the ‘c’ unless it’s at the end of a sentence.

rule_summary: Use two digits after the decimal point for decimal currency amounts.
rule_detail: If the amount is a decimal number, always use 2 digits after the decimal point.

rule_summary: Use a leading zero for amounts of less than 10 cents.
rule_detail: If the amount is less than 10 cents, use a zero before the number of cents.

rule_summary: Use $ for amounts clearly referring only to Australian dollars.
rule_detail: Where content is clearly only referencing Australian dollars, use ‘$’.

rule_summary: Use A$ when the currency could be confused with another dollar currency.
rule_detail: If users could be confused about the currency being referenced, place ‘A’ before the ‘$’. Don’t insert a space between them.

rule_summary: Avoid non-Australian currency symbols where possible for accessibility.
rule_detail: Non-Australian currency symbols may be inaccessible to people who access content using screen readers. Screen readers may be unable to interpret and describe the symbols. Avoid the use of non-Australian currency symbols where possible.

rule_summary: Use IBAN currency codes to reference currencies.
rule_detail: Use the 3-letter International Bank Account Number [(IBAN) currency codes](https://www.iban.com/currency-codes) – for example, THB, USD, VND. This is the preferred method because it doesn’t use symbols and makes content more accessible.

rule_summary: Use country prefixes with dollar currencies when referencing foreign currencies.
rule_detail: When referencing ‘dollar’ currencies, use a country prefix followed by the ‘$’ symbol – for example, A$, C$, NZ$, US$. If there is any chance of confusion, use the 3-letter IBAN codes.

rule_summary: Use the currency symbol only for non-dollar currencies if it best meets user needs.
rule_detail: Use the currency symbol only, for example ‘£’ for the British pound, if you have evidence that it is the best way to meet a user need.

rule_summary: Use IBAN codes for all currencies, including Australian dollars, when you choose that format.
rule_detail: Use them for all currencies referenced in the content (including Australian dollars).

rule_summary: Do not leave a space between an IBAN code and numerals.
rule_detail: Don’t place a space between the IBAN currency code and the numerals.

rule_summary: Use the same number of decimal places for all currencies mentioned together.
rule_detail: Use the same number of decimal places for all the currencies you refer to.

rule_summary: Explain foreign currency symbols on first use unless they are very widely known.
rule_detail: If using foreign currency symbols: Explain them on first use unless they are very widely known (for example, US$).

rule_summary: Place foreign currency symbols before numerals without a space.
rule_detail: Place them before the numerals and don’t insert a space.

rule_summary: Do not combine foreign currency symbols with IBAN codes.
rule_detail: Don’t also use the IBAN currency code.

rule_summary: Write former Australian currency units in words rather than symbols.
rule_detail: Use words rather than symbols for former Australian currency.

rule_summary: Write out former Australian currency units in full.
rule_detail: Before 14 February 1966, pounds (£), shillings (s) and pence (d) were Australia’s units of currency. Few people would recognise these symbols now, so write them out in full.

rule_summary: State former Australian pounds or use A£ when there is a risk of confusion with other pound currencies.
rule_detail: Some countries still use pounds as their currency. If there is any chance of confusion, state ‘former Australian pounds’ or use the symbol ‘A£’.

rule_summary: Use the level of precision needed for large money amounts.
rule_detail: Use the level of precision needed for the content.

rule_summary: Use words for inexact money amounts.
rule_detail: Use words for amounts of money that are an expression rather than an actual amount.

rule_summary: Write dates and times consistently so content is readable and clear.
rule_detail: Dates and expressions of time need to be readable and clear, particularly in content that contains detailed timelines. Write, abbreviate and punctuate dates and times consistently so people can understand your content.

rule_summary: Follow international and Australian standards for data systems and international communication.
rule_detail: Follow international and Australian standards to write dates and times for data systems and international communication.

rule_summary: Use numerals and words for dates in most content.
rule_detail: Use numerals and words for dates in most content. Use numeric dates when space is limited and in content types like tables.

rule_summary: Use numeric dates when space is limited or in tables.
rule_detail: Use numerals and words for dates in most content. Use numeric dates when space is limited and in content types like tables.

rule_summary: Use the Australian date sequence day month year.
rule_detail: In Australia, the conventional sequence for dates is ‘day month year’. Use this sequence when expressing dates in numerals and words.

rule_summary: Write body-text dates with numerals for day and year and the month spelled out.
rule_detail: For dates in body text, use numerals for the day and year and spell out the name of the month. Don’t include a comma or any other punctuation.

rule_summary: Spell out the day name in a date, but do not add a comma after it.
rule_detail: Spell out the name of the day if it is being used, but don’t include a comma after the day.

rule_summary: Capitalize month and day names as proper nouns.
rule_detail: The names of months and days start with an initial capital because they are proper nouns.

rule_summary: Use a non-breaking space between the day and month in written dates.
rule_detail: Insert a non-breaking space between the day and the month so they stay together on one line. A non-breaking space means that a line break will split the date before the year.

rule_summary: Do not use ordinal numbers when writing dates in body text.
rule_detail: Don’t use an ordinal number (12th, 21st etc.) when writing dates in body text.

rule_summary: Spell out the month when writing incomplete dates that omit the day or year.
rule_detail: Follow the general rules above when writing incomplete dates. Spell out the month in words if you need to leave out either the day or the year.

rule_summary: Use an ordinal number when the day is given but the month is omitted.
rule_detail: If you refer to the day but not the month, use an ordinal number.

rule_summary: Do not superscript ordinal suffixes in dates.
rule_detail: Don’t put the ordinal suffix (‘st’, ‘nd’, ‘rd’ or ‘th’) in superscript. Superscript can cause problems for people who use screen readers.

rule_summary: Write years in full when the year is shown on its own.
rule_detail: If you refer to the year only, use the full numerical year. Don’t abbreviate it.

rule_summary: Use abbreviations for dates only when space is limited.
rule_detail: Only use abbreviations if space is limited – for example, in tables, illustrations, charts and notes. Ensure that it is obvious to users which days of the week or months you are referring to.

rule_summary: Use standard abbreviations for days of the week.
rule_detail:
The standard abbreviations for the days of the week are:

- Monday – ‘Mon’ or ‘M’
- Tuesday – ‘Tues’ (‘Tue’) or ‘Tu’
- Wednesday – ‘Wed’ or ‘W’
- Thursday – 'Thurs’ (‘Thur’,‘Thu’) or ‘Th’
- Friday – ‘Fri’ or ‘F’
- Saturday – ‘Sat’ or ‘Sa’
- Sunday – ‘Sun’ or ‘Su’.

rule_summary: Use alternative weekday abbreviations only when the context makes their meaning clear.
rule_detail: The abbreviations in parentheses are alternatives for the standard abbreviation they follow. Only use the alternatives when the context ensures their meaning is clear.

rule_summary: Treat Monday as the first day of the week.
rule_detail: Style Manual lists Monday as the first day of the week. This is consistent with the order of calendar days in a calendar week as defined in the international standard adopted by Australia.

rule_summary: Use standard abbreviations for months.
rule_detail:
The standard abbreviations for the months are:

- January – ‘Jan’
- February – ‘Feb’
- March – ‘Mar’
- April – ‘Apr’
- May – retain as ‘May’
- June – retain as ‘June’ or shorten to ‘Jun’
- July – retain as ‘July’ or shorten to ‘Jul’
- August – ‘Aug’
- September – ‘Sept’ or shorten to ‘Sep’
- October – ‘Oct’
- November – ‘Nov’
- December – ‘Dec’.

rule_summary: Use the shortest forms of days and months only in limited applications.
rule_detail: Only use the shortest form of days and months – ‘F’, ‘M’, ‘N’ and so on – in limited applications. An example is a time-series chart where the context and order allow users to understand the difference between each capital letter.

rule_summary: Do not use full stops after shortened days and months.
rule_detail: Don’t use a full stop after shortened days and months. No full stop is the correct Australian Government style for all abbreviations, acronyms and initialisms and contractions.

rule_summary: Avoid abbreviating dates in body text.
rule_detail: Avoid abbreviated words when writing dates in body text. Words written in full are usually easier to read and understand.

rule_summary: Do not write general-content dates as numerals unless space is limited.
rule_detail: Avoid writing dates entirely in numerals for general content. Use numeric dates only when space is limited (such as in tables).

rule_summary: Use Australia’s conventional date order unless writing for a country with a different style.
rule_detail: Use Australia’s conventional order of ‘day month year’ unless you are writing for users in a country that uses a different style.

rule_summary: Separate numbers in numeric dates with unspaced forward slashes.
rule_detail: Separate the numbers in a numeric date with an unspaced forward slash, using the format ‘day/month/year’. This format uses single digits for single-digit days and months.

rule_summary: Use single digits for single-digit days and months in numeric dates.
rule_detail: Separate the numbers in a numeric date with an unspaced forward slash, using the format ‘day/month/year’. This format uses single digits for single-digit days and months.

rule_summary: Use two-digit elements in numeric dates only in the specified situations.
rule_detail:
You can also use 2 digits for each element. Only use this style for the year:

- in financial data
- if it is clear which century you are referring to
- if users understand the order of the elements (‘day month year’ for Australian users).

rule_summary: Use date formats consistently.
rule_detail: Whichever style you use for date formats, use it consistently.

rule_summary: Use decimal values in text as numerals.
rule_detail: In text, write decimal values as numerals. Write fractions as words.

rule_summary: Use fractions in text as words.
rule_detail: In text, write decimal values as numerals. Write fractions as words.

rule_summary: Use decimals when precision matters.
rule_detail: Use decimals when you need to be precise.

rule_summary: Use fractions when exactness is not important.
rule_detail: Use fractions when: an exact number is not important; the user needs only a general idea of the values.

rule_summary: Write a leading zero before decimal values less than one.
rule_detail: Decimal values less than one have a ‘0’ before the decimal point.

rule_summary: Use a full stop, not a comma, as the decimal point.
rule_detail: Always use a full stop, not a comma, for the decimal point. This is the style for Australian content.

rule_summary: Describe mathematical relationships in words in most general content.
rule_detail: In most content, the connection should be described in words. Only use symbols if there’s a user need.

rule_summary: Code mathematical symbols correctly to keep them accessible.
rule_detail: Code symbols correctly to ensure they are accessible.

rule_summary: Use words instead of symbols in most content to improve accessibility.
rule_detail: In most content, explain mathematical relationships using words instead of symbols.

rule_summary: Write numbers as numerals in all mathematical expressions.
rule_detail: In all mathematical expressions, write numbers as numerals. This applies even when you use words to explain a relationship between the numbers.

rule_summary: Use standard units of measurement to support readability and accuracy.
rule_detail: Standard units of measurement support readability and accuracy. Express precise values for users by combining numerals with the correct unit symbol.

rule_summary: Use the standard units of measurement.
rule_detail: Use the standard units of measurement

rule_summary: Use the metric system for most quantities in Australia.
rule_detail: Australia uses the metric system for most quantities:

rule_summary: Avoid using non-SI legal units in international content unless users will understand and accept them.
rule_detail: Don’t use the non-SI legal units of measurement for international content. The exception is when you have checked that users will understand and accept them.

rule_summary: Do not place a full stop after a unit of measurement.
rule_detail: Punctuation: don’t place a full stop after a unit of measurement.

rule_summary: Use capitals only when the unit represents a proper name.
rule_detail: Capitalisation: use capitals only if the unit represents a proper name.

rule_summary: Do not use plural or possessive forms for units.
rule_detail: Plural and possessive: units don’t have a plural or possessive form.

rule_summary: Write units in full at the start of a sentence.
rule_detail: Start of a sentence: write out the unit in full.

rule_summary: Use a non-breaking space between the number and the unit.
rule_detail: Spacing: use a non-breaking space between the number and the unit.

rule_summary: Use numerals, not words, when referring to a unit of measurement.
rule_detail: Use numerals, not words, for numbers when you are referring to a unit of measurement:

rule_summary: Always use numerals next to a unit of measurement.
rule_detail: Always use numerals next to a unit of measurement.

rule_summary: Include a non-breaking space between the number and the unit.
rule_detail: Include a non-breaking space between the number and the unit.

rule_summary: Use symbols for common units of measurement.
rule_detail: Use symbols for common units of measurement

rule_summary: Do not spell out common units if users will know what they mean.
rule_detail: You don’t need to spell out units of measurement, even for the first use, if they’re well known and users will know what they mean.

rule_summary: Spell out units the first time if users will not immediately understand them.
rule_detail: Spell out units of measurement the first time you use them if users won’t immediately understand them. After that, use the symbols.

rule_summary: Use only the symbol or the word for a unit, not both together.
rule_detail: Don’t combine symbols and words for units.

rule_summary: Use internationally accepted SI prefixes and their symbols in government content.
rule_detail: Internationally accepted prefixes and their symbols make it easier for users to read, understand and compare numbers. Use them in government content.

rule_summary: Use the internationally accepted spelling 'deca' unless using the Australian legal spelling 'deka'.
rule_detail: Note: the International Bureau of Weights and Measures uses ‘deca’ but this is spelled ‘deka’ in Schedule 3 of the National Measurement Regulations.

rule_summary: Do not use non-standard units.
rule_detail: Don’t use non-standard units.

rule_summary: Use storage and transfer prefixes according to the data-specific byte scale.
rule_detail: The prefixes for data storage and transfer work differently to those used for SI units. ‘Byte’ (B) is the unit of storage and data transfer speed. For this purpose, use:

rule_summary: Spell out days, years, hours and minutes unless they are in a table, list or chart and are easy to understand.
rule_detail: Days, years, hours and minutes measure time. These are not SI units. Spell them out in full – unless they’re in a table, list or chart and are easy to understand.

rule_summary: Use symbols for units derived from time measurements, such as speed.
rule_detail: Use symbols for units that are derived from time measurements, such as speed.

rule_summary: Put a non-breaking space between numbers and units.
rule_detail: Put a non-breaking space between numbers and units

rule_summary: Use a non-breaking space so the number and unit stay together.
rule_detail: People will read the number and its unit as a measurement only if the 2 components sit together. To do this, use a non-breaking space between numbers and their units of measurement.

rule_summary: Keep the number and unit together so line breaks do not separate them.
rule_detail: Without a non-breaking space, a unit could reflow to the next line. This would separate it from the quantity, making it difficult for users to understand the information being presented.

rule_summary: Use a non-breaking space because small screens make reflow more likely.
rule_detail: Although this is important for all content, it’s more likely to happen on smaller screens, such as those on mobile devices.

rule_summary: Do not add an 's' to symbols for plural units.
rule_detail: Symbols for units of measurement represent both the singular and the plural forms. Don’t use an ‘s’ to show plural with the symbols for units.

rule_summary: Use the same units, prefixes and decimal places when comparing measurements.
rule_detail:
Make it easy for users to compare quantities. Use the same:

- unit and prefix
- number of decimal places.

rule_summary: Use the same unit and prefix when comparing measurements.
rule_detail:
Use the same:

- unit and prefix
- number of decimal places.

rule_summary: Use the same number of decimal places when comparing measurements.
rule_detail:
Use the same:

- unit and prefix
- number of decimal places.

rule_summary: Use words for ordinals up to ninth and numerals for 10th and above.
rule_detail: Use words for ordinals up to ‘ninth’ and numerals for ‘10th’ and above

rule_summary: Spell out ordinal numbers from first to ninth and use numerals from 10th onwards.
rule_detail: Spell out ordinal numbers from ‘first’ to ‘ninth’. Use numerals for ordinals from ‘10th’ onwards.

rule_summary: Write ordinal numerals with an appropriate suffix.
rule_detail:
Ordinals written as numerals always have a suffix:

- ‘-st’ (‘first’, ‘21st’)
- ‘-nd’ (‘second’, ‘32nd’)
- ‘-rd’ (‘third’, ‘103rd’)
- ‘-th’ (‘fourth’, ‘15th’, ‘55th’ and so on).

rule_summary: Do not write ordinal suffixes in superscript.
rule_detail: Don’t write suffixes in superscript. Superscript may not be accessible to people who use screen readers.

rule_summary: Use numerals, not words, for ordinals with centuries.
rule_detail: Use numerals, not words, when writing ordinals with [centuries](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-conventions/numbers-and-measurements/dates-and-time#refer_to_specific_days_events_and_periods_with_capitals). This is an exception to the general rule to spell out ‘first’ to ‘ninth’ for ordinals.

rule_summary: Write century and centuries in lower case.
rule_detail: Write ‘century’ and ‘centuries’ in lower case.

rule_summary: Spell out very large ordinals as words and include the relevant suffix.
rule_detail: People find very large rounded numbers easier to read in [words rather than numerals](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/grammar-punctuation-and-measurements/choosing-numerals-or-words#combine_numerals_and_words_for_large_rounded_numbers). This also applies to ordinal numbers. Spell out the number and include the relevant suffix.

rule_summary: Use words for ordinal numbers in reference lists for publication editions.
rule_detail: In reference lists, use numerals with a suffix for editions of a publication. This is an exception to the rule to use words for ordinal numbers up to ninth.

rule_summary: Write organisation names as the organisation does when they include a numeral.
rule_detail: If an organisation’s name includes a numeral, write the name as the organisation does. This is an exception to the rule to use words for ordinal numbers up to ninth.

rule_summary: Use a numbered list rather than ordinals to order points in general content.
rule_detail: Don’t use ordinals to order points in general content. Reword the content so it doesn’t need ordinals or use a numbered list instead. A list can make it easier for people to follow the sequence.

rule_summary: Use numbered lists for series of items or steps in recommendations or instructions.
rule_detail: Always use numbered lists rather than ordinals when you’re expressing a series of items or steps – for example, in recommendations or instructions.

rule_summary: Mark up ordered lists with the ol tag for accessibility.
rule_detail: Code lists so they are understood correctly. Mark up ordered lists in HTML with the <ol> tag.

rule_summary: Use firstly and secondly as a pair in journal and report-style content.
rule_detail: ‘Firstly’ and ‘secondly’ work as a pair. Don’t use one without the other.

rule_summary: Do not use thirdly; write the points as a run-on list instead.
rule_detail: Don’t use ‘thirdly’. Instead, omit ordinals and write the points as a run-on list in a sentence.

rule_summary: Use numerals without suffixes in dates.
rule_detail: Use numerals without a suffix for dates.

rule_summary: Do not confuse ordinals with regnal numbers.
rule_detail:
Regnal numbers are upper case roman numerals that are used for the titles of monarchs and popes and in family names.

Even though you might pronounce regnals as ordinal numbers, don’t write them like that.

rule_summary: Use a non-breaking space between a name and a regnal number.
rule_detail:
Put a non-breaking space between the name and the regnal number. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t split up both elements of the name. The name and number will stay together on one line.

You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

In HTML, use the entity to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.

rule_summary: Use a narrow no-break space between a name and a regnal number in print.
rule_detail:
Use a narrow no-break space between the name and the regnal number.

The narrow no-break space ensures that the:

- name and number stay together on one line
- spacing between name and number doesn’t change when text is justified.

You can insert a narrow no-break space using the Unicode character U+202F.

rule_summary: Use chunks of digits to make telephone numbers easier to read.
rule_detail:
Use ‘chunks’ of digits to help people read telephone numbers

Break telephone numbers into shorter blocks of digits or ‘chunks’.

Telephone numbers are easier to read when their digits are chunked, rather than written in one large group.

rule_summary: Limit Australian telephone numbers in general use to no more than 10 digits.
rule_detail:
Australian telephone numbers in general use have no more than 10 digits:

- Landlines – 2 digits for the area code followed by 8 digits for the rest of the telephone number.
- Mobiles – 10 digits (there is no area code).

There are also categories of telephone numbers that don’t have 10 digits – for example, ‘13’ numbers have 6 digits.

rule_summary: Separate telephone number chunks with a non-breaking space.
rule_detail:
Put a non-breaking space between the chunks of digits

Use a non-breaking space between chunks of digits in a telephone number. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t split up the number. The telephone number will stay together on one line.

You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

In HTML, use the entity to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.

rule_summary: Use a narrow no-break space between telephone number chunks in print.
rule_detail:
### Print considerations

Use a narrow no-break space between chunks of digits in a telephone number.

The narrow no-break space ensures that the:

- telephone number stays together on one line
- spacing between digits doesn’t change when text is justified.

You can insert a narrow no-break space using the Unicode character U+202F.

rule_summary: Use the national format for Australian telephone numbers used within Australia.
rule_detail:
Write telephone numbers in the national or international format

Write telephone numbers in a format appropriate for the location of the users.

### National format for telephone numbers

Use Australia’s national format when writing Australian telephone numbers for content that will be used within Australia.

rule_summary: Write Australian landline numbers with the 2-digit area code followed by the rest in 2 chunks of 4 digits.
rule_detail: For landline telephone numbers, write the 2-digit area code followed by a non-breaking space. Then write the rest of the number in 2 chunks of 4 digits.

rule_summary: Write Australian mobile numbers in 1 chunk of 4 digits and 2 chunks of 3 digits.
rule_detail: Write mobile telephone numbers in 1 chunk of 4 digits and then 2 chunks of 3 digits.

rule_summary: Use the international format for content used outside Australia.
rule_detail:
### International format for telephone numbers

Use international format for content that will be used outside Australia.

rule_summary: Write international telephone numbers with a plus symbol and country code.
rule_detail:
The international format uses a plus symbol ’+’ to represent the international prefix, followed by a country code (‘61’ for Australia).

For landline numbers:

- start with a plus symbol ‘+’ and add the country code (‘61’ for Australia)
- add the area code without the ‘0’
- write the telephone number in 2 chunks of 4 digits.

For mobile numbers:

- start with a plus symbol ‘+’ and add the country code (‘61’ for Australia)
- omit the first ‘0’
- write the telephone number in 3 chunks of 3 digits.

rule_summary: Write foreign telephone numbers in international format.
rule_detail: Always write foreign telephone numbers in the international format.

rule_summary: Make telephone numbers clickable with tel: links and remove spaces from the URL.
rule_detail:
Make telephone numbers accessible through ‘click-to-call’ functionality

‘Click-to-call’ allows users to call a telephone number by selecting (clicking) the number shown in content. When the user selects the number, the user’s mobile phone, other mobile device or personal computer (if it has a supporting application) calls the number.

Click-to-call makes telephone numbers more accessible because users don’t need to copy the number manually. Click-to-call also works with screen readers.

Devices sometimes recognise when a number in content is a telephone number and automatically treat the number as a click-to-call link. This is not always the case, so use HTML code to support this functionality. Seek specialist advice if you’re unsure of how to do this.

### Using HTML for click-to-call

Use ‘tel:[telephone number]’ as the URL. Remove spaces between the numbers.

Remember that all webpages can be accessed internationally. Include the international dialling prefix if appropriate.

rule_summary: Do not use phone words; display telephone numbers only as digits.
rule_detail:
Don't use ‘phone words’

Always display the telephone number as digits. Don’t use ‘phone words’. Use the relevant 13 or 1300 number instead.

Some organisations use phone words to advertise their telephone number as a digit-word combination. Don’t do this, because some people find it hard to convert letters to numbers.

rule_summary: Use numerals when they are easier for people to scan.
rule_detail: Numbers as numerals are generally easier for people to scan.

rule_summary: Use words for numbers when that is the expected convention in a type of content.
rule_detail: Numbers as words remain a convention that people expect in some types of content.

rule_summary: Use the correct numbers, words and symbols for currency.
rule_detail: Use the correct numbers, words and symbols for currency so people are clear about the amount.

rule_summary: Write dates and times clearly and consistently.
rule_detail: Dates and expressions of time need to be readable and clear, particularly in content that contains detailed timelines.
