Write, abbreviate and punctuate dates and times consistently so people can understand your content. Follow international and Australian standards to write dates and times for data systems and international communication.

rule_summary: Use decimals for precise values.
rule_detail: Decimals are useful when people need a precise value.

rule_summary: Use fractions when an exact value is not important.
rule_detail: Fractions are useful when an exact value is not important.

rule_summary: Describe mathematical relationships in words in most content.
rule_detail: In most content, the connection should be described in words. Only use symbols if there’s a user need. Code symbols correctly to ensure they are accessible.

rule_summary: Use symbols for mathematical relationships only when there is a user need.
rule_detail: In most content, the connection should be described in words. Only use symbols if there’s a user need. Code symbols correctly to ensure they are accessible.

rule_summary: Code mathematical symbols correctly so they are accessible.
rule_detail: In most content, the connection should be described in words. Only use symbols if there’s a user need. Code symbols correctly to ensure they are accessible.

rule_summary: Use standard units of measurement to support readability and accuracy.
rule_detail: Standard units of measurement support readability and accuracy.

rule_summary: Express precise values by combining numerals with the correct unit symbol.
rule_detail: Express precise values for users by combining numerals with the correct unit symbol.

rule_summary: Use ordinal numbers to show order, position or importance in a list or sequence.
rule_detail: Ordinal numbers, such as ‘first’, ‘second’ and ‘third’, show the order, position or importance of things in a list or sequence.

rule_summary: Use numerals with the percentage sign.
rule_detail: Use numerals with the percentage sign.

rule_summary: Be concise when writing about percentages.
rule_detail: Be concise when you write about percentages.

rule_summary: Write telephone numbers so people can read and use them easily.
rule_detail: Write telephone numbers so people can read and use them easily. There are rules for grouping the numbers, using spacing and creating links.

rule_summary: Use at least one verb in a clause.
rule_detail: Clauses contain at least one verb

rule_summary: Define a clause as a group of words containing a subject and a verb.
rule_detail: A clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb.

rule_summary: Distinguish main clauses from subordinate clauses.
rule_detail:
A clause can be:

- a main clause
- a subordinate clause – noun, adjectival or adverbial.

rule_summary: Treat main clauses as capable of standing alone, unlike subordinate clauses.
rule_detail: A main clause can usually stand alone as a sentence, but a subordinate clause can’t.

rule_summary: Use a main clause as a sentence-capable clause.
rule_detail: A main clause can stand alone as a sentence

rule_summary: Recognise every sentence as containing at least one main clause.
rule_detail:
Every sentence has at least one main clause. The main clause is also known as:

- a principal clause
- an independent clause.

rule_summary: Identify a main clause as containing at least one complete finite verb and standing alone as a sentence.
rule_detail: The main clause has at least one complete (finite) verb and can stand alone as a sentence.

rule_summary: Join two or more main clauses with a coordinating conjunction to form a compound sentence.
rule_detail: A compound sentence contains 2 or more main clauses joined by a [coordinating conjunction](/node/129#coordinating_conjunctions_join_things_of_equal_importance). Each clause has a complete verb and could stand on its own.

rule_summary: Treat subordinate clauses as dependent on the main clause for meaning.
rule_detail: A subordinate clause can’t stand alone as a sentence. Subordinate clauses depend on the main clause to make sense. This is why they are also called ‘dependent clauses’.

rule_summary: Recognise noun clauses as functioning like nouns in a sentence.
rule_detail: Noun clauses act as [nouns](/node/122) in a sentence, even though they may consist of other types of words. You can replace a noun clause with ‘it’ and the sentence will still make sense.

rule_summary: Start noun clauses with a relative pronoun or subordinating conjunction when applicable.
rule_detail:
Noun clauses often start with a:

- relative pronoun – such as ‘that’ or ‘who’
- subordinating conjunction – such as ‘although’ or ‘because’.

rule_summary: Allow noun clauses to begin with a verb in its basic form using to.
rule_detail: They can also start with a verb in its basic form, which means it has the word ‘to’ (such as ‘to sleep’, ‘to sit’).

rule_summary: Use adjectival clauses to describe nouns.
rule_detail: An adjectival (or relative) clause acts as an [adjective](/node/126). It describes a noun.

rule_summary: Usually introduce adjectival clauses with a relative pronoun.
rule_detail: Adjectival clauses are usually, but not always, introduced by a relative pronoun (such as ‘that’, ‘which’, ‘who’, ‘whom’, ‘whose’).

rule_summary: Check that a sentence still makes sense after removing the adjectival clause.
rule_detail: The sentence should still make sense if you remove the adjectival clause.

rule_summary: Use adverbial clauses to stand in for adverbs and describe time, place, manner, reason, condition, purpose or concession.
rule_detail: Adverbial clauses stand in for [adverbs](/node/127). They describe time, place, manner, reason, condition, purpose or concession.

rule_summary: Check that a sentence still makes sense after removing the adverbial clause.
rule_detail: The sentence should still make sense if you remove the adverbial clause.

rule_summary: Usually introduce adverbial clauses with a relative pronoun or a preposition.
rule_detail:
Adverbial clauses are usually, but not always, introduced by:

- a relative pronoun – such as ‘that’, ‘which’, ‘who’, ‘whom’, ‘whose’
- a preposition.

rule_summary: Use a comma after an adverbial clause when it helps readers find the subject.
rule_detail: In the last example, the comma after the adverbial clause helps users find the subject in the sentence (‘she’).

rule_summary: Use a comma when a subject would be hard to find without it after an introductory adverbial clause.
rule_detail: In some sentences, the subject isn’t easy to find without the [comma](/node/109#mark_out_nonessential_information_within_a_sentence).

rule_summary: Use if for conditions that must exist for the main clause to be true.
rule_detail: ‘If’ is conditional. It defines a condition that needs to exist for the main clause to be true.

rule_summary: Use whether to show two possibilities.
rule_detail: ‘Whether’ shows 2 possibilities. Sometimes one of the possibilities can be understood rather than explicitly mentioned.

rule_summary: Choose the correct subordinating conjunction when writing, because if and whether are not always interchangeable.
rule_detail: ‘If’ and ‘whether’ are both subordinating conjunctions. They can often be interchangeable, particularly in spoken English. Yet they have different meanings. When you’re writing, choose the right one:

rule_summary: Use whether when there are two concrete possibilities to avoid ambiguity.
rule_detail: When there are 2 concrete possibilities, using ‘if’ instead of ‘whether’ can lead to ambiguous sentences.

rule_summary: Write and punctuate phrases correctly so they give people clear and useful information.
rule_detail: Phrases are groups of words that add meaning to a sentence. Write and punctuate them correctly to give people clear and useful information.

rule_summary: Use phrases only to add meaning to a sentence.
rule_detail: Phrases can only add meaning to a sentence. They can’t stand on their own.

rule_summary: Use noun phrases as nouns in a sentence.
rule_detail: A noun phrase is a group of words that works in a sentence as a noun. A noun phrase always includes a noun. It can also include determiners, adjectives, adverbs and other nouns.

rule_summary: Use possessive phrases to show that one noun belongs to another.
rule_detail: A possessive phrase is a particular type of noun phrase. It shows that one noun in the phrase belongs to another noun in the phrase. Possessive phrases usually have an apostrophe.

rule_summary: Use an apostrophe in possessive phrases, usually.
rule_detail: Possessive phrases usually have an apostrophe.

rule_summary: Do not use apostrophes in non-possessive and generic phrases.
rule_detail: Non-possessive and generic phrases use plural nouns as adjectives. No apostrophes are needed.

rule_summary: Use adverbial phrases to describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs.
rule_detail: An adverbial phrase is a group of words that describes a verb, adjective or other adverb.

rule_summary: Use adverbial phrases to describe the manner or reason for a verb’s action.
rule_detail: Adverbial phrases can describe the manner of or reason for a verb’s action.

rule_summary: Use adverbial phrases to describe time and place.
rule_detail:
Adverbial phrases can also describe time and place. These are known as ‘prepositional phrases’. Prepositional phrases consist of:

- the preposition
- any adjectives or determiners that accompany it.

rule_summary: Use adjectival phrases as adjectives to modify a pronoun, noun, or noun phrase.
rule_detail: An adjectival phrase is a group of words that works as an adjective. It modifies a pronoun, noun or noun phrase.

rule_summary: Place adjectival phrases after the verb ‘to be’ when they modify a pronoun, noun, or noun phrase.
rule_detail: Adjectival phrases that modify a pronoun, noun or noun phrase can also appear after the verb ‘to be’.

rule_summary: Use prepositional phrases to start adjectival phrases.
rule_detail: Adjectival phrases can start with a preposition. They are also known as prepositional phrases.

rule_summary: Structure the parts of a sentence so meaning is easy to understand.
rule_detail: Structure the parts of a sentence so meaning is easy to understand.

rule_summary: Use a full sentence that is grammatically complete and expresses a complete idea.
rule_detail:
A full sentence is grammatically complete

Sentences can be statements, questions, exclamations or commands. A full sentence expresses a complete idea.

rule_summary: Include at least a subject and a verb in every sentence.
rule_detail: Sentences contain at least a subject and a verb.

rule_summary: Treat the verb plus the object or complement as the predicate when a sentence has one.
rule_detail: The verb plus the object or complement form the ‘predicate’. Not all sentences contain an object or complement as part of the predicate.

rule_summary: Use a subject and verb alone when they complete the subject–predicate structure of a sentence.
rule_detail: A subject and verb can be enough to complete the subject–predicate structure of a sentence.

rule_summary: Recognise the subject as the person or thing doing the action in the sentence.
rule_detail: The subject is the person or thing that is doing the action in the sentence. The subject can be a pronoun, noun, noun phrase or noun clause.

rule_summary: Use the verb to carry information about the subject and its effect on any object or complement.
rule_detail: The verb carries information about the subject. It affects the object or complement (if there is one). It can convey an action, an event, a change or a state.

rule_summary: Identify an object as the thing, person or concept that complements the verb.
rule_detail: An object is the thing, person or concept that complements the verb. Objects can be direct or indirect.

rule_summary: Use complements to describe a quality or characteristic of the subject when a verb has no action.
rule_detail: Some verbs have no action. They have complements that describe a quality or characteristic of the subject.

rule_summary: Make a simple sentence contain only one main clause and one complete verb.
rule_detail: A simple sentence contains only one [main (or principal) clause](/node/143). This means it has only one complete verb in it.

rule_summary: Use the imperative mood to imply the subject in a simple sentence.
rule_detail: The subject can be implied by using a verb in the imperative mood.

rule_summary: Make a compound sentence contain two or more main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.
rule_detail: A compound sentence contains 2 or more main clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’). Each clause has a complete verb and could stand on its own.

rule_summary: Use a comma before the coordinating conjunction when compound clauses have different subjects.
rule_detail: If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.

rule_summary: Do not repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction when the two compound clauses share the same subject.
rule_detail: If the 2 clauses share the same subject, don’t repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.

rule_summary: Use a complex sentence with a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
rule_detail: A complex sentence contains a main clause and at least one [subordinate clause](/node/143#subordinate_clauses_depend_on_the_main_clause).

rule_summary: Start a complex sentence with either the main clause or the subordinate clause depending on the emphasis you want.
rule_detail:
You can start the sentence with the main clause.

You can also start the sentence with the subordinate clause to change the emphasis.

rule_summary: Build most sentences in standard subject–verb–object order using active voice with active verbs.
rule_detail:
Simple subject–verb–object sentences are standard in English. This order is clearer and more accessible for people.

Build most sentences in this order with active voice when using active verbs (doing or action verbs).

rule_summary: Use passive voice only when there is a good reason, such as when you cannot identify the actor or must conceal the information for ethical or legal reasons.
rule_detail: Use passive voice only if there is a good reason – for example, if you can’t say who did the action or because information has to be concealed for ethical or legal reasons.

rule_summary: Use apostrophes to show possession and contractions.
rule_detail: Apostrophes show possession and contractions.

rule_summary: Avoid apostrophes in descriptive phrases.
rule_detail: Don’t use them in descriptive phrases or to make nouns and shortened forms plural.

rule_summary: Use an apostrophe to mark possession when the first noun in a pair or noun phrase is related to the other words.
rule_detail: When the first of 2 consecutive nouns has an apostrophe, it means those nouns have a relationship. If the first noun in a noun phrase has an apostrophe, it means the noun is related to the other words in the phrase.

rule_summary: Treat apostrophe-marked noun relationships as possessives or genitives.
rule_detail: The type of relationship shown by the apostrophe differs, but all are known collectively as ‘possessives’ and sometimes as ‘genitives’.

rule_summary: Use possession to mean any apostrophe-marked relationship between nouns or noun-phrase words.
rule_detail: On this page, ‘possession’ or ‘possessive’ means any relationship between nouns – or between words in a noun phrase – that is shown by an apostrophe.

rule_summary: Add apostrophe-s after a singular noun to show possession.
rule_detail: Singular noun | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’

rule_summary: Add only an apostrophe after a singular noun phrase ending in a plural noun in s.
rule_detail: Singular noun of 2 or more words, the last word being a plural ending in ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe only

rule_summary: Add only an apostrophe after plural nouns ending in s to show possession.
rule_detail: Plural nouns that end in letter ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe only

rule_summary: Add apostrophe-s after plural nouns that do not end in s to show possession.
rule_detail: Plural nouns that don’t end in ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’

rule_summary: Add apostrophe-s to proper names ending in s, even if the final s is not pronounced.
rule_detail: Proper names ending in letter ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe and another ‘s’, even if you don’t pronounce that final ‘s’

rule_summary: Add apostrophe-s after each noun for individual possession by more than one noun.
rule_detail: More than one noun: individual possession | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ after each noun

rule_summary: Add apostrophe-s only after the last noun for joint possession by more than one noun.
rule_detail: More than one noun: joint possession | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ after the last noun only

rule_summary: Add apostrophe-s after a singular compound noun to show possession.
rule_detail: Singular compound noun | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ after the compound

rule_summary: Add only an apostrophe after plural compound nouns ending in s.
rule_detail: Plural compound nouns ending in ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe after the compound

rule_summary: Add apostrophe-s after plural compound nouns that do not end in s.
rule_detail: Plural compound nouns that don’t end in ‘s’ | Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ after the compound

rule_summary: Do not use apostrophes in descriptive noun phrases.
rule_detail: A descriptive phrase doesn’t need an apostrophe

rule_summary: Do not separate the nouns in a descriptive phrase.
rule_detail: For this reason, never separate the nouns in a descriptive phrase.

rule_summary: Add apostrophes only when showing possession in contrasted examples.
rule_detail: Only add an apostrophe when showing possession.

rule_summary: Use apostrophe-s to form possessive shortened forms.
rule_detail: Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ to form a possessive shortened form

rule_summary: Use shortened forms only if users will understand them in context.
rule_detail: Only use shortened forms if users will understand them.

rule_summary: Make shortened forms appropriate for the content's context, purpose and tone.
rule_detail: Make sure they are appropriate for your content’s context, purpose and tone.

rule_summary: Use apostrophe-s to show possession for shortened forms.
rule_detail: Add an apostrophe and ‘s’ to show possession for shortened forms.

rule_summary: Consider using a descriptive phrase instead of a possessive shortened form.
rule_detail: Consider whether the possessive form is necessary or can be replaced by a descriptive phrase.

rule_summary: Do not use apostrophes to make the plural of shortened forms such as acronyms and initialisms.
rule_detail: Add an ‘s’ to form the plural of shortened forms such as acronyms and initialisms. Don’t write an apostrophe before the ‘s’.

rule_summary: Add only s to form the plural of nouns.
rule_detail: The same rule applies when making nouns plural.

rule_summary: Use apostrophe-s to show possession for plural shortened forms.
rule_detail: Add an apostrophe to plural shortened forms to show possession.

rule_summary: Do not use a possessive apostrophe when defining a shortened form.
rule_detail: Don’t use a possessive apostrophe when you do this.

rule_summary: Define a shortened form on first use unless users will already understand it.
rule_detail: Define a shortened form the first time you use it (unless you’re certain users will understand it without a definition).

rule_summary: Follow a defined shortened form with the shortened form in parentheses.
rule_detail: Follow the spelt-out term with its shortened form in parentheses.

rule_summary: Use the shortened form rather than the full term on subsequent mentions.
rule_detail: Use the shortened form rather than the full term if you mention the term again.

rule_summary: Use brackets only when the enclosed text can be removed without changing the meaning.
rule_detail: Only use brackets if you can remove the enclosed text and the meaning does not change.

rule_summary: Use brackets for text users can skip over.
rule_detail: Use brackets for text users can skip over

rule_summary: Use brackets only for non-essential text that can be removed without breaking grammar.
rule_detail: Brackets can help you break up information. They enclose parts of the sentence that aren’t essential to the meaning. Sentences must be grammatically correct if you remove the text in brackets.

rule_summary: Use brackets sparingly for non-essential information, references and insertions.
rule_detail:
Use brackets sparingly for:

- non-essential information
[shortened forms](/node/92)- references
- insertions.

rule_summary: Use brackets only where they make content clearer to readers.
rule_detail: Use brackets only where they make content clearer to people. For example, always use brackets in [author–date citations](/node/165#examples_of_authordate_citations).

rule_summary: Avoid using too many or badly used brackets because they make writing harder to understand.
rule_detail: Too many brackets, or badly used brackets, can make a sentence more complex and difficult to understand. You can usually rewrite a sentence so the content in brackets can be its own sentence or can even be removed.

rule_summary: Avoid using curly brackets and slant brackets in most content.
rule_detail: Other types of brackets, such as curly brackets and slant brackets, are used in fields such as mathematics and linguistics. These are specialist uses, so don’t use them in most content.

rule_summary: Use parentheses for less important information.
rule_detail: Information in parentheses is less important than information that is between [spaced en dashes](/node/199) or pairs of [commas](/node/109).

rule_summary: Use parentheses to enclose definitions.
rule_detail: Parentheses enclose definitions.

rule_summary: Use parentheses to introduce a shortened form after the full term.
rule_detail: Parentheses introduce a shortened form after it has been spelt out in full. You can then use the shortened form through the rest of the page or publication.

rule_summary: Use parentheses to enclose cross-references to other parts of the content.
rule_detail: Parentheses enclose cross-references to other parts of the content.

rule_summary: Use parentheses to enclose citations in the author–date system.
rule_detail: Parentheses enclose citations in the author–date system of referencing.

rule_summary: Use parentheses to enclose extra detail.
rule_detail: Parentheses enclose extra detail.

rule_summary: Use parentheses to enclose clarification, extra information and asides.
rule_detail: Parentheses enclose text that doesn’t have a grammatical relationship to the rest of the sentence. This type of text includes extra information, clarifications and asides.

rule_summary: Avoid square brackets inside parentheses where possible.
rule_detail: Reword the text to avoid square brackets inside of parentheses wherever possible.

rule_summary: Avoid nested parentheses and use square brackets if parenthetical information must appear inside parentheses.
rule_detail: Don’t use sets of parentheses inside each other. Instead, use square brackets if you must put parenthetical information within parentheses.

rule_summary: Use square brackets in quoted material to show insertions or paraphrases.
rule_detail:
Use square brackets in [quoted material](/node/114) to show that you have:

- paraphrased the original content
- inserted text that was not in the original content.

rule_summary: Use square brackets to clarify quoted material when needed.
rule_detail: You can also use square brackets to clarify quoted material.

rule_summary: Use square brackets with italicised sic to show an error from the original writer.
rule_detail: Square brackets with an italicised ‘*sic*’ show that the error in the text is from the original writer.

rule_summary: Follow normal punctuation rules for bracketed content.
rule_detail: Punctuation in brackets depends on what is inside the brackets. Punctuate content in brackets as you would if it were outside the brackets.

rule_summary: Use a comma after a closing bracket only when the sentence would take a comma without brackets.
rule_detail: A comma follows a closing bracket only if you would have used a comma if there were no brackets.

rule_summary: Place end punctuation inside brackets when the bracketed content is a full sentence.
rule_detail: If the content inside the brackets is a full sentence, include the end punctuation inside the brackets.

rule_summary: Do not use brackets to enclose a sentence within a sentence.
rule_detail: Don’t use brackets to enclose a sentence within a sentence. Rewrite the text instead.

rule_summary: Match bracket styling to the surrounding text formatting.
rule_detail: Brackets should be in the same type (roman, italics, bold) as the text around the brackets. This is regardless of the type of the text inside the brackets.

rule_summary: Use colons only when they are essential.
rule_detail: Only add colons that are essential. Use them to introduce examples, contrasts, lists and block quotations.

rule_summary: Use a colon to introduce a word, phrase or clause that adds detail.
rule_detail: Use a colon to: introduce a word, phrase or clause that provides more detail

rule_summary: Use a colon to introduce a question.
rule_detail: Use a colon to: introduce a question

rule_summary: Use a colon to give an example.
rule_detail: Use a colon to: give an example

rule_summary: Use a colon to summarise or contrast with what comes before it.
rule_detail: Use a colon to: summarise or contrast with what comes before it.

rule_summary: Use a colon only when you are sure it is needed.
rule_detail: Use a colon only if you are sure it is needed. Incorrect use creates confusion for users.

rule_summary: Do not use a colon when a list flows on as part of a full sentence.
rule_detail: Don’t include a colon when the list flows on as part of a full sentence. This is a common error.

rule_summary: Use a colon to introduce a list of words, phrases or clauses.
rule_detail: Use a colon to introduce a list of words, phrases or clauses.

rule_summary: Use a colon to restructure content into a bulleted list.
rule_detail: Include the colon to restructure content into [bulleted lists](/node/56).

rule_summary: Start the word after a colon with a lower case letter in most cases.
rule_detail: Start the word after the colon with a lower case letter unless: the word that follows the colon is a proper noun - the text after the colon is a question that is a complete sentence.

rule_summary: Capitalize the first word of a complete-sentence question after a colon.
rule_detail: After a colon, capitalise the first word of questions that are complete sentences. This makes it clear that the question mark applies only to the text after the colon.

rule_summary: Use a lead-in and a colon to introduce a series of sentences or questions in a list.
rule_detail: If the colon introduces a series of sentences or questions, use a lead-in and colon to introduce them in a [bulleted or numbered list](/node/56).

rule_summary: Use a colon before the subtitle of a book or article.
rule_detail: Use a colon before the subtitle of a book or article. Follow the colon with a lower case letter, unless it’s a proper noun.

rule_summary: Use a colon to introduce a block quotation.
rule_detail: Use a colon to introduce a block quotation. Block quotations should also be coded with the HTML <blockquote> element.

rule_summary: Write mathematical ratios with a colon and no space after it.
rule_detail: Use a colon to give a [mathematical ratio](/node/145). Don’t put a space after the colon.

rule_summary: Use commas to separate parts of a sentence when needed for clarity.
rule_detail: Commas separate parts of a sentence so the meaning is clear. Sentence structure determines their correct use.

rule_summary: Separate introductory words, phrases and clauses from the main clause with a comma.
rule_detail: A comma separates introductory words, phrases and clauses from the main clause of the sentence.

rule_summary: Omit the comma when an introductory phrase can move to the end of the sentence without changing the meaning.
rule_detail: Many introductory phrases can be moved to the end of sentences without changing the meaning. In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase. This simpler structure can be easier to read.

rule_summary: Place a comma after introductory words such as greetings, adverbs and forms of address.
rule_detail: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone. Using an introductory word gives it emphasis.

rule_summary: Omit the comma after an introductory word in a very short sentence.
rule_detail: You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short. This minimises punctuation in very short sentences.

rule_summary: Use a comma after introductory adverbial phrases and clauses that modify the whole sentence.
rule_detail: Use commas after [adverbial phrases](/node/127) and [adverbial clauses](/node/127). Adverbs – such as ‘first’ and ‘during’ – modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs.

rule_summary: Use a comma after a conditional adverbial clause when it begins the sentence.
rule_detail: Conditional clauses are adverbial clauses (for example, beginning with ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’). They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.

rule_summary: Avoid starting a sentence with a numeric phrase followed immediately by another numeral.
rule_detail:
Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral. It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.

Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

rule_summary: Set off non-essential information in a sentence with comma pairs.
rule_detail:
Commas isolate information in a sentence when it isn’t essential to:

- meaning
- grammatical structure.

Within a sentence, use a pair of commas to separate non-essential or supplementary information. Always check for the second comma where there should be a pair.

Generally, if you can take out part of the sentence and it is still grammatically correct, it should be between a pair of commas.

Check carefully. Using comma pairs can completely change the meaning of a sentence.

rule_summary: Use commas around non-essential clauses that add information without changing the sentence's meaning.
rule_detail:
Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.

Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.

If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

Non-essential clauses are also called ‘non-restrictive’ or ‘non-defining’ [clauses](/node/143).

rule_summary: Avoid commas around clauses that are essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rule_detail: Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.

rule_summary: Use a pair of commas when two adjacent noun phrases define the same thing.
rule_detail: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.

rule_summary: Ensure the noun phrase between comma pairs is removable without making the sentence ungrammatical.
rule_detail: You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

rule_summary: Set off question tags at the end of a sentence with a comma.
rule_detail: Questions can be tagged onto the end of sentences. Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.

rule_summary: Use commas around the phrase 'for example' when it appears mid-sentence or at the start of a sentence.
rule_detail:
Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.

If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an [introductory phrase](/node/144). Follow it with a comma.

rule_summary: Use a colon, not commas, when introducing a bullet list after 'for example'.
rule_detail: If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.

rule_summary: Do not follow Latin shortened forms such as 'e.g.' and 'i.e.' with a comma.
rule_detail: If you use [Latin shortened forms](/node/91), such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.

rule_summary: Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining principal clauses with different subjects.
rule_detail:
Use commas to connect 2 or more [principal clauses](/node/143#a_principal_clause_can_stand_alone_as_a_sentence) joined by a [coordinating conjunction](/node/129#coordinating_conjunctions_join_things_of_equal_importance) (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).

If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.

rule_summary: Do not use this comma rule to create sentences longer than 25 words.
rule_detail: Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words. Shorter sentences are easier to read.

rule_summary: Omit the comma before a coordinating conjunction when two clauses share the same subject.
rule_detail: If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.

rule_summary: Use a comma when more than two principal clauses share the same subject.
rule_detail: The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

rule_summary: Do not splice two stand-alone sentences with a comma unless you add a coordinating conjunction.
rule_detail: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction. This kind of error is called a ‘comma splice’.

rule_summary: Separate list items in sentence lists with commas and omit the comma before the final item.
rule_detail:
Use commas between items in a sentence list. Avoid using a comma before the last item in the list.

This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists. Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.

rule_summary: Use the Oxford comma only when the final list item contains 'and' or when it prevents ambiguity.
rule_detail:
If the last item combines 2 words or phrases with the word ‘and’, use a comma before that final item. This use of the comma is known as the ‘Oxford comma’ or ‘serial comma’.

The Oxford comma can prevent ambiguity in complex sentence lists. For example, use the Oxford comma before the last item if you’re using a defining phrase applicable only to that final item.

rule_summary: Use commas in a string of adjectives of the same type.
rule_detail: Use commas in strings of adjectives of the same type (for example, a string of descriptive adjectives).

rule_summary: Do not use commas in a string of adjectives of different types.
rule_detail: Don’t use commas in strings of adjectives of different types.

rule_summary: Use commas to separate numerals with four or more digits.
rule_detail:
Numbers with 4 or more digits (starting from 1,000) need a comma. Use commas for numerals in text and in tables.

Don’t use a space between the digits, because screen readers can read them as separate numbers.

rule_summary: Group numerals in threes using commas for numbers of 1,000 or more.
rule_detail: When you are using numbers of 1,000 or more, use commas to separate the numerals into groups of 3 (working right to left).

rule_summary: Do not use commas to the right of a decimal point.
rule_detail: Commas are not used to the right of a decimal point.

rule_summary: Use en dashes to show a relationship.
rule_detail: Dashes show a relationship.

rule_summary: Prefer a phrase over an en dash for spans in general content.
rule_detail: Generally, en dashes for spans are less accessible for users than a phrase.

rule_summary: Use spaced en dashes to set off non-essential information in sentences.
rule_detail: Use spaced en dashes to set off non-essential information in sentences.

rule_summary: Use the correct symbols for the en dash and minus symbol.
rule_detail: Use the correct symbols for en dash and minus symbol

rule_summary: Treat en dashes as punctuation marks.
rule_detail: En dashes are half the width of the font height. Use them as a type of punctuation.

rule_summary: Do not use an en dash instead of a minus symbol.
rule_detail: Don’t use an en dash instead of a minus symbol. Screen readers will read dashes as dashes, not as the minus symbol.

rule_summary: Use U+2013 for the en dash in Unicode and the HTML entity –.
rule_detail: In Unicode, the en dash is U+2013. Use the entity – in HTML.

rule_summary: Use the mathematical minus symbol for minus and the HTML entity −.
rule_detail: To make sure screen readers read the minus symbol, use the mathematical symbol for minus. In Unicode, this is U+2212. Use the entity − in HTML.

rule_summary: Do not confuse a dash or minus symbol with a hyphen.
rule_detail: Don’t confuse the dash or the minus symbol for a [hyphen](/node/105).

rule_summary: Use a phrase instead of an en dash for most spans of numbers.
rule_detail: Use a phrase instead of an en dash for most spans of numbers

rule_summary: Use en dashes for spans with numerals, such as financial years, ranges of values, or spans of time.
rule_detail: En dashes show a span when used with numerals, such as in a financial year, a range of values or span of time. En dashes sometimes appear in a span of words, such as in a span of days of the week.

rule_summary: Avoid using en dashes in most content.
rule_detail: Avoid using en dashes in most content.

rule_summary: Use phrases for spans in general content instead of en dashes.
rule_detail:
Avoid using en dashes for spans in body text and headings. Instead, use the phrases:

- ‘from’ paired with ‘to’ – for example, ‘from 57 to 65 years’
- ‘between’ paired with ‘and’ – for example, ‘between Monday and Friday’.

rule_summary: Do not mix ‘from’ or ‘between’ with an en dash.
rule_detail: Never mix ‘from’ or ‘between’ with an en dash.

rule_summary: Use en dashes only for the listed exceptions in general-content date spans.
rule_detail:
There are exceptions to the rule of using phrases for spans in general content. The exceptions are for particular date spans and time spans.

Use en dashes for date spans in:

- financial years
- calendar years
- the titles of publications and programs
- terms of office
- lifespans (birth and death)
- limited space.

rule_summary: Use the general rule for date spans in headings, except in the listed exceptions.
rule_detail:
Date spans in headings should follow the general rule, except when:

- the heading contains a title that has an en dash
- using words would push the character count over 70 characters (including spaces).

rule_summary: Use en dashes for time spans only when space is limited.
rule_detail: Only use en dashes for time spans when you have limited space.

rule_summary: Use an unspaced en dash for financial years.
rule_detail: For financial years, use 4 digits for the first number and only 2 digits for the second. Join them with an unspaced en dash.

rule_summary: Use the phrases ‘financial year’ and ‘financial years’ at first mention unless the meaning is clear.
rule_detail: Use the phrases ‘financial year’ and ‘financial years’ at first mention, unless the context makes the meaning clear.

rule_summary: Use 4 digits on both sides of an en dash for financial years that cross centuries.
rule_detail: For financial years that cross centuries, use 4 digits on either side of the en dash.

rule_summary: Use an unspaced en dash for calendar years.
rule_detail: For calendar years, use 4 digits for the first number and either 4 or 2 digits for the second number. Join them with an unspaced en dash.

rule_summary: Use the phrases ‘calendar year’ and ‘calendar years’ at first mention unless the meaning is clear.
rule_detail: Use the phrases ‘calendar year’ and ‘calendar years’ at first mention, unless the context makes the meaning clear.

rule_summary: Use en dashes in titles of publications and programs with the specified year-span style.
rule_detail:
When you create a title, use 4 digits for the first year and 2 digits for the second year. If you cross the century, always use 4 digits for both years.

Use 4 digits on both sides of the span for these titles if that is your organisation’s house style.

When you refer to a title published by another person or organisation, retain the style that was originally used for year spans.

rule_summary: Reproduce titles with en dashes when citing them as references.
rule_detail: Reproduce titles with en dashes when you cite them as a reference.

rule_summary: Use an unspaced en dash for a term of office and keep both dates in 4-digit form.
rule_detail: A person’s term of office usually appears in parentheses after the person’s name. Always use 4 digits for both dates, joined by an unspaced en dash.

rule_summary: Use an unspaced en dash for a person’s lifespan and keep both dates in 4-digit form.
rule_detail: Dates of birth and death usually appear in parentheses after the person’s name. Always use 4 digits for both dates, joined by an unspaced en dash.

rule_summary: Use en dashes for date spans when space is limited.
rule_detail: Using en dashes for date spans is allowed when you have limited space. This could be in display text, tables, lists or in social media posts.

rule_summary: Space en dashes in day-and-month spans when the date appears on both sides.
rule_detail:
Use the following style for en dashes in spans of days and months:

- The en dash is spaced when the day and month appear on both sides of the span.
- The en dash is unspaced when the month only appears at the end of the span.

rule_summary: Restrict en dashes in headings to the listed cases.
rule_detail:
Only use en dashes for date spans in headings when:

- your heading includes a title that contains en dashes
- using words pushes the character count above 70 characters (including spaces).

In all other cases, write date spans in headings with words. Use the phrases ‘from … to’ and ‘between … and’.

rule_summary: Use an en dash for a time span only when space is limited.
rule_detail: Use en dashes for time spans only when you have limited space. This could be in display text, tables, lists or in social media posts.

rule_summary: Use an unspaced en dash for time spans in 24-hour format or when only the end uses am or pm.
rule_detail:
The spacing of the en dash depends on the position of elements in the span.

Use an unspaced en dash when:

- the ‘am’ or ‘pm’ appears only at the end of the span
- the time is in 24-hour clock format.

rule_summary: Use ellipses to show that ideas or words are missing from a sentence or a quote.
rule_detail: Ellipses show users that ideas or words are missing from a sentence or a quote. Don’t use ellipses to change the intent of the original source.

rule_summary: Use a 3-dot ellipsis character.
rule_detail: The ellipsis (plural ‘ellipses’) is a character of exactly 3 dots.

rule_summary: Use an ellipsis to omit words in quoted text.
rule_detail: Use the ellipsis: - if you omit words in quoted text - to mark an unfinished [phrase, clause or sentence](/node/120).

rule_summary: Use an ellipsis to mark an unfinished phrase, clause or sentence.
rule_detail: Use the ellipsis: - if you omit words in quoted text - to mark an unfinished [phrase, clause or sentence](/node/120).

rule_summary: Add the phrase 'ellipsis in original' after a quotation when the original text already contains an ellipsis.
rule_detail: If there is an ellipsis in the original text you’re quoting, add the phrase ‘ellipsis in original’ in square brackets after the quote. Use the same font as the surrounding text.

rule_summary: Use the same font as the surrounding text for the phrase 'ellipsis in original'.
rule_detail: If there is an ellipsis in the original text you’re quoting, add the phrase ‘ellipsis in original’ in square brackets after the quote. Use the same font as the surrounding text.

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop, comma or semicolon after an ellipsis.
rule_detail: Don’t use a full stop, comma or semicolon after an ellipsis.

rule_summary: Allow a question mark or exclamation mark after an ellipsis when necessary.
rule_detail: You can use a question mark or exclamation mark after an ellipsis if necessary.

rule_summary: Place an ellipsis on its own line when you omit a paragraph or more from a block quotation.
rule_detail: If a paragraph or more is omitted from a [block quotation](/node/114), you can place the ellipsis on a line of its own.

rule_summary: Use the ellipsis symbol rather than a string of full stops.
rule_detail: Do not use a string of full stops. Use the symbol for the ellipsis. Don’t use a string of full stops. Insert it using: - the unicode character U+2026 - the HTML code <…> - in many software applications, Alt+Ctrl+. or Option;.

rule_summary: Insert an ellipsis with the Unicode character U+2026.
rule_detail: Use the symbol for the ellipsis. Don’t use a string of full stops. Insert it using: - the unicode character U+2026 - the HTML code <…> - in many software applications, Alt+Ctrl+. or Option;.

rule_summary: Insert an ellipsis with the HTML code <…>.
rule_detail: Use the symbol for the ellipsis. Don’t use a string of full stops. Insert it using: - the unicode character U+2026 - the HTML code <…> - in many software applications, Alt+Ctrl+. or Option;.

rule_summary: Insert an ellipsis with Alt+Ctrl+. or Option+.
rule_detail: Use the symbol for the ellipsis. Don’t use a string of full stops. Insert it using: - the unicode character U+2026 - the HTML code <…> - in many software applications, Alt+Ctrl+. or Option;.

rule_summary: Use a single space before and after each ellipsis.
rule_detail: Use a single space before and after each ellipsis.

rule_summary: Do not put a space between punctuation and an ellipsis when the quote ends with a question mark or exclamation mark.
rule_detail: The exception to this rule is if the quote ends in an exclamation mark or question mark. Include the final punctuation mark after the ellipsis. Don’t include a space between the punctuation and the ellipsis.

rule_summary: Include the final punctuation mark after an ellipsis when the quote ends with a question mark or exclamation mark.
rule_detail: The exception to this rule is if the quote ends in an exclamation mark or question mark. Include the final punctuation mark after the ellipsis. Don’t include a space between the punctuation and the ellipsis.

rule_summary: Use ellipses sparingly.
rule_detail: Use ellipses sparingly. Overusing ellipses can lead to a suspicion that you are misquoting. Don’t leave out important details or change the original intent of the quoted material.

rule_summary: Do not leave out important details or change the original intent of quoted material.
rule_detail: Use ellipses sparingly. Overusing ellipses can lead to a suspicion that you are misquoting. Don’t leave out important details or change the original intent of the quoted material.

rule_summary: Use exclamation marks only in informal content.
rule_detail: Exclamation marks show emphasis and convey emotion. Only use them in informal content.

rule_summary: Avoid exclamation marks in formal government content.
rule_detail: Exclamation marks aren’t part of [government voice](/node/40). Don’t use exclamation marks in formal content, such as government reports or briefings.

rule_summary: Use exclamation marks sparingly in less formal content.
rule_detail: Use them sparingly in less formal content such as promotional material and social media posts. Be aware that exclamation marks can create a sense of panic or stress.

rule_summary: Allow exclamation marks to appear as themselves in instructions to users of government services.
rule_detail: Exclamation marks often appear ‘as themselves’ in instructions to users of government services.

rule_summary: Use only one exclamation mark at the end of an emphasized sentence.
rule_detail: At the end of each sentence you want to emphasise, use only one exclamation mark.

rule_summary: Avoid using multiple exclamation marks.
rule_detail: Don’t use exclamation marks too often. Exclamation marks can lose their emphasis if you use too many.

rule_summary: Do not use several exclamation marks at the end of a sentence.
rule_detail: Some people use multiple exclamation marks in [social media](/node/43). This is not suitable for government content.

rule_summary: Limit forward slashes to specific uses.
rule_detail: Limit the forward slash to specific uses

rule_summary: Use forward slashes in some shortened forms.
rule_detail:
Use forward slashes:

- in some shortened forms

rule_summary: Use forward slashes in mathematical expressions.
rule_detail:
Use forward slashes:

- in mathematical expressions

rule_summary: Use forward slashes to present lines of poetry in body text.
rule_detail:
Use forward slashes:

- to present lines of poetry in body text

rule_summary: Use forward slashes instead of per, an or a when abbreviating units of measurement.
rule_detail:
Use forward slashes:

- instead of ‘per’, ‘an’ or ‘a’ when abbreviating units of measurement

rule_summary: Use forward slashes in web addresses.
rule_detail:
Use forward slashes:

- in web addresses

rule_summary: Use forward slashes in dates if you cannot write them out.
rule_detail:
Use forward slashes:

- in dates if you can’t write them out – for example, in tables

rule_summary: Use forward slashes in some place names.
rule_detail:
Use forward slashes:

- in some place names.

rule_summary: Do not add spaces around most forward slashes.
rule_detail: Don’t add spaces around most forward slashes

rule_summary: Omit spaces around forward slashes except for official dual place names and poetry lines in body text.
rule_detail:
There is no need to include a space on either side of a forward slash.

The exceptions are for:

[official dual place names](/node/134#check_official_dual_place_names_and_style_them_correctly)- lines of poetry in body text – use forward slashes with spaces around them to show the line breaks.

rule_summary: Avoid using forward slashes either side of a line break where possible.
rule_detail: As far as possible, avoid using forward slashes either side of a line break.

rule_summary: Place the slash before the line break if you must split it across lines.
rule_detail: If you must, include the slash before the line break so that the reader anticipates it as they read the next line.

rule_summary: Write shortened units of measurement with a forward slash.
rule_detail: Write shortened units of measurement with a forward slash

rule_summary: Do not use forward slashes when spelling out units of measurement.
rule_detail: Don’t use forward slashes when spelling out [units of measurement](/node/147).

rule_summary: Use an en dash, not a slash, for financial years.
rule_detail:
Use an en dash for financial years, not a slash

Don’t use a forward slash as a replacement for an en dash in financial years.

rule_summary: Use or instead of a slash for alternatives.
rule_detail:
Write ‘or’ instead of a slash for alternatives

When showing alternatives, use ‘or’ instead of a forward slash. This is easier for people to understand.

rule_summary: Do not use and/or in text.
rule_detail: Do not use ‘and/or’* *in text. It could mean either ‘and’ or ‘or’, which confuses many users. Rewrite the sentence to make the meaning clear.

rule_summary: Do not join words with a slash.
rule_detail:
Don’t join words with a slash

Don’t use a forward slash between words that retain their separate identities. Instead, either use an en dash or reword the sentence. Forward slashes can make it look like you mean to show an alternative.

rule_summary: Use a full stop to end a sentence that is not a question or exclamation.
rule_detail: Full stops mark the end of a sentence that is not a question or an exclamation.

rule_summary: Use a final full stop for the last item in a list made up of sentence fragments.
rule_detail: Following the same rule, use full stops at the end of the last item in a [list that’s made up of sentence fragments](/node/56#lists_can_be_fragments_whole_sentences_and_standalone_items).

rule_summary: Use a full stop as the decimal point in numbers and currency.
rule_detail: Also use full stops: - as the decimal point in numbers and currency – for example, ‘$3.55’

rule_summary: Use a full stop in numbering subsections and paragraphs in a document.
rule_detail: Also use full stops: - in numbering subsections and paragraphs in a document – for example, ‘Section 7.3’

rule_summary: Use full stops in some Latin shortened forms and shortened forms used in referencing.
rule_detail: Also use full stops: - in some [Latin shortened forms](/node/91)and[shortened forms used in referencing](/node/92).

rule_summary: Do not use full stops with contractions or most abbreviations.
rule_detail: Don’t use full stops with [contractions](/node/191) or most [abbreviations](/node/184).

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop after a web or email address when it is part of a sentence fragment or on a line by itself.
rule_detail: Do not use a full stop after a web or email address if it’s part of a sentence fragment or on a line by itself.

rule_summary: Write full stops in email and web addresses when you use the full form rather than link text.
rule_detail: Write full stops in email and web addresses when you use the full form rather than link text (for example, ‘dfat.gov.au’ instead of linking ‘the DFAT website’).

rule_summary: Do not include a full stop in link text.
rule_detail: Ensure link text doesn’t include a full stop

rule_summary: Put the full stop after the sentence, not inside the linked text.
rule_detail: Use full stops at the end of sentences with link text, but don’t include the full stop in the link itself.

rule_summary: Do not use full stops in headings, stand-alone lists, page headers or footers.
rule_detail: Don’t use full stops in: [headings](/node/51)[stand-alone lists](/node/56#lists_can_be_fragments_whole_sentences_and_standalone_items)(stand-alone lists have a heading without a colon)- page headers or footers.

rule_summary: Do not put full stops after symbols, units of measurement, captions or titles unless they end a sentence.
rule_detail: Full stops do not go after: - symbols or [units of measurement](/node/147)(unless the symbol or unit is also at the end of a sentence) [captions and titles](/node/49).

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop at the end of government social media posts that end with a URL, tag, hashtag, emoji or sentence fragment.
rule_detail: Use correct punctuation in government [social media](/node/43). You don’t need a full stop if your post ends in: - a web address (URL) - a tag or handle - a hashtag - an emoji - a sentence fragment.

rule_summary: Include a full stop at the end of a text message if it ends with a sentence.
rule_detail: Include a full stop at the end of a text message if it finishes with a sentence. Don’t include a full stop if the message ends with a fragment or sign off.

rule_summary: Do not include a full stop at the end of a text message if it ends with a fragment or sign-off.
rule_detail: Include a full stop at the end of a text message if it finishes with a sentence. Don’t include a full stop if the message ends with a fragment or sign off.

rule_summary: Use a dictionary and your organisation’s preferred hyphenation practices when you are unsure about hyphen spelling.
rule_detail:
Refer to your organisation’s preferred dictionary when you are not sure if you need to use a hyphen for spelling.

Follow hyphenation rules in the dictionary your organisation uses

rule_summary: Use hyphens to clarify meaning and avoid ambiguity.
rule_detail: Hyphens clarify meaning by connecting words and parts of words into a single unit of meaning. Use hyphens to avoid ambiguity.

rule_summary: Use the accepted naming conventions for compass points, names of people and names of places.
rule_detail: Follow the accepted naming conventions for [compass points](/node/135), [names of people](/node/90) and [names of places](/node/134).

rule_summary: Do not break short words over a line, especially words with fewer than 6 letters, one-syllable words and 2-syllable words.
rule_detail:
Don’t break short words over a line, especially:

- words of fewer than 6 letters
- one-syllable words
- 2-syllable words.

rule_summary: Break words between syllables so the hyphen falls between the components of a compound word, the base word and a suffix or prefix, or before a consonant unless that would mislead readers.
rule_detail:
Break words between syllables so that the hyphen:

- is between 2 components of a compound word (for example, ‘data-base’)
- is between the base word and the suffix or prefix (for example, ‘neat-ness’)
- comes before a consonant (for example, write ‘fic-tion’ not ‘fict-ion’) unless this is misleading (for example, write ‘draw-ings’ not ‘dra-wings’).

rule_summary: Do not add extra hyphens when breaking URLs or email addresses across lines.
rule_detail: Don’t include extra hyphens if you need to break up URLs or email addresses. People could read them as part of the address.

rule_summary: Use the part of the word before the hyphen and surrounding vowels and consonants to guide line breaks.
rule_detail: Use the part of the word before the hyphen to suggest the rest of the word. Consider the vowels and consonants when breaking words over a line.

rule_summary: Use hyphens with certain prefixes such as anti-, auto-, counter-, extra-, intra-, re- and sub-.
rule_detail:
Hyphens are useful in some sets of words formed with prefixes such as:

- ‘anti-’
- ‘auto-’
- ‘counter-’
- ‘extra-’
- ‘intra-’
- ‘re-’
- ‘sub-’.

rule_summary: Use hyphens in prefixes when they help avoid doubled-up vowels or clarify words that might be confused with existing words.
rule_detail:
They’re especially useful for:

- doubled-up vowels
- clarifying new words that could be confused with existing ones.

rule_summary: Use a hyphen in some prefixed words to distinguish them from other words that look the same.
rule_detail: A hyphen is used in some words with prefixes to distinguish them from words that would otherwise look the same.

rule_summary: Use a second hyphen when a hyphenated phrase takes a prefix such as non-, pre- or anti-.
rule_detail: Sometimes a prefix such as ‘non-’, ‘pre-’ or ‘anti-’ acts on more than one word. If the phrase is already hyphenated, use a second hyphen to link the prefix to all words in the phrase.

rule_summary: Use a hyphen when a single-syllable prefix ending in a vowel is followed by the same vowel.
rule_detail: Use a hyphen when the last letter of a single-syllable prefix is a vowel and the word that follows begins with the same vowel.

rule_summary: Treat some well-known doubled-vowel forms as dictionary exceptions.
rule_detail:
This practice is less important if a word is well known. Check a dictionary if you are unsure.

#### Write this

- coordinate
- cooperate

#### Not this

- co-ordinate
- co-operate

rule_summary: Use hyphens to avoid double letters or misunderstanding in prefixed or suffixed forms.
rule_detail: Hyphens link a prefix or suffix to a word to avoid a double letter or prevent a misunderstanding.

rule_summary: Use hyphens with prefixes before capital letters.
rule_detail: Hyphens link a prefix to a word that starts with a capital letter.

rule_summary: Do not hyphenate when two words end and start with different vowels.
rule_detail: Don’t use hyphens if the 2 words end and start with different vowels. The combined word doesn’t place the same vowel together.

rule_summary: Use a hyphen when a prefix attaches to a single-syllable word beginning with a vowel.
rule_detail: Use a hyphen, however, if the prefix is attached to a single-syllable word beginning with a vowel. This punctuation means the vowels aren’t read as one sound.

rule_summary: Usually hyphenate two-syllable prefixes ending in a vowel other than o when the base word begins with a vowel, but write them as one word if the base word begins with a consonant.
rule_detail: Two-syllable prefixes ending in a vowel other than ‘o’ and followed by another vowel are often hyphenated. If the base word begins with a consonant, the term is usually written as one word.

rule_summary: Usually write two-syllable prefixes ending in o without a hyphen.
rule_detail: Two-syllable prefixes ending in ‘o’ are often attached without a hyphen, regardless of what the base word starts with.

rule_summary: Rarely hyphenate two-syllable prefixes ending in a consonant.
rule_detail: Two-syllable prefixes ending in a consonant are rarely followed by a hyphen.

rule_summary: Use hyphens with many co- words meaning joint and with all ex- words meaning former.
rule_detail:
Regardless of whether the rest of the word starts with a vowel:

- Many words with the prefix ‘co-’, meaning ‘joint’, have hyphens after the ‘co’.
- All words formed with ‘ex-’, meaning ‘former’, are hyphenated.

rule_summary: Follow the spelling in your preferred dictionary for co- and ex- words.
rule_detail: Follow the spelling in your preferred dictionary.

rule_summary: Use a hyphen after a prefix when it is followed by a number or italicised expression.
rule_detail: Use a hyphen if a prefix is followed by a number or an expression that’s in italics.

rule_summary: Attach most suffixes directly to the base word without a hyphen.
rule_detail:
Suffixes are normally attached directly to the base word without any hyphen. The commonest suffixes include:

- -able
- -ate
- -ation
- -fold
- -ful
- -ise
- -ish
- -ly
- -ment
- -ness
- -y.

rule_summary: Use a hyphen with the suffix -fold after numerals, but not after spelled-out numbers.
rule_detail: A hyphen precedes ‘-fold’ when that suffix is used with a numeral, but not a spelled out number.

rule_summary: Always use a hyphen with the suffix -odd.
rule_detail: Always use a hyphen with the suffix ‘-odd’, whether it’s with a word or numeral.

rule_summary: Hyphenate compound adjectives only when they are used before a noun, not after it.
rule_detail: Hyphens link elements of compound words as a phrase, but usually only when they are used before a noun as [adjectives](/node/126). Don’t use hyphens when the phrase is after the noun in the [sentence structure](/node/204).

rule_summary: Use a hyphen in compound nouns made up of a verb plus an adverb.
rule_detail: Use a hyphen in compound nouns made up of a verb plus an adverb. This shows that the adverb is part of the compound rather than modifying other elements of the sentence.

rule_summary: Use minimal punctuation and capitalisation to make content more readable.
rule_detail: Punctuation and capitalisation have rules for correct use. Use minimal punctuation and capitalisation to make content more readable.

rule_summary: Use only punctuation that is grammatically correct and makes meaning clear.
rule_detail: Only use punctuation that makes the sentence grammatically correct and the meaning clear.

rule_summary: Do not add full stops to headings, page headers, footers or captions.
rule_detail: Don’t add full stops to the ends of headings, page headers, footers or captions.

rule_summary: Do not use a semicolon at the end of each item in a bullet list.
rule_detail: Don’t use a semicolon at the end of each item in a bullet list.

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop for bullet-list items unless each item is a full sentence or the last item in a list.
rule_detail: Unless each item is a full sentence or the last item in a list, don’t use a full stop for items in bullet lists.

rule_summary: Do not use full stops between the letters of an acronym or initialism.
rule_detail: Don’t use full stops between letters in an acronym or initialism.

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop at the end of most abbreviations.
rule_detail: Don’t use a full stop at the end of most abbreviations.

rule_summary: Use punctuation marks to end sentences, break up sentences, show possession and contractions, and connect related words.
rule_detail: Use punctuation marks to: end sentences (full stops, exclamation marks and question marks); break up sentences and show the relationship between words and phrases (commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, forward slashes and ellipses); show possession and contractions (apostrophes); connect related words (hyphens and dashes).

rule_summary: Include a single space after a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence.
rule_detail: Include a single space after a punctuation mark at the end of a sentence.

rule_summary: Never use double spaces.
rule_detail: Never use double spaces.

rule_summary: Check documents for double and multiple spaces and delete them.
rule_detail: Check each document for double and multiple spaces and delete them.

rule_summary: Capitalise the first word in a sentence and in headings.
rule_detail: Capitalise the first word in a sentence and in headings.

rule_summary: Use lower case for all other words in a sentence unless they include proper nouns.
rule_detail: Use lower case for all other words, unless those words include proper nouns.

rule_summary: Do not use all capitals for headings unless the visual design meets WCAG in all respects.
rule_detail: Do not use all capitals for headings, unless the visual design for the content meets WCAG in all respects.

rule_summary: Use sentence case with italics for titles of works mentioned in the content.
rule_detail: Use sentence case with italics for titles of works mentioned in the content. This applies even when the reference is included in a heading within the content.

rule_summary: Minimise capitals for common nouns and adjectives.
rule_detail: Minimise capitals for common nouns and adjectives.

rule_summary: Capitalise proper nouns generally with an initial capital letter for each word.
rule_detail: Proper nouns generally have an initial capital letter for each word in the noun.

rule_summary: Do not use initial capitals for common nouns and adjectives except in specified cases.
rule_detail: Common nouns and adjectives don’t use initial capitals, with few exceptions. For example, adjectives often have capitals when they refer to a national, religious or linguistic group.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms only when they support plain English.
rule_detail: Use shortened forms only when this choice supports plain English.

rule_summary: Use the standard capitalisation rules for shortened forms according to whether they represent proper or common nouns.
rule_detail: Rules for capitalisation and punctuation differ from rules for terms spelt out in full. The rules depend on where the terms are in the sentence. The spelt-out form might not need initial capitals, even if an acronym or initialism has them. Use normal capitalisation practices for proper and common nouns. If in doubt, check a dictionary.

rule_summary: Write out shortened forms of proper nouns with capital letters for each word.
rule_detail: If the shortened form represents a proper noun, start each word with a capital letter.

rule_summary: Write out shortened forms of common nouns without initial capitals.
rule_detail: If the shortened form represents a common noun, do not begin each word of the full form with a capital letter.

rule_summary: Use capitals for symbols of units of measurement only when the style is standardised or specified in regulations.
rule_detail: Only use capitals when the style is standardised or specified in regulations, for symbols of units of measurement.

rule_summary: Follow the conventions for capitals in titles, honours and forms of address.
rule_detail: Follow conventions for using capitals for titles, honours and forms of address. Use capitals when an official title precedes the name of the office holder. This includes titles for executives specified in legislation.

rule_summary: Use capitals when an official title precedes the name of the office holder.
rule_detail: Use capitals when an official title precedes the name of the office holder. This includes titles for executives specified in legislation.

rule_summary: Avoid using capitals in body text for a position or role within an organisation unless advised in the manual.
rule_detail: Unless advised in this manual, avoid using capitals in body text for a particular position or role within an organisation. This practice goes against readability and does not support clarity.

rule_summary: Do not use capitals when the title is an organisational name given to an office holder.
rule_detail: You do not need to use capitals when the title is an organisational name given to an office holder.

rule_summary: Use house style only within the organisational context.
rule_detail: Deference for positions within an organisation might follow house style. Do not use house style outside of the organisational context. Detail any special use of capitals in a style sheet.

rule_summary: Record any special use of capitals in a style sheet.
rule_detail: Detail any special use of capitals in a style sheet.

rule_summary: Use title preferences for traditional owner, elder and custodian titles from the relevant First Nations community.
rule_detail: Preferences for capitals when the terms ‘traditional owner’, ‘elder’ and ‘custodian’ are used as titles should come directly from the relevant First Nations community.

rule_summary: Use a question mark to end direct questions and requests.
rule_detail: Users expect direct questions and requests to end with a question mark.

rule_summary: Use other punctuation for indirect questions, commands and rhetorical questions when appropriate.
rule_detail: Indirect questions, commands and rhetorical questions can take other punctuation.

rule_summary: Place a question mark immediately after the last letter of the sentence it refers to.
rule_detail: Question marks usually go after the last letter in a sentence. Like other punctuation marks, question marks stay with the text they refer to. Usually, this is immediately after the last letter of the last word of the sentence.

rule_summary: Place a question mark before a closing bracket or quotation mark when the question belongs inside the bracketed or quoted text.
rule_detail: For brackets and quotation marks, place the question mark: before a closing bracket or quotation mark if the question is part of the text in the brackets or quotation marks

rule_summary: Place a question mark after a closing bracket or quotation mark when the question belongs to the surrounding text.
rule_detail: For brackets and quotation marks, place the question mark: after the closing bracket or quotation mark if the question is part of the surrounding text.

rule_summary: Use a question mark to indicate uncertainty in dates or other specific details.
rule_detail: Question marks can express doubt and uncertainty about dates or other specific details.

rule_summary: End direct questions with a question mark.
rule_detail: Direct questions end with a question mark.

rule_summary: End requests that are framed as questions with a question mark.
rule_detail: Requests are often framed as questions.

rule_summary: Do not end indirect questions with a question mark.
rule_detail: Indirect questions don’t end with question marks, even if they include a word such as ‘who’ or ‘does’.

rule_summary: Treat indirect questions used as headings according to the guidance to avoid questions as headings, except in Easy Read materials.
rule_detail: Indirect questions are often used in headings. Guidance in this manual recommends to [avoid questions as headings](/node/51#write_headings_that_are_clear_and_short), except for [Easy Read materials](/node/63).

rule_summary: Use question marks only when a sentence is truly a question, not just because it can be rearranged as one.
rule_detail: Spellcheckers often recommend that you change indirect questions to end with a question mark. This isn’t always correct. It depends on whether you *are* asking a question.

rule_summary: Do not end instructions and commands with a question mark.
rule_detail: Instructions and commands aren’t framed as questions. They don’t start with words such as ‘what’, ‘are’ or ‘does’,* *and don’t end with a question mark.

rule_summary: Use either a question mark or an exclamation mark for rhetorical questions, depending on the context.
rule_detail: Depending on the context, a rhetorical question can end in a question mark or an exclamation mark.

rule_summary: Use single quotation marks for most direct speech.
rule_detail: Write most direct speech in single quote marks

rule_summary: Use block quotations without quotation marks for long quotes.
rule_detail: For long quotes, use block quotations without quotation marks.

rule_summary: Use single quotation marks for short quotations of direct speech.
rule_detail: Short quotations of direct speech are enclosed in single quotation marks.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks to show direct speech, quoted work, certain titles, and emphasis on defined or special-use words.
rule_detail:
Use them to:

- show direct speech and the quoted work of other writers
- enclose the title of certain works
- draw attention to a word you’re defining.

rule_summary: Avoid double quotation marks except for quotations within quotations.
rule_detail: Double quotation marks aren’t Australian Government style. Use them only for quotations within quotations.

rule_summary: Use double quotation marks inside single quotation marks for quotations within quotations.
rule_detail: For quotations within quotations, use double quotation marks inside one single quotation marks.

rule_summary: Use ellipses only when omitted words do not mislead readers about the source.
rule_detail: If you use ellipses for omitted words, ensure that the omission won’t mislead readers about the content or tone of the source you’re quoting.

rule_summary: Add square-bracketed context only when it is correct and preserves the original meaning.
rule_detail: If the quotation needs the information for context, add specific detail in [square brackets]. You must be sure that the specific detail is correct and that it retains the meaning intended by the original speaker.

rule_summary: Use square brackets to paraphrase omitted material in quoted speech.
rule_detail: If you paraphrase omitted material, place the paraphrasing in square brackets.

rule_summary: Use italicised sic in non-italicised square brackets to show an error comes from the original.
rule_detail: To show the error is in the original, insert an italicised ‘sic’ in non-italicised square brackets after the error. This shows the reader that the error comes from the original.

rule_summary: Preserve the original spelling and capitalisation of quoted non-Australian English material.
rule_detail: In quoted material use the original spelling of the quoted material, even if it uses US spellings such as ‘color’. The capitalisation of words must also be the same as in the original.

rule_summary: Update US quotation marks to the Australian convention when quoting US material.
rule_detail: If the US material uses the US conventions for quotation marks, you can update them to the Australian convention.

rule_summary: Format quotations longer than about 30 words as block quotations.
rule_detail: Quotations that are longer than about 30 words are:

rule_summary: Indent block quotations and may use a smaller font or different font.
rule_detail:
Quotations that are longer than about 30 words are:

- usually indented from the text margin
- sometimes set in a smaller font size or a different font.

rule_summary: Do not use quotation marks to identify block quotations.
rule_detail: Don’t use quotation marks to identify the quoted material – the formatting does that instead. Block quotations should also be coded with the HTML <blockquote> element.

rule_summary: Code block quotations with the HTML blockquote element.
rule_detail: Block quotations should also be coded with the HTML <blockquote> element.

rule_summary: Use an opening quote mark at the start of each paragraph in multi-paragraph quoted speech and a closing quote mark only at the end of the last paragraph.
rule_detail:
To include several paragraphs of quoted speech without the attribution tag, such as in a media release, use a quotation mark:

- at the beginning of each paragraph
- at the end of the last paragraph only.

rule_summary: Omit quotation marks in transcripts and plays when the speaker name comes first.
rule_detail: Quotation marks are unnecessary in transcripts and plays if the name of the speaker comes before the direct speech.

rule_summary: Omit quotation marks in Q&As.
rule_detail: The same applies for questions and answers (Q&As).

rule_summary: Use quotation marks for certain kinds of titles in references and citations.
rule_detail:
When referring to these titles, use quotation marks in references and citations:

- a chapter in a book or report
- an article in a periodical
- an essay
- a lecture
- a poem
- a song.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks to draw attention to words in defined or special senses.
rule_detail:
You can use quotation marks instead of italics to make words stand out from your sentence. Examples include:

- a technical term on its first mention in a non-technical document
- a word or phrase that has been coined or that you’re using in a specific sense
- colloquial words, nicknames, slang, or ironic or humorous words and phrases, in formal writing.

rule_summary: Do not repeat quotation marks unnecessarily on later mentions of the same word.
rule_detail: You don’t usually need to repeat the quotation marks the next time you use the word. They might be useful if the next mention is a long way from the first.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks for words introduced by titled, marked, the term, or defined as.
rule_detail: Another use of quotation marks is for words introduced by expressions such as ‘titled’, ‘marked’, ‘the term’ and ‘defined as’.

rule_summary: Place punctuation belonging to the quoted text before the closing quotation mark.
rule_detail: If the punctuation mark is part of the quoted text, place the punctuation mark before the closing quotation mark.

rule_summary: Place punctuation outside the closing quotation mark when it belongs to the sentence outside the quote.
rule_detail: If the punctuation mark is part of the sentence outside the quoted text, it follows the closing quotation mark.

rule_summary: Place quotation marks inside surrounding sentence punctuation when quoted material is parenthetical.
rule_detail: Quoted material can appear as parenthetical information, enclosed in parentheses, dashes or commas. In these cases, place the quotation marks inside the sentence punctuation.

rule_summary: Place the final full stop before the closing quotation mark when the quotation ends a sentence or is a sentence on its own.
rule_detail: If the quotation ends a sentence or is a sentence in its own right, place the final full stop before the final quotation mark.

rule_summary: Use only the stronger of two competing punctuation marks; do not use both.
rule_detail: Sometimes, there are 2 punctuation marks – one for the quotation and one for the sentence. Decide which is stronger and use it. Don’t use both punctuation marks.

rule_summary: Avoid using semicolons to link sentences unless the relationship between the sentences is closely related.
rule_detail:
Semicolons link sentences. They complicate sentences for users if overused. Avoid using a semicolon to link sentences
