Semicolons can create a break that is stronger than a comma but weaker than a full stop. They can link 2 sentences that share or develop an idea. The information must be closely related.

rule_summary: Do not use semicolons at the end of bullet and numbered list items.
rule_detail:
Do not use them at the end of bullet and numbered list items

Don’t end bullet and numbered list items with semicolons

You don’t need a semicolon at the end of each list item for bullet and numbered lists. It clutters the list and makes it hard to read.

rule_summary: Prefer a full stop or a comma plus conjunction instead of a semicolon where possible.
rule_detail:
Instead of a semicolon, it’s usually best to use either:

- a full stop followed by a new sentence
- a comma before the last item, followed by a
[conjunction](/node/129).

rule_summary: Avoid semicolons when they only make a sentence longer.
rule_detail: Sentences should be in plain language and no longer than 25 words. Don’t use a semicolon if all it does is make your sentence longer.

rule_summary: Use semicolons only between two full sentences when you need one.
rule_detail: If you have to use a semicolon, on both sides of the semicolon write [full sentences](/node/120). Other than in some sentence lists, it’s incorrect to have a sentence fragment on one side of the semicolon.

rule_summary: Separate multiple in-text references in brackets with semicolons.
rule_detail: Use a semicolon between each reference when you have more than one in-text [reference in brackets](/node/181).

rule_summary: Use bullets or numbered lists instead of semicolons in complex lists when possible.
rule_detail:
Use a bullet or numbered list instead of semicolons in a complex sentence

Complex lists in sentences can be hard to read. If you can’t use a bullet or numbered list, separate list items with:

- commas if the list is simple, such as a list of single words
- semicolons if the list is complex, such as a list of items that already contain commas or conjunctions.

In complex lists, you need semicolons to show what goes with what.

It is almost always better to break a complex list into a bullet or numbered list to make it easier to read.

rule_summary: Use punctuation correctly to support readability and comprehension.
rule_detail: Use punctuation correctly to help readability and comprehension.

rule_summary: Avoid overusing punctuation marks.
rule_detail: Don't overuse punctuation marks.

rule_summary: Use minimal punctuation and capitalisation.
rule_detail: The Style Manual follows the principles of minimal punctuation and capitalisation.

rule_summary: Use apostrophes to show possession and contractions.
rule_detail: Apostrophes show possession and contractions.

rule_summary: Do not use apostrophes in descriptive phrases.
rule_detail: Don’t use them in descriptive phrases or to make nouns and shortened forms plural.

rule_summary: Do not use apostrophes to make nouns plural.
rule_detail: Don’t use them in descriptive phrases or to make nouns and shortened forms plural.

rule_summary: Do not use apostrophes to make shortened forms plural.
rule_detail: Don’t use them in descriptive phrases or to make nouns and shortened forms plural.

rule_summary: Use brackets only when removing the enclosed text does not change the meaning.
rule_detail: Only use brackets if you can remove the enclosed text and the meaning does not change.

rule_summary: Use colons only when they are essential.
rule_detail: Only add colons that are essential.

rule_summary: Use colons to introduce examples, contrasts, lists and block quotations.
rule_detail: Use them to introduce examples, contrasts, lists and block quotations.

rule_summary: Use commas according to sentence structure.
rule_detail: Sentence structure determines their correct use.

rule_summary: Use dashes to show a relationship.
rule_detail: Dashes show a relationship.

rule_summary: Prefer a phrase over an en dash for spans when accessibility matters.
rule_detail: Generally, en dashes for spans are less accessible for users than a phrase.

rule_summary: Use spaced en dashes to set off non-essential information in sentences.
rule_detail: Use spaced en dashes to set off non-essential information in sentences.

rule_summary: Do not use ellipses to change the intent of the original source.
rule_detail: Don’t use ellipses to change the intent of the original source.

rule_summary: Use exclamation marks only in informal content.
rule_detail: Only use them in informal content.

rule_summary: Use forward slashes in mathematical expressions, dates, web addresses and some shortened forms.
rule_detail: Users are familiar with them in mathematical expressions, dates, web addresses and in some shortened forms.

rule_summary: Use full stops to end sentences that are not questions or exclamations.
rule_detail: Full stops mark the end of sentences which aren't questions or exclamations.

rule_summary: Use full stops to help users scan text and recognise decimal values.
rule_detail: Users need them to scan text and to recognise decimal values.

rule_summary: Use hyphens to connect words and prefixes when meaning needs to be clear.
rule_detail: Hyphens connect words and prefixes so meaning is clear.

rule_summary: Consult your organisation's preferred dictionary when unsure about hyphen use for spelling.
rule_detail: Refer to your organisation’s preferred dictionary when you are not sure if you need to use a hyphen for spelling.

rule_summary: End direct questions and requests with a question mark.
rule_detail: Users expect direct questions and requests to end with a question mark.

rule_summary: Allow indirect questions, commands and rhetorical questions to take other punctuation.
rule_detail: Indirect questions, commands and rhetorical questions can take other punctuation.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks to draw attention to words and to reference certain kinds of titles.
rule_detail: Quotation marks draw attention to words and reference certain kinds of titles.

rule_summary: Write most direct speech in single quote marks.
rule_detail: Write most direct speech in single quote marks.

rule_summary: Use block quotations without quotation marks for long quotes.
rule_detail: For long quotes, use block quotations without quotation marks.

rule_summary: Use semicolons to link sentences.
rule_detail: Semicolons link sentences.

rule_summary: Avoid overusing semicolons.
rule_detail: They complicate sentences for users if overused.

rule_summary: Do not use semicolons at the end of bullet and numbered list items.
rule_detail: Do not use them at the end of bullet and numbered list items.

rule_summary: Limit the use of abbreviations.
rule_detail: Limit the use of abbreviations

rule_summary: Avoid using abbreviations in general content where possible.
rule_detail: Abbreviations are generally not good for readability and can be misunderstood. Avoid using them in general content where possible.

rule_summary: Use abbreviations only in limited circumstances such as tables, charts, or continuing text markers.
rule_detail:
Abbreviations are useful in very limited circumstances:

- in a table or chart, where space is unavailable for the full form of the word – provide a note under the table or chart giving the full form
- when using ‘cont’ to show continuing text in another part of content (for example, on another page of a print newsletter) – the full form of the word is more helpful where space allows.

rule_summary: Use abbreviations only if users will understand them, and define them on first use when there is any doubt.
rule_detail: Semi-formal and informal content uses abbreviations more often. Use abbreviations only if users will understand what they mean. If there’s any doubt, define the abbreviation on first use.

rule_summary: Avoid using abbreviations in any public-facing content.
rule_detail: Avoid using abbreviations in any public-facing content.

rule_summary: Do not put a full stop after most abbreviations.
rule_detail: Don’t put a full stop after most abbreviations

rule_summary: Do not place a full stop after an abbreviation.
rule_detail: Don’t place a full stop after an abbreviation.

rule_summary: Omit the full stop when an abbreviation ends a sentence and is not followed by another punctuation mark.
rule_detail:
There are exceptions:

- when the abbreviation ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark

rule_summary: Omit the full stop for abbreviations of scientific names for plants and animals.
rule_detail:
There are exceptions:

- for abbreviations of scientific names for
[plants and animals](/node/96) - for the abbreviation ‘n.d.’(meaning ‘no date’) for the year of publication in references.

rule_summary: Use the same capitalisation as the unabbreviated word.
rule_detail: Use the same capitalisation as for the unabbreviated word.

rule_summary: Write out an abbreviation in full when it would be the first word in a sentence.
rule_detail:
Don’t abbreviate the first word in a sentence

Write out the abbreviated term in full.

rule_summary: Add an s to form plural abbreviations, except for pp for pages.
rule_detail:
Add ‘s’ to create plural abbreviations

Add an ‘s’. One exception is ‘pp’* *(pages), which is used when referring to multiple pages.

rule_summary: Use acronyms and initialisms only when people will recognise and understand them.
rule_detail: Acronyms and initialisms are shortened forms. They replace full names and special terms in text. Use them only if people recognise and understand them.

rule_summary: Choose acronyms and initialisms that people will recognise.
rule_detail: Choose acronyms and initialisms people will recognise

rule_summary: Define shortened forms the first time you use them, unless you are certain all users will understand them.
rule_detail:
To make sure all shortened forms are accessible:

- Define them the first time you use them in content (unless you’re certain all users will understand them without a definition – consult a dictionary first).
- Include them with their spelt-out forms in the glossary. This is particularly important if the content contains many specialist shortened forms.

rule_summary: Include shortened forms and their spelt-out forms in the glossary when needed.
rule_detail: Include them with their spelt-out forms in the glossary. This is particularly important if the content contains many specialist shortened forms.

rule_summary: Spell out most acronyms or initialisms on first use.
rule_detail: If there’s a chance users won’t know the meaning of an acronym or initialism, define it at first mention. Write the term in full first and follow with the acronym or initialism in parentheses. Use the shortened form rather than the full term for later mentions.

rule_summary: Use the full term first and the shortened form in parentheses for unfamiliar acronyms or initialisms.
rule_detail: If there’s a chance users won’t know the meaning of an acronym or initialism, define it at first mention. Write the term in full first and follow with the acronym or initialism in parentheses. Use the shortened form rather than the full term for later mentions.

rule_summary: Use the shortened form for later mentions after you define an acronym or initialism.
rule_detail: If there’s a chance users won’t know the meaning of an acronym or initialism, define it at first mention. Write the term in full first and follow with the acronym or initialism in parentheses. Use the shortened form rather than the full term for later mentions.

rule_summary: Write well-known acronyms or initialisms first and follow them with the full term in parentheses.
rule_detail: Write well-known acronyms or initialisms first and follow with the full term in parentheses.

rule_summary: Do not define certain familiar acronyms or initialisms on first use.
rule_detail:
You don’t need to define some acronyms and initialisms on first use. These include:

- some place names (NT, ACT)
- time of day (am, pm)
- some organisational names (BHP, Qantas)
- terms that began as acronyms but are now words in their own right (radar, scuba, sonar).

rule_summary: Repeat the full term more than once if readers may encounter the shortened form out of context.
rule_detail:
If you use the shortened form only a few times in long-form content, consider writing out the full term more than once.

People could come across the shortened form without reading the text where it is first defined. For example, a user might click straight to a section that only includes the shortened form.

rule_summary: Spell out government agency names in full the first time, then use the generic name afterwards when that is clearer.
rule_detail:
Rather than using acronyms or initialisms, it can be easier for people if you:

- spell out the agency’s name in full the first time you use it
- then use the generic name (‘department’, ‘agency’, ‘bureau’) afterwards.

This is usually more useful to non-specialist users.

rule_summary: Provide a glossary when content relies on many specialised acronyms and initialisms.
rule_detail: For content with many specialised acronyms and initialisms, provide a glossary – a list of terms and their meaning that users can refer to.

rule_summary: Place the glossary at the end of the content or on a separate webpage and link to it from the text.
rule_detail: Include the glossary at the end of the content or on a separate webpage. Use a hyperlink in the text to help people access the glossary.

rule_summary: Do not include a glossary if there are only a few unfamiliar shortened forms, they appear in a limited section, or each is defined on first mention.
rule_detail:
You don’t need to include a glossary if:

- there are only a few unfamiliar shortened forms
- each one is only in a very limited section of text
- each one is spelt out when first mentioned.

rule_summary: Place the glossary before references in print materials.
rule_detail: The glossary usually appears before the references (with the endmatter).

rule_summary: Do not end acronyms or initialisms with a full stop.
rule_detail:
Don’t end acronyms and initialisms with a full stop

Don’t place a full stop after the acronym or initialism.

rule_summary: Allow a full stop only when the acronym or initialism ends a sentence and no other punctuation follows.
rule_detail: The exception is if the shortened form ends a sentence and isn’t followed by another punctuation mark.

rule_summary: Use all capitals for most acronyms and initialisms.
rule_detail:
Acronyms are usually all capitals, but use lower case for some familiar acronyms (taser, captcha, laser). Use an initial capital for familiar acronyms that are proper nouns (Qantas, Anzac).

Initialisms are often all upper case (VOIP, FOI) but there are exceptions (bpm). Consult a dictionary if you’re unsure of the capitalisation.

rule_summary: Use lower case for some familiar acronyms.
rule_detail: Acronyms are usually all capitals, but use lower case for some familiar acronyms (taser, captcha, laser). Use an initial capital for familiar acronyms that are proper nouns (Qantas, Anzac).

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for familiar acronyms that are proper nouns.
rule_detail: Acronyms are usually all capitals, but use lower case for some familiar acronyms (taser, captcha, laser). Use an initial capital for familiar acronyms that are proper nouns (Qantas, Anzac).

rule_summary: Use uppercase for initialisms unless there is an exception.
rule_detail: Initialisms are often all upper case (VOIP, FOI) but there are exceptions (bpm). Consult a dictionary if you’re unsure of the capitalisation.

rule_summary: Do not capitalise every word in the full form when the acronym or initialism represents common nouns.
rule_detail: If the acronym or initialism represents common nouns, don’t begin each word of the full form with a capital letter.

rule_summary: Capitalise each main word in the full form when the acronym or initialism represents a proper noun.
rule_detail: If the acronym or initialism represents a proper noun, start each word with a capital letter (excluding words such as ‘of’ and ‘and’).

rule_summary: Avoid contractions in formal content.
rule_detail: Contractions are shortened words. People will read and understand them depending on their context. Avoid them in formal content.

rule_summary: Use single-word contractions carefully.
rule_detail: Shorten single words and grammatical phrases with care

rule_summary: Use grammatical contractions only when the context supports them.
rule_detail: Legal documents and many specialist and professional publications use specific contractions. Look at examples of existing content to see whether you can use grammatical contractions. Don’t use them if you’re unsure.

rule_summary: Avoid single-word contractions in more formal content except for formal titles.
rule_detail: Avoid using contractions of single words in more formal content such as high-level briefing and responses to official inquiries. The exceptions are contractions used in formal writing, such as ‘Dr’ and other titles.

rule_summary: Use English rather than Latin shortened forms in most content.
rule_detail: Use English rather than Latin shortened forms, except in some cases. People will prefer the English equivalent unless the context requires special use.

rule_summary: Avoid using Latin shortened forms except in limited situations.
rule_detail: Avoid using Latin shortened forms in most content

rule_summary: Use Latin forms only in limited situations.
rule_detail:
Use Latin forms only in limited situations – for example:

- where there’s limited space, such as in tables
- in technical and specialist publications that use them.

rule_summary: Use full stops with i.e. and e.g.
rule_detail: The terms ‘i.e.’ and ‘e.g.’ need full stops after each letter. This helps screen readers announce them.

rule_summary: Do not follow e.g. or i.e. with a comma.
rule_detail: Don’t follow ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ with a comma, regardless of whether you would use a comma in the sentence.

rule_summary: Prefer the English words for example and that is instead of e.g. and i.e.
rule_detail: Rather than using ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ write the English words out in full. Write ‘for example’ and ‘that is’ instead, particularly in more formal publications.

rule_summary: Avoid using etc. in lists introduced by for example, such as, or including.
rule_detail: Use of ‘etc.’ is redundant in a list introduced by ‘for example’, ‘such as’ or ‘including’. These expressions show that the list is incomplete.

rule_summary: Include the additional ideas in the sentence instead of adding etc.
rule_detail: If you think you need to include ‘etc.’ because there’s more to say, include these ideas in your sentence instead.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms only if they help users understand quicker.
rule_detail: Use shortened forms if they help the user understand quicker. Make sure everyone understands them.

rule_summary: Make sure everyone understands shortened forms before using them.
rule_detail: Use shortened forms if they help the user understand quicker. Make sure everyone understands them.

rule_summary: Use abbreviations sparingly because they can hinder understanding.
rule_detail: Abbreviations are shortened words. They can hinder people’s understanding, so they have limited uses.

rule_summary: Use acronyms and initialisms only if people recognise and understand them.
rule_detail: Acronyms and initialisms are shortened forms. They replace full names and special terms in text. Use them only if people recognise and understand them.

rule_summary: Avoid contractions in formal content.
rule_detail: Contractions are shortened words. People will read and understand them depending on their context. Avoid them in formal content.

rule_summary: Use English rather than Latin shortened forms unless the context requires special use.
rule_detail: Use English rather than Latin shortened forms, except in some cases. People will prefer the English equivalent unless the context requires special use.

rule_summary: Check a dictionary if you are unsure about a word’s spelling.
rule_detail: If you’re not sure about the spelling of a word, check a dictionary.

rule_summary: Follow one dictionary consistently to check variable spellings.
rule_detail: Follow one dictionary for consistency and use it to check variable spellings.

rule_summary: Use the correct spelling and word choice to keep content readable and clear.
rule_detail: Correct word use makes content readable and clear to users. Getting words wrong risks losing users’ engagement with, and trust of, your content.

rule_summary: Use 'accept' to mean agree or receive.
rule_detail: The verb ‘to accept’ means ‘to agree’ or ‘to receive’.

rule_summary: Use 'except' to mean exclude.
rule_detail: The verb ‘to except’ means ‘to exclude’.

rule_summary: Use 'affect' to mean produce an effect on.
rule_detail: The word ‘affect’ means ‘to produce an effect on’.

rule_summary: Use 'effect' to mean the result of an action or to bring about something.
rule_detail: The word ‘effect’ means ‘the result of an action’ or, as a verb, ‘to bring about or make something happen’.

rule_summary: Use 'allusion' to mean a reference.
rule_detail: The word ‘allusion’ means ‘a reference’. It is often followed by 'to’.

rule_summary: Use 'illusion' to mean a mistaken belief.
rule_detail: The word ‘illusion’ means ‘a mistaken belief’.

rule_summary: Use 'ascent' to mean upward movement.
rule_detail: The word ‘ascent’ means ‘upward movement’.

rule_summary: Use 'assent' to mean agree.
rule_detail: The word ‘assent’ means ‘to agree’. It is often followed by ‘to’.

rule_summary: Use 'complement' to mean something that completes something else.
rule_detail: The noun ‘complement’ means ‘something that completes something else’ or, as a verb, ‘to complete something’.

rule_summary: Use 'compliment' to mean praise.
rule_detail: The noun ‘compliment’ means ‘an expression of praise’ or, as a verb, ‘to praise’.

rule_summary: Use 'council' to mean a formal advisory body of people.
rule_detail: The word ‘council’ means ‘a formal advisory body of people’.

rule_summary: Use 'counsel' to mean advice or to advise.
rule_detail: The word ‘counsel’ means ‘advice’ and ‘to advise’. It also refers to a barrister or other ‘legal adviser’.

rule_summary: Use 'conscience' to mean a moral sense of right and wrong.
rule_detail: The word ‘conscience’ means ‘a moral sense of right and wrong’.

rule_summary: Use 'conscious' to mean awake and aware.
rule_detail: The word ‘conscious’ means ‘awake and aware of one’s surroundings and identity’.

rule_summary: Use 'dependant' for a person who relies on another.
rule_detail: A ‘dependant’ is a person who relies on another, especially for financial support.

rule_summary: Use 'dependent' to mean conditional or subordinate, usually followed by 'on'.
rule_detail: The word ‘dependent’ is usually followed by ‘on’, and means ‘conditional’ or ‘subordinate’.

rule_summary: Use 'discreet' to mean careful or prudent.
rule_detail: The word ‘discreet’ means ‘careful’ or ‘prudent’.

rule_summary: Use 'discrete' to mean distinct.
rule_detail: The word ‘discrete’ means ‘distinct’.

rule_summary: Use 'disinterested' to mean impartial and unbiased by personal interest.
rule_detail: The word ‘disinterested’ means ‘impartial’ and ‘unbiased by personal interest’.

rule_summary: Use 'uninterested' to mean not interested, indifferent or unconcerned.
rule_detail: The word ‘uninterested’ means ‘not interested’, ‘indifferent’ or ‘unconcerned’.

rule_summary: Use 'dived' as the Australian English past tense of 'dive'.
rule_detail: In Australian English, write ‘dived’ to use the past tense of the verb ‘to dive’.

rule_summary: Use 'dove' only as the American English past tense of 'dive'.
rule_detail: The word ‘dove’ is the past tense of ‘dive’ in American English.

rule_summary: Use 'drank' as the past tense of 'drink'.
rule_detail: The verb ‘drank’ is the past tense of ‘to drink’.

rule_summary: Use 'drunk' as a participle with has, have or had.
rule_detail: The verb ‘drunk’ is a participle and is used with ‘has’, ‘have’ or ‘had’.

rule_summary: Follow one Australian English dictionary for consistency.
rule_detail: Government organisations should choose one dictionary of Australian English.

rule_summary: Use either the Australian concise Oxford dictionary or the Macquarie dictionary.
rule_detail:
This manual recommends either:

- the
*Australian concise Oxford dictionary*(ACOD) - the
*Macquarie dictionary*.

rule_summary: Use your organisation's preferred dictionary as the spelling reference.
rule_detail: Use your organisation’s preferred dictionary as a spelling reference when you write.

rule_summary: Use an up-to-date dictionary edition that reflects current language usage.
rule_detail: Make sure you use an up-to-date edition that reflects current language usages.

rule_summary: Use the first listed dictionary spelling for variable spellings.
rule_detail: Dictionaries include any variable spellings for words. Always use the first entry in the list.

rule_summary: Use an alternative spelling only when evidence shows it meets a user need.
rule_detail: Only use an alternative spelling listed for a word if you have evidence it will meet a user need.

rule_summary: Record alternative spelling decisions in a style sheet.
rule_detail: Record decisions you make about alternative spellings in a style sheet.

rule_summary: Use specialist dictionaries for scientific or technical writing.
rule_detail: Specialist dictionaries are essential for scientific or technical writing.

rule_summary: Include specialist terms in the content style sheet.
rule_detail: The style sheet for the content should include specialist terms.

rule_summary: Use an Australian English dictionary for Australian spellings.
rule_detail: For Australian spellings, always use an Australian English dictionary.

rule_summary: Follow the Style Manual's guidance for specific terms and phrases.
rule_detail: Follow our guidance for specific terms and phrases.

rule_summary: Use the spelling guidance in the punctuation and capitalisation section where relevant.
rule_detail: There is also guidance related to spelling at punctuation and capitalisation.

rule_summary: Use the sixth edition of the ACOD as the spelling basis for this manual.
rule_detail: The spelling in this manual follows the sixth edition of the ACOD.

rule_summary: Use the Style Manual's recognised government-content spellings where they differ from the dictionary.
rule_detail: Style Manual also recognises conventions and spellings particular to government content.

rule_summary: Accept either recommended dictionary as long as you apply it consistently.
rule_detail: This is perfectly acceptable – choose either of our recommended dictionaries (or a specialist dictionary) and follow it consistently.

rule_summary: Use the Style Manual's guidance for specific terms and phrases.
rule_detail: Always follow our guidance for specific terms and phrases.

rule_summary: Use 'gement' spelling in acknowledgement, lodgement and judgement.
rule_detail: For example, we now write ‘ement’ not ‘ment’ in acknowledgement, lodgement and judgement (but we use ‘judgment’ for legal material).

rule_summary: Use 'judgment' in legal material.
rule_detail: For example, we now write ‘ement’ not ‘ment’ in acknowledgement, lodgement and judgement (but we use ‘judgment’ for legal material).

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals.
rule_detail:
Use initial capitals for the titles of individual academics and professionals

The academic and professional titles held by individuals usually have initial capitals. This includes honorary titles.

Use lower case if you use a title generically.

rule_summary: Use full titles in specific display and formal contexts.
rule_detail:
Use full titles in certain contexts

Academics and professionals are often addressed by their ‘full title’. A full title includes the title or honorific (with initial capitals), name, post-nominals, position and organisation.

Use a full title:

- to introduce an individual as speaker
- in address and signature blocks in correspondence
- in official records of proceedings
- in lists in organisational publications such as annual reports
- if it is important to know where an individual works.

A full title is often about using titles in a display or presentation context (display text).

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for titles that appear immediately before a person's name unless the title is generic.
rule_detail:
Titles immediately before a name

Use initial capitals for titles that appear immediately before a person’s name. Do this unless the title is generic.

Also use initial capitals for the shortened forms of titles.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms of titles only in limited circumstances and spell out confusing forms.
rule_detail:
Shortened forms for titles immediately before a name

Only use shortened forms of titles in limited circumstances. People might understand common contractions like ‘Prof’ for ‘Professor’, but some shortened forms are confusing. For example, the initialism for ‘Pro Vice-Chancellor’ is ‘PVC’. To ensure your content is readable, write the title in full.

Shortened forms are sometimes necessary because of limited space. For example, shortened forms often appear in tables. List the full form of any title that people might find confusing in a note.

The space available for image captions can be limited, but write the full names and titles as a default. If you have to use initials and the shortened forms of titles in a caption, always include the full forms in body text to provide context.

‘Dr’ is an exception in all instances. Like ‘Ms’ and ‘Mr’, ‘Dr’ is easy to understand when it appears before a name.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for official titles that replace a name when addressing someone directly or in salutations.
rule_detail:
Titles that replace a name

Use initial capitals for official titles that replace a name.

Titles replacing a name also have initial capitals:

- when you address someone directly
- for salutations in correspondence.

For all other uses, titles that replace a name should be lower case.

These other uses include abbreviated titles and titles given by an organisation to a role or position. Academic and professional organisations might capitalise such titles as a mark of respect or status, but this is not Australian Government style. Treat them as generic and use lower case.

rule_summary: Use lower case for most titles that appear after a name.
rule_detail:
Titles after a name

Use lower case for most titles that appear after a name. These titles describe the individual and are generic.

There is one exception. Only use initial capitals for titles after a name in a full title.

This includes for:

- address and signature blocks in correspondence
- lists in organisational publications such as annual reports.

Follow your organisation’s template style for signature blocks. Templates apply design elements and list all elements in correct order. Some organisations prefer all capitals for names, titles and the organisation’s name.

rule_summary: Use lower case for titles used generically, including plural titles, common nouns and descriptive titles.
rule_detail:
Use lower case for titles used in a generic way

Generic use of academic and professional titles includes:

- titles that describe a named individual
- plural titles
- common nouns.

As shown in the previous section, most titles that appear after a name are generic.

Some titles appearing immediately before a name are also generic because they describe the individual. These titles are usually preceded by ‘the’ or a modifier. Adjectives are modifiers because they restrict the meaning of a noun.

rule_summary: Use a person's title, name and post-nominals at first mention.
rule_detail:
Use title, name and post-nominals at first mention

When you write about an individual, it’s respectful to use their title.

The first time you mention someone in body text, use their academic or professional title before their first name and last name, followed by post-nominals.

If you mention the individual again, only use the title and last name. Some academic titles have an accepted abbreviated title you can use after the first mention.

rule_summary: Do not use shortened forms of academic titles in body text except for 'Dr'.
rule_detail:
Never use the shortened form of the title in body text (‘Prof’ for example), except for the contraction ‘Dr’.

This year’s graduate cohort asked Deputy Vice-Chancellor Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

DVC Jonquil Johansson to moderate their debate.

rule_summary: Place post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles and do not use commas around them.
rule_detail:
Write post-nominals after the name in academic and professional titles

Post-nominals are letters after a name that stand for academic, civil and military awards and honours.

Make sure you write post-nominals in the right order.

Don’t use commas before or between post-nominals.

rule_summary: Use post-nominals only at first mention in body text.
rule_detail:
Use post-nominals at first mention only

The first time you write a name in body text, use the academic and professional title along with the first and last name. Include the post-nominal for a civil or military honour in the title.

If you mention the name again, use the title and last name, but don’t include the post-nominal.

rule_summary: Retain post-nominals when using shortened forms of titles.
rule_detail:
Include post-nominals in the shortened forms of titles

Retain any post-nominals for civil and military honours when using the shortened forms of titles.

rule_summary: Use academic and professional qualification post-nominals only for academic correspondence or to show relevant expertise.
rule_detail:
Use post-nominals for academic and professional qualifications in 2 contexts

Post-nominals can also stand for tertiary and professional qualifications.

Use these post-nominals:

- for correspondence within the academic community
- to show relevant expertise.

Don’t include both ‘Dr’ (doctorate) and ‘PhD’ (Doctor of Philosophy) for the one name. It is conventional to use either the title or the post-nominal. This also applies to PhD equivalents such as ‘LLD’ (Doctor of Laws).

Don’t include post-nominals for master and bachelor degrees in correspondence.

rule_summary: Use full titles for academics in most contexts.
rule_detail:
Titles for academics

In most contexts, address academics with their full title: title or honorific, name, position, post-nominals and academic institution.

rule_summary: Place Sir or Dame after the academic title for a knighted academic.
rule_detail:
An academic who is knighted

Use ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’ after the academic title.

rule_summary: Keep the initial capital for the title in correspondence to a specific academic.
rule_detail:
Emails and letters to academics

Keep the initial capital for the title in correspondence when you’re writing to a specific person.

rule_summary: Use the specified salutations and closings in formal and less formal correspondence to academics.
rule_detail:
In formal correspondence:

- Open with ‘Chancellor’ (or ‘Vice-Chancellor’, ‘Professor’ and so on).
- Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

In less formal correspondence:

- Open with ‘Dear Chancellor’ (or ‘Vice-Chancellor’, ‘Professor’ and so on).
- Conclude with ‘Yours sincerely’.

Don’t include a comma after these phrases. Australian Government style is to write salutations without punctuation.

rule_summary: Address associate and assistant professors as 'Associate Professor' and 'Assistant Professor' in Australian correspondence.
rule_detail: For Australian correspondence, write ‘Dear Associate Professor’ and ‘Dear Assistant Professor’ not ‘Dear Doctor’ or ‘Dear Professor’.

rule_summary: Address people with doctorates as 'Doctor' or 'Dr' and omit the full stop.
rule_detail:
People with doctorates

You can address people who hold a doctorate as ‘Doctor’ or ‘Dr’ (without a full stop). Today, it is acceptable to use ‘Dear Dr Name’ for both formal and informal correspondence.

When writing ‘Dear’ without the person’s name in emails and letters, write the title ‘Doctor’ in full.

Don’t include a comma after these phrases.

rule_summary: Address a knighted holder of a doctorate as Sir or Dame rather than Doctor.
rule_detail:
A holder of a doctorate who is knighted

If the holder of a doctorate is knighted, don’t address them as ‘Doctor’.

Instead, address the person by ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’. Write the post-nominals for the knighthood after the name, followed by any other post-nominals. Don’t insert commas before or between the post-nominals.

rule_summary: Use the correct title and style to refer to members of the armed services.
rule_detail: Use the correct title and style to refer to members of the armed services. This guidance is intended primarily for users outside the Department of Defence and the Australian Defence Force.

rule_summary: Use ‘Defence’ to refer to both the Department of Defence and the Australian Defence Force.
rule_detail: Use the term ‘Defence’ when you mean both the Department of Defence and the Australian Defence Force (ADF). ‘Defence’ is used to represent the organisation as a whole.

rule_summary: Capitalize ‘Defence’ in formal names and titles, and use lower case for generic references.
rule_detail: ‘Defence’ has an initial capital when it is part of a formal name or title. Use lower case for generic references.

rule_summary: Use ‘Australian Defence Force’ and ‘ADF’ for the Navy, Army and Air Force collectively.
rule_detail: Use ‘Australian Defence Force’ and ‘ADF’ when referring to the Royal Australian Navy, Australian Army and Royal Australian Air Force, commanded by the Chief of the Defence Force.

rule_summary: Use ‘Department of Defence’ when referring to the department.
rule_detail: Use ‘Department of Defence’ when referring to the department, headed by the Secretary of the Department of Defence.

rule_summary: Follow the ADF order of precedence for the services.
rule_detail: When referring to the services, follow the order of precedence established by the Defence Act 1903: Royal Australian Navy, Australian Army, Royal Australian Air Force.

rule_summary: Write the short names of the services with initial capitals.
rule_detail: Always use initial capitals when writing the short names of the services: Navy, Army, Air Force.

rule_summary: Address ADF members by rank, name and post-nominals in the specified order.
rule_detail: Use the following order to address members of the ADF: rank, given name or initials, family name, post-nominals, service (for commissioned officers in the Navy only).

rule_summary: Use the full rank, given name or initials, family name and post-nominals when first mentioning an ADF member in specified contexts.
rule_detail: Do this: the first time you write their name in body text; in address blocks in correspondence; when introducing an ADF member as speaker; in official records of proceedings; in lists in organisational publications such as annual reports.

rule_summary: Use rank and family name for subsequent mentions of an ADF member in body text.
rule_detail: If you mention the name again in body text, use rank and family name.

rule_summary: Do not hyphenate military ranks made of more than one word.
rule_detail: Write military ranks of more than one word as separate words. Do not hyphenate the rank.

rule_summary: Hyphenate Air Vice-Marshal.
rule_detail: There is one exception from the Air Force: Air Vice-Marshal. It is always hyphenated.

rule_summary: Place post-nominals after the family name.
rule_detail: Write post-nominals after the family name. Place post-nominals before the shortened form showing service (‘RAN’).

rule_summary: Place ‘RAN’ after the family name and any post-nominals.
rule_detail: Use ‘RAN’ (Royal Australian Navy) for all commissioned officers of the Navy. Place ‘RAN’ after the family name and any post-nominals.

rule_summary: Do not use service acronyms for Army or Air Force officers.
rule_detail: Don’t use an acronym to show service for officers in the Army or Air Force.

rule_summary: Put the military rank before other titles such as Sir or Dame.
rule_detail: When someone has a military rank and another title such as ‘Sir’, ‘Dame’ or ‘the Honourable’, place the military rank first.

rule_summary: Address chaplains and maritime spiritual wellbeing officers by their titles, not military rank.
rule_detail: Address chaplains with their chaplaincy title, not a military rank. MSWOs have been part of the Navy since 2020. Address them with their MSWO title, not a military rank. Include any post-nominals.

rule_summary: Use the specified chaplaincy titles for ADF chaplains.
rule_detail: The chaplaincy titles are: Principal Chaplain (Navy and Army) and Principal Air Chaplain (Air Force); Senior Chaplain (Navy) and Chaplain (Navy, Army and Air Force).

rule_summary: Use the specified titles for MSWOs.
rule_detail: The MSWO titles include: Principal Maritime Spiritual Wellbeing Officer; Senior Maritime Spiritual Wellbeing Officer; Maritime Spiritual Wellbeing Officer.

rule_summary: Allow retired commissioned officers to retain their rank and add ‘(Retd)’ after post-nominals.
rule_detail: Commissioned officers who retire can continue to use their military rank. When writing their name, use their rank and include ‘(Retd)’ after any post-nominals.

rule_summary: Write full rank with an initial capital outside Defence rather than abbreviated rank forms.
rule_detail: Avoid using the shortened forms of ranks. For internal Defence use, it is common to write the ranks in abbreviated form using capital letters. Don’t follow this convention in other types of content. Write the full rank with an initial capital letter.

rule_summary: Apply the address-block format to all ADF members.
rule_detail: The style rule for address blocks applies to all members of the ADF. The style of address blocks is the same for all ranks.

rule_summary: Format address blocks in the specified order.
rule_detail: To write an address block, follow all preceding rules on this page. The style of address blocks is the same for all ranks. rank; given name or initials; family name; post-nominals; ‘RAN’ for commissioned officers in the Navy; ‘(Retd)’ for retired commissioned officers who retain rank; postal address.

rule_summary: Follow the rank-specific salutation rules.
rule_detail: The style of salutations depends on rank. Don’t include post-nominals in salutations. Never add a comma after salutations.

rule_summary: Use ‘Dear [Rank]’ for senior commissioned officer ranks.
rule_detail: Use the rule for these ranks: Admiral, Rear Admiral, Commodore and Captain (Navy); General, Lieutenant General, Major General, Brigadier and Colonel (Army); Air Chief Marshal, Air Marshal, Air Vice-Marshal, Air Commodore and Group Captain (Air Force).

rule_summary: Use ‘Dear [Rank Family name]’ for the specified commissioned officer ranks.
rule_detail: Use the rule for these ranks: Commander, Lieutenant Commander and Lieutenant (Navy); Lieutenant Colonel, Major and Captain (Army); Wing Commander, Squadron Leader and Flight Lieutenant (Air Force).

rule_summary: List post-nominals in the correct order, with the highest honour first.
rule_detail:
Post-nominals and titles of status show the awards and honours an individual has. List them in the correct order.

Post-nominals are the shortened forms for academic awards and civil and military honours.

There is an order in which to write the post-nominals.

In summary, the rule is to write the highest honour first. The order is:
- post-nominals for honours and awards
- King’s Counsel (KC) or Senior Counsel (SC) or Justice of the Peace (JP)
- university degrees and diplomas
- membership of professional associations
- membership of parliament.

rule_summary: Omit full stops and spaces within post-nominals.
rule_detail: Don’t use full stops or spaces within post-nominals.

rule_summary: Do not use commas before or between post-nominals.
rule_detail: Don’t use commas before or between post-nominals.

rule_summary: Place vice-regal, ecclesiastical and Australian Defence Force titles before all other titles.
rule_detail: Vice-regal and ecclesiastical titles and Australian Defence Force ranks usually precede all other titles.

rule_summary: Place other titles immediately before a person's name after the higher-ranking titles.
rule_detail: Follow these with any other titles (such as ‘Dame’, ‘Sir’ and ‘Dr’) immediately before a person’s name.

rule_summary: Use the correct diplomatic title for the country or authority the person represents.
rule_detail: The title for diplomats depends on what they represent: High commissioners represent Commonwealth countries. Ambassadors represent non-Commonwealth countries. Nuncios represent the Holy See, the governing body of the Roman Catholic Church.

rule_summary: Use initial capitals for the titles of high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios.
rule_detail: Use initial capitals when writing to ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios.

rule_summary: Capitalise 'His' and 'Her' when they are part of a diplomatic title.
rule_detail: The pronouns ‘His’ and ‘Her’ are part of the title. Write these with an initial capital as well.

rule_summary: Address high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios as 'His Excellency' or 'Her Excellency'.
rule_detail: Use ‘His Excellency’ or ‘Her Excellency’ to address high commissioners, ambassadors and nuncios.

rule_summary: Open formal correspondence with ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios with 'Your Excellency'.
rule_detail: In formal correspondence with ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios: Open with ‘Your Excellency’. Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

rule_summary: Conclude formal correspondence with ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios with 'Yours faithfully'.
rule_detail: In formal correspondence with ambassadors, high commissioners and nuncios: Open with ‘Your Excellency’. Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

rule_summary: Open informal correspondence with ambassadors and high commissioners with 'Dear High Commissioner' or 'Dear Ambassador'.
rule_detail: In informal correspondence: Open with ‘Dear High Commissioner’ or ‘Dear Ambassador’. Conclude with ‘Yours sincerely’.

rule_summary: Conclude informal correspondence with ambassadors and high commissioners with 'Yours sincerely'.
rule_detail: In informal correspondence: Open with ‘Dear High Commissioner’ or ‘Dear Ambassador’. Conclude with ‘Yours sincerely’.

rule_summary: Address other diplomatic staff by name and official position.
rule_detail: Use the name and official position to address: diplomatic staff (such as chargés d’affaires and counsellors) consular appointees (such as consuls general, vice-consuls and honorary consuls).

rule_summary: Use the correct titles to refer to members of the judiciary.
rule_detail: Use the correct titles to refer to members of the judiciary.

rule_summary: Refer to judges of the High Court, Federal Court, Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1), and supreme courts as Justice and The Honourable.
rule_detail:
Refer to judges of the following courts as ‘Justice’ and use the title ‘The Honourable’:

- High Court
- Federal Court
- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1)
- supreme courts in the states and territories.

rule_summary: Use Your Honour, His Honour or Her Honour for judges of Division 2, district courts and county courts.
rule_detail:
Use the titles ‘Your Honour’, ‘His Honour’ or ‘Her Honour’ for judges of:

- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2)
- district courts
- county courts.

rule_summary: Address High Court and Federal Court judges and registrars using the linked court guidance.
rule_detail:
Instructions for addressing judges and registrars are at:

- High Court –
[How do I address a High Court judge? [PDF 31 KB]](https://www.hcourt.gov.au/assets/education/How%20to%20address%20a%20high%20court%20justice.pdf) - Federal Court –
[How to address [Federal Court] judges & judicial registrars](https://www.fedcourt.gov.au/going-to-court/forms_address).

rule_summary: Retain the title The Honourable for life for judges of the High Court and Federal Court.
rule_detail: Judges of these courts retain the title ‘The Honourable’ for life.

rule_summary: Abbreviate Honourable to Hon without a full stop when using the shortened form of the title.
rule_detail: You can also abbreviate the term ‘Honourable’ to ‘Hon’ without a full stop.

rule_summary: Refer to judges of Division 1 and supreme courts as Justice and The Honourable.
rule_detail:
Refer to judges of the following courts as ‘Justice’ and use the title ‘The Honourable’:

- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1)
- supreme courts in the states and territories.

rule_summary: Keep the title The Honourable for life for Division 1 judges and chief justices of supreme courts.
rule_detail: Judges of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1) and chief justices of the supreme courts in states and territories retain the title ‘The Honourable’ for life. Supreme court justices also generally retain the title for life.

rule_summary: Address Division 1 and supreme court judges in emails and letters as Dear Justice [Family name].
rule_detail:
In emails and letters, use ‘Dear Justice [Family name]’ to address:

- a justice of the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 1)
- a judge of a state or territory supreme court.

rule_summary: Conclude correspondence with Yours faithfully when writing to Division 1 or supreme court judges.
rule_detail: Conclude correspondence with ‘Yours faithfully’.

rule_summary: Address Division 2, district court and county court judges as Judge.
rule_detail:
Address judges of the following courts as ‘Judge’:

- Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Division 2)
- district courts
- county courts.

rule_summary: Use His Honour or Her Honour for judges of Division 2, district courts and county courts.
rule_detail: Use the title ‘His Honour’ or ‘Her Honour’ for judges of these courts.

rule_summary: Open correspondence to Division 2, district court and county court judges with Dear Judge [Family name].
rule_detail:
In emails and letters:

- Open with ‘Dear Judge [Family name]’.
- Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

rule_summary: Address magistrates in court as Your Honour.
rule_detail: Address magistrates in court as ‘Your Honour’*.

rule_summary: Address magistrates outside court as Magistrate.
rule_detail: *When outside court, address them as ‘Magistrate’.

rule_summary: Address envelopes to magistrates as Her Honour Magistrate or His Honour Magistrate.
rule_detail: When addressing an envelope use ‘Her Honour Magistrate’ or ‘His Honour Magistrate’.

rule_summary: Address a knighted judge as The Honourable Sir or The Honourable Dame.
rule_detail: Address a judge who is a knight or dame as ‘The Honourable Sir’ or ‘The Honourable Dame’.

rule_summary: Use Sir or Dame with the person’s given name on subsequent mention of a knighted judge.
rule_detail: On subsequent mention, you can use ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’ and the person’s given name.

rule_summary: Capitalise the titles of the current prime minister and treasurer.
rule_detail: Capitalise the titles of the current prime minister and treasurer

rule_summary: Capitalise the titles of current holders of the Prime Minister and Treasurer positions, even when abbreviated.
rule_detail:
Capitalise the titles of the current holders of the positions of:

- Prime Minister
- Treasurer.

Do this even when the titles are abbreviated.

rule_summary: Use lower case when referring to prime ministers or treasurers generically.
rule_detail: If referencing prime ministers or treasurers generically, use lower case.

rule_summary: Use lower case for former prime ministers and treasurers of Australia.
rule_detail: Use lower case letters for former prime ministers and treasurers of Australia.

rule_summary: Capitalize titles for current senators and members of the Australian Parliament.
rule_detail: Capitalise titles for current senators and members of the Australian Parliament

rule_summary: Write the specified parliamentary titles in the listed forms.
rule_detail:
Write these titles as follows:

- the Prime Minister
- the President of the Senate
- the Speaker of the House of Representatives
- ministers (Senate)
- ministers (House of Representatives)
- assistant ministers (Senate)
- assistant ministers (House of Representatives)
- senators
- members (House of Representatives).

rule_summary: Place the title Senator before a person’s given name if they are elected to the upper house.
rule_detail: People elected to the upper house take the title ‘Senator’ before their given name.

rule_summary: Place MP after members of the House of Representatives and after any other post-nominals.
rule_detail: Members of the House of Representatives take the initialism ‘MP’ after their name. Write it after any other post-nominals. Don’t use commas before or between post-nominals.

rule_summary: Use the title Honourable for ministers and parliamentary secretaries in the Australian Parliament.
rule_detail: Use the title ‘Honourable’ for ministers (including the prime minister) and parliamentary secretaries in the Australian Parliament. The title is given to these office holders because they are members of the Federal Executive Council. They retain the title for life.

rule_summary: Abbreviate Honourable as Hon without a full stop.
rule_detail: The abbreviation for ‘Honourable’ is ‘Hon’ without a full stop.

rule_summary: Use Senator before The Hon when the minister or parliamentary secretary is a member of the Senate.
rule_detail: Use the title ‘Senator’ before ‘the Honourable’ if the minister or parliamentary secretary is a member of the Senate.

rule_summary: Use Honourable for the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives.
rule_detail: The President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives (the presiding officers) use the title ‘Honourable’.

rule_summary: Use Honourable for former state ministers and former presiding officers of state parliaments.
rule_detail:
‘Honourable’ is also given to members of the Australian Parliament who are:

- former members of state ministries
- former presiding officers of state parliaments.

rule_summary: Use Dear Minister and Yours faithfully in formal emails and letters to a minister.
rule_detail:
In formal emails and letters to a minister:

- Open with ‘Dear Minister’.
- Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

rule_summary: Use My dear Minister and Yours sincerely in less formal correspondence to a minister.
rule_detail:
In less formal correspondence:

- Open with ‘My dear Minister’.
- Conclude with ‘Yours sincerely’.

rule_summary: Address members of state and territory parliaments using the relevant post-nominal after their name in formal emails and letters.
rule_detail: In formal emails and letters, address members of state and territory parliaments with the relevant post-nominal after their name.

rule_summary: Use MLC for members of the Legislative Council in NSW, SA, Tas, Vic and WA.
rule_detail:
Use MLC for members of the Legislative Council of:

- NSW
- SA
- Tas
- Vic
- WA.

rule_summary: Use MLA for members of the Legislative Assembly in the ACT, NT and WA.
rule_detail:
Use MLA for members of the Legislative Assembly of:

- ACT
- NT
- WA.

rule_summary: Use MP for members of the Legislative Assembly in NSW, Queensland and Victoria.
rule_detail:
Use MP for members of the Legislative Assembly of:

- NSW
- Qld
- Vic.

rule_summary: Use MP for members of the House of Assembly in South Australia and Tasmania.
rule_detail:
Use MP for members of the House of Assembly of:

- SA
- Tas.

rule_summary: Write other post-nominals in the same way the parliamentarian uses them and check with the office if unsure.
rule_detail:
A parliamentarian may have other post-nominals after their name. These can include:

- civilian and military honours
- educational and professional qualifications.

If so, write these in the same way the parliamentarian does. If you’re unsure, check with the parliamentarian’s office.

rule_summary: Use Dear Ms or similar and Yours faithfully in formal correspondence to members of a state or territory parliament.
rule_detail:
In formal correspondence with a member of a state or territory parliament:

- Open with ‘Dear Ms’ (or ‘Mr’, ‘Mrs’, ‘Mx’, ‘Dr’ and so on).
- Conclude with ‘Yours faithfully’.

rule_summary: Use Dear Mr or similar and Yours sincerely in less formal correspondence to members of a state or territory parliament.
rule_detail:
In less formal correspondence:

- Open with ‘Dear Mr’ (or ‘Ms’, ‘Mrs’, ‘Mx’, ‘Dr’ and so on).
- Conclude with ‘Yours sincerely’.

rule_summary: Use Honourable when addressing specified state and NT office holders and former ministers.
rule_detail:
Use ‘Honourable’ when addressing all members of the executive councils of the states and the NT:

- premiers and ministers in all states
- chief minister and ministers in the NT
- former ministers in all states and the NT.

Use ‘Honourable’ when addressing these parliamentarians:

- members of all state legislative councils except in Victoria
- Leader of the Opposition in Tasmania
- presidents of all legislative councils
- speakers of all parliaments except in the ACT.

rule_summary: Address royalty and representatives of the royal family with their correct title.
rule_detail: Royalty and representatives of the royal family should be addressed with their correct title.

rule_summary: Capitalize the titles of current royals.
rule_detail: Always capitalise the titles of current royals

rule_summary: Capitalize the title of the current Australian monarch.
rule_detail: Always use capitals for the title of the current Australian monarch.

rule_summary: Use the full current monarch title when referring to Australia’s monarch.
rule_detail: The full title of the current monarch of Australia is ‘Charles the Third, by the Grace of God King of Australia and His other Realms and Territories, Head of the Commonwealth’.

rule_summary: Address letters to the King via his private secretary.
rule_detail: Address letters to the King to his private secretary.

rule_summary: Use the title Her Majesty The Queen for Queen Camilla.
rule_detail: The title of the King’s wife, Queen Camilla, is ‘Her Majesty The Queen’.

rule_summary: Use the title Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II for Queen Elizabeth II.
rule_detail: The title of the late Queen Elizabeth II is ‘Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II’.

rule_summary: Use the title His Royal Highness The Duke of Edinburgh for Prince Philip.
rule_detail: The title of the late Queen’s husband, Prince Philip, is ‘His Royal Highness The Duke of Edinburgh’.

rule_summary: Use the title His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales for Prince William.
rule_detail: The King’s elder son, Prince William, is titled ‘His Royal Highness The Prince of Wales’.

rule_summary: Use the title Her Royal Highness The Princess of Wales for Catherine.
rule_detail: Prince William’s wife, Catherine, is titled ’Her Royal Highness The Princess of Wales’.

rule_summary: Address letters to Prince William via his private secretary.
rule_detail: Address letters to Prince William to his private secretary. You can use the shortened form for ‘His Royal Highness’ in this instance.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for The in the formal titles of the King and his immediate family.
rule_detail: Use an initial capital for ‘The’ for the formal titles of the King and his immediate family.

rule_summary: Use regnal numbers in upper-case Roman numerals for monarchs and religious leaders.
rule_detail: Regnal numbers are upper case roman numerals that are used for the titles of monarchs and popes.

rule_summary: Do not use digits or ordinal numbers for regnal numbers.
rule_detail: Don’t use digits or ordinal numbers, even though you might pronounce them like that.

rule_summary: Use a non-breaking space between a name and its regnal number.
rule_detail: Put a non-breaking space between the name and the regnal number. A non-breaking space means that line breaks won’t split up both elements of the name. The name and number will stay together on one line.

rule_summary: Use U+00A0 as the non-breaking space character for regnal numbers.
rule_detail: You can insert a non-breaking space using the Unicode character U+00A0.

rule_summary: Use the HTML entity to insert a non-breaking space.
rule_detail: In HTML, use the entity to insert a non-breaking space. You can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar in Word.

rule_summary: Use a narrow no-break space in print between a name and its regnal number.
rule_detail: Use a narrow no-break space between the name and the regnal number.

rule_summary: Keep the name and regnal number together on one line.
rule_detail: The narrow no-break space ensures that the: - name and number stays together on one line - spacing between name and number doesn’t change when text is justified.

rule_summary: Use U+202F as the narrow no-break space character for print.
rule_detail: You can insert a narrow no-break space using the Unicode character U+202F.

rule_summary: Capitalize Governor-General when it is part of a formal title.
rule_detail: Capitalise ‘Governor-General’ when it’s part of the formal title

rule_summary: Use vice-royalty to refer to the office of Governor-General in Australia.
rule_detail: The position of governor-general in Australia is known as vice-royalty. The Governor-General represents the King in Australia.

rule_summary: Address the Governor-General using the prescribed formal order and components.
rule_detail:
Address the Governor-General of Australia in the following style and order:

- ‘His/Her Excellency the Honourable’
- prefixed titles
- given name and family name
- post-nominals
- ‘Governor-General of the Commonwealth of Australia’.

rule_summary: Vary the title order to suit the incumbent’s titles when needed.
rule_detail:
You might need to vary the order of the items in the title to suit the titles of the incumbent. For example, place:

- military rank before ‘the Honourable’
- ‘Sir’ or ‘Dame’ after ‘the Honourable’.

rule_summary: Use lower case governor-general when referring to the generic term or multiple officeholders.
rule_detail: When you are referring to the generic term, use lower case ‘governor-general’. When you are referring to 2 or more people who hold or have held the title, use lower case and refer to them as ‘governors-general’.

rule_summary: Use correct titles and capitalisation for academics, diplomats, judges, government officials, royalty and members of the armed forces.
rule_detail: Use correct titles and capitalisation for academics, diplomats, judges, government officials, royalty and members of the armed forces.

rule_summary: Address and title academics and professionals correctly.
rule_detail: Follow these rules to address and title academics and professionals correctly. The guidance focuses on academics, medical practitioners, dentists and veterinarians. Apply the rules when writing about individuals in other professions.

rule_summary: Use the correct title and style for members of the Australian Defence Force.
rule_detail: Use the correct title and style to refer to members of the armed services. This guidance is intended primarily for users outside the Department of Defence and the Australian Defence Force.

rule_summary: List post-nominals and titles of status in the correct order.
rule_detail: Post-nominals and titles of status show the awards and honours an individual has. List them in the correct order.

rule_summary: Use the correct term when referring to ambassadors, high commissioners, nuncios and other diplomatic staff.
rule_detail: Use the correct term when referring to ambassadors, high commissioners, nuncios and other diplomatic staff.

rule_summary: Use the correct titles for members of the judiciary.
rule_detail: Use the correct titles to refer to members of the judiciary.

rule_summary: Refer to members of Australian parliaments and councils in the correct style.
rule_detail: Refer to members of Australian parliaments and councils in the correct style. Follow these rules to address and title people correctly.

rule_summary: Address royalty and representatives of the royal family with their correct title.
rule_detail: Royalty and representatives of the royal family should be addressed with their correct title.

rule_summary: Use adjectives to describe, compare and define nouns and words that act as nouns.
rule_detail: Adjectives describe, compare and define nouns and words that act as nouns.

rule_summary: Use adjectives to help people understand meaning.
rule_detail: Use adjectives to help people understand meaning.

rule_summary: Place adjectives immediately before the noun when possible.
rule_detail: Adjectives usually go immediately before the noun.

rule_summary: Allow adjectives to appear elsewhere in a sentence when needed.
rule_detail: They can go elsewhere in a sentence – for example, as a predicate.

rule_summary: Use adjectives sparingly and only when they are essential for meaning.
rule_detail: Use adjectives sparingly and only when they are essential for meaning. Remove any adjective that doesn’t play a critical function in a sentence.

rule_summary: Remove adjectives that do not play a critical function in a sentence.
rule_detail: Use adjectives sparingly and only when they are essential for meaning. Remove any adjective that doesn’t play a critical function in a sentence.

rule_summary: Use hyphens to form some compound adjectives.
rule_detail: Adjectives can be joined with hyphens to make compound adjectives.

rule_summary: Use a hyphen in a compound adjective when it appears before the noun it describes.
rule_detail: A compound adjective usually has a hyphen if the adjective is before the noun it is describing.

rule_summary: Avoid hyphens with most adverbs ending in -ly when they form compound adjectives.
rule_detail: Don’t use hyphens with most adverbs finishing in ‘-ly’.

rule_summary: Check a dictionary if you are unsure about hyphenating compound adjectives with adverbs ending in -ly.
rule_detail: There are few exceptions to this rule, so check a dictionary if you are unsure.

rule_summary: Form the comparative and superlative of most adjectives by adding -er and -est.
rule_detail: These adjectives usually follow the pattern of adding ‘-er’ or ‘-est’ to the end to show the degree.

rule_summary: Use irregular comparative and superlative forms for adjectives with irregular degree patterns.
rule_detail: Not all adjectives follow the regular pattern of ‘fast–faster–fastest’. These irregular adjectives have different patterns.

rule_summary: Use more and most for adjectives that do not change form for degree.
rule_detail: Some adjectives don’t have a different form to show degree. They show degree by using ‘more’ for comparative or ‘most’ for superlative.

rule_summary: Do not compare adjectives that cannot logically be compared.
rule_detail: Some adjectives don’t have degree because you can’t compare them. For example, nothing can be more unique than something else.

rule_summary: Order strings of adjectives to sound more natural.
rule_detail: Write strings of adjectives in an order that creates a more natural-sounding English.

rule_summary: List adjectives in the order evaluative, descriptive, then definitive.
rule_detail:
List adjectives in this order:

- evaluative – features of a noun that you can measure or compare
- descriptive – features of a noun that you can’t measure
- definitive – features of a noun that are intrinsic to the noun.

rule_summary: Separate adjectives of the same type with commas.
rule_detail:
Strings of adjectives have:

- commas between adjectives of the same type
- no commas between adjectives of different types
- no commas and no ‘and’ before definitive adjectives.

rule_summary: Do not use commas between adjectives of different types.
rule_detail:
Strings of adjectives have:

- commas between adjectives of the same type
- no commas between adjectives of different types
- no commas and no ‘and’ before definitive adjectives.

rule_summary: Do not use commas or and before definitive adjectives.
rule_detail:
Strings of adjectives have:

- commas between adjectives of the same type
- no commas between adjectives of different types
- no commas and no ‘and’ before definitive adjectives.

rule_summary: Use and instead of commas when it improves sentence flow.
rule_detail: You can also use ‘and’ instead of commas to help the sentence flow more smoothly.

rule_summary: Avoid adjectives that repeat a quality already inherent in the noun.
rule_detail: Don’t use an adjective if it repeats a quality or property that is part of the noun.

rule_summary: Use adverbs occasionally to show how, when, where or the extent to which something happens.
rule_detail: Use them occasionally to show people how, when, where, or the extent to which something happens.

rule_summary: Use adverbs sparingly and remove any adverb that does not play a critical function in a sentence.
rule_detail: Use adverbs sparingly. Remove any adverb that doesn’t play a critical function in a [sentence](/node/204).

rule_summary: Use conjunctions to connect words, phrases and clauses.
rule_detail: Use conjunctions to connect words, phrases and clauses.

rule_summary: Keep both parts of paired conjunctions before the same type of word, phrase or clause.
rule_detail: Some conjunctions come in pairs, such as ‘whether/or’, 'both/and', ‘either/or’ and ‘neither/nor’. Each conjunction in the pair should appear before the same type of word, phrase or clause.

rule_summary: Use coordinating conjunctions to join words, phrases and clauses of equal importance.
rule_detail: Coordinating conjunctions include ‘and’, ‘but’ and ‘or’. They link words, phrases and clauses that are of the same importance.

rule_summary: Use coordinating conjunctions to join clauses that could stand alone as sentences.
rule_detail: Coordinating conjunctions can also join clauses that could stand alone as sentences.

rule_summary: Use subordinating conjunctions to join a main clause to a subordinate clause or phrase.
rule_detail: Subordinating conjunctions join the main clause to a subordinate (or ‘dependent’) clause or phrase.

rule_summary: Treat the main clause as a complete sentence and the dependent clause as information that relies on it.
rule_detail: The main clause can stand alone as a sentence. Dependent clauses add to the main clause: they depend on it to form a complete sentence.

rule_summary: Use conjunctive adverbs to join two main clauses and modify another word or clause.
rule_detail:
A conjunctive adverb is a word that does 2 things at the same time.

- It joins 2 main clauses.
- It modifies a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole clause.

rule_summary: Use conjunctive adverbs sparingly.
rule_detail: Conjunctive adverbs are often not needed. They add nuance to writing, but use them sparingly. You can usually delete them and keep meaning clear.

rule_summary: Do not use 'with' to add a clause at the beginning or end of a sentence.
rule_detail: Don’t use ‘with’ to add a clause at the beginning or end of a sentence. Reword or split the sentence to prevent this misuse. This helps create shorter, simpler sentences that are easier to read.

rule_summary: Use determiners with a noun.
rule_detail: Determiners always go with a noun. They tell people something specific or general about the noun.

rule_summary: Use determiners to introduce a noun or noun phrase.
rule_detail: Determiners introduce a [noun](/node/122) or a [noun phrase](/node/144). Determiners give more information about the noun they are introducing. They are also called ‘articles’.

rule_summary: Use determiners to show what you are referring to, whether it is specific or generic, and how many there are.
rule_detail:
They show users:

- which things you are referring to
- whether you are referring to specific or to generic things and ideas
- how many things there are.

rule_summary: Use articles, pronouns, and numbers as determiners.
rule_detail:
Determiners include:

- articles such as ‘a’, ‘an’ or ‘the’
- pronouns such as ‘those’, ‘my’ or ‘some’
- numbers such as ‘2’, ‘14’ or ‘23 million’.

rule_summary: Use ‘the’ to refer to a specific thing or things.
rule_detail: The word ‘the’ is the ‘definite article’. It defines which specific thing you are referring to.

rule_summary: Use ‘the’ for a group only when you are referring to a specific group.
rule_detail: You can use ‘the’ for a group of things, but only if you refer to a specific group.

rule_summary: Do not use ‘the’ when making a generalisation.
rule_detail: Don’t use ‘the’ when you make a generalisation.

rule_summary: Use ‘a’ and ‘an’ to make generalisations about generic things or ideas.
rule_detail: The words ‘a’ and ‘an’ are ‘indefinite articles’. Use them when you are referring to a generic thing or idea rather than a specific one.

rule_summary: Choose ‘a’ or ‘an’ according to the sound of the following word.
rule_detail:
Choose ‘a’ or ‘an’ according to the sound of the word after it:

- Use ‘a’ if the following word starts with a consonant sound.
- Use ‘an’ if the following word starts with a vowel sound.

The same rule applies to shortened words and phrases ([abbreviations](/node/184), [acronyms and initialisms](/node/190), and [contractions](/node/191)).

rule_summary: Use ‘a’ before a vowel letter with a hidden initial ‘y’ consonant sound.
rule_detail:
Some vowels have a hidden ‘y’ consonant sound at the beginning. For example, you would read ‘universal’ as ‘yew-nee-ver-sahl’.

Say the noun out loud. If it starts with the hidden ‘y’ sound, use ‘a’.

rule_summary: Use ‘an’ before a vowel sound and in specific examples such as ‘error’, ‘office’, and ‘university degree’.
rule_detail:
- It was an error. [The ‘e’ sound in ‘error’ is a vowel.]
- It was a cold office. [The ‘c’ sound in ‘cold’ is a consonant.]
- The job required a university degree. [The ‘u’ sound in ‘university’ sounds like the consonant ‘y’.]

rule_summary: Use ‘an’ before words starting with a silent ‘h’.
rule_detail:
For words that start with ‘h’:

- Use ‘an’ only before words that start with a silent ‘h’, such as ‘honour’ or ‘hour’.

rule_summary: Use ‘a’ before words starting with spoken ‘h’.
rule_detail: Use ‘a’ for all other words starting with ‘h’, such as ‘historian’ or 'hotel’, when the ‘h’ is spoken.

rule_summary: Use pronouns as determiners when they introduce nouns.
rule_detail: Some pronouns introduce nouns, so they work as determiners. Examples of these pronouns are ‘any’, ‘some’, ‘this’, ‘that’, ‘these’, ‘those’, ‘my’, ‘your’, ‘his’, ‘her’.

rule_summary: Use determiner pronouns to show which noun you are referring to.
rule_detail: Pronouns, working as determiners, can show which noun you are referring to.

rule_summary: Use pronouns as determiners to quantify the noun.
rule_detail: Pronouns can also quantify the noun.

rule_summary: Use numbers as determiners to show quantity.
rule_detail: Numbers work as determiners because they give information about how many nouns they are introducing.

rule_summary: Capitalise proper nouns.
rule_detail: Proper nouns always start with capital letters, except for [some commercial terms](/node/89).

rule_summary: Treat a name for a specific person, organisation, place or thing as a proper noun.
rule_detail: Any name for a specific person, organisation, place or thing is a ‘proper noun’.

rule_summary: Capitalize common nouns only when they begin a sentence.
rule_detail: Common nouns describe people, places, times or things in a general sense. They have a capital letter only when they are the first word in a sentence.

rule_summary: Capitalise nouns only when they are part of a proper noun.
rule_detail: Capitalise nouns only if they are part of a proper noun. Don’t capitalise them if you use them as common nouns.

rule_summary: Use concrete nouns for things you can identify through the senses.
rule_detail: Concrete nouns name things you can identify through one or more of the 5 senses.

rule_summary: Use abstract nouns for intangible things.
rule_detail: Abstract nouns name intangible things. These include ideas, emotions and physical feelings.

rule_summary: Recognise that some nouns can be concrete or abstract depending on context.
rule_detail: Some nouns can be either concrete or abstract, depending on the context.

rule_summary: Treat gerunds as nouns formed by adding -ing to a verb.
rule_detail: Gerunds are nouns that form by attaching an ‘-ing’ to a verb.

rule_summary: Use determiners with gerunds and other verbal nouns where needed.
rule_detail: You can combine gerunds and other verbal nouns with a [determiner](/node/132#pronouns_can_function_as_determiners) (such as ‘my’ or ‘your’).

rule_summary: Recognise verbal nouns formed with suffixes such as -ation or -ment as non-gerunds.
rule_detail: Verbal nouns also include nouns that relate to verbs in another way. For example, the noun can form by adding other types of suffix to a verb like ‘-ation’ or ‘-ment’. These are not gerunds.

rule_summary: Use context to distinguish nouns that share the same spelling as verbs.
rule_detail: Other verbal nouns don’t have any suffix but have the same spelling as the verb. It is context that gives the distinction.

rule_summary: Form most plural nouns by adding -s or -es, but check exceptions in a dictionary.
rule_detail: Nouns can be singular or plural. Most English words add an ‘-s’ or ‘-es’ to form the plural, but there are many exceptions. Check a dictionary if you’re not sure.

rule_summary: Do not use an apostrophe to show a plural.
rule_detail: Don’t use an apostrophe before (or after) the ‘s’ to show the plural.

rule_summary: Use a singular verb with a collective noun in most cases.
rule_detail: A collective noun usually has a [singular verb](/node/128). This is so, even if it’s made up of component parts.

rule_summary: Use a plural verb with a collective noun when you need to highlight the individual parts.
rule_detail: An exception is when you need to draw attention to the individual parts of the collective noun.

rule_summary: Use countable nouns when the noun can be separated into individual units and counted.
rule_detail: You can sort nouns by whether they can be separated into individual units and counted: - You can count countable nouns. - You cannot count uncountable nouns.

rule_summary: Require a determiner with a countable singular noun.
rule_detail: A countable singular noun must have a determiner.

rule_summary: Treat uncountable nouns as singular and do not require a determiner.
rule_detail: An uncountable noun has no plural and only a singular verb. Uncountable nouns don’t need to have a determiner. Whether it has one depends on the meaning of the sentence.

rule_summary: Interpret nouns that can be countable or uncountable according to context and meaning.
rule_detail: Some nouns can be used both ways. The meaning depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable in the way it is used: - In the uncountable form, it refers to the whole idea or quantity. - In the countable form, it refers to a specific example or type.

rule_summary: Avoid noun trains by rewriting sentences that contain strings of three or more nouns.
