rule_detail: Strings of 3 or more nouns are known as ‘noun trains’. Each noun in a noun train modifies the next.

rule_summary: Rewrite noun trains to improve plain language.
rule_detail: Rewrite a sentence to avoid using a noun train. This will help you [write in plain language](/node/55).

rule_summary: Use prepositions to show relationships between words or phrases.
rule_detail: A preposition creates relationships between words or phrases. Prepositions show a relationship between a noun or verb. Use prepositions to give information about the time and place of an action or thing.

rule_summary: Choose prepositions deliberately to convey meaning to users.
rule_detail: Some words only work with specific prepositions. Choose them deliberately to convey meaning to users.

rule_summary: Use specific prepositions only where the word or phrase requires them.
rule_detail: Not all prepositions work for every word or phrase. Some words are always followed by particular prepositions. For example, 'different' is always followed by 'to' or 'from', but not by 'than'. Check a dictionary if you are not sure.

rule_summary: Use pronouns to replace nouns, noun phrases, or noun clauses.
rule_detail: Pronouns stand in for nouns. They stand in for groups of words that function as nouns (noun phrases and noun clauses). They can also act like determiners.

rule_summary: Use pronouns in singular or plural forms as appropriate.
rule_detail: Pronouns can be singular or plural.

rule_summary: Recognise the six main types of pronouns by their function.
rule_detail: There are 6 main types of pronouns: Personal pronouns replace the names of people or things. Reflexive pronouns reflect the action of the verb back to the subject. Relative pronouns refer to nouns that are already known from the context. Interrogative pronouns ask questions. Demonstrative pronouns specify which noun you are referring to. Indefinite pronouns don’t specify quantity or number.

rule_summary: Use gender-neutral singular pronouns instead of gendered forms.
rule_detail: Singular pronouns have a gender-neutral form. Use the forms: ‘they’ instead of ‘he’ or ‘she’; ‘them’ instead of ‘him’ or ‘her’; ‘their’ instead of ‘his’ or ‘hers’.

rule_summary: Use the plural verb form when singular 'they' is used as a gender-neutral term.
rule_detail: When the singular ‘they’ is used in a sentence as a gender-neutral term, it takes the plural form of a verb.

rule_summary: Use the subjective case for pronouns acting as subjects.
rule_detail: A pronoun used as the subject in a sentence is in the subjective case (for example, ‘I’, ‘they’).

rule_summary: Use the objective case for pronouns acting as objects.
rule_detail: A pronoun used as the object in a sentence is in the objective case (for example, ‘me’, ‘them’).

rule_summary: Check whether a pronoun should be in the subjective or objective case.
rule_detail: Use the correct case when writing pronouns. Check whether the pronoun should be in the subjective or the objective case – whether it is the subject or object.

rule_summary: Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object are the same.
rule_detail: Sentences can have reflexive pronouns when the subject is also the object of the verb. The manager emailed themself. [‘Themself’ is the object but refers to ‘the manager’, which is the subject.]

rule_summary: Do not use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object are not the same.
rule_detail: Don’t use a reflexive pronoun if the subject and the object are not the same person or thing.

rule_summary: Do not use reflexive pronouns as the subject of a verb.
rule_detail: Don’t use reflexive pronouns such as ‘yourself’ and ‘myself’ as the subject of the verb.

rule_summary: Use 'that' for essential relative clauses.
rule_detail: To make your writing clear, use: ‘that’ for essential information.

rule_summary: Use 'which' with punctuation for non-essential relative clauses.
rule_detail: To make your writing clear, use: ‘which’, with punctuation, for non-essential information.

rule_summary: Use punctuation to show whether information is essential or non-essential.
rule_detail: It is important to show users whether information is essential or non-essential by using punctuation, for example commas.

rule_summary: Treat choosing between relative pronouns as a matter of style in some situations.
rule_detail: Choosing between relative pronouns can be a matter of style in some situations, depending on voice and tone. It is the use of punctuation with the relative pronoun that clarifies meaning.

rule_summary: Use verbs to show when something happened or whether it is continuing or finished.
rule_detail: Verbs express when something happened, or that something is continuing or finished.

rule_summary: Use verbs to help make sense of other parts of a sentence or clause.
rule_detail: Verbs help people make sense of other parts of a sentence or clause.

rule_summary: Recognise that verbs can describe an action, a state, an event or a change.
rule_detail: Verbs describe an action, a state, an event or a change

rule_summary: Match the form of the verb to the grammatical subject and tense.
rule_detail: The form of the verb changes depending on the grammatical subject and tense.

rule_summary: Make the verb agree with the subject.
rule_detail: Verbs must ‘agree’ with the subject

rule_summary: Use singular verb forms with singular subjects and plural verb forms with plural subjects.
rule_detail: The form of the verb changes to show whether the subject is singular or plural (the number). This is called ‘subject–verb agreement’.

rule_summary: Use the subject to decide which verb form you need.
rule_detail: To decide which form of the verb you need, find its subject and ask ‘who’ or ‘what’ is doing the verb.

rule_summary: Use the singular verb form with a singular subject such as one specific person.
rule_detail: [There is one specific analyst, so the verb takes the singular form ‘works’.]

rule_summary: Avoid using a plural verb form with a singular subject.
rule_detail: [There is one person, Jan, so the verb should not take the plural form ‘work’.]

rule_summary: Use a plural verb with collective nouns when the collective noun is being treated as a group.
rule_detail: For example, a common mistake is to use the plural form of a verb with a [collective noun](/node/122#collective_nouns_describe_a_group_in_a_single_word).

rule_summary: Keep the relationship between the grammatical subject and the verb clear to users.
rule_detail: Keep the relationship between the grammatical subject and the verb clear to users.

rule_summary: Write plain language sentences with a clear subject-verb relationship.
rule_detail: This relationship is the basis for writing [plain language sentences](/node/204#write_plain_language_sentences).

rule_summary: Use transitive verbs with an object.
rule_detail: Some verbs need an object to have meaning. For example, you don’t just need or take – you need ‘something’ or take ‘something’. These are ‘transitive’ verbs.

rule_summary: Use intransitive verbs without an object.
rule_detail: Some verbs don’t have an object. These are ‘intransitive’ verbs.

rule_summary: Use an adverb or adverbial phrase as a complement with some intransitive verbs.
rule_detail: Intransitive verbs can instead have a complement in the form of an [adverb](/node/127) or [adverbial phrase](/node/144).

rule_summary: Allow a verb to function transitively or intransitively depending on the sentence.
rule_detail: Some verbs can be transitive or intransitive. They can have meaning with or without an object, depending on the rest of the sentence.

rule_summary: Use a complement, not an object, to link a subject to an attribute, quality or characteristic.
rule_detail: A complement can go with a verb that links the subject to an attribute, quality or characteristic. This type of complement is not an object, but completes the sentence. They are often [adjectival phrases](/node/144#adjectival_phrases_function_as_adjectives) or [adjectives](/node/126).

rule_summary: Use tense to show when something happened and whether it is continuing or finished.
rule_detail:
The form of the verb can also change to show:

- when something happened (past, present or future) – this is the tense of the verb
- whether something is continuing or has finished.

rule_summary: Use auxiliary verbs with the main verb to form tense or aspect.
rule_detail: Verbs like ‘will’ change the form of the main verb ‘to write’. Verbs added to the main verb are ‘auxiliary’ verbs.

rule_summary: Use the indicative mood for simple statements and questions.
rule_detail: This mood expresses simple statements or questions.

rule_summary: Use the imperative mood for urgency, commands, pleas and requests.
rule_detail: This is the mood for expressing urgency, commands, pleas and requests.

rule_summary: Use the imperative mood for instructions and when space is limited.
rule_detail: The imperative mood is direct. It works well for instructions and where there is limited space, such as in [forms](/node/177).

rule_summary: Be deliberate about the tone imperative commands convey.
rule_detail: Be deliberate about the tone the content needs to convey. Imperative commands can seem blunt, even if you use the word ‘please’.

rule_summary: Use the subjunctive mood to express possibility, hypothetical situations or desirability.
rule_detail: This is the mood for expressing possibility. It shows that something is hypothetical, possible, conceivable or desirable.

rule_summary: Use the subjunctive mood in conditional constructions.
rule_detail: Verbs in the subjunctive mood can work together with other words to express a condition.

rule_summary: Use the subjunctive mood in recommendations.
rule_detail: The subjunctive mood doesn’t always need an auxiliary verb to show the mood, only the main verb. Recommendations can follow this formula.

rule_summary: Use auxiliary verbs such as can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must and ought to to convey ability, possibility, permission or obligation.
rule_detail:
You can use auxiliary verbs to convey ability, possibility, permission or obligation. This affects the [tone of your writing](/node/40).

These verbs are:

- can
- could
- may
- might
- will
- would
- shall
- should
- must
- ought to.

rule_summary: Use phrasal verbs with the correct preposition or adverb.
rule_detail: Phrasal verbs are verbs paired with one or more [prepositions](/node/130). They can also go with an [adverb](/node/127). Check the dictionary entry for the verb to use the correct combination.

rule_summary: Place the object either after both parts of a phrasal verb or between its parts when needed.
rule_detail: When phrasal verbs need an object, you can put the object between the verb and its other part.

rule_summary: Keep the functions of words in mind to write clear content.
rule_detail: Keep the functions of words in mind to write clear content. Grammar and sentence structure help people understand meaning.

rule_summary: Use punctuation correctly to help readability and comprehension.
rule_detail: Use punctuation correctly to help readability and comprehension. Don't overuse punctuation marks. The Style Manual follows the principles of minimal punctuation and capitalisation.

rule_summary: Follow one dictionary for consistency and use it to check variable spellings.
rule_detail: Spelling errors detract from readability. Follow one dictionary for consistency and use it to check variable spellings.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms if they help the user understand quicker.
rule_detail: Use shortened forms if they help the user understand quicker. Make sure everyone understands them.

rule_summary: Make sure everyone understands shortened forms.
rule_detail: Use shortened forms if they help the user understand quicker. Make sure everyone understands them.

rule_summary: Use style for numbers and measurements that supports accessibility and readability.
rule_detail: Style for numbers and measurements supports accessibility and readability for users.

rule_summary: Use italics sparingly.
rule_detail: Italic type contrasts with roman type. It draws people’s attention to convey meaning. Use italic type sparingly as it can affect readability.

rule_summary: Check official sources for correct names and terms.
rule_detail: Check official sources for correct names and terms. Use consistent capitalisation and punctuation.

rule_summary: Use consistent capitalisation and punctuation for names and terms.
rule_detail: Check official sources for correct names and terms. Use consistent capitalisation and punctuation.

rule_summary: Use correct titles and capitalisation for specified people and roles.
rule_detail: Use correct titles and capitalisation for academics, diplomats, judges, government officials, royalty and members of the armed forces.

rule_summary: Use the Style Manual when creating Australian Government content.
rule_detail: Use the Style Manual when creating Australian Government content.

rule_summary: Create content that meets users' needs.
rule_detail: Use it to create clear and consistent content that meets the needs of users.

rule_summary: Use companion resources to style Australian Government content consistently.
rule_detail: Use these resources as companions to the Style Manual. They will help you style Australian Government content consistently.

rule_summary: Use this guidance to create clear and findable content.
rule_detail: Use this guidance to create content that’s clear and findable.

rule_summary: Reference the grammar, punctuation and conventions section for definitive Australian Government style rules and examples.
rule_detail: Reference this section for definitive rules and examples of Australian Government style.

rule_summary: Use the format that best meets the user's need.
rule_detail: Use the format that helps meet the user’s need. This could be a form, a blog, an image or another format.

rule_summary: Design content with a structure that helps users navigate and understand.
rule_detail: Design content with a structure that helps the user navigate and understand.

rule_summary: Reference sources correctly so users can identify them.
rule_detail: Reference correctly so users can identify the sources you use.

rule_summary: Cite film, television, radio and podcast programs so people can find the source material.
rule_detail: Cite film, television, radio and podcast programs so people can find the source material. Use the right style and comply with copyright laws.

rule_summary: Use sentence case for media titles, keeping initial capitals for the first word, proper nouns and proper adjectives.
rule_detail: Use sentence case – retain initial capitals for the first word, proper nouns and proper adjectives.

rule_summary: Use italics for published works and roman type for unpublished works.
rule_detail: Use italics for published works and roman type for unpublished works.

rule_summary: Use roman type and quotation marks for parts of works, such as episodes.
rule_detail: Use roman type and quotation marks for parts of works, such as episodes.

rule_summary: Use the company’s spelling and capitalisation for channels, streaming services and networks.
rule_detail: Use roman type and the spelling and capitalisation that the company uses for the names of channels, streaming services and networks.

rule_summary: Use full organisation names the first time you mention them.
rule_detail: Use full names of organisations the first time you mention them.

rule_summary: Italicise the titles of films, television and radio programs, and podcasts.
rule_detail: Italicise the titles of films, television and radio programs, and podcasts.

rule_summary: Put episode names in quotation marks and use roman type.
rule_detail: Place the names of episodes in quotation marks and roman type.

rule_summary: Use the author-date system for the examples on this page.
rule_detail: Examples of in-text citations and reference lists on this page follow the author–date system, as this is the most common way of citing film, television and radio programs in government content.

rule_summary: Attribute all copyright material you reference, including video and audio.
rule_detail: You must attribute copyright material you reference. This includes video and audio.

rule_summary: Include the details required by open access licences.
rule_detail: Include all the details required by open access licences (read how to attribute Creative Commons).

rule_summary: Apply the government copyright rules in the Australian Government intellectual property manual.
rule_detail: Read the government copyright rules in the Australian Government intellectual property manual.

rule_summary: Use italics and sentence case for film titles.
rule_detail: Write the title as it appears in film information. Include punctuation marks and any intentional misspelling. Italicise the title and use sentence case.

rule_summary: Keep the original format of a film series number.
rule_detail: If the film is part of a series, include the number of the series in the same format as in the original title of the film. For example, if the original title has the number written as a word, use the word.

rule_summary: Place a film’s year of production after the title in roman type and parentheses.
rule_detail: In-text citations of films often include the year of production. Place this after the title in roman type and enclosed in parentheses.

rule_summary: Omit the film year in parentheses if you mention the date in the text.
rule_detail: If you mention the date in the text, you don’t have to include it in parentheses.

rule_summary: Shorten a film title after the first mention if the shorter form remains clear.
rule_detail: After the first mention, you can abbreviate the title as long as it makes sense. You can also omit the date in parentheses. This often happens with well-known and longer titles because it improves the flow of the text.

rule_summary: Use the director and year of release for a film reference list entry, or the producer if there is no credited director.
rule_detail: In a reference list, use the director and the year of release. Include the place of production if known. If there is no credited director, use the name of the producer.

rule_summary: Format a film reference list entry as Director or Producer, year, title, motion picture, publisher and place of production.
rule_detail: Rule: Director D (director) or Producer P (producer) (Year) *Title of film: subtitle of film* [motion picture], Name of Studio or Publisher, Place of Production.

rule_summary: Use sentence case, roman type and quotation marks for television episode titles.
rule_detail: Use sentence case, roman type and quotation marks for episodes of a program.

rule_summary: Use roman type and no quotation marks for production companies, networks, channels and streaming services.
rule_detail:
Use roman type and no quotation marks for the names of:

- production companies
- networks
- channels
- streaming services.

rule_summary: Include the year of production for television programs in roman type and brackets.
rule_detail: Include the year of production of television programs in roman type and brackets.

rule_summary: Use Arabic numerals for season numbers.
rule_detail: Use arabic – not roman – numerals for the numbers of seasons.

rule_summary: Format a television reference list entry as director or producer, year, episode title, series name, season and episode numbers, station or studio, and place of production.
rule_detail: Rule: Director D (director) or Producer P (producer) (Year) ‘Title of episode: subtitle of episode’ [television program], *Name of series* (season number, episode number), Name of Station or Studio, Place of Production.

rule_summary: If a television episode has no title, write the program name first.
rule_detail: If the episode doesn’t have a name, write the name of the program first.

rule_summary: Cite classics in line with the author–date system.
rule_detail: Cite titles in line with the author–date system.

rule_summary: Treat classics titles as book titles in references and in-text citations.
rule_detail: In references and in-text citations, treat the titles of classics as you would other book titles.

rule_summary: Use sentence case for titles of classics.
rule_detail: Use sentence case – capitalise only the first letter of the title and the first letter of any proper noun.

rule_summary: Italicise titles of books, series and anthologies.
rule_detail: Use italics for the titles of books, series and anthologies.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks for titles of chapters, poems or sections.
rule_detail: Use quotation marks for the titles of chapters, poems or sections.

rule_summary: Include cited classics in the reference list when using one.
rule_detail: If you’re using a reference list, include any classics that you cite.

rule_summary: Use the documentary–note system if your organisation requires it, and adjust the citation style accordingly.
rule_detail: If your organisation uses the documentary–note system, change the citation and style of reference list accordingly.

rule_summary: Include the information you know in in-text citations for classics.
rule_detail: Include the information that you know in in-text citations.

rule_summary: Do not use Anon, unknown or Anonymous when the author is not known.
rule_detail: If you don’t know the name of the author, don’t use ‘Anon’*, *‘unknown’ or ‘Anonymous’ in the in-text citation.

rule_summary: Use the translator’s name and publication date when the author and date are unknown.
rule_detail: If you don’t know the author or the date of a work, use the name of the translator (trans) and the date of publication of the edition you’re working with. Place the date at the end of the reference.

rule_summary: Use the author’s common name for classical and medieval authors.
rule_detail: Use the author’s common name in text, in-text citations and reference lists.

rule_summary: Do not repeat the author’s name in brackets when the author is already named in the sentence.
rule_detail: As with other books, if you mention the author in the sentence, don’t place the author’s name in brackets with the title of the work.

rule_summary: Include divisions in in-text citations whenever possible.
rule_detail: Some classics have divisions. Divisions organise prose and poetry into, for example, books, chapters, sections, lines and verses.

rule_summary: Spell out divisions the first time you cite a work with divisions.
rule_detail: If the work you’re citing has divisions, quote them in the in-text citation. The first time you cite a work, spell out the divisions. Place a comma between the title of the work and the first division. Separate divisions with a comma.

rule_summary: Use only division numbers in subsequent citations.
rule_detail: For subsequent citations, don’t spell out the divisions. You only need the division numbers. Separate divisions with a full stop. Don’t place a comma between the title of the work and the division numbers.

rule_summary: Spell out a single division in the citation.
rule_detail: If you have only one division to cite, always spell it out. Place a comma between the title and the division.

rule_summary: Use page numbers for editions without divisions.
rule_detail: If you’re referring to an edition that doesn’t have divisions, you can refer to specific page numbers. In these cases, place the date of the translation – or edition – you’re working with and the page number after the title of the work. Separate the date from the page numbers with a colon, not a full stop. Don’t use spaces around the colon.

rule_summary: Use the English title in in-text citations for translated works.
rule_detail: In in-text citations, refer to the English title that appears on the source you’re citing. If you include the work in a reference list, use the date of the translation and the name of the translator (‘trans’).

rule_summary: Use the original-language title when citing works in the original language.
rule_detail: In these cases, cite the title in the original language. If the original language uses a different alphabet to English – ancient Greek for example – use the anglicised spelling.

rule_summary: Include classics in the reference list when you are already using one for other works.
rule_detail:
You don’t usually need a reference list for classics.

If you are using a reference list because you’re citing other works as well, then include the classics you have cited.

rule_summary: Cite the specific translation and edition used in the reference list.
rule_detail:
If you include a classics work in the reference list, cite the particular translation and edition you are working with. Make sure you:

- specify the date of the edition, not the date of the creation of the work
- acknowledge the translator (‘trans’)
- place the date at the end of the reference list entry – this is contrary to author–date style, but it stops possible confusion caused by, for example, ‘Plato (1954)’
- hyperlink titles in digital content where available.

rule_summary: Cite musical compositions using the author-date system.
rule_detail: Cite musical compositions using the author–date system.

rule_summary: Attribute compositions with correct references so people can find a particular piece of music.
rule_detail: Attribute compositions with correct references to help people find a particular piece of music.

rule_summary: Use title case and quotation marks for Australia’s National Anthem.
rule_detail: Use title case (maximal capitalisation) and quotation marks for Australia’s National Anthem.

rule_summary: Use roman type and no quotation marks for unnamed compositions.
rule_detail: For compositions with no given name, use roman type and no quotation marks. Always use a capital letter for the key of musical compositions.

rule_summary: Use a capital letter for the key of musical compositions.
rule_detail: Always use a capital letter for the key of musical compositions.

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop after no when a composition is numbered as part of a series.
rule_detail: For compositions numbered as one of a series, do not use a full stop for the contraction for the word numero (or ‘number’).

rule_summary: Do not capitalise the generic type of composition.
rule_detail: Don’t capitalise the generic type of composition.

rule_summary: Use the English word for most composition types.
rule_detail: Use the English word for most types of compositions (Table 1).

rule_summary: Use the English plural form for most composition types.
rule_detail: Use the English plural form for most types of compositions (Table 2).

rule_summary: Use a full stop after the abbreviation Op.
rule_detail: ‘Op.’ is the abbreviated form of the Latin ‘opus’, meaning ‘work’. It is a common catalogue term for many composers' works. Always use a full stop with this abbreviation.

rule_summary: Never spell out shortened catalogue forms such as BWV.
rule_detail: Never spell out these shortened forms.

rule_summary: Use italics for long works and compilations and roman type for songs.
rule_detail: Use italics for long works and compilations, roman type for songs

rule_summary: Place song and short-piece titles in single quotation marks and use sentence case.
rule_detail: Place the titles of songs or short, discrete pieces in single quotation marks. Use sentence case.

rule_summary: Refer to composition titles as the composer or producer gave them, or by a popular name.
rule_detail: Composition titles can be the name that the composer or producer gave the work or they can be a popular name.

rule_summary: Style hymns the same way as song titles.
rule_detail: The titles of hymns follow the same style.

rule_summary: Keep original-language titles in the original language unless they have an English title.
rule_detail: If a title is in another language, refer to it in the original language unless it has an English title. Apply the capitalisation rules of the original language.

rule_summary: Apply the capitalisation rules of the original language.
rule_detail: If a title is in another language, refer to it in the original language unless it has an English title. Apply the capitalisation rules of the original language.

rule_summary: Use ft for featured artists on song recordings.
rule_detail: Use the abbreviation ‘ft’ for artists named as featuring on song recordings.

rule_summary: Use italics and sentence case for long-work titles.
rule_detail: Use italics and sentence case for the titles of long works. If the title is in a language other than English, refer to it in the original language. Apply the capitalisation rules of that language.

rule_summary: Use italics and sentence case for album, compilation, playlist and collection titles.
rule_detail: Use italics and sentence case for the titles of albums, compilations, playlists and collections. Use the same punctuation as the original title of the album or compilation.

rule_summary: Match the punctuation of the original album or compilation title.
rule_detail: Use the same punctuation as the original title of the album or compilation.

rule_summary: Use italics and sentence case for soundtrack names.
rule_detail: For names of the soundtracks of films and video games, use italics and sentence case.

rule_summary: Use single quotation marks and roman type for individual pieces in a soundtrack.
rule_detail: For individual pieces in the soundtrack, use single quotation marks and roman type.

rule_summary: Cite the song when you use someone’s lyrics.
rule_detail: Cite the song when you use someone’s lyrics

rule_summary: Put the song name, author and year in parentheses when citing lyrics.
rule_detail: Write the name of the song, the author and the year of publication in parentheses when you cite lyrics in a text.

rule_summary: If you mention the song name in text, include only the author and year in parentheses.
rule_detail: If you mention the name of the song in the text, place only the author and the year in parentheses.

rule_summary: If you mention the author in text, place the date in parentheses immediately after the author name.
rule_detail: If you mention the author in text, put the date in parentheses straight after the author’s name.

rule_summary: Use single quotation marks and sentence case for song titles in lyric citations.
rule_detail: Use single quotation marks and sentence case for the name of the song.

rule_summary: Do not usually create a reference list for musical compositions in government content.
rule_detail: In government content, you don’t need to create a reference list to cite musical compositions. If you have a reference list already, add musical compositions to your list.

rule_summary: Add musical compositions to an existing reference list.
rule_detail: If you have a reference list already, add musical compositions to your list.

rule_summary: Check whether musical compositions need to be added to a reference list in other content types.
rule_detail: If you’re writing another type of content, check whether you need to add musical compositions to a reference list.

rule_summary: Cite plays and poetry using the author–date system.
rule_detail: Cite plays and poetry using the author–date system.

rule_summary: Attribute works with correct references so people can find the play or poem.
rule_detail: Attribute works with correct references to help people find the play or poem.

rule_summary: Make references to plays and poetry accurate and complete.
rule_detail:
References to plays and poetry must be accurate and complete so that they:

- provide all the information someone needs to identify the work properly
- comply with copyright laws.

rule_summary: Attribute copyright material you reference.
rule_detail: You must attribute copyright material you reference. This includes plays, poems and scripts.

rule_summary: Include all details required by open access licences.
rule_detail: Include all the details required by open access licences (read how to attribute Creative Commons).

rule_summary: Use italics and sentence case for play titles.
rule_detail: Write titles of plays in italics and use sentence case. This means the first word and any proper nouns have an initial capital letter.

rule_summary: Use a forward slash with spaces to show line breaks in plays.
rule_detail: When you quote lines spoken by a character in a play, use a forward slash to show line breaks appearing in the original. Insert spaces around the forward slash. If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.

rule_summary: Omit quotation marks in scripts of plays when direct speech follows the speaker's name.
rule_detail: In plays, you don’t need quotation marks if the direct speech follows the name of the speaker.

rule_summary: Cite plays using divisions such as acts, scenes and lines.
rule_detail: Use divisions for in-text citations of plays. Citations to plays are more helpful if you use divisions – acts, scenes and lines. Readers who wish to read the quote in context can use the divisions to find it in any edition of the play.

rule_summary: Use the full name of the playwright unless the surname alone identifies them.
rule_detail: Use the full name of the playwright, unless people can identify the playwright by the surname. Use roman type (not italics), lower case and numerals for divisions.

rule_summary: Do not create a reference list solely to cite plays.
rule_detail: In government content, you don’t need to create a reference list just to cite plays. If you have a reference list already, then add plays to your list. You can also add reviews of plays to the list.

rule_summary: Cite plays using the edition cited, adding the original date in parentheses when needed.
rule_detail: Use the edition of the play you cited. If the play was written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition’s publishing date.

rule_summary: Format play reference list entries as author, year, title, publisher and place.
rule_detail: Rule: Author A (Year of Original Publication/Year of Edition) *Title of play: subtitle of play*, Name of Publisher of Edition, Place of Publication.

rule_summary: Use the author–date system for in-text citations in documents with a reference list.
rule_detail: Use the author–date system for in-text citations in documents with a reference list. Include a page number after a colon if you’re citing a specific page. Use the original and edition dates if citing an old work.

rule_summary: Add reviews of plays to a reference list using the source publication's citation rules.
rule_detail: Follow the rules of citation for the source (for example, a newspaper) that published the review. Use italics for the title of the play.

rule_summary: Enclose poem titles in quotation marks.
rule_detail: Enclose titles of poems in quotation marks. If the title is part of a quotation, enclose it in double quotation marks.

rule_summary: Italicise poem titles when the poem is published as a freestanding book.
rule_detail: Poems can be published as a freestanding work in book form. In this case, follow the citation rules for books. Use italics for the poem’s title.

rule_summary: Use the author's capitalisation and punctuation for poem titles.
rule_detail: A poem’s title is part of its artistic integrity. Apply the author’s own style for capitalisation and punctuation. If the title is all lower case or all upper case, follow suit.

rule_summary: Use sentence case for poem titles when the author's style is unclear.
rule_detail: If you’re unsure of the author’s style, write the titles of poems using sentence case. Sentence case can usually replace title case (maximal capitalisation), which is often a publishing style rather than an artistic choice.

rule_summary: Italicise titles of filmpoems and preserve their original capitalisation and punctuation.
rule_detail: Italicise titles of filmpoems and use the original capitalisation and punctuation.

rule_summary: Use the first line as the title for untitled published poems.
rule_detail: Some poems do not have titles. They often become known by their first line and are usually cited that way. Even if the poem isn’t well known, use the first line as a title for untitled poems. The aim is to give readers enough information to find the poem.

rule_summary: Describe untitled unpublished spoken word poems so readers can identify them.
rule_detail: The nature of spoken word and performance poetry means the text often isn’t published. Give people enough information to appreciate and identify the poem. It’s possible a performance was recorded. To help people find it online, name the poet and the event, or quote some of the poet’s words.

rule_summary: Italicise collection titles and use quotation marks for poems within collections.
rule_detail: If a poem is part of a published collection, italicise the title of the collection and use sentence case. Use quotation marks for the poems in the collection.

rule_summary: Use a forward slash with spaces to show line breaks in poems.
rule_detail: Separate lines of poetry in a sentence with a forward slash. Insert spaces around the forward slash. If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.

rule_summary: Always cite quotations from poems in text.
rule_detail:
In government writing, mentioning the poet and the title of the poem is usually enough.

Always cite quotations in text. Follow the quotation with the poet’s name in roman type and the title of the poem in quotation marks. Use the poet’s full name, unless people can identify the poet by the surname alone.

rule_summary: Use divisions in poetry citations when available.
rule_detail:
Use divisions if they are available. Use lower case and numerals for divisions.

Divisions are cantos, verses, stanzas and lines marked and numbered on the text of some longer, older poems. Divisions are the same for all editions of these poems. This means that people who want to read a quotation in context can use divisions to find the quotation in any edition.

rule_summary: Use a reputable online version and hyperlink the poem title if the poem has no divisions.
rule_detail: If a poem does not have divisions, use a reputable online version and hyperlink the poem’s title. Users can then search to find the cited lines on the webpage.

rule_summary: Include poems in a reference list if you already have one.
rule_detail: You don’t need to create a separate reference list to cite poems, but if you have a reference list already, then add poems to your list.

rule_summary: Cite poems using the edition cited and add the original date when the poem predates the edition.
rule_detail: Use the edition of the poem you cited. If the poem was written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition’s publishing date.

rule_summary: Cite works of art using the author-date system.
rule_detail: Cite works of art using the author–date system.

rule_summary: Attribute artwork with correct references to help people find the source and relevant information.
rule_detail: Attribute artwork with correct references to help people find the source and relevant information.

rule_summary: Include works of art such as paintings, sculptures, maps, photographs and digital art in the category of works of art.
rule_detail:
Works of art include:

- paintings, drawings, prints, sculptures and ceramics
- other physical artworks such as street and neon sign art
- ephemeral and performance artwork
- antiquities – objects from ancient times such as coins and pottery
- posters, maps, clip art, photographs and cartoons
- digital art – art created using technology such as video, computer or laser beam.

rule_summary: Ensure references for works of art identify the work properly and comply with copyright laws.
rule_detail:
The reference must:

- provide all the information someone needs to identify the work properly
- comply with copyright laws.

rule_summary: Attribute copyright material you reference.
rule_detail: You must attribute copyright material you reference.

rule_summary: Attribute images and works of art as copyright material.
rule_detail: This includes images and works of art.

rule_summary: Include all details required by open access licences.
rule_detail: Include all the details required by open access licences (read how to attribute Creative Commons).

rule_summary: Read the government copyright rules in the Australian Government intellectual property manual.
rule_detail: Read the government copyright rules in the Australian Government intellectual property manual.

rule_summary: Ensure images of art meet accessibility needs.
rule_detail:
Images, including works of art, may be inaccessible to:

- people who have low vision
- people who use screen readers to access content
- users of mobile phones.

rule_summary: Size images for easier viewing.
rule_detail:
When including images of art in content, ensure they:

- are sized for easier viewing
- will display correctly on mobile phones or other small screen devices
- can be made larger by people, without loss of content or functionality
- include alt text so that descriptions of the image can be read by screen readers or mobile users wishing to limit data usage.

rule_summary: Ensure images display correctly on mobile phones or other small screen devices.
rule_detail:
When including images of art in content, ensure they:

- are sized for easier viewing
- will display correctly on mobile phones or other small screen devices
- can be made larger by people, without loss of content or functionality
- include alt text so that descriptions of the image can be read by screen readers or mobile users wishing to limit data usage.

rule_summary: Make images enlargable without loss of content or functionality.
rule_detail:
When including images of art in content, ensure they:

- are sized for easier viewing
- will display correctly on mobile phones or other small screen devices
- can be made larger by people, without loss of content or functionality
- include alt text so that descriptions of the image can be read by screen readers or mobile users wishing to limit data usage.

rule_summary: Include alt text for images.
rule_detail:
When including images of art in content, ensure they:

- are sized for easier viewing
- will display correctly on mobile phones or other small screen devices
- can be made larger by people, without loss of content or functionality
- include alt text so that descriptions of the image can be read by screen readers or mobile users wishing to limit data usage.

rule_summary: Use the author–date system with in-text citations and a full reference list.
rule_detail: The author–date system includes details for author and date in the text with a full citation in a list of references. This system is suitable for most Australian Government content.

rule_summary: Include the author’s name and date in in-text citations.
rule_detail: An in-text citation gives the author’s name and the date of publication.

rule_summary: Use the shortened form of an organisation’s name in in-text citations.
rule_detail: Use the shortened form of an organisation’s name in the in-text citation. (In the reference list, you can use the shortened form followed by the spelt-out form in parentheses.)

rule_summary: Use both authors’ names for a work by 2 authors.
rule_detail: For a work by 2 authors, include both names in the in-text citation.

rule_summary: Use the first author’s name plus et al. for a work by 3 or more authors.
rule_detail: For a work by 3 or more authors, use the first author’s name plus the Latin term ‘et al.’ (meaning ‘and others’). Don’t use italics for ‘et al.’. All authors’ names are included in the reference list.

rule_summary: Use and between names rather than an ampersand.
rule_detail: Use the word ‘and’ between names outside and inside parentheses. Don’t use the ampersand (‘&’).

rule_summary: Include page numbers only for direct quotations when the source has page numbers.
rule_detail: Include page numbers in the in-text citation only when the work has page numbers and you’re including a direct quotation. Use a colon between the date and page numbers.

rule_summary: Separate multiple works in one citation with semicolons and sort them alphabetically by author name.
rule_detail: To cite multiple works in the same in-text citation, use semicolons between each work. Arrange the works alphabetically by author name.

rule_summary: Separate multiple works by the same author in different years with commas and list them chronologically.
rule_detail: To cite multiple works published by the same author in different years, write the author’s name. Follow the name with each date of publication separated by a comma. Arrange the dates chronologically, starting with the earliest date.

rule_summary: Add letter suffixes to works by the same author in the same year.
rule_detail: To cite multiple works by the same author in the same year, put a letter after the date of each citation. Put an ‘a’ after the date of the first work you cite, then a ‘b’ after the date of the second, and so on.

rule_summary: Use n.d. when a work has no publication date.
rule_detail: For works without a date, write ‘n.d.’ (for ‘no date’) instead of the year of publication.

rule_summary: Use the References heading for reference lists.
rule_detail: A reference list includes the full details of every cited work. Use the heading ‘References’.

rule_summary: Place webpage reference lists immediately after the content.
rule_detail: On a webpage, place the reference list immediately after the content and under the heading ‘References’. In print, place the reference list after any appendices but before an index.

rule_summary: Add separate reference lists for sections by different authors or subjects.
rule_detail: If the content has sections written by different authors or on different subjects, include a reference list at the end of each section. This helps users who are interested in only one section and keeps reference lists manageable.

rule_summary: Include a reference for each source cited in text.
rule_detail: Include a reference in your list for each source you cite in text. All other sources can go in a list called ‘More reading’ or ‘More information’. This list should appear after the reference list.

rule_summary: Keep specialised sources in separate reference lists when required.
rule_detail: Some types of specialised sources, such as works of art, need their own reference list. Others, like legislation, are only included in a reference list if there are references to other types of works as well. Check each type of specialised source that you’re using to see if you need to include it in a reference list.

rule_summary: Order reference-list elements by source type and include the relevant core details.
rule_detail: References in the list will have different elements depending on the type of source. For example, when citing a book, include the name of the publisher. When citing a website, include the date you accessed it. The general order is: author or authoring organisation’s name; publishing date; title (and series or issue details); publisher details; accessed date (for digital content). Some elements have shortened forms used in referencing. Use the shortened form when appropriate. Follow the examples of author–date citations.

rule_summary: Write personal author names as family name followed by initials with no comma or full stops.
rule_detail: Write the family name of the authors, editors or translators before writing their initials. Use the original spelling for all author names. Don’t separate the family name from the initials with a comma. Don’t separate initials with full stops.

rule_summary: List all authors’ names in reference lists.
rule_detail: Unlike for in-text citations, include all of the authors’ names in a reference list.

rule_summary: Use the author name that appears on the source for changed government names.
rule_detail: Organisations change names over time. Use the name that appears on the source. For example, the Services Australia annual report for 2016–17 has the author as the Department of Human Services. That was the name of the agency at the time, so use Department of Human Services as the author when you cite the report.

rule_summary: Use the documentary–note system only when it best suits the publishing mode and user needs.
rule_detail: Choose this system only if it best suits the mode of publishing content and user needs.

rule_summary: Use superscript reference markers in text and footnotes or endnotes with full source information.
rule_detail:
The documentary–note system uses:

- superscript reference markers – numbers or symbols – in the text
- footnotes or endnotes with the full information about the source.

rule_summary: Place the corresponding superscript reference marker before each note.
rule_detail: Each note has the corresponding superscript reference marker before it.

rule_summary: Hyperlink reference markers in digital content when possible.
rule_detail: In digital content, the reference markers can be hyperlinked to help users access the note.

rule_summary: Use notes for sources cited in the text and list other sources separately.
rule_detail: Use notes for the sources you cite in the text. All other sources can be listed in a section called ‘More reading’ or ‘More information’. This list should appear at the end of a page of digital content, or at the end of a section in print.

rule_summary: Attribute all copyright material you reference.
rule_detail: You must attribute copyright material you reference. This includes text, images, video and sounds.

rule_summary: Include all details required by open access licences.
rule_detail: Include all the details required by open access licences (read how to attribute Creative Commons).

rule_summary: Use the heading 'Notes' for footnotes in digital content and for endnotes.
rule_detail: Use the heading ‘Notes’ for footnotes in digital content and for endnotes. Don’t use a heading for footnotes in print-only publications.

rule_summary: Prefer footnotes for digital content.
rule_detail: Footnotes are preferable for digital content, which has no set page length. The user can find the source information on the page they’re accessing.

rule_summary: Use footnotes sparingly in print if you only have a few citations.
rule_detail: In print, footnotes work well if you only have a few citations. If you have many citations, the footnote section at the bottom of the page can become quite long. This leaves you with little space on the page for content.

rule_summary: Use endnotes for print where page length is fixed.
rule_detail: Endnotes work better for print, which has a set page length, because they don’t take up space on a page.

rule_summary: Include a list of endnotes at the end of each section when sections have different authors or subjects.
rule_detail: In print, if you have sections written by different authors or on different subjects, include a list of endnotes at the end of each section. This helps users who are only interested in one section and keeps lists of notes manageable.

rule_summary: Use reference numbers instead of symbols in most content.
rule_detail: Use reference numbers instead of symbols in most content. Numbers are easier for users to match and they’re in an intuitive sequence.

rule_summary: Restart numbering on each page or section when content has many citations.
rule_detail: In content that uses a lot of citations, restart numbering on each page of digital content or in each section of a document.

rule_summary: Use reference symbols only for content with many numbers or where exponents could be confused.
rule_detail:
Reference symbols are best for content with many numbers, such as content with mathematical equations.

Use symbols if there’s a risk that users will confuse superscript numbers for exponents.

rule_summary: Use footnotes rather than endnotes when using symbols.
rule_detail: If you use symbols, use footnotes instead of endnotes. It’s easier for users to match symbols if they’re closer together.

rule_summary: Use reference symbols in the prescribed order.
rule_detail:
Use the symbols in this order:

- * (asterisk)
- † (dagger)
- ‡ (double dagger)
- § (section sign)
- # (hash sign).

rule_summary: Restart symbol sequences on each page and double symbols after five notes.
rule_detail: Restart the symbols on each page. If you have more than five notes on a page, double the symbols (**, ††).

rule_summary: Place reference markers immediately after quoted material, phrases, clauses or sentences.
rule_detail: Place reference markers immediately after quoted material, or after phrases, clauses or sentences. Don’t interrupt a phrase or clause with a reference marker.

rule_summary: Place reference markers after commas and other sentence punctuation.
rule_detail: Place reference markers after commas and other sentence punctuation.

rule_summary: Place reference markers before footnotes or endnotes with a single space before the note text.
rule_detail: Place reference markers before the footnote or endnote. Add a single space between the reference marker and the beginning of the reference.

rule_summary: Cite multiple works in one note rather than using more than one marker at the same location.
rule_detail: Don’t use more than one reference marker in the same place, such as when citing 2 works. Instead cite both works in one footnote or endnote, separating the entries in the note with a semicolon.

rule_summary: Format all notes consistently.
rule_detail: Format all notes consistently to help users find the source.

rule_summary: Order note elements as author, title, publisher, publishing date and accessed date where relevant.
rule_detail:
The general order is:

- author or authoring organisation’s name
- title
- publisher
- publishing date
- accessed date (for digital content).

rule_summary: Use a shortened citation for repeated references to the same work after the first mention.
rule_detail: If you cite the same work more than once, give it its own reference marker. In the notes, use a shortened form of the citation after the first mention, instead of citing the full source again.

rule_summary: Limit short citations to the author family name or organisation name plus title.
rule_detail: Short forms include only the author’s family name (or authoring organisation name) and the title of the source.

rule_summary: Use the long form first in each section when endnotes are placed at the end of each section.
rule_detail: If you’re using endnotes at the end of each section, use the long form of the reference note the first time you cite the work in that section.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms when appropriate.
rule_detail: Some elements have shortened forms used in referencing. Use the shortened form when appropriate.

rule_summary: Do not use ibid., op cit. or loc cit. for repeated citations.
rule_detail: Don’t use the Latin abbreviations ‘ibid.’, ‘op cit.’ or ‘loc cit.’ for repeated citations.

rule_summary: Write initials before family names and preserve original spelling for personal author names.
rule_detail: Write the initials of given names before writing the family name of the authors, editors or translators. Use the original spelling for all author names.

rule_summary: Do not separate initials with full stops.
rule_detail: Don’t separate initials with full stops.

rule_summary: Do not include initials in short citations.
rule_detail: Short citations include only the author’s name and the title. Don’t include initials in short citations.

rule_summary: Use et al. in short citations when a work has more than two authors.
rule_detail: Shortened forms include up to 2 author family names. When you have more than 2 authors, use the Latin term ‘et al.’ (meaning ‘and others’) in short citations. Don’t use italics for ‘et al.’.

rule_summary: Use the shortened organisation name in short citations for organisational authors.
rule_detail: If the author is an organisation, short citations use the shortened form of the organisation’s name.

rule_summary: Use title case for Act titles and italicise the first mention.
rule_detail: Use title case (maximal capitalisation) for the titles of Acts. Use italics for the first mention of these titles.

rule_summary: Use roman type for Act titles in reference lists and other long lists.
rule_detail: Use roman type for the titles of Acts in reference lists and other long lists. Blocks of italics are difficult to read.

rule_summary: Include the year in the Act title and do not use a comma before it.
rule_detail: The year the legislation is first enacted forms part of the title. Don’t use a comma before the year.

rule_summary: Include all words in an Act title, including any leading article.
rule_detail: Include all the words in the title. If the title begins with ‘The’, ‘An’ or ‘A’, make sure you include it.

rule_summary: Preserve numerals and the full stop in 'No.' exactly as written in Act titles.
rule_detail: If the Act’s title has a number, include the number exactly as written. The contraction ‘No.’ retains the full stop in this situation, which is an exception to the general rule for the shortened form for ‘number’.

rule_summary: Recognise that each Act has both a short title and a long title.
rule_detail: An Act has a short title (its name) and long title (a description). Both appear after the list of contents in the text of the Act. The long title appears as a heading before section 1 of the Act. The short title is named in section 1.

rule_summary: Use the Act's short title in italics at first mention.
rule_detail: At first mention, use the short title in italics. The first time you name the Act in text, use the short title in italics.

rule_summary: Use the short title in roman type without the year after first mention.
rule_detail: If there are subsequent mentions of the Act, use the short title in roman type without the year. Always use the short title in italics the first time you cite the Act in your text.

rule_summary: Add a shortened form in parentheses at first mention when it does more than remove the year or 'Act'.
rule_detail: Add the shortened form in parentheses at the first mention if it does more than just remove the year or the word ‘Act’ from the title.

rule_summary: Use an informal title in roman type and title case after the full title at first mention.
rule_detail: At first mention, include the informal title in parentheses after the title. Use the informal title after that. Use title case and roman type for the informal title.

rule_summary: Include series numbers when citing Acts.
rule_detail: Each Act has a series number to use in citations. Acts are also identified by series. Every Act made in a year is given a number starting at 1. The series appears in the text of the Act immediately under the title, for example ‘Act No. 137 of 1979’. Using the series in general content helps people identify the particular Act and find it in the Legislation Register. Series are also used in annotations and in notes.

rule_summary: Identify the jurisdiction of an Act.
rule_detail: It is important to identify the jurisdiction of the Act – that is, whether it is an Act of: the Commonwealth; a state or territory.

rule_summary: State the jurisdiction of an Act in a sentence when that is the chosen method.
rule_detail: The first way is to write a sentence that explains where the Act originates. This method is useful in documents that don’t mention legislation frequently.

rule_summary: Use the jurisdiction's shortened form in parentheses after the italicised title when appropriate.
rule_detail: Alternatively, insert the jurisdiction’s shortened form in roman type in parentheses after the italicised title.

rule_summary: Use the approved non-punctuated jurisdiction abbreviations.
rule_detail: Use these shortened forms: Cth (the Commonwealth); ACT (Australian Capital Territory); NT (Northern Territory); NSW (New South Wales); Qld (Queensland); SA (South Australia); Tas (Tasmania); Vic (Victoria); WA (Western Australia). None of these shortened forms for jurisdictions are punctuated.

rule_summary: Use capital letters for 'Act' and 'Acts' when referring to legislation.
rule_detail: Always use capitals for the words ‘Act’ and ‘Acts’ when you write about Acts of parliament. This avoids possible confusion in publications, even those that are mostly about the law. The words ‘act’ and ‘acts’ have several meanings.

rule_summary: Use lower case for sections, subsections, paragraphs and subparagraphs unless they begin a sentence.
rule_detail: An Act contains sections, which are often divided into subsections. Subsections might be divided into paragraphs and subparagraphs. Use lower case for these units unless they begin a sentence.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for Chapter, Part, Division and Subdivision when referring to a specific unit.
rule_detail: Sections are usually grouped into parts, divisions and subdivisions. An Act only has subdivisions if there are divisions. Some larger Acts – for example, the Criminal Code Act 1995 – group these units into chapters. Always use an initial capital for a specific reference to a ‘Chapter’, ‘Part’, ‘Division’ or ‘Subdivision’.

rule_summary: Cite units below section level at the smallest unit in Commonwealth Acts when that suits the context.
rule_detail: Commonwealth Acts cite units at the smallest unit below section level. This is a convention used by the Office of Parliamentary Counsel in legislative drafting. Some jurisdictions cite at section level. Whether to cite at section level or below will depend on the context for your content. You can choose which method to follow. Content that discuss the operation and effect of certain subsections, paragraphs and subparagraphs will cite at the smallest unit level. A general discussion about the provisions of an Act might only cite at section level. Follow in-house style. Otherwise, be guided by the type of content you’re writing, and its purpose and audience.

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop after shortened forms of Act units in citations or notes.
rule_detail: Don’t use a full stop after the shortened form when you use it in a citation or note.

rule_summary: Write titles of foreign Acts in roman type and add the country abbreviation.
rule_detail: Write all legislation from foreign countries in roman type, followed by the country abbreviation. If you’re not sure of an abbreviation, write the sentence to make the jurisdiction clear.

rule_summary: Capitalise 'Constitution' when referring to Australia's Constitution.
rule_detail: Always capitalise ‘Constitution’ when writing about Australia’s Constitution. The Constitution was enacted by the British Parliament. The long title of the Act is the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution Act 1900 (UK). Like all foreign Acts of parliament, it is written in roman type, not italics. The original version is available on the UK Government Legislation website. A compilation including amendments is on the Legislation Register.

rule_summary: Use 'the Constitution' when the reference is clear, or 'the Australian Constitution' when it is not.
rule_detail: How you refer to Australia’s Constitution depends on the context. Write ‘the Constitution’ when it’s clear that you’re referring to Australia’s Constitution. If you’re unsure, use ‘the Australian Constitution’ so there’s no confusion.

rule_summary: Use the correct abbreviations for Australian law report series.
rule_detail: Case citations rely on authorised and unauthorised law report series. Use the correct abbreviations for Australian law report series. This will help people find the judgements you cite.

rule_summary: Generally cite a law report when referring to case law.
rule_detail: When you are referring to case law, you will generally cite a law report.

rule_summary: Prefer citing an authorised law report wherever possible.
rule_detail: Wherever you can, cite an authorised law report using the relevant abbreviation.

rule_summary: Use unauthorised law report abbreviations only when no authorised version exists.
rule_detail: If the law report has no authorised version, you might need to use the abbreviations from this select list of unauthorised law report series:

rule_summary: Use roman type and title case for bill titles.
rule_detail: Style for bill titles is roman type, title case

rule_summary: Write the titles of bills in roman type rather than italics.
rule_detail: Write the titles of bills in roman type, not italics.

rule_summary: Use the short title of a bill in general.
rule_detail: In general, use the short title. Use title case (maximal capitalisation). There is no comma between the title and year.

rule_summary: Use title case for the short title of a bill.
rule_detail: In general, use the short title. Use title case (maximal capitalisation). There is no comma between the title and year.

rule_summary: Omit the comma between a bill title and the year.
rule_detail: In general, use the short title. Use title case (maximal capitalisation). There is no comma between the title and year.

rule_summary: Use sentence case for the long title of a bill.
rule_detail: The long title uses sentence case.

rule_summary: Capitalise Bill when referring to a specific bill.
rule_detail: Always use an initial capital for the word ‘Bill’ when you write about a specific bill: ‘the Bill’, ‘this Bill’.

rule_summary: Use lower case bill when referring to multiple bills.
rule_detail: If you are writing about 2 or more bills, use the lower case: ‘the bills’, ‘these bills’.

rule_summary: Use lower case bill when referring to bills in a general sense.
rule_detail: If you write about a bill or bills generally, use the lower case: ‘a bill’, ‘some bills’.

rule_summary: Use a capital B if lower case bill may confuse readers.
rule_detail: For bills, people are unlikely to find the lower case forms confusing. If there’s any chance the text is unclear to readers, use a capital ‘B’.

rule_summary: Use lower case for clause-level bill units unless they begin a sentence.
rule_detail: Bills contain clauses, which become sections when bills become Acts. Clauses can be divided into subclauses, then into paragraphs and then into subparagraphs. Use lower case for these units of a bill unless they begin a sentence.

rule_summary: Capitalise Part, Division and Subdivision in long bills.
rule_detail: Long bills have clauses grouped into parts, divisions and subdivisions. Always use an initial capital for these units, for example ‘Part 1’.

rule_summary: Use the smallest unit of text when citing Commonwealth bills below clause level.
rule_detail: Commonwealth bills refer to units below clause level using the smallest unit of text. This is a convention used by the Office of Parliamentary Counsel in legislative drafting. Some jurisdictions cite at clause level.

rule_summary: Choose clause-level or below-clause-level citation based on context.
rule_detail: Whether to cite at clause level or below will depend on the context for your content. You can choose which method to follow.

rule_summary: Cite material discussing operation and effect at the smallest unit level.
rule_detail: Content that discusses the operation and effect of certain subclauses, paragraphs and subparagraphs will cite at the smallest unit level. A general discussion about the provisions of a bill will cite at clause level.

rule_summary: Follow in-house style unless the content's type, purpose and audience indicate otherwise.
rule_detail: Follow in-house style. Otherwise, be guided by the type of content you’re writing, and its purpose and audience.

rule_summary: Write cl and cls in lower case without a full stop.
rule_detail: The shortened forms of ‘clause’ and ‘clauses’ are ‘cl’ and ‘cls’. Write them in lower case and without a full stop.

rule_summary: Use subcl and subcls as the shortened forms of subclause and subclauses.
rule_detail: The shortened forms of ‘subclause’ and ‘subclauses’ are ‘subcl’ and ‘subcls’.

rule_summary: Use either the long or shortened forms of bill units for in-text citation and notes as appropriate.
rule_detail: You can use both the long and shortened forms of units for in-text citation and notes. To decide which to use, think about the type of content, its users and the amount of legal material cited in it. If the long form better helps people understand the text, use it.

rule_summary: Use roman type and title case for explanatory material titles.
rule_detail: Explanatory material titles use roman type, title case

rule_summary: Write explanatory material titles in roman type.
rule_detail: Write titles in roman type. Use title case for the titles of explanatory material.

rule_summary: Use title case for explanatory material titles.
rule_detail: Write titles in roman type. Use title case for the titles of explanatory material.

rule_summary: Use lower case explanatory memoranda and explanatory statements in general discussion.
rule_detail: Don’t use capitals for ‘explanatory memoranda’ and ‘explanatory statements’ when writing about explanatory material in the general sense.

rule_summary: Use EM, EMs and ES as shortened forms for explanatory material after first mention.
rule_detail:
For content that mentions explanatory material often, use these shortened forms:

-
EM (explanatory memorandum)

-
EMs (explanatory memoranda or memorandums)

-
ES (explanatory statement or statements).


Write them in parentheses at first mention and use the shortened form after that.

rule_summary: Put shortened forms for explanatory material in parentheses at first mention.
rule_detail:
For content that mentions explanatory material often, use these shortened forms:

-
EM (explanatory memorandum)

-
EMs (explanatory memoranda or memorandums)

-
ES (explanatory statement or statements).


Write them in parentheses at first mention and use the shortened form after that.

rule_summary: Use explanatory material titles as in-text citations to provide context.
rule_detail: Write the titles of explanatory material as in-text citations to give context.

rule_summary: Cite cases, rulings and determinations using the correct style.
rule_detail: Cite cases, rulings and determinations using the correct style. Accuracy helps people find the source material. Specify the law report or online legal authority that hosts the relevant judgment or decision.

rule_summary: Use title case for case names.
rule_detail: Style for case names is title case, not always italics

rule_summary: Capitalise party names and use a lowercase v without a full stop between them.
rule_detail: The people or organisations named in the case are known as ‘parties’. Capitalise the names of the parties but use a lower case ‘v’ between the party names. There is no full stop after ‘v’.

rule_summary: Write case names in the form Party v Party.
rule_detail: Case names have this basic form: *Party v Party.*

rule_summary: Italicise case names when they are mentioned briefly in general content.
rule_detail: Write the name of the case in italics. This rule is for case names that are mentioned briefly in general content.

rule_summary: Use roman type for case names in reference lists and other long lists.
rule_detail: Use roman type for cases in reference lists and other long lists. Blocks of italics are difficult to read.

rule_summary: Keep case names exactly as they appear in the source.
rule_detail: Always write the names as they appear in your source.

rule_summary: Use the abbreviated title in italics and title case on first mention after the full case name.
rule_detail: Cases are often known by an abbreviated title. On first mention of the case name, follow it with the abbreviated title in parentheses. For in-text references, write this title in italics and use title case (maximal capitalisation). You can then use the abbreviated title throughout the content.

rule_summary: Do not capitalise the words the case or this case.
rule_detail: Do not capitalise ‘the case’ or ‘this case’.

rule_summary: Provide a full citation for most government writing about cases.
rule_detail: Most government writing about cases requires a full citation. Citations show people where to find the published authorised judgments and decisions of courts, commissions and tribunals. They also tell people who made the decision and what year it was made.

rule_summary: Cite reported decisions in authorised law reports when available.
rule_detail:
Reported decisions are published in authorised law reports (a report series). For example:

- Commonwealth Law Reports (CLR) contain authorised reports of High Court decisions.
- Federal Court Reports (FCR) contain authorised reports of the Federal Court.
- Industrial Reports (IR) contain decisions of the Commonwealth Fair Work Commission.

Always cite an authorised report if it is available.

rule_summary: Cite unreported decisions using the legal authority's own report series.
rule_detail:
Unreported decisions are published in report series from the legal authorities themselves. For example:

- High Court of Australia (HCA)
- Federal Court of Australia (FCA)
- Fair Work Commission (FWC).

rule_summary: Use parentheses for reported decisions that use consecutive volume numbers for the whole series.
rule_detail: Use parentheses (round brackets) for reported decisions that use consecutive volume numbers for the whole series. This means you don’t have to use the year to find the volume on the shelf.

rule_summary: Use square brackets for reported decisions that use the year as a volume number.
rule_detail: Use square brackets for reported decisions that use the year as a volume number. This means you must look for the year first, then for volume 1, 2 and so on. Other years would also have a volume 1.

rule_summary: Use square brackets for unreported decisions and omit a volume number.
rule_detail: Unreported decisions are always in square brackets. There is no volume number, as the case is not part of an authorised report series. The legal authority publishes the report in its own series.

rule_summary: List the first plaintiff and defendant in civil case titles.
rule_detail: For civil case titles, specify the first plaintiff and defendant

rule_summary: Use sentence case and italics for Re and Ex parte in civil case titles.
rule_detail: In civil cases, use sentence case and italics for ‘*Re*’ and ‘*Ex parte*’* *

rule_summary: List all defendants in criminal case titles.
rule_detail: For criminal case titles, list all defendants

rule_summary: Use R without a full stop for the Crown in criminal cases.
rule_detail: If prosecuting, the Crown is signified by an ‘R’ without a full stop. This is a Latin abbreviation for ‘*Rex*’ or ‘*Regina*’, meaning ‘King’* *or ‘Queen’.

rule_summary: Reverse the parties in a criminal appeal when the Crown is the respondent.
rule_detail: If the Crown is the respondent in a criminal appeal, reverse the parties and write ‘Appellant v The King’ (not ‘R’). If the Crown is the appellant, ‘The King’ is the first party cited.

rule_summary: Retain The King or The Queen as first published in the title.
rule_detail: 'The King' or 'The Queen' in the title is always retained as first published. The title does not change when the monarch changes.

rule_summary: Use the full citation first in notes, then cite only the first party in subsequent notes.
rule_detail: When citing cases using notes, always use a full citation as the first citation. After that, you can use the name of the first party, followed by the case citation.

rule_summary: Use at for pinpoint page numbers in notes.
rule_detail: If you use notes, write pinpoint page numbers for the citation using ‘at [page number]’.

rule_summary: Add paragraph pinpoints in square brackets after the page number.
rule_detail: You can follow the page number with the number of the relevant paragraph as it appears in the judgment. Write the paragraph number in square brackets.

rule_summary: Separate pinpoint citations with a comma.
rule_detail: Use a comma to list separate pinpoint citations.

rule_summary: Identify the judicial officer whose judgment you are citing.
rule_detail: Identify the judicial officer whose judgment you are citing. Cite the case fully and add ‘per [name] [judicial office abbreviation]’.

rule_summary: Use the specified judicial office abbreviations for judge citations.
rule_detail:
Use these abbreviations:

- J (Justice)
- JJ (Justices)
- CJ (Chief Justice)
- ACJ (Acting Chief Justice)
- FM (Federal Magistrate)
- JA (Justice of Appeal)
- DCJ (District Court Judge).

rule_summary: Cite delegated legislation using the correct style so readers can find the source material.
rule_detail: Follow the correct style to cite delegated legislation made under the authority of an Act. This will help people find the source material.

rule_summary: Use title case and roman type for regulation titles.
rule_detail: Use title case (maximal capitalisation) and roman type for the titles of regulations.

rule_summary: Capitalise Regulation or Regulations when citing a regulation title or referring to a specific regulation.
rule_detail: Always capitalise ‘Regulations’ or ‘Regulation’ when you write the title of regulations and refer to particular regulations.

rule_summary: Cite regulation titles exactly as written, including the year, and do not insert a comma before the year.
rule_detail: Cite the title exactly without altering the spelling. The year forms part of the title. There is no comma between title and year.

rule_summary: Use lower case for an individual regulation or subregulation unless it begins a sentence.
rule_detail: Use lower case when citing an individual regulation or subregulation, unless they begin a sentence.

rule_summary: Check whether a regulation title is singular or plural and cite it accordingly.
rule_detail: Some titles are singular so check to make sure you write the title correctly. A singular regulation still contains regulations and subregulations.

rule_summary: Use the shortened forms reg, regs, subreg and subregs for regulations and subregulations.
rule_detail:
The shortened forms of regulations and subregulations are:

- reg
- regs
- subreg
- subregs.

rule_summary: Use title case and roman type for other delegated legislation titles.
rule_detail:
Style for all other titles of delegated legislation is the same as for regulations.

Use roman type and title case for citations that give the full title.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital for a reference to a specific delegated instrument and lower case for a generic reference.
rule_detail: Use an initial capital for a reference to a specific instrument. Use lower case for generic references.

rule_summary: Use the long form Determination for in-text citations and notes.
rule_detail: Use the long form ‘Determination’ for in-text citations and notes.

rule_summary: Capitalise Determination when referring to a particular determination and use lower case for generic determinations.
rule_detail:
Use a capital ‘D’ when you refer to a particular determination or to determinations.

Use a lower case ‘d’ when you write about generic determinations.

rule_summary: Use the long form Order and Orders for in-text citations and notes.
rule_detail: Use the long forms ‘Order’ and ‘Orders’ for in-text citations and notes.

rule_summary: Capitalise Order for a particular order and use lower case for generic orders.
rule_detail:
