Use a capital ‘O’ when you refer to a particular order or to orders.

Use a lower case ‘o’ when you write about generic orders.

rule_summary: Use the long form Ordinance and Ordinances for in-text citations and notes.
rule_detail: Use the long forms ‘Ordinance’ and ‘Ordinances’ for in-text citations and notes.

rule_summary: Capitalise Ordinance for a particular ordinance and use lower case for generic ordinances.
rule_detail:
Use a capital ‘O’ when you refer to a particular ordinance.

Use a lower case ‘o’ when you write about generic ordinances.

rule_summary: Use the capitalised form Rule for a particular rule and lower case for generic rules.
rule_detail:
Use a capital ‘R’ when you refer to a particular rule or rules.

Use a lower case ‘r’ when you write about generic rules.

rule_summary: Use the shortened forms r, subr, rr and subrr for rules and subrules.
rule_detail:
Units for rules are ‘rules’ and ‘subrules’.

Use lower case for their shortened forms:

- r (rule)
- subr (subrule)
- rr (rules)
- subrr (subrules).

rule_summary: Refer to schedules that appear at the end of legislation using style conventions.
rule_detail: Refer to schedules that appear at the end of legislation using style conventions. Follow the drafting rules for amending and non-amending schedules so people can find the source information.

rule_summary: Use schedule-level citations for most content rather than citing the basic unit level.
rule_detail: Cite at schedule level, not the basic unit level, for most content.

rule_summary: Capitalise schedule titles with an initial capital.
rule_detail: Style for schedule titles is an initial capital

rule_summary: Capitalise 'Schedule' and 'Schedules' when naming or referring to specific schedules.
rule_detail: Always capitalise ‘Schedule’ or ‘Schedules’ when you write the title of schedules or refer to particular schedules.

rule_summary: Use 'Sch' as the shortened form for both singular and plural schedule references.
rule_detail: The shortened form is ‘Sch’ for singular and plural.

rule_summary: Treat the basic unit of an amending schedule as an item.
rule_detail: The basic unit of an amending schedule is an item

rule_summary: Divide amending schedules into parts and then into divisions.
rule_detail: Amending schedules are divided into parts, then into divisions.

rule_summary: Number parts and divisions with arabic numerals.
rule_detail: Both are given arabic numerals – for example, Part 1 Division 3.

rule_summary: Number items and subitems using parentheses for subitems.
rule_detail: Divisions contain items divided into subitems, which are given numbers in parentheses – (1), (2) and so on.

rule_summary: Do not use a shortened form for item or subitem.
rule_detail: There is no shortened form for ‘item’ or ‘subitem’.

rule_summary: Use the correct treaty style to help readers access titles, series information and detailed citations.
rule_detail: Treaties are made under international law. Follow the correct style to help people to access titles, series information and detailed citations.

rule_summary: Write treaty titles in roman type and title case.
rule_detail: Write titles of treaties in roman type with title case (maximal capitalisation). Follow the full title with the short title in parentheses and use the short title after that.

rule_summary: Add the short title in parentheses after the full treaty title and use the short title thereafter.
rule_detail: Write titles of treaties in roman type with title case (maximal capitalisation). Follow the full title with the short title in parentheses and use the short title after that.

rule_summary: Omit the year from the treaty title unless you place it in the sentence or after the short title in parentheses.
rule_detail: The year the treaty is made does not form part of the title. If you include it, write it into the sentence or add it in parentheses after the short title.

rule_summary: Use only the treaty title in general publications when that is sufficient.
rule_detail: In general publications, citing the title of the treaty is usually enough.

rule_summary: Format detailed treaty citations in the prescribed element order.
rule_detail:
Write the citation this way:

- title
- (place of making, date of making)
- [year treaty entered into force]
- treaty series and volume number
- page number in the series volume.

rule_summary: Do not use punctuation between the elements of a detailed treaty citation.
rule_detail: Don’t use any punctuation between the elements.

rule_summary: Use square brackets for the year the treaty entered into force.
rule_detail: The square brackets follow the style used in the Australian Treaties Database.

rule_summary: Use the short title in notes if it has already been introduced and used in the text.
rule_detail: If a short title has been introduced and used in the text, you can use the short title in the note.

rule_summary: Use the long title in reference list entries for treaties.
rule_detail: Always use the long title in a reference list.

rule_summary: Follow one citation style consistently for legal material.
rule_detail: There are different conventions for how to cite legal material. Follow one style consistently to help people read and use the information.

rule_summary: Cite legal material consistently and accurately.
rule_detail: Cite legal material consistently and accurately

rule_summary: Use Style Manual guidance to cite legal material in any content type.
rule_detail: Use the Style Manual guidance to cite legal material for any type of content. If you work on non-government material, follow the appropriate style for your publication.

rule_summary: Put the title first in citations unless the title is obvious from context.
rule_detail:
Unless it is obvious from the context:

- Put the title first when writing in-text citations, footnotes and endnotes.
- Follow the title with the rest of the citation.

rule_summary: Use authorised legislation titles from the relevant jurisdictional databases.
rule_detail:
Use the following databases to find the authorised titles of legislation from each Australian jurisdiction.

### Commonwealth

### States and territories

__ACT Legislation Register____NSW legislation____Northern Territory legislation____Queensland legislation____South Australian legislation____Tasmanian legislation____Victorian legislation and parliamentary documents____Western Australian legislation__

rule_summary: Use consolidated or in-force legislation when searching databases.
rule_detail: When you search or browse databases – such as the databases in the lists above – look for legislation that is ‘consolidated’ or ‘in force’. This is current law. Consolidated legislation includes all amendments made by other laws since the legislation was first enacted. It is sometimes called the ‘principal legislation’.

rule_summary: Distinguish amending legislation from consolidated legislation and use the correct version for the purpose.
rule_detail:
Amending legislation changes existing law. In legal databases, the version that was originally enacted (not including later amendments) is called ‘as made’, ‘as passed’ or, for Acts, ‘as enacted’.

The work of government has its basis in legislation. When you write about a particular policy, service or program, you often need to refer to recent changes to the relevant law (amending legislation). You will also name the legislation that currently applies (consolidated legislation). You might have to write about changes in the law over time. In this case, you would mention amending legislation that is no longer in force.

rule_summary: Use endnote history sections to track changes to consolidated legislation.
rule_detail:
The text of consolidated legislation includes information to show how it has been amended over time. Look in the endnotes named ‘Legislation history’ and ‘Amendment history’ to find this information.

A useful way to track the history of legislation, particularly for historical material not published online is to use The Office of Parliamentary Counsel (OPC) [Legislation tables](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Content/LegislationTables).

rule_summary: Use in-text citations or notes to provide accurate and complete legal details.
rule_detail: You can use in-text citations and footnotes or endnotes (notes) to provide accurate and complete details.

rule_summary: Use in-text citations to give general readers all the information they need.
rule_detail: For general content, in-text citations often give people all the information they need.

rule_summary: List the legislation or case name first in a basic note.
rule_detail: Always list the legislation or case name first in a basic note.

rule_summary: Use explanatory notes to add information that would otherwise clutter the content.
rule_detail: Explanatory notes might vary. They can be a useful way to add extra information that would otherwise clutter the content.

rule_summary: Place the corresponding superscript reference marker before each note.
rule_detail: Each note has the corresponding superscript reference marker before it. Users find the note by matching the number.

rule_summary: Use hyperlinked endnotes in digital content.
rule_detail: In digital content, the reference markers can be hyperlinked to help users access the note. Use hyperlinked endnotes in digital content.

rule_summary: Ensure reference markers and endnotes meet accessibility requirements.
rule_detail:
Reference markers and endnotes can be inaccessible to:

- people who have low vision
- people who use screen readers to access content
- users of mobile phones.

If using reference markers and endnotes, ensure they:

- are sized for easier readability
- will display correctly on mobile phones or other small screen devices
- can be made larger by users without loss of content or functionality
- can be read by screen readers.

Seek specialist advice to ensure you achieve this functionality.

rule_summary: Follow your organisation's preference for footnotes or endnotes in print.
rule_detail: In print, follow your organisation’s style preference for footnotes or endnotes. Choose the style that people will find most useful.

rule_summary: Include a legal reference list only when people need it, non-legal references already use one, or agency style requires it.
rule_detail:
Most government writers should only include a reference list if one of these applies:

- People need the list to understand the content.
- The content includes a reference list for non-legal sources.
- It is agency style to have a reference list.

rule_summary: Use separate reference list headings for legislation and legal cases.
rule_detail: Set up separate lists under the subheadings ‘Legislation’ and ‘Legal cases’*. *Arrange legislation and legal cases in alphabetical order under these headings.

rule_summary: Arrange legislation and legal cases alphabetically under their headings.
rule_detail: Set up separate lists under the subheadings ‘Legislation’ and ‘Legal cases’*. *Arrange legislation and legal cases in alphabetical order under these headings.

rule_summary: Write titles of Acts and legal cases in roman type in reference lists.
rule_detail: Write the titles of Acts and legal cases in roman type, even though they’re italicised in the text. Blocks of italics are difficult to read.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms in referencing to help readers quickly identify sources.
rule_detail: Shortened forms are used in referencing to help people quickly identify sources.

rule_summary: Set shortened forms in roman type rather than italics.
rule_detail: In referencing, present shortened forms in roman type (not italics).

rule_summary: Start shortened forms with a lower case letter.
rule_detail: Always start them with a lower case letter, even when they are derived from Latin words.

rule_summary: Use full stops only in some Latin shortened forms and in 'n.d.'.
rule_detail: Only some Latin shortened forms and ‘n.d.’ take full stops.

rule_summary: Avoid Latin shortened forms in referencing unless a publisher requires them.
rule_detail: These terms should be avoided unless they are required by a publisher.

rule_summary: Use 'ibid.' to refer to the same publication cited immediately before it.
rule_detail: The term ‘ibid.’ refers users to the same publication that was cited immediately before it.

rule_summary: Use 'ibid.' for the same page or a different page in the same publication.
rule_detail: It can refer to the same page or to a different one.

rule_summary: Use 'op. cit.' to refer back to information from different pages in the same publication.
rule_detail: The term ‘op. cit.’ refers users back to information from different pages in the same publication.

rule_summary: Use 'loc. cit.' to refer the reader back to the same page of a publication already cited.
rule_detail: The term ‘loc. cit.’ refers the reader back to the same page of a publication already cited.

rule_summary: Use 'id.' to signal that the second note is by the same author as the first note.
rule_detail: The term ‘id.’ signifies that the work in the second note is by the same author as the work in the first note.

rule_summary: Reference correctly so users can identify the sources you use.
rule_detail: Reference correctly so users can identify the sources you use.

rule_summary: Use the author–date system for most Australian Government content.
rule_detail: The author–date system includes details for author and date in the text with a full citation in a list of references. This system is suitable for most Australian Government content.

rule_summary: Use the documentary–note system only when it best suits the mode of publishing content and user needs.
rule_detail: The documentary–note system uses a symbol or number in the text to mark detailed references in footnotes or endnotes. Choose this system only if it best suits the mode of publishing content and user needs.

rule_summary: Follow one consistent style when citing legal material.
rule_detail: There are different conventions for how to cite legal material. Follow one style consistently to help people read and use the information.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms in referencing to help people quickly identify sources.
rule_detail: Shortened forms are used in referencing to help people quickly identify sources. Unlike other shortened forms, some Latin shortened forms retain full stops.

rule_summary: Organise content using clear heading levels.
rule_detail: Organise content using clear heading levels.

rule_summary: Begin each heading with keywords and keep it to the point.
rule_detail: Begin each heading with keywords and keep it to the point.

rule_summary: Write headings that are clear and short.
rule_detail: Write headings that are clear and short

rule_summary: Make headings specific to the topic they describe.
rule_detail: Clear headings are specific to the topic they describe.

rule_summary: Keep headings brief.
rule_detail: Keep them brief.

rule_summary: Write clear page titles that align with the first heading on the page.
rule_detail: Write clear page titles. This is the first topic a screen reader user will hear and should align with the first heading on the page.

rule_summary: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings.
rule_detail: Organise content with a clear structure using section headings. Clearly describe the topics or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Make sure all users can navigate all content in the intended order.
rule_detail: Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they are using. Use the same navigation elements consistently across services.

rule_summary: State the main point in each heading.
rule_detail: Headings should state the main point. This helps users find and use content in search results and on social media.

rule_summary: Use words that accurately describe the content below a heading.
rule_detail: Use words that accurately describe the content. Don’t use empty words or phrases (for example, ‘more’ or ‘related information’).

rule_summary: Keep only relevant information under a heading.
rule_detail: Only include information in the section that is relevant to the heading. If the information isn’t relevant, move it or rewrite the heading.

rule_summary: Write headings that tell the user what is in the content below.
rule_detail: Write headings that tell the user what is in the content below it.

rule_summary: Use no more than 70 characters in a heading.
rule_detail: Write headings that are no more than 70 characters (including spaces).

rule_summary: Avoid using questions as headings.
rule_detail: Avoid questions as headings

rule_summary: Start headings and subheadings with keywords.
rule_detail: Use keywords to start headings

rule_summary: Organise heading levels in a logical order.
rule_detail: Organise heading levels in a logical order

rule_summary: Write headings in a complete organised hierarchy.
rule_detail: Write headings in a complete organised hierarchy.

rule_summary: Use just one level 1 heading per webpage.
rule_detail: Use just one level 1 heading per webpage. Make it unique to your site. This helps users understand the content and find it using search engines.

rule_summary: Make every heading and subheading relate to the heading above it.
rule_detail: Every heading and subheading must relate to the heading above it so the grouping of information is logical and clear for users.

rule_summary: Avoid level 5 and deeper heading levels.
rule_detail: Avoid level 5 and deeper heading levels

rule_summary: Separate each heading from the next one with text.
rule_detail: Separate each heading from the next one by some text, even if it’s only a sentence. This helps create a clear distinction between ideas.

rule_summary: Give each heading level at least one other heading at the same level.
rule_detail: Give each heading level in a section at least one other heading at the same level. This avoids the appearance of stranded ideas.

rule_summary: Use numbered headings only for steps.
rule_detail: Use numbered headings only when they relate to a series of steps. Numbered headings can help users through a sequential structure.

rule_summary: Keep all headings in a level consistent in message and grammatical form.
rule_detail: All headings in a level should be consistent. They should have the same: overall message (for example, they are all steps in a process) grammatical form (called ‘parallel structure’).

rule_summary: Format headings so each level is visibly different.
rule_detail: Format headings so the heading levels are visibly different. This helps users scan the text.

rule_summary: Do not underline headings or any other text.
rule_detail: Don’t underline headings or any other text.

rule_summary: Use styles, tags and HTML elements to identify headings in digital content.
rule_detail: Use styles, tags and HTML elements to identify headings in digital content.

rule_summary: Use the correct HTML element for the heading level.
rule_detail: Use the correct HTML element for the heading level.

rule_summary: Apply inbuilt heading styles so they can be added automatically to navigation and contents pages.
rule_detail: Apply correct inbuilt heading styles so they can be automatically added to navigation and contents pages.

rule_summary: Use template styles if your organisation uses templates.
rule_detail: If your organisation uses templates, use the template styles.

rule_summary: Use sentence case for headings.
rule_detail: Write all headings in sentence case and use minimal punctuation

rule_summary: Use a capital letter only for the first word, proper nouns, acronyms and initialisms.
rule_detail: This means you should use a capital letter only for: the first letter of the first word the first letter of any proper nouns letters in acronyms and initialisms.

rule_summary: Do not write headings in all capital letters.
rule_detail: Don’t write headings in all capital letters as users could misread words.

rule_summary: Do not use a full stop to end headings.
rule_detail: Don’t use a full stop to end headings

rule_summary: Avoid using shortened forms in headings unless they are better known than the full term.
rule_detail: Avoid using shortened forms in headings. Don’t use a shortened form in a heading unless it is better known than the full term (for example, ‘DNA’ and ‘CSIRO’).

rule_summary: Include links only when they support user journeys or meet a user need.
rule_detail: Include links when they support user journeys and for search engine optimisation.

rule_summary: Link to something only if it helps meet the user’s need.
rule_detail: Link to something only if it helps meet the user’s need

rule_summary: Use link text that is accurate and accessible.
rule_detail: Write link text that is accurate and accessible.

rule_summary: Use text links in most cases.
rule_detail: Use text for links in most cases. These links are called anchor text.

rule_summary: Use images for links only when they meet a user need.
rule_detail: Use images for links only if they meet a user need.

rule_summary: Describe image links accurately with alt text.
rule_detail: If you do use images, accurately describe the link with [alt text](/node/49). Don’t describe the image itself.

rule_summary: Use external links only when they are essential to the user journey.
rule_detail: Use them only when they are an essential part of the user journey.

rule_summary: Include external links when the user needs to complete a task on another website or access authoritative external information.
rule_detail:
Include external links when the user needs:

- to complete their task on an external website
- to access original, authoritative information that’s provided by another government agency or external source.

rule_summary: Follow your agency’s external linking policy for non-government websites.
rule_detail: Follow your agency’s external linking policy when linking to non-government websites.

rule_summary: Avoid implying endorsement of commercial websites in external links.
rule_detail: Avoid implying endorsement to commercial websites in external links.

rule_summary: Link to sources rather than duplicating content.
rule_detail: If it does, link to it rather than duplicating it.

rule_summary: Link directly to the specific page the user needs.
rule_detail: Link directly to the specific page that the user needs to go to, not the homepage. This is known as ‘deep linking’.

rule_summary: Provide document title, file type and size when linking to files.
rule_detail:
Give users the information they need to decide whether to download the file by providing the:

- document title (not the file name)
- the file type
- the file size in kilobytes (kB) or megabytes (MB).

rule_summary: Include file details in the link text.
rule_detail: Include all this information in the link text, but remember that this adds extra information for all users. Minimise the number of links where you can.

rule_summary: Use unusual or specialist file types only if you explain them in support pages.
rule_detail: If your website uses an unusual or specialist file type, consider explaining this in your support pages.

rule_summary: Treat file type icons carefully because they can create clutter and accessibility issues.
rule_detail:
For some users, file type icons can be a useful way of recognising different kinds of files. These icons have disadvantages though:

- File type icons can create ‘clutter’ for users, including those who use assistive technology. This is especially true when there are lists of links.
- File type icons are images and require the same consideration for all
[images on websites](/node/49). This includes alternative text. - File type icons may require resources to apply and maintain. They can be difficult for content authors to use if your content management system does not apply them automatically.
- They may not support the branding or overall look and feel of your site. There is a large variety of icons available and selecting or designing an inappropriate icon may confuse users.

rule_summary: Make link text clearly indicate the destination.
rule_detail: Write link text that makes the destination clear

rule_summary: Avoid vague link text such as 'click here' or 'more information'.
rule_detail: Links like ‘click here’ or ‘more information’ don’t give the user any information about the destination.

rule_summary: Describe the destination in clear language.
rule_detail: Write link text that describes the destination in clear language.

rule_summary: Match link text to the content on the linked page.
rule_detail: Match the content on the linked page so the user knows they have reached the right place.

rule_summary: Make links understandable out of context.
rule_detail: For these reasons, links need to make sense when read out of the context of surrounding content.

rule_summary: Make link purpose clear for assistive technology users.
rule_detail: Write link text that makes the destination and purpose of the link clear.

rule_summary: Use short, frontloaded link text with the most important words first.
rule_detail: Keep them concise and put the most important words at the start of the link.

rule_summary: Write links about a single idea and link only the keywords.
rule_detail: Write links that are about a single idea, to help people to decide whether to click. Only link the keywords.

rule_summary: Put most links at the end of sentences.
rule_detail: If it’s important for users to understand all your content, put links at the end of sentences.

rule_summary: Place a link earlier in a sentence only when the whole sentence is essential.
rule_detail: If a link makes more sense at the start of a sentence, consider if everything in the sentence is essential.

rule_summary: Use concise call-to-action text or buttons that accurately describe the next step.
rule_detail: Use concise keywords for call-to-action text or buttons. Accurately describe what will happen next.

rule_summary: Use the email address as the link text for email links.
rule_detail: To link to an email address, use the email address as the link text so it’s not mistaken for a website address.

rule_summary: Use the mailto: prefix in the URL, but not in the link text.
rule_detail: Use the mailto: prefix in the URL but not in the link text.

rule_summary: Open links in the same browser tab or window by default.
rule_detail: Set links to open in the same browser window or tab by default.

rule_summary: Consider opening links in a new tab or window only after careful thought about user tasks.
rule_detail: Consider carefully how users move through your website before you set a link to open in a new tab or window.

rule_summary: Explain in the link why it will open in a new window or tab.
rule_detail: In all cases, give users contextual information in the link to explain why a link will open in a new window or tab.

rule_summary: Create internal links that support the user’s journey.
rule_detail: Create internal links that support the user’s journey

rule_summary: Use internal links to help users orient, move sequentially, and find related information.
rule_detail:
Build internal links to help users move through each stage of the user journey. Use them to help users:

- orient themselves when using your digital product or service
- move sequentially through a step-by-step task
- find information that’s directly related to a topic.

rule_summary: Include a homepage link in your main navigation.
rule_detail: You must include a homepage link in your main navigation.

rule_summary: Add homepage links to the agency name or site title and the Commonwealth Coat of Arms image.
rule_detail: Add homepage links to the agency name or site title and the Commonwealth Coat of Arms image.

rule_summary: Use lists to help users scan and understand a series of items.
rule_detail: Lists make it easy for users to scan and understand a series of items. Structure and style lists with the user in mind. Set up grammatical structure for list items with a lead-in.

rule_summary: Use a lead-in or heading to introduce every list.
rule_detail: All lists have a 'lead-in' (a phrase or sentence) or heading to introduce the list.

rule_summary: Use lists to group related information, show steps, and arrange items by importance.
rule_detail:
Use lists to:

- help users skim information
- group related information
- help users understand how items relate to each other
- show an order of steps
- arrange information by importance.

rule_summary: Distinguish ordered and unordered lists by whether order matters.
rule_detail: Lists can be ordered or numbered (the order is important) or unordered (the order is not critical).

rule_summary: Treat bullet lists as either ordered or unordered, and numbered lists as ordered.
rule_detail:
- A bullet list can be ordered or unordered.
- A numbered list is always ordered.

rule_summary: Do not use a list for a single item.
rule_detail: Don’t use a list if you have only one item. Lists are only for a series of items.

rule_summary: Use lists to make content easier to skim and navigate for accessibility.
rule_detail: Fundamental requirement: use lists to make it easier for users to skim content and navigate pages.

rule_summary: Move long lists to a separate page or appendix.
rule_detail: Move long lists to a separate page or an appendix.

rule_summary: Limit the number of lists so content remains easy to follow.
rule_detail: Content with too many lists is hard to follow. The content should flow so people can read it easily.

rule_summary: Write list items in a consistent pattern.
rule_detail: Write items in a list so they follow a consistent pattern. The pattern is made up by the number of words you use and grammatical structure.

rule_summary: Use parallel structure for list items.
rule_detail: Write list items so they have parallel structure

rule_summary: Use the same word type, tense and sentence type across list items.
rule_detail:
To make a parallel structure, use the same:

- word type to start each item (such as a noun or a verb)
- tense for each item (past, present or future)
- sentence type (such as a question, direction or statement).

rule_summary: Move repeated words in list items to the lead-in.
rule_detail: Move any words repeated in the list items to the lead-in.

rule_summary: End phrase lead-ins with a colon.
rule_detail: Phrase lead-ins always end in a colon (:).

rule_summary: Use one punctuation mark consistently for sentence lead-ins.
rule_detail: Sentence lead-ins can end in a colon or a full stop. Choose one punctuation mark and use it for all sentence lead-ins in your document. If in doubt, choose a colon; it is used more commonly.

rule_summary: Do not punctuate headings in lists.
rule_detail: Headings do not have punctuation marks.

rule_summary: Omit semicolons and commas at the end of list items.
rule_detail:
In a bullet or numbered list, don’t use:

- semicolons (;) or commas (,) at the end of list items
- ‘and’ or ‘or’ after list items.

rule_summary: Do not add 'and' or 'or' after list items unless it is critical to meaning.
rule_detail:
In a bullet or numbered list, don’t use:

- semicolons (;) or commas (,) at the end of list items
- ‘and’ or ‘or’ after list items.

Only include ‘and’ or ‘or’ after the second-last list item if it is critical to meaning – for example, you are writing in a legal context. Make sure the lead-in is a clear guide for how this kind of list should be interpreted.

rule_summary: Use 'for example', 'including' or 'includes' to introduce incomplete lists.
rule_detail: Lead-ins for incomplete lists can use ‘for example’, ‘including’ or ‘includes’.

rule_summary: Do not write 'etc.' at the end of a list.
rule_detail: Don’t write ‘etc.’ at the end of the list to show the list is incomplete.

rule_summary: Explain variables in a lead-in when items may be additional or optional.
rule_detail: When listing items that may be additional or optional, write a lead-in to explain any variables.

rule_summary: Finish each item in a sentence list with a full stop.
rule_detail: - Finish each item in a sentence list with a full stop, including the last one.

rule_summary: Finish fragment lists with a full stop only after the last item.
rule_detail: - Finish fragment lists with a full stop only after the last item.

rule_summary: Use sentence lists for series of complete sentences.
rule_detail:
### Use sentence lists for a series of complete sentences

If you have a paragraph with a series of related sentences, you can consider breaking it into a sentence list.

rule_summary: Capitalize and punctuate each sentence list item as a complete sentence.
rule_detail:
Rules for sentence lists:

- Follow normal sentence structure in each list item.
- Start each list item with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.

rule_summary: Align run-over lines with the text in sentence lists.
rule_detail: Align run-over lines with the text, not the bullet or number.

rule_summary: Avoid multiple sentences in a single bullet or numbered item.
rule_detail:
Avoid using multiple sentences in each bullet or numbered item. If you include more than one sentence per list item, consider whether:

- all list items conform to a similar pattern
- the list builds
[rhythm for readability](/node/60#rhythm_changes_can_help_or_hinder_reading).

rule_summary: Use full sentence list items for imperative items when the lead-in has no stated subject.
rule_detail: Use full sentence list items for imperative list items where there is no stated subject in the lead-in.

rule_summary: Consider breaking long in-sentence lists into fragment lists.
rule_detail: If you list more than 3 items in a sentence, consider breaking the sentence into a fragment list. This will aid readability.

rule_summary: Use fragment lists for incomplete sentences.
rule_detail:
Fragments are words, phrases or incomplete sentences. Another name for fragment lists is ‘phrase lists’.

Fragment lists have a:

- lead-in phrase or sentence followed by a colon
- list of fragments, each marked by a bullet.

rule_summary: Use fragment list items when the lead-in states the grammatical subject.
rule_detail: Use fragment list items when the lead-in states the [grammatical subject](/node/120#a_full_sentence_is_grammatically_complete).

rule_summary: Use lowercase for fragment list items unless they are proper nouns.
rule_detail:
Rules for fragment lists:

- Use lower case for the first letter of each fragment, unless it’s a proper noun.

rule_summary: Capitalize only the last fragment list item with a full stop.
rule_detail: - Add a full stop to the last list item only.

rule_summary: Use parallel structure in fragment list items.
rule_detail: - Use a grammatically parallel structure for each list item.

rule_summary: Make each fragment complete the phrase lead-in.
rule_detail: - Make sure each fragment can complete a phrase lead-in.

rule_summary: Keep phrase-lead-in fragment lists very short if the fragments run on into full sentences.
rule_detail: If list items run-on from a phrase lead-in, the list should be very short. The full sentence should be 25 words or less.

rule_summary: Keep each paragraph focused on one topic.
rule_detail: One topic per paragraph helps users absorb information.

rule_summary: Organise paragraphs under headings to help users scan content.
rule_detail: Organise them under headings to help users scan the content.

rule_summary: Write short paragraphs that begin with a topic sentence or a transition sentence.
rule_detail: Write short paragraphs, each starting with a topic sentence or a transition sentence.

rule_summary: Limit each paragraph to one topic or theme.
rule_detail: People find it easier to understand content when a paragraph contains only one topic or theme. Don’t introduce a new topic in the middle or at the end of a paragraph. Start a new paragraph instead.

rule_summary: Group introduction or summary paragraphs by theme.
rule_detail: Introduction or summary paragraphs recap ideas covered in the content. Group sentences in these paragraphs by theme – for example, to help users understand [how the content is structured](/node/75).

rule_summary: Put paragraphs in the order that makes sense to the user.
rule_detail: Put paragraphs in the order that makes sense to the user

rule_summary: Order paragraphs in a logical sequence.
rule_detail:
Order paragraphs in a logical sequence, such as:

- steps in a transaction
- the order of importance
- cause then effect
- problem then solution
- pros then cons.

rule_summary: Arrange paragraphs under brief, meaningful headings.
rule_detail: Arrange paragraphs under brief, meaningful [headings](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/structuring-content/headings). Headings help users understand what the paragraphs cover.

rule_summary: Expand on the heading in the first paragraph.
rule_detail: Expand on the heading in the first paragraph

rule_summary: Use the first paragraph to make the purpose of the content easy to find in searches.
rule_detail: Use the first paragraph to make the purpose of your content easier to find in [searches](/node/72). It should include a topic sentence and summarise the following paragraphs.

rule_summary: Use first paragraphs to improve long-form content.
rule_detail: You can use first paragraphs to improve long-form content, such as reports. First paragraphs can summarise the main points in each section.

rule_summary: Ensure the first sentence in each paragraph is a topic or transition sentence.
rule_detail: The first sentence in each paragraph should be a topic or transition sentence. A topic sentence tells people what the paragraph is about. A transition sentence explicitly connects the previous paragraph with the new.

rule_summary: Keep the sentences in a paragraph logically related to its topic.
rule_detail: Each paragraph should contain sentences that are arranged logically and relate only to the topic.

rule_summary: Make the concluding sentence summarise the topic or lead into the next paragraph.
rule_detail: A paragraph’s concluding sentence usually summarises the topic or leads into the next paragraph.

rule_summary: Begin most paragraphs with a topic sentence.
rule_detail: Most paragraphs will begin with a topic sentence. When users skim content, topic sentences help them to follow your meaning.

rule_summary: Use active voice in topic sentences.
rule_detail: To write an effective topic sentence, use [active voice](/node/204#write_in_active_voice). This approach makes the topic of the paragraph the [grammatical subject of the topic sentence](/node/120#passive_voice_changes_standard_sentence_order).

rule_summary: Start topic sentences with the paragraph topic as the grammatical subject.
rule_detail: This approach makes the topic of the paragraph the [grammatical subject of the topic sentence](/node/120#passive_voice_changes_standard_sentence_order).

rule_summary: Use a transition sentence to link a paragraph to the previous paragraph and the next topic.
rule_detail: The transition sentence includes words that link the topic of the previous paragraph with the topic to follow. This is particularly useful when the concluding sentence of one paragraph doesn’t explicitly link to the next.

rule_summary: Use transition sentences when a paragraph needs to stay connected to a larger narrative.
rule_detail: Transition sentences are also useful if it's important to stress that your new paragraph is part of a larger narrative. Transition sentences keep the narrative flowing and help users make connections.

rule_summary: Begin a new paragraph with a clear pronoun only when its referent is already obvious.
rule_detail: Be clear when using pronouns to start paragraphs

rule_summary: Make sure a paragraph-starting pronoun clearly refers to a known noun.
rule_detail: Take care if you start a paragraph with a [pronoun](/node/131). It should already be clear who or what the pronoun is referring to. If not, make sure to mention the noun in each paragraph before using the pronoun that substitutes the [noun](/node/122).

rule_summary: Keep most paragraphs to two or three sentences.
rule_detail: Keep most paragraphs to 2 or 3 sentences

rule_summary: Use short paragraphs to help people understand content.
rule_detail:
Short paragraphs help people understand content. The ideal length depends on what you are writing, for example:

- Media releases and news articles have 1 or 2 sentences in a paragraph.
- Content designed for mobile screens has no more than 2 or 3 sentences in a paragraph.
- Reports (and other long-form content) usually have a limit of 6 sentences in a paragraph.

rule_summary: Treat one- or two-sentence paragraphs as appropriate for media releases and news articles.
rule_detail: Media releases and news articles have 1 or 2 sentences in a paragraph.

rule_summary: Limit mobile-screen content to no more than two or three sentences per paragraph.
rule_detail: Content designed for mobile screens has no more than 2 or 3 sentences in a paragraph.

rule_summary: Allow reports and other long-form content to have up to six sentences per paragraph.
rule_detail: Reports (and other long-form content) usually have a limit of 6 sentences in a paragraph.

rule_summary: Break up paragraphs or sentences that are too long.
rule_detail: If your paragraphs or sentences are too long, you might be trying to say too much in one place.

rule_summary: Start a new paragraph or use an itemised list when content is too long for one paragraph.
rule_detail: Consider starting a new paragraph or using an [itemised list](/node/56). Make sure the items relate to each other and are grammatically parallel.

rule_summary: Ensure items in a list relate to each other and are grammatically parallel.
rule_detail: Make sure the items relate to each other and are grammatically parallel.

rule_summary: Use a one-sentence paragraph only carefully.
rule_detail: A paragraph can be one sentence, but be careful. Overusing single-sentence paragraphs reduces their effectiveness and can disrupt the flow of content.

rule_summary: Use responsive design so users can read content on any device.
rule_detail: Use responsive design methods to make sure users can read the content on any device. Short paragraphs are critical in responsive design: [Criterion 6. Consistent and responsive design](https://www.dta.gov.au/help-and-advice/digital-service-standard/digital-service-standard-criteria/6-consistent-and-responsive-design).

rule_summary: Test content on a mobile device first.
rule_detail: Many people do not use a desktop computer or printed material to access government services and information. Test your content on a mobile device first.

rule_summary: Write clear sentences using 25 words or fewer.
rule_detail: Write clear sentences using a maximum of 25 words

rule_summary: Use plain language in all sentences.
rule_detail: All sentences should use [ plain language](/node/204#write_plain_language_sentences). Even in technical documents, keep sentences to 25 words or less. Long sentences often cause long paragraphs.

rule_summary: Use sentences in a paragraph to develop the main idea from the topic sentence.
rule_detail:
Sentences in a paragraph develop the main idea from a topic or transition sentence by:

- giving examples or details
- comparing or contrasting
- showing cause and effect
- drawing conclusions from evidence.

rule_summary: Use tables only when they make content easier to read.
rule_detail: Use tables if they make content easier to read

rule_summary: Use a table only when there is no simpler way to present the content.
rule_detail: Use a table only if there isn’t a simpler way to present your content, such as a list, paragraph of text or diagram.

rule_summary: Use tables for exact values or very detailed information.
rule_detail: Use tables for exact values and information that is too detailed for the text.

rule_summary: Do not create a table for only one or two items.
rule_detail: Don’t create a table for only one or 2 items. Report them in the body of the text instead.

rule_summary: Design tables so users can scan the information.
rule_detail:
Design tables to allow users to:

- scan the information
- find an exact value
- compare values in different categories
- understand how you have categorised the information.

rule_summary: Do not nest tables inside other tables.
rule_detail: Don’t make tables with other tables inside them (known as ‘nested’* *tables).

rule_summary: Make tables self-explanatory.
rule_detail: Some people will look at tables before they read the text. For this reason, design tables so they are self-explanatory. You must still refer to the table in the body of the text. Place the table immediately after the reference to it in the text.

rule_summary: Provide a title, row and column headings, entries and a cross-reference for every table.
rule_detail:
You must give a table:

- a title (also called a[caption](/node/49))

- row and column headings

- information (entries)

- a cross-reference in the text. - You may also need to add notes below the table to help users understand the information and where it comes from.

rule_summary: Do not rely on colour as the only way to convey information in tables.
rule_detail: Don’t rely on colour as the only visual means of conveying information in tables.

rule_summary: Do not leave table cells empty.
rule_detail: Don’t leave cells empty. Use ‘zero’ or ‘nil’ or 'n/a' where there is no data. If it is numeric data, use the numeric zero (0). Only use zero if it is the true value.

rule_summary: Publish long and detailed tables separately or in an appendix.
rule_detail: Publish long and detailed tables separately or in an appendix.

rule_summary: Refer to tables in the text.
rule_detail: Refer to the table in the text

rule_summary: Place tables close to the text that refers to them.
rule_detail:
When using a table:

- Place the table close to where you mention it in the text and after the paragraph that refers to it. In print, the table should be on the same or facing page.

rule_summary: Match the table number in the text to the table number in the title.
rule_detail: Ensure that the table number referenced in the text matches the table number in the title.

rule_summary: Do not repeat the full table title in the text.
rule_detail: Don’t repeat the whole title of the table in the text.

rule_summary: Do not refer to the table above or below.
rule_detail: Don’t refer to ‘the table below’ or ‘the table above’.

rule_summary: Keep the text consistent with the table.
rule_detail: Ensure that the information in the text is consistent with the information in the table.

rule_summary: Avoid repeating the table text or data word for word in the surrounding text.
rule_detail: Your text comments on or interprets the table. Where possible, avoid repeating the text or data in the table word for word.

rule_summary: Avoid referring to page numbers in table references.
rule_detail: Avoid referring to a page number in the text. Page numbers can change during the publishing process.

rule_summary: Include only the information the user needs in a table.
rule_detail: Limit tables to only the information the user needs

rule_summary: Keep table content precise, relevant, credible and consistent with the title and text.
rule_detail:
Be informative, but don’t include too much information. Use only as much text or data as you need to make sure the table is easy to understand. Make sure information is:

- precise
- relevant to the title or caption
- from a credible source and backed by evidence
- consistent with how it’s presented in the text.

rule_summary: Check table data against the same information in the body text.
rule_detail: Check text and data in the table against the same information in the body of your content. It is easy to make a last-minute change to one and forget to correct the other.

rule_summary: Group table information correctly under the right headings.
rule_detail: Ensure that information in the table is correctly grouped and sits under the correct headings.

rule_summary: Use the same grammatical form for all items in a table.
rule_detail: The text or data in a table should use the same grammatical form (for example, [noun](/node/122), [noun phrase](/node/144) or [sentence](/node/204)).

rule_summary: Order table data sequentially.
rule_detail: Organise data in a sequential order. For example, order a list of names alphabetically by family name.

rule_summary: Avoid merged cells where possible.
rule_detail: Merged cells can reduce usability for many people, including screen reader users. They can be made accessible in HTML and PDF. Avoid using them in word processing applications.

rule_summary: Keep tables from becoming too long or too wide.
rule_detail:
To design usable tables:

- Don’t make tables too long or too wide.
- Consider splitting a large, complex table into smaller tables.
- If the content includes a large number of tables, consider putting them in an appendix.
- Check the structure and content of all the tables in your content. If you repeat or duplicate information, combine or delete tables.

rule_summary: Use simple language in table headings.
rule_detail: Use simple language in row and column headings for tables. This makes it easier for people to understand the information. It also helps screen reader users navigate tables.

rule_summary: Put the column headings in the first row.
rule_detail:
Structure tables so:

- the first row contains the column headings
- the first column (also known as the ‘stub’) contains the row headings.

rule_summary: Put the row headings in the first column.
rule_detail:
Structure tables so:

- the first row contains the column headings
- the first column (also known as the ‘stub’) contains the row headings.

rule_summary: Make column and row headings relate to each other.
rule_detail: The column and row headings must relate to each other so users can make sense of the information.

rule_summary: Mark up tables to distinguish header cells from data cells.
rule_detail: Mark up tables to show header cells and data cells. PDF software and web authoring programs have tools to help you with this.

rule_summary: Use the same grammatical form for each entry in a column.
rule_detail: Use the same grammatical form for each entry in a column.

rule_summary: Define column and row groups in complex tables.
rule_detail: Complex tables have header cells that span more than one column or row. If you use a complex table, you must define the column and row groups and mark up the table accordingly. This is so screen reader users can access the information in the table.

rule_summary: Repeat column headings at the top of each printed page for a table that runs over pages.
rule_detail:
If a table runs over pages when printed, ensure:

- column headings appear at the top of each page
- you repeat row headings on each page.

rule_summary: Limit the use of text boxes and callouts.
rule_detail: Limit the use of text boxes and callouts

rule_summary: Use text boxes and callouts only when they help people understand or use the information.
rule_detail: Before you include a text box or callout in your content, consider how it will help people understand or use the information.

rule_summary: Avoid overusing text boxes and callouts.
rule_detail: Don’t overuse text boxes or callouts: they become a distraction. Avoid putting content in a text box or callout just because you can’t make it fit into the flow of the text.

rule_summary: Use text boxes for supporting content rather than main text.
rule_detail: Use text boxes for supporting content, not main text

rule_summary: Place text boxes close to the text they support.
rule_detail: Text boxes sit close to the text they support.

rule_summary: Use text boxes for summaries, examples or expansions of the body text.
rule_detail:
Text boxes should contain a summary, examples or an expansion of ideas in the body of the text. This is because people:

- scan text boxes before they read the body text
- often read text boxes separately from the main body of the text.

rule_summary: Use text boxes for useful supporting information that is not part of the main content.
rule_detail:
Use text boxes to set information apart from the content. You can use text boxes for information that is useful but not part of the main content, for example:

- summaries
- checklists
- examples
- case studies
- quotes
- links to related information
- definitions.

rule_summary: Treat pull-quotes as a type of callout.
rule_detail:
Pull-quotes are a type of callout. They are often in the form of an incomplete quote and are set apart with distinct formatting. They are not the same as ‘[block quotations](/node/114#format_long_quotes_as_block_quotes_with_no_quotation_marks)’.

Pull-quotes are a device to draw the user back into the content.

rule_summary: Format pull-quotes distinctly and as incomplete quotes.
rule_detail:
Pull-quotes are a type of callout. They are often in the form of an incomplete quote and are set apart with distinct formatting. They are not the same as ‘[block quotations](/node/114#format_long_quotes_as_block_quotes_with_no_quotation_marks)’.

Pull-quotes are a device to draw the user back into the content.

rule_summary: Do not treat pull-quotes as block quotations.
rule_detail:
Pull-quotes are a type of callout. They are often in the form of an incomplete quote and are set apart with distinct formatting. They are not the same as ‘[block quotations](/node/114#format_long_quotes_as_block_quotes_with_no_quotation_marks)’.

Pull-quotes are a device to draw the user back into the content.

rule_summary: Use pull-quotes to draw the user back into the content.
rule_detail: Pull-quotes are a device to draw the user back into the content.

rule_summary: Treat sidebars as a type of callout.
rule_detail: Sidebars are a type of callout. They sit beside the main content and are more common in print publications.

rule_summary: Use the same presentation for the same type of content.
rule_detail: Use the same presentation for the same type of content. For example, present example text boxes consistently, but differently to summary information.

rule_summary: Apply the same rules for capitalisation, punctuation and lists as for other text.
rule_detail: Use the same rules for capitalisation, punctuation and lists as other text.

rule_summary: Add a heading or title to longer text boxes.
rule_detail: Longer text boxes should have a heading or title to show people the purpose of the text box at a glance. Make it distinct from the other headings in the text so you don’t interrupt the [heading hierarchy](/node/51#organise_heading_levels_in_a_logical_order).

rule_summary: Make the text-box heading distinct so it does not interrupt heading hierarchy.
rule_detail: Longer text boxes should have a heading or title to show people the purpose of the text box at a glance. Make it distinct from the other headings in the text so you don’t interrupt the [heading hierarchy](/node/51#organise_heading_levels_in_a_logical_order).

rule_summary: Use text boxes in technical or long-form content for short supporting articles.
rule_detail: In technical or long-form content, text boxes often contain short articles that support the main body of the text. Examples include case studies and descriptions of processes. They often contain [images](/node/46).

rule_summary: Number text boxes when they feature repeatedly in content.
rule_detail: Number text boxes if they feature repeatedly in content. Refer to numbered text boxes in the body text. You can use an appropriate identifier, such as ‘Box 1’ or ‘Case study 1’.

rule_summary: Refer to numbered text boxes in the body text.
rule_detail: Number text boxes if they feature repeatedly in content. Refer to numbered text boxes in the body text. You can use an appropriate identifier, such as ‘Box 1’ or ‘Case study 1’.

rule_summary: Use an appropriate identifier for numbered text boxes, such as Box 1 or Case study 1.
rule_detail: Number text boxes if they feature repeatedly in content. Refer to numbered text boxes in the body text. You can use an appropriate identifier, such as ‘Box 1’ or ‘Case study 1’.

rule_summary: Make text boxes accessible in HTML.
rule_detail: Make text boxes accessible in HTML

rule_summary: Make sure text boxes are readable by all users and on all devices.
rule_detail: Make sure boxes are readable by all users and on all devices.

rule_summary: Use the aside element for text boxes in HTML.
rule_detail: For text boxes in HTML, use the <aside> element.

rule_summary: Use aria complementary landmarks for text boxes outside the main content.
rule_detail: You can also use the <role=“complementary”> attribute to define an ARIA complementary landmark. Use this when it sits outside the <main> content.

rule_summary: Use aria region landmarks with a name when text boxes must sit within the main content.
rule_detail: Alternatively, use the <role=“region”> attribute and assign a name if the content needs to sit within the <main> section of a page.

rule_summary: Do not use text boxes in Microsoft Office documents.
rule_detail: You should not use text boxes in Word and PowerPoint. They are not accessible for most users of screen readers.

rule_summary: Do not use text boxes in Word and PowerPoint because they are not accessible to most screen-reader users.
rule_detail: You should not use text boxes in Word and PowerPoint. They are not accessible for most users of screen readers.

rule_summary: Use borders and paragraph styles instead of text boxes in Office documents.
rule_detail: Instead of text boxes, use borders and paragraph styles to highlight content visually. If these styles don't work for your content, there are other solutions.

rule_summary: Consider a one-by-one table as an alternative when text-box styles do not work.
rule_detail: A one-by-one table is an option. If your document has complex formatting, [accessible PDF (Portable Document Format)](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/format-writing-and-structure/content-formats/pdf-portable-document-format#make_pdf_content_accessible_to_all_users) may be a better option.

rule_summary: Use accessible PDF for complex Office documents if needed.
rule_detail: A one-by-one table is an option. If your document has complex formatting, [accessible PDF (Portable Document Format)](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/format-writing-and-structure/content-formats/pdf-portable-document-format#make_pdf_content_accessible_to_all_users) may be a better option.

rule_summary: Show how categories relate to one another in a hierarchy.
rule_detail: Show how categories relate to one another

rule_summary: Structure content by category so the relationship to the main idea or theme is clear.
rule_detail: Hierarchies structure content by category. They show how different categories relate to each other, and how they relate to the main idea or theme.

rule_summary: Plan what information fits under each heading.
rule_detail: Plan what information fits under each heading.

rule_summary: Plan subheadings.
rule_detail: Plan subheadings.

rule_summary: Keep the hierarchy shallow and use no more than 4 heading levels.
rule_detail: Keep the hierarchy shallow – use no more than 4 heading levels.

rule_summary: Check headings for consistency and logic.
rule_detail: Check the headings for consistency and logic.

rule_summary: Write clear page titles.
rule_detail: Write clear page titles. The title is the first thing a screen reader user will hear and is the first item to appear in search results.

rule_summary: Organise content in a clear order using section headings.
rule_detail: Organise content in a clear order using section headings. Describe the topics or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Use section headings to describe the topics or the following section.
rule_detail: Organise content in a clear order using section headings. Describe the topics or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Make sure all users can navigate content in the intended order regardless of technology.
rule_detail: Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they're using. Use the same navigation elements across services.

rule_summary: Use the same navigation elements across services.
rule_detail: Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they're using. Use the same navigation elements across services.

rule_summary: Start with what the user most needs to know.
rule_detail: The inverted pyramid starts with what the user most needs to know. Order the rest of the page from most to least important information.

rule_summary: Use the inverted pyramid for most content.
rule_detail: Use the inverted pyramid for most content

rule_summary: Structure content with a heading and details ordered from most to least important.
rule_detail:
The basic structure of the inverted pyramid is:

- a heading
- details in order, from the most to the least important.

rule_summary: Place the most important idea first, above the fold.
rule_detail: The most important idea comes first or ‘above the fold’. This is the top part of a screen or a newspaper, where people can see the main idea at a glance.

rule_summary: Use the inverted pyramid to help users scan content on any device.
rule_detail: This structure helps users scan content on any device.

rule_summary: Write the main idea in as few words as possible.
rule_detail: Write the main idea in as few words as possible. It can be a summary, a conclusion or recommendation, or the action someone needs to take.

rule_summary: Describe the main ideas in headings.
rule_detail:
Describe the main ideas in
[headings](/node/51).

rule_summary: Group content under subheadings below top-level headings.
rule_detail:
Under each of the top-level headings, group the content under
[subheadings](/node/51#organise_headings_in_a_logical_order). This helps people find supporting information.

rule_summary: Write supporting paragraphs.
rule_detail:
Write supporting
[paragraphs](/node/53).

rule_summary: Organise information in order of importance.
rule_detail: Organise the information in order of importance.

rule_summary: Use a summary or a list of recommendations in preliminary pages for long-form content.
rule_detail: For long-form content, use a summary or a list of recommendations in the preliminary pages. This helps people read the main information with ease.

rule_summary: Start with the topic sentence when structuring a paragraph using the inverted pyramid.
rule_detail: To structure a paragraph using the inverted pyramid, start with a topic sentence. Use the rest of the paragraph to explain the topic sentence.

rule_summary: Use narrative structure for long-form content and other content that benefits from a beginning, middle and end.
rule_detail: Narrative structure works well in long-form content like research reports, speeches, technical writing and books. It's also used in other digital content – for example, in human-interest news articles. In narrative structure, users expect a beginning, middle and end.

rule_summary: Use narrative structure to tell a story.
rule_detail: Use narrative structure to tell a story

rule_summary: Adapt the narrative to the genre, users, format, complexity and scope of the content.
rule_detail:
Content creators will adapt their narrative to the:

- genre
- users
- format – for example, text, video, audio, games, presentations
- complexity and scope of the content.

rule_summary: Base narratives on evidence from authoritative sources or actual events.
rule_detail: So, it’s important to ensure your narrative is based on evidence from authoritative sources or actual events.

rule_summary: Do not include details that are not factual or that assume cause and effect without evidence.
rule_detail: Government content must be evidence-based and created transparently. Don’t include details that might work with the story but aren’t factual. And never include any information based on an assumption that something happened because of something else. Without supporting evidence, any assertions you make about cause and effect will result in a biased narrative.

rule_summary: Use simple narrative structures for government writing.
rule_detail: Simple structures are best for government writing.

rule_summary: Use a linear structure when a chronology or hierarchy of importance suits the content.
rule_detail: A linear structure follows a sequence, such as a chronology or a hierarchy of importance. This can work well when reporting on projects.

rule_summary: Use a parallel structure when comparing evidence or balancing arguments.
rule_detail: A parallel structure is useful when comparing evidence because arguments can be balanced against each other.

rule_summary: Choose a combination of narrative structures when it suits the content’s purpose and format.
rule_detail: A combination of narrative structures can work, depending on the content’s purpose and its format. An example is a new policy proposal that has 2 structural elements. It may have costings, project points, dependencies and implications (parallel) laid out against an agreed timeline (linear).

rule_summary: Use a consistent beginning, middle and end in all narrative structures, including linear structures.
rule_detail: All types of narrative structure, including linear, follow a consistent pattern: they have a beginning, middle and end. In other words, the story is a 3-part sequence of events. Most users are familiar with this sequence and will expect your narrative to follow it.

rule_summary: Write the beginning, middle and end in the order that suits the content format while keeping the sequence consistent.
rule_detail: You can apply the beginning–middle–end sequence to content published in a variety of formats. While the order of the sequence usually remains the same, elements of the 3 parts will vary depending on the type of content. For example, the beginnings of a novel, a blog post and an academic article introduce their content in very different ways.

rule_summary: Start a narrative with an introduction or set-up.
rule_detail: Narrative structure starts with an introduction (‘exposition’ or ‘set-up’).

rule_summary: Use the beginning to introduce characters, set the scene, provide background and frame the topic.
rule_detail:
Use it to:

- introduce characters and set the scene
- grab attention and hook users
- give the background
- make general statements about the topic
- introduce the problem to overcome
- describe the thing that needs to change
- list what users need to do
- briefly summarise the most important information or main findings
- provide an abstract that establishes the context and summarises the main findings.

rule_summary: Write introductions so users can understand the context without reading from beginning to end.
rule_detail: A good introduction helps users decide if they need to read more. Users shouldn’t need to read from beginning to end to understand the context. An effective introduction also ensures that users don’t miss the main points in longer narratives.

rule_summary: Use the middle to provide detail, build engagement and support the position.
rule_detail: The middle (‘rising action’ or ‘plot progression’) gives users more detail.

rule_summary: Use the middle to describe action, explain events, compare evidence and lay out arguments for change.
rule_detail:
Use it to:

- describe action, introduce tension or reach a climax
- present characters with a problem or challenge
- explain what happened
- discuss new ideas
- outline the consequences of action or inaction
- give examples, tell anecdotes or present case studies
- anticipate, raise and answer questions
- compare evidence
- discuss pros and cons
- lay out the argument for change
- set expectations
- suggest what needs to be done
- present research materials, methods, results and a discussion.

rule_summary: Omit content in the middle that is not related to the primary message.
rule_detail: A good middle supports your position and continues to engage users. Omit anything that isn’t related to your primary message.

rule_summary: End a narrative with a conclusion or resolution.
rule_detail: Narrative structure has a conclusion (‘resolution’ or ‘falling action’).

rule_summary: Use the end to resolve events, summarise information, present findings and recommend next actions.
rule_detail:
Use it to:

- resolve tension and events
- describe the change to characters or circumstances
- summarise information given in the middle
- recap results
- present findings
- make recommendations
- achieve an outcome flagged earlier
- flag unresolved questions
- outline next steps in the process
- issue a call to action.

rule_summary: End a story by reinforcing the takeaway and encouraging action.
rule_detail: A good end to a story reinforces why users found the narrative so relatable. It leaves an impression, gives users a clear takeaway and encourages them to act.

rule_summary: Flag future content that will continue the narrative when needed.
rule_detail: To keep users engaged, you can also flag any future content that will continue the narrative.

rule_summary: Create a content outline to plan the story and map narrative elements across the beginning, middle and end.
rule_detail: An effective narrative tells a coherent story. Writing a content outline helps you to achieve this. Use it to plot the story and the elements of narrative structure against the beginning, middle and end.There must be a logical connection between the 3 parts. Within them, use [headings as signposts](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-manual-resources/government-writing-handbook/editors-tips/headings) and [paragraphs that flow smoothly from one to the next](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-manual-resources/government-writing-handbook/editors-tips/paragraphs-structure-and-narratives-flow).

rule_summary: Use headings as signposts and paragraphs that flow smoothly from one to the next within the narrative.
rule_detail: An effective narrative tells a coherent story. Writing a content outline helps you to achieve this. Use it to plot the story and the elements of narrative structure against the beginning, middle and end.There must be a logical connection between the 3 parts. Within them, use [headings as signposts](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-manual-resources/government-writing-handbook/editors-tips/headings) and [paragraphs that flow smoothly from one to the next](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/style-manual-resources/government-writing-handbook/editors-tips/paragraphs-structure-and-narratives-flow).

rule_summary: Make sure users can understand the relationship between people, events and design elements.
rule_detail: Users must be able to understand the relationship between any people and events you describe and the design elements you include.

rule_summary: Ensure the narrative helps users identify with the story, stay engaged, understand detail and act when required.
rule_detail:
An effective narrative will:

- ensure that users identify with the story
- keep users’ attention
- explain things using the right amount of detail
- convince users to act when required.

rule_summary: Use a sequential structure to explain steps or a specific order.
rule_detail: Use a sequential structure to explain steps or a specific order

rule_summary: Use a sequential structure for instructions.
rule_detail:
Use a sequential structure for:

- instructions – such as how-to guides, recipes and directions
- step-by-step content formats – such as forms
- reports of events – such as incident reports, histories and case studies.

rule_summary: Use a sequential structure for step-by-step content formats.
rule_detail:
Use a sequential structure for:

- instructions – such as how-to guides, recipes and directions
- step-by-step content formats – such as forms
- reports of events – such as incident reports, histories and case studies.

rule_summary: Use a sequential structure for reports of events.
rule_detail:
Use a sequential structure for:

- instructions – such as how-to guides, recipes and directions
- step-by-step content formats – such as forms
- reports of events – such as incident reports, histories and case studies.

rule_summary: Use a more direct writing style for instructions and transactions.
rule_detail: Use the right writing style. For example, instructions and transactions are more direct and use the [imperative](/node/128). Reports of events usually use the [past tense of the verb](/node/128).

rule_summary: Use the imperative mood for instructions and transactions.
rule_detail: Use the right writing style. For example, instructions and transactions are more direct and use the [imperative](/node/128). Reports of events usually use the [past tense of the verb](/node/128).

rule_summary: Use the past tense for reports of events.
rule_detail: Use the right writing style. For example, instructions and transactions are more direct and use the [imperative](/node/128). Reports of events usually use the [past tense of the verb](/node/128).

rule_summary: Write clear page titles.
rule_detail: Write clear page titles. The title is the first thing a screen reader user will hear and is the first item to appear in search results.

rule_summary: Order content in a sequence that is meaningful for the user.
rule_detail: Order the content in a sequence that is meaningful for the user.

rule_summary: Organise content in a clear order using section headings.
rule_detail: Organise content in a clear order using section headings. Describe the topics or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Describe the topics or the following section in headings.
rule_detail: Organise content in a clear order using section headings. Describe the topics or the following section in the headings.

rule_summary: Make sure all users can navigate content in the intended order.
rule_detail: Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they're using. Use the same navigation elements across services.

rule_summary: Use the same navigation elements across services.
rule_detail: Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they're using. Use the same navigation elements across services.

rule_summary: Split processes into a balanced number of steps.
rule_detail:
Split processes into balanced steps

Dividing a process into a sequence of steps can be challenging. Create the right number of steps.

- Too few steps might mean you have left out important information or grouped too many actions under one heading.
- Too many steps might mean you have divided the process into steps so small they are meaningless.

rule_summary: Create the right number of steps.
rule_detail: Dividing a process into a sequence of steps can be challenging. Create the right number of steps.

rule_summary: Group very complex processes into broader stages.
rule_detail: If the process is very complex, group steps into broader stages of the process.

rule_summary: Design menu and link items based on how users find information when combining structures.
rule_detail: If you use a combination of structures, design menu and link items based on [how users find their way through the content](/node/74#learn_how_users_search_for_information). Be consistent in the language, style and design of headings at the same level across the content.

rule_summary: Be consistent in the language, style and design of same-level headings.
rule_detail: If you use a combination of structures, design menu and link items based on [how users find their way through the content](/node/74#learn_how_users_search_for_information). Be consistent in the language, style and design of headings at the same level across the content.

rule_summary: Write clear instructions users can follow.
rule_detail: Write clear instructions users can follow

rule_summary: Keep instructional and transactional content concise and focused on what users need to do.
rule_detail: For instructional and transactional content, people want to know what they need to do. They don’t need long explanations of the process.

rule_summary: Consider whether a link would be more useful than extra explanation.
rule_detail:
If an explanation is needed, consider:

- how you can help people keep their focus
- what the minimum amount of information is
- whether a link would be more useful.

rule_summary: Help people keep their focus when an explanation is needed.
rule_detail:
If an explanation is needed, consider:

- how you can help people keep their focus
- what the minimum amount of information is
- whether a link would be more useful.

rule_summary: Use the minimum amount of information needed when an explanation is required.
rule_detail:
If an explanation is needed, consider:

- how you can help people keep their focus
- what the minimum amount of information is
- whether a link would be more useful.

rule_summary: Break a task into smaller steps if users need too much extra information to complete it.
rule_detail: If users need a lot of extra information to do a task, you might have tried to include too much in a single step. You need to break the task into smaller steps.

rule_summary: Design content with a structure that helps users navigate and understand.
rule_detail: Design content with a structure that helps the user navigate and understand.

rule_summary: Use the type of structure that suits the content and how people will need to consume it.
rule_detail: Structure supports the user as they search for information. Use the type of structure that suits the content and how people will need to consume it.

rule_summary: Organise content using clear heading levels.
rule_detail: Headings help users scan content and find what they need. Organise content using clear heading levels. Begin each heading with keywords and keep it to the point.

rule_summary: Begin each heading with keywords and keep it to the point.
rule_detail: Headings help users scan content and find what they need. Organise content using clear heading levels. Begin each heading with keywords and keep it to the point.

rule_summary: Include links when they support user journeys and search engine optimisation.
rule_detail: Links can help users navigate content. Include links when they support user journeys and for search engine optimisation. Write link text that is accurate and accessible.

rule_summary: Write link text that is accurate and accessible.
rule_detail: Links can help users navigate content. Include links when they support user journeys and for search engine optimisation. Write link text that is accurate and accessible.

rule_summary: Structure and style lists with the user in mind.
rule_detail: Lists make it easy for users to scan and understand a series of items. Structure and style lists with the user in mind. Set up grammatical structure for list items with a lead-in.

rule_summary: Set up grammatical structure for list items with a lead-in.
rule_detail: Lists make it easy for users to scan and understand a series of items. Structure and style lists with the user in mind. Set up grammatical structure for list items with a lead-in.

rule_summary: Organise paragraphs under headings to help users scan the content.
