rule_detail: One topic per paragraph helps users absorb information. Organise them under headings to help users scan the content. Write short paragraphs, each starting with a topic sentence or a transition sentence.

rule_summary: Write short paragraphs that begin with a topic sentence or transition sentence.
rule_detail: One topic per paragraph helps users absorb information. Organise them under headings to help users scan the content. Write short paragraphs, each starting with a topic sentence or a transition sentence.

rule_summary: Design accessible tables and organise data so it is easy for users to scan.
rule_detail: Tables provide a structure for complex and detailed information. Design accessible tables and organise data so it’s easy for users to scan.

rule_summary: Make text boxes, pull-quotes and sidebars accessible to everyone.
rule_detail: Text boxes, pull-quotes and sidebars draw attention from body text. Make sure they are accessible to everyone.

rule_summary: Display only blog posts from the last year.
rule_detail: We only display blog posts from the last year.

rule_summary: Link older blog items to the blog archive page.
rule_detail: For older items, please visit our [blog archive page](/blog/archive).

rule_summary: Provide an accessible PDF version of the Government writing handbook for download.
rule_detail: The *Government writing handbook* is designed for print. You can download an accessible version of the [Government writing handbook [PDF 3 MB]](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/sites/default/files/2024-12/Government%20writing%20handbook%20accessible%20PDF%202.53%20MB.pdf).

rule_summary: Review your writing and get others to check it too.
rule_detail: Review what you’ve written and, ideally, get others to check it too.

rule_summary: Check whether your writing has tics that annoy, distract or weaken readers' understanding.
rule_detail:
They’re the style habits we pick up and use unconsciously when writing. Granted, they can put the ‘you’ into writing and save it from being drearily bland. But it’s also possible your tics will:

- annoy and distract readers
- make the writing repetitive
- add redundant words
- get in the way of your message.

rule_summary: Ask colleagues whether you have writing tics that bother them.
rule_detail: Be brave and ask your colleagues if you have writing tics that drive them nuts.

rule_summary: Use spellcheck set to Australian spelling.
rule_detail: Check that your spellcheck is set to Australian spelling (*see* ‘[Always use an Australian dictionary](/node/280)’).

rule_summary: Check in-app editor suggestions against Style Manual guidance before accepting them.
rule_detail: In-app ‘Editor’ tools are useful, but some suggested edits differ from Australian Government style. Check any suggestions against Style Manual guidance and follow our style. Using one style across government helps build trust in our content.

rule_summary: Use readability tools to identify potential issues, not as the sole guide to good writing.
rule_detail:
The tools highlight areas where you can improve readability to make your writing easier to understand. Good writing is much more than that.

Don’t edit and revise your writing simply to improve a readability score. Use the tool’s editing suggestions to identify potential issues, then exercise judgement.

rule_summary: Create a word list to record preferred terms and spelling.
rule_detail: Word lists are alphabetical lists of preferred terms and spelling. They record your decisions about what term to use and when.

rule_summary: Add every checked dictionary word to your word list.
rule_detail: Add every word you check in the dictionary to the list.

rule_summary: Add acronyms and their long forms to your word list.
rule_detail: Add acronyms and their long forms.

rule_summary: Include the meanings of confusing words in your word list.
rule_detail: Include the meanings of words that trip you up (like ‘affect’ and ‘effect’).

rule_summary: Include stakeholder-preferred terms in your word list.
rule_detail: Include terms your stakeholders use or prefer.

rule_summary: Reread your work before sending it.
rule_detail: Always take a minute to reread your work before you hit send.

rule_summary: Use active voice for government writing.
rule_detail: We recommend active voice for government writing.

rule_summary: Use active voice to emphasise the person or thing doing the action.
rule_detail: Active voice emphasises the person or thing doing the action.

rule_summary: Use passive voice to emphasise the receiver of the action.
rule_detail: Passive voice emphasises the receiver of the action.

rule_summary: Prefer active voice because it is more direct than passive voice.
rule_detail: The active voice is more direct than the passive voice.

rule_summary: Use active voice to make it easier for readers to understand who is doing what.
rule_detail: This makes it easier for readers to understand who is doing what.

rule_summary: Use active voice because active sentences are usually shorter.
rule_detail: Active sentences speak more to ‘you’ and are usually shorter.

rule_summary: Provide context when using the agentless passive so readers can work out who is responsible.
rule_detail: Frustrated readers must search for some context to work out who’s responsible. Make sure you provide that context.

rule_summary: Use passive voice when you want to emphasise the receiver of the action.
rule_detail: Sometimes, passive sentences have their place. You might want to emphasise the receiver of the action.

rule_summary: Use passive voice to focus on the students and their protest rather than on the resolution.
rule_detail: Here, we want to focus on the students and their protest, not on the resolution.

rule_summary: Allow the agentless passive when no one knows who is doing the action, when the actor is implied, or when the actor does not need to be known.
rule_detail:
Even the agentless passive is acceptable when:
- no-one knows who is doing the action
- who is doing the action is implied
- we don’t need to know (or shouldn’t know) who is doing the action.

rule_summary: Use Australian English consistently when writing for government.
rule_detail: When you write for government, use Australian English and use it consistently.

rule_summary: Use the first word in a dictionary entry as the preferred spelling.
rule_detail: Our tip is to use the first word in the entry (the headword).

rule_summary: Use another dictionary option only when it matches your agency's style and then use it consistently.
rule_detail: It’s okay to use another option when it’s your agency’s style. Just make sure you always use that option (see ‘Create a word list’ in ‘Review your writing effectively’).

rule_summary: Write ‘it’s’ when you mean ‘it is’.
rule_detail: Rule 1: write ‘it’s’ when you mean ‘it is’

rule_summary: Use ‘its’ as the possessive form of the pronoun ‘it’.
rule_detail: Rule 2: write ‘its’ for the possessive form of the pronoun ‘it’

rule_summary: Do not use an apostrophe in possessive pronouns like ‘its’.
rule_detail: But pronouns like the possessive ‘its’ (e.g. my, our, yours, theirs) never have an apostrophe.

rule_summary: Use words for zero and one.
rule_detail: Use words for ‘zero’ and ‘one’.

rule_summary: Use numerals for 2 and above.
rule_detail: Use numerals for ‘2’ and above.

rule_summary: Use a comma in numbers from 1,000.
rule_detail: Use a comma in numbers from 1,000.

rule_summary: Use numerals for large numbers when precision matters.
rule_detail: Use numerals for large numbers when it’s important to be precise.

rule_summary: Combine numerals and words for large, rounded numbers from a million.
rule_detail: Combine numerals and words for large, rounded numbers from a million.

rule_summary: Allow words for numbers below 10 when following journalistic style.
rule_detail: Government writing that follows journalistic conventions can use words for numbers below 10. Media releases usually follow journalistic style.

rule_summary: Use words for numbers that start a sentence.
rule_detail: Use words for a number that starts a sentence.

rule_summary: Use numerals for zero and one in measurement and time contexts.
rule_detail: In some contexts, we write ‘zero’ and ‘one’ as numerals, not words. For example, we use numerals for units of measurement (1.05 cm) and times of day (00:45 AEDT).

rule_summary: Use numerals to compare numbers.
rule_detail:
Write ‘0’ and ‘1’:

- to compare numbers

rule_summary: Use numerals in a series of numbers.
rule_detail:
Write ‘0’ and ‘1’:

- in a series of numbers.

rule_summary: Compare numerals, not words and numerals.
rule_detail: Always compare numerals, not words and numerals.

rule_summary: Use numerals for related items in a series.
rule_detail: Always use numerals for a group of related items.

rule_summary: Use paragraphs as the basic structural units of writing.
rule_detail: Paragraphs are the basic structural units of our writing.

rule_summary: Order words into groups of ideas or discussion points.
rule_detail: - order words into groups of ideas or discussion points

rule_summary: Use paragraphs to work together to tell a coherent story.
rule_detail: - work together to tell a coherent story.

rule_summary: Start a section with a heading that signals the related paragraphs.
rule_detail: A heading says, ‘all the paragraphs that follow are related to me by meaning’. It gives readers an inkling of what the paragraphs are about.

rule_summary: Write short paragraphs that cover one topic.
rule_detail: Write short paragraphs containing one topic.

rule_summary: Begin a paragraph with a topic sentence that tells readers what it is about.
rule_detail: topic sentence that tells readers what the paragraph is about

rule_summary: Begin a paragraph with a transition sentence that connects to the previous paragraph.
rule_detail: transition sentence that smoothly connects the previous paragraph to the new.

rule_summary: Place the body of a paragraph after the topic or transition sentence.
rule_detail: After the topic or transition sentence comes the body of the paragraph.

rule_summary: Arrange sentences in a paragraph in a logical order.
rule_detail: It contains sentences in a logical order.

rule_summary: Ensure each sentence develops the topic.
rule_detail: Each sentence must contain an idea that develops the topic.

rule_summary: End a paragraph with a concluding sentence that summarises the topic or leads into the next paragraph.
rule_detail:
The paragraph’s concluding sentence usually does one of these things:

summarises the topic

leads into the next paragraph.

rule_summary: Limit paragraph length to the number of sentences appropriate for the format.
rule_detail:
The ideal number of sentences in a paragraph depends on what you are writing. For example, paragraphs for:

- media releases usually have 1 or 2 sentences
- short-form content for mobile screens have 2 or 3 sentences
- long-form content, like a report, have up to 6 sentences.

rule_summary: Allow a paragraph to be one sentence long.
rule_detail: A paragraph can also be one sentence.

rule_summary: Avoid making a paragraph one long sentence.
rule_detail: But it should never be one long sentence.

rule_summary: Apply structure to text so that paragraphs stay on one topic and sentences and paragraphs are arranged logically.
rule_detail: Apply structure to your text. Limit paragraphs to one topic and arrange sentences and paragraphs in logical order. The narrative will flow and make your writing easier to read.

rule_summary: Match each list item to the style of the lead-in.
rule_detail: The items in each list: - match the style of the lead-in - start with the same type of word (e.g. noun or verb) - have the same tense (e.g. past, present or future) - are the same type of sentence (e.g. question or statement).

rule_summary: Start list items with the same type of word.
rule_detail: The items in each list: - start with the same type of word (e.g. noun or verb)

rule_summary: Use the same tense for all list items.
rule_detail: The items in each list: - have the same tense (e.g. past, present or future)

rule_summary: Use the same sentence type for all list items.
rule_detail: The items in each list: - are the same type of sentence (e.g. question or statement).

rule_summary: Make list items parallel so they flow logically from the lead-in and read more easily.
rule_detail: This is called ‘parallel structure’ and it’s very important. It ensures that list items flow logically from the lead-in. And it shows that each item in the list is the same kind of thing. Parallel structure makes lists easier to read.

rule_summary: Do not repeat the same opening word in every list item; move repeated words to the lead-in instead.
rule_detail: A parallel structure doesn’t mean using the same word to start each list item. If you find yourself doing this, move the repeated word up to the lead-in.

rule_summary: Include only a single item in a list when there is more than one item to list.
rule_detail: If you only have one item, you don’t need a list.

rule_summary: Write in a positive, affirming way unless research shows there is a good reason not to.
rule_detail: Write in a positive, affirming way, unless research shows there’s a good reason not to.

rule_summary: Use positive sentences when asking people to do something.
rule_detail: When you ask people to do something, they are more likely to respond to a positive sentence.

rule_summary: Prefer positive sentences because they are often shorter and use fewer words.
rule_detail: You will also use fewer words. Positive sentences are often shorter than their negative counterparts.

rule_summary: Use negative sentences only when user research shows they are appropriate.
rule_detail: User research shows when it’s appropriate to use negative sentences.

rule_summary: Use negative sentences in rule-based writing such as requests, instructions or commands.
rule_detail: They usually appear in rule-based writing as requests, instructions or commands – known as ‘imperatives’.

rule_summary: Use a negative imperative sentence when supported by agency research.
rule_detail: Don’t accept friend requests from strangers. [Agency’s research supports using a negative imperative sentence]

rule_summary: Place punctuation inside quotation marks when it belongs to the quoted material.
rule_detail: The punctuation mark goes inside the closing quotation mark when it belongs to the quote.

rule_summary: Use a comma instead of a full stop at the end of a quote when attribution follows the quote.
rule_detail: When you quote a sentence that is followed by an attribution, replace the quote’s full stop with a comma.

rule_summary: Keep the full stop inside the closing quotation mark when the quote ends the sentence.
rule_detail: If the quote finishes the sentence, keep its full stop inside the closing quotation mark.

rule_summary: Place punctuation outside quotation marks when it belongs to the surrounding sentence rather than the quoted material.
rule_detail: The punctuation mark goes outside the closing quotation mark when it belongs to the sentence, not the quote.

rule_summary: Choose the stronger of two competing punctuation marks and do not use both.
rule_detail: When there are 2 punctuation marks – one for the quote and one for the sentence – decide which is stronger and use it. Don’t use both.

rule_summary: Use short sentences in plain language writing.
rule_detail: Plain language writing means using short sentences.

rule_summary: Keep sentences short so they are easier to read and understand.
rule_detail:
Short sentences are easier to:

- read and understand because they limit the scope of an idea
- scan because they have fewer words, phrases and clauses than long sentences.

rule_summary: Avoid letting a long sentence hide your message.
rule_detail: It’s easy to lose your message in a long sentence.

rule_summary: Keep sentences to an average of 15 words and no more than 25 words.
rule_detail: Keep sentences to an average of 15 words and no more than 25 words.

rule_summary: Break sentences longer than 25 words into two sentences.
rule_detail: Break sentences over 25 words long into 2 sentences.

rule_summary: Start a sentence with And, Or, or But when needed to make it shorter.
rule_detail: Start a sentence with ‘And’, ‘Or’ or ‘But’ to make a shorter sentence (it’s allowed).

rule_summary: Move words into a list if that helps avoid a long sentence.
rule_detail: Move some of the words into a list if you can’t avoid a long sentence.

rule_summary: Include a mix of sentence lengths for variety and rhythm.
rule_detail: Include a mix of sentence lengths in your document – readers like variety and rhythm.

rule_summary: Use the standard subject–verb–object order readers expect.
rule_detail: A standard sentence uses the order readers expect: subject–verb–object.

rule_summary: Rewrite or punctuate a sentence if the word order is wrong.
rule_detail: If you do get it wrong, you should rewrite or punctuate to impose order and meaning.

rule_summary: Use rewriting when you need to restore clarity by changing the sentence structure.
rule_detail: Option: rewrite

rule_summary: Use punctuation when it helps impose order and meaning.
rule_detail: If you do get it wrong, you should rewrite or punctuate to impose order and meaning.

rule_summary: Use punctuation when it helps preserve or clarify the intended emphasis.
rule_detail: If the emphasis shift doesn’t suit, then try another option.

rule_summary: Use a comma pair to mark supplementary information in a sentence.
rule_detail: We added a comma pair to mark out the supplementary information in the sentence. The meaning is clear.

rule_summary: Test whether a comma pair is usable by removing the supplementary phrase and checking that the remaining sentence is grammatically correct.
rule_detail: If we remove ‘which John arranged’, the sentence that remains is grammatically correct: ‘I have a meeting in the seminar room’. This is how to work out if you can use a comma pair.

rule_summary: Test whether a phrase is correct by removing 'you and' and checking whether the sentence still makes sense.
rule_detail: Simply take ‘you and’ out of the sentence. If the sentence still makes sense, then you’ve used the correct phrase.

rule_summary: Use 'you and me' when the phrase is the object of a verb or preposition.
rule_detail: The director prefers the words drafted by you and me. The director prefers the words drafted by me.

rule_summary: Use 'you and I' when the phrase is the subject of a verb.
rule_detail: You and I attended the meeting. I attended the meeting.

rule_summary: Apply the same subject-versus-object test when writing about yourself and another person or thing.
rule_detail: Use a similar approach when writing about yourself and someone or something else.

rule_summary: Use active voice and passive voice appropriately.
rule_detail: Active and passive voice

rule_summary: Use an Australian dictionary.
rule_detail: Always use an Australian dictionary

rule_summary: Use headings to organise content.
rule_detail: Headings

rule_summary: Use it's and its correctly.
rule_detail: It’s and its

rule_summary: Use numerals or words for numbers according to the context.
rule_detail: Numbers: choosing numerals or words

rule_summary: Write paragraphs, structure, and narratives so they flow.
rule_detail: Paragraphs, structure and narratives that flow

rule_summary: Use parallel structure in lists.
rule_detail: Parallel structure for lists

rule_summary: Use positive sentences.
rule_detail: Positive sentences

rule_summary: Use punctuation and quotation marks correctly.
rule_detail: Punctuation and quotation marks

rule_summary: Keep sentence length appropriate.
rule_detail: Sentence length

rule_summary: Use word order effectively.
rule_detail: Word order

rule_summary: Use you and me or you and I correctly.
rule_detail: ‘You and me’ or ‘you and I’?

rule_summary: Write the handbook title in italics with an initial capital when mentioning it in your content.
rule_detail: When you mention the handbook in your content, write the title in italics with an initial capital.

rule_summary: Cite the handbook whenever you paraphrase it or quote it.
rule_detail: Always cite the handbook when you paraphrase it or quote it in your content. The following examples show how to do this using our preferred referencing styles.

rule_summary: Use the noun “writing” more often than “content” in the handbook.
rule_detail: We use the noun ‘writing’ more often than ‘content’ (the term prevalent in the Style Manual). Writing is the words that are set down in a document, a draft or a complete written work.

rule_summary: Use “content” in the broader sense of government material that includes non-text elements.
rule_detail: We use ‘content’ in a broader sense. Content is the range of government material (including web content) that includes visual, auditory or interactive elements as well as text.

rule_summary: Use “text” to mean a group of words or a written work.
rule_detail: ‘Text’ is a group of words or a written work.

rule_summary: Use “document” to mean the thing people write in, amend and send for approval.
rule_detail: ‘Document’ is writing software’s equivalent of paper. It is the thing people write in, amend and send for approval.

rule_summary: Use “readers” throughout the handbook except in the two named topics, where use “users”.
rule_detail: We use ‘readers’ throughout the handbook. There are 2 exceptions. In ‘Understand who you are writing for and why’ and ‘Make it accessible and inclusive’, we use the standard term for these topics – ‘users’.

rule_summary: Use “APS” throughout the handbook to refer to the Australian Public Service, including state and territory public servants.
rule_detail: We refer to the ‘APS’, the Australian Public Service, throughout the handbook. This is for convenience. Please read APS to include public servants working for state and territory governments.

rule_summary: Build a persuasive argument with facts and logic, emotional appeal, and credibility.
rule_detail:
A good persuasive argument has 3 parts. Each part has a different role, so you need all 3:

- facts and logic – the verified evidence that your argument is true
- emotional appeal – the human side of your argument
- credibility – why you are a trusted source of information.

rule_summary: Back your argument with quantitative or qualitative evidence.
rule_detail: You must back your argument with quantitative or qualitative evidence.

rule_summary: Explain the relevance and importance of your evidence and how you collected it.
rule_detail: Be clear about the relevance and importance of your evidence, as well as how you collected it.

rule_summary: Cite any sources you quote.
rule_detail: Cite any sources you quote.

rule_summary: Describe the impact on people.
rule_detail: Be sure to describe the impact on people.

rule_summary: Explain the impact in terms of benefits to people or the human problem you want to solve.
rule_detail: Explain the impact in terms of the benefits to them, or the human problem you want to solve.

rule_summary: Demonstrate your credibility rather than stating that you should be trusted.
rule_detail: Demonstrate your credibility rather than stating you should be trusted.

rule_summary: Make sure your actions reflect your words.
rule_detail: Make sure your actions reflect your words.

rule_summary: Show that you understand and respect readers' values.
rule_detail: Show that you understand and respect readers’ values (*see* ‘[Understand who you are writing for and why](/node/260)’).

rule_summary: Use active voice and first person to show you take responsibility for your statements.
rule_detail: Use active voice and first person (‘I’, ‘we’) to show you take responsibility for your statements (*see* ‘[Active and passive voice](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/about-style-manual/government-writing-handbook/editors-tips/active-and-passive-voice)’, ‘[Relate to your readers](https://www.stylemanual.gov.au/about-style-manual/government-writing-handbook/section-1-write-your-readers/relate-your-readers)’).

rule_summary: Improve writing by practising regularly.
rule_detail: Writing is a skill that gets better with practice. Like any skill, there are ways of working that help you to improve faster.

rule_summary: Edit text after drafting content.
rule_detail: Editing text is usually easier than writing it. So, your first step is to come up with words to edit.

rule_summary: Dump ideas onto the page when starting a draft.
rule_detail: Dump everything out of your brain and onto the page.

rule_summary: Group ideas and impose a structure on the initial draft.
rule_detail: Group ideas and impose a structure on the initial chaos.

rule_summary: Remove ideas and phrases that do not fit the structure.
rule_detail: Ditch any clever ideas and favourite phrases that don’t fit into your structure (this can hurt).

rule_summary: Write down what must be included in the document.
rule_detail: Write down what needs to be in the document.

rule_summary: Use as few words as possible for each idea.
rule_detail: Use as few words as possible for each idea.

rule_summary: Reorder ideas until they are in the right sequence.
rule_detail: Shuffle the ideas around until they are in the right order.

rule_summary: Check that facts come from reliable sources.
rule_detail: Make sure you know where your facts come from. A quick search online is rarely enough. Find a reputable source and look for robust evidence.

rule_summary: Exclude material if you cannot find supporting evidence.
rule_detail: If you can’t find it, there are 2 options: Don't include the material.

rule_summary: Include material only when you clearly state the limits of its evidence.
rule_detail: If you can’t find it, there are 2 options: Include the material and be clear about the limitations of its supporting evidence.

rule_summary: Cite the sources you quote.
rule_detail: Always cite the sources you quote.

rule_summary: Include citations or references in reports and briefs.
rule_detail: Reports and briefs usually include citations or a list of references.

rule_summary: Organise the narrative in a logical order.
rule_detail: The narrative should make sense with your ideas in a logical order (*see* ‘[Tell the story and follow the flow](/node/262)’).

rule_summary: Ensure there is a clear chain of logic between facts and conclusions.
rule_detail: There must be a clear chain of logic between your facts and your conclusions.

rule_summary: Have someone else read your work.
rule_detail: The best option is to get someone else to read your work.

rule_summary: Use the read-aloud function in writing software to check your text.
rule_detail: You can also check by using the ‘read aloud’ function in writing software.

rule_summary: Follow your agency’s version control rules.
rule_detail: Follow your agency’s version control rules.

rule_summary: Create a new version at every stage if your agency requires it.
rule_detail: You might be required to create a new version at every stage of the drafting process.

rule_summary: Save a separate file at each major milestone.
rule_detail: At the very least, it’s a good idea to save a separate file each time you reach a major milestone.

rule_summary: Save a new file before and after incorporating stakeholder feedback.
rule_detail: For example, you could save a new file before and after you incorporate stakeholder feedback.

rule_summary: Keep a record of comments and changes before accepting or removing them.
rule_detail: This means you have a record of all comments and changes before accepting or removing them.

rule_summary: Agree on a tone and voice for all authors.
rule_detail: Everyone writes differently, so agree on a tone and voice that all authors should aim for (*see* ‘[Relate to your readers](/node/261)’).

rule_summary: Edit the complete document to a consistent style.
rule_detail: This makes it much easier to edit the complete document to a consistent style.

rule_summary: Assign sections to the best expert when specialised knowledge is needed.
rule_detail: How you divide tasks depends on your team’s skills and knowledge. When there is a lot of specialised knowledge, decide on the best expert to write each section.

rule_summary: Use team members’ writing and editing strengths appropriately.
rule_detail: If some team members are better at writing and some at editing, make use of these strengths.

rule_summary: Set the formality of your tone to match the relationship you want with your readers.
rule_detail: Set the formality of your tone to match the relationship you want with your readers.

rule_summary: Use a formal tone for legal writing, policies, reports and ministerial briefs.
rule_detail: Legal writing, policies, reports and ministerial briefs are usually written in a formal tone. It is professional, neutral and objective. Avoid contractions, personal pronouns, idioms, metaphors, humour and slang.

rule_summary: Use a standard tone for most government writing, including emails, letters, online services, corporate communications, media releases and articles.
rule_detail: This is the easiest tone for most people to understand and is a good choice for a lot of government writing. It is used for emails and letters, online government services, corporate communications, media releases and articles. You can use contractions and some personal pronouns. But still avoid idioms, metaphors, humour and slang.

rule_summary: Use an informal tone for social media, blogs and some newsletter articles.
rule_detail: An informal tone is best used for social media, blogs and some types of newsletter articles. You can use: contractions; personal pronouns; idioms and metaphors; humour; references to popular culture; personal anecdotes to replace case studies.

rule_summary: Be aware of your cultural assumptions when writing informally.
rule_detail: Be aware of your cultural assumptions when you write informally. Idioms, metaphors and humour can make your writing engaging but risk excluding some of your readers.

rule_summary: Use basic government voice as the basis for government writing.
rule_detail: Basic government voice is a good place to start. It is: clear; direct; objective; impartial. Use basic government voice as the basis for the many personas that can shape your writing. Different voices are useful for different types of communication.

rule_summary: Use a supportive, friendly, positive and empowering voice for instructions, guidance, explanations of policy and other external-facing content.
rule_detail: Instructions, guidance, explanations of policy, other external-facing content | Supportive, friendly, positive, empowering

rule_summary: Use an expert, factual and balanced voice for formal advice, research reports and statutory reports.
rule_detail: Formal advice, research reports and statutory reports | Expert, factual, balanced

rule_summary: Use a reasonable, authoritative and measured voice for policy documents, explanations of government decisions, general advice and information.
rule_detail: Policy documents, explanations of government decisions, general advice and information | Reasonable, authoritative, measured

rule_summary: Use a calm, authoritative and compliance-based voice for emergency instructions relating to personal or national safety.
rule_detail: Emergency instructions relating to personal or national safety | Calm, authoritative, compliance-based

rule_summary: Put the key information at the beginning of the document.
rule_detail: The answers to these questions should be clear and at the beginning of your document.

rule_summary: Use workplace labels like ‘For action’, ‘For information’ and ‘For decision’ to help readers understand what they need to do.
rule_detail: Within the workplace, phrases like ‘For action’, ‘For information’ and ‘For decision’ help readers understand what they need to do.

rule_summary: Summarise what you need in the subject line of emails.
rule_detail: In emails, summarise what you need in the subject line.

rule_summary: Use headings like ‘About this service’ or ‘Submitting your claim’ to direct readers outside the APS to the information they need.
rule_detail: For readers outside the APS, headings like ‘About this service’ or ‘Submitting your claim’ direct them to the information they need.

rule_summary: Ensure information is accurate.
rule_detail: The information in everything we write must be accurate.

rule_summary: Research and verify information when writing about topics outside your expertise or understanding.
rule_detail: But often we have to write about something that is outside our expertise or that we don’t fully understand. Research is the answer. Find experts to ask, and use trustworthy sources. Check back to make sure your information is correct. Do what you can in the time available, then flag any uncertainties in the document you send for approval.

rule_summary: Do not invent information.
rule_detail: In other words, don’t make stuff up.

rule_summary: Write only the background information that directly helps your readers.
rule_detail: Background information should directly help your readers.

rule_summary: Avoid telling readers every interesting thing you know about a topic.
rule_detail: Resist the temptation to tell them every interesting thing you know about a topic.

rule_summary: Write less rather than more when in doubt.
rule_detail: When in doubt, write less rather than more.

rule_summary: Move details you cannot remove to an attachment.
rule_detail: If you can’t bear to remove the fascinating details, move them to an attachment.

rule_summary: Understand the story's primary message before writing.
rule_detail: To tell an effective story, you must understand its primary message – the point of the story. Once you know that, you know the overall goal of your writing.

rule_summary: Structure writing so it leads the reader to the goal.
rule_detail: Work out what structure will lead your reader to the goal.

rule_summary: Start with a brief summary of the most important information.
rule_detail: Start your document with a brief summary of the most important information. Then go on to explain the information in more detail. The summary helps readers decide if they need to read the detail.

rule_summary: Use a beginning-middle-end structure for the detail.
rule_detail:
A common structure that works well for the detail is:
- the beginning state or thing we want to change
- one or more events needed to transform it
- the end state where we have the desired outcome.

rule_summary: Follow the chosen structure in order.
rule_detail: Once you have your structure, stick to it. Make sure you tell the story in order and that each paragraph flows into the next. If you forget to include something, go back and put it where it belongs in the structure.

rule_summary: Read writing aloud to check flow.
rule_detail: A good technique is to read your writing aloud or use the ‘read aloud’ function in writing software. This usually shows whether you have a clear flow from beginning to end or are jumping backwards and forwards.

rule_summary: Understand who needs your content and why they need it.
rule_detail: It is vital to understand who needs your content and why they need it.

rule_summary: Write with accessibility in mind.
rule_detail: If you don’t understand who you’re writing for, you risk writing something that isn’t accessible or useful.

rule_summary: Make sure content is accessible.
rule_detail: The APS has a legal obligation to provide information that’s accessible.

rule_summary: Understand users’ diverse needs before writing.
rule_detail: We must understand our users’ diverse needs before we start writing.

rule_summary: Use inclusive language and follow accessibility guidelines.
rule_detail: Use inclusive language and follow accessibility guidelines (*see* ‘[Make it accessible and inclusive](/node/270)’).

rule_summary: Remove barriers to access and make content welcoming.
rule_detail: People bring different perspectives to their interactions with government. It’s important to remove any barriers to access and to make content welcoming to all.

rule_summary: Respect people’s time.
rule_detail: Respect people’s time by producing content that is readable and usable.

rule_summary: Write content that is readable and usable.
rule_detail: Respect people’s time by producing content that is readable and usable.

rule_summary: Ask what users need to know and what they are trying to do.
rule_detail: Ask yourself: What do my users need to know? What are they trying to do?

rule_summary: Use user research to understand users and meet their needs.
rule_detail: One of the best ways to understand users and meet their needs is through user research.

rule_summary: Check whether people understand your content and how they interact with it.
rule_detail: It shows whether people understand your content and how they interact with it.

rule_summary: Use user research to write and design effective products and services.
rule_detail: Doing user research helps you write and design effective products and services.

rule_summary: Use existing data.
rule_detail: Use existing data.

rule_summary: Check whether your agency has done research previously.
rule_detail: Check if your agency has done research previously.

rule_summary: Use research insights to better understand your audience.
rule_detail: Any insights will help you better understand who you are writing for.

rule_summary: Encourage users to provide feedback and monitor analytics data for web content.
rule_detail: Encourage users to provide feedback, and monitor analytics data for web-based content.

rule_summary: Use feedback and analytics to respond to evolving user needs.
rule_detail: Feedback and analytics help you respond to user needs as they evolve.

rule_summary: Use information to keep content current and fit for purpose.
rule_detail: Use the information to ensure your content remains current and fit for purpose.

rule_summary: Ask colleagues who engage regularly with your intended users.
rule_detail: Ask questions and talk to colleagues who engage regularly with your intended users.

rule_summary: Use colleague input to uncover common problems, user queries and accessibility requirements.
rule_detail: This can uncover common problems, user queries and any accessibility requirements.

rule_summary: Follow Style Manual guidance.
rule_detail: Follow Style Manual guidance.

rule_summary: Write content that people can understand.
rule_detail: The manual helps you write content that people can understand.

rule_summary: Use complete sentences that contain a subject, a verb and an object where appropriate.
rule_detail: Typically, sentences contain a subject, a verb and an object. A complete sentence can stand alone and retain its meaning – it has a central idea.

rule_summary: Avoid incomplete sentences.
rule_detail: An incomplete sentence feels wrong to a reader and is a distracting irritant. For example, ‘Before I go’, ‘Behind the tree’ and ‘Where you walk’ are not complete sentences. They leave you looking for the rest of the idea.

rule_summary: Prefer simple sentences with one idea when possible.
rule_detail: Simple sentences contain one idea. Complex sentences have one idea and extra information that contributes to that idea.

rule_summary: Keep sentences to 25 words or fewer where possible.
rule_detail: Where possible, keep your sentences to 25 words or fewer. Shorter sentences lighten the reader’s cognitive load.

rule_summary: Make verbs agree with singular or plural subjects.
rule_detail: In English, the form of a verb changes according to whether the subject is singular or plural. This rule is called ‘subject–verb agreement’: the form of the verb must agree with the form of the subject.

rule_summary: Use a singular verb with collective nouns.
rule_detail: Collective nouns are singular, so they are followed by the singular form of the verb.

rule_summary: Treat staff, committee and department as collective nouns in government writing.
rule_detail: ‘Staff’, ‘committee’ and ‘department’ are nearly always collective nouns in government writing. This means you will use a singular verb.

rule_summary: Use a plural verb with committee or staff when the individuals act independently.
rule_detail: But occasionally, ‘committee’ and ‘staff’ do use a plural verb. This happens when the individual parts of these nouns (e.g. the people) operate independently. The individual parts are implied in the sentence, rather than written.

rule_summary: Treat department as a collective noun unless you are sure it is not collective.
rule_detail: It is rare for ‘department’ to use a plural verb. Treat it as a collective noun unless you’re sure it isn’t.

rule_summary: Use plain language to benefit readers.
rule_detail: Using plain language benefits everyone. It builds trust, improves comprehension and makes content accessible for more people.

rule_summary: Use plain language to open writing up rather than “dumbing it down”.
rule_detail: Using plain language is not ‘dumbing down’ your writing – it’s opening it up. Using plain language lessens the cognitive load for all readers. This includes people with high literacy levels who are time-poor and have a lot to read.

rule_summary: Understand your readers and their needs before writing plain language.
rule_detail: The most important element of plain language is understanding your readers and their needs (*see* ‘[Understand who you are writing for and why](/node/260)’).

rule_summary: Use four basic elements of plain language.
rule_detail:
After identifying your readers, we suggest you start with 4 basic elements of plain language:

- structure
- word choice
- active voice
- short sentences.

rule_summary: Choose words that let readers focus on the message rather than decoding the text.
rule_detail: When people read your writing, their focus should be on your message, not on trying to decode it. Readers have to decode words before they can decode sentences.

rule_summary: Prefer common usage and shorter words when choosing words.
rule_detail:
Two things to think about when choosing words are common usage and word length. Most people find:

- common words easier to read than uncommon words
- shorter words easier to read than longer words.

rule_summary: Use short everyday words and phrases when possible.
rule_detail: More people will understand short everyday words and phrases. The right words, used in context, can convey complex text in ways that are easy to understand.

rule_summary: Prefer simpler alternatives to long complicated words and phrases.
rule_detail: Most long complicated words and phrases have simpler alternatives.

rule_summary: Avoid jargon unless you are sure readers understand it.
rule_detail: Avoid jargon unless you’re sure readers understand it. If you can’t avoid technical terms, make sure you explain them in plain language. Large technical documents should include a glossary.

rule_summary: Explain technical terms in plain language if you cannot avoid them.
rule_detail: If you can’t avoid technical terms, make sure you explain them in plain language. Large technical documents should include a glossary.

rule_summary: Include a glossary in large technical documents.
rule_detail: If you can’t avoid technical terms, make sure you explain them in plain language. Large technical documents should include a glossary.

rule_summary: Be concise and avoid using too many words.
rule_detail:
Be concise

Don’t use too many words, even if they are short and simple. It’s important to be concise.

rule_summary: Ask whether every word is needed to make your meaning clear.
rule_detail: Concise writing is a skill that takes practice. A good first step is to ask, ‘Do I need all these words to make my meaning clear?’

rule_summary: Produce accessible content.
rule_detail: Government agencies must produce accessible content.

rule_summary: Use WCAG as the baseline accessibility standard for Australian Government digital content.
rule_detail: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the baseline accessibility standard for all Australian Government digital content.

rule_summary: Write for users so they can find and understand the content.
rule_detail: I need to find and understand the content.

rule_summary: Write for users so they can operate navigation and interface elements.
rule_detail: I need to operate the navigation and interface.

rule_summary: Write content that assistive technologies can interpret.
rule_detail: My assistive technologies can interpret the content.

rule_summary: Use respectful language that talks to the person, not their difference.
rule_detail: We must use respectful language that talks to the person, not their difference.

rule_summary: Use only terms that are necessary to give context and meaning when describing people.
rule_detail: When you describe people, only use the terms that are necessary to give context and meaning to your writing.

rule_summary: Avoid language that stereotypes age groups.
rule_detail: ‘Old people’ and ‘youths’ convey a stereotype of each age group.

rule_summary: Avoid words that suggest a stereotype or harmful effect.
rule_detail: Stereotypes are often negative and do not reflect diversity. They can have a harmful effect on people’s wellbeing.

rule_summary: Use structural elements to help readers scan and understand content.
rule_detail:
Structural elements are signposts for readers. Before they read your paragraphs, people will scan headings, tables, lists, images and links.

A successful structure supports:

- navigation
- readability
- understanding
- assistive technologies.

rule_summary: Use bullet lists to present content that benefits from clear structure and readability.
rule_detail: A list that is styled correctly is readable and conveys meaning concisely. But don’t overdo it. Too many lists will make readers feel like they’ve run an obstacle race.

rule_summary: Format sentence lists so each item is a complete sentence with an initial capital and a full stop.
rule_detail: They are named ‘sentence lists’ because each list item is a complete sentence. Each list item has an initial capital and a full stop.

rule_summary: Use a colon or a full stop in the lead-in for a sentence list, depending on whether the lead-in is a sentence or a phrase.
rule_detail:
| These hints will help your writing: | Sentence lead-in with a colon |
These hints will help your writing. | Sentence lead-in with a full stop |
To write well: | Phrase lead-in with a colon |
Hints to help your writing | Heading with no punctuation |

rule_summary: Use any type of sentence in a sentence list.
rule_detail: You can use any type of sentence in a sentence list. The list items above are all examples of positive ‘imperative’ sentences (*see* ‘[Positive sentences](/node/277)’).

rule_summary: Format fragment lists so each item starts in lower case unless it is a proper noun.
rule_detail: They are named ‘fragment lists’ because each list item is a sentence fragment. The first word of each list item is in lower case, unless it’s a proper noun.

rule_summary: End only the final item in a fragment list with a full stop.
rule_detail: Only the final list item has a full stop.

rule_summary: Make the lead-in and each fragment form a complete sentence in fragment lists.
rule_detail:
Adelaide is famous for its:
| Phrase lead-in with a colon The phrase lead-in and each fragment must make a sentence:
Ensure each sentence is 25 words or fewer

rule_summary: Format stand-alone lists with an initial capital and no full stop on each item.
rule_detail:
They are named ‘stand-alone lists’ because they can stand independently. Brochures, display material and technical content often contain stand-alone lists.

Each list item has an initial capital and no full stop.

rule_summary: Use a stand-alone list for words or phrases rather than full sentences.
rule_detail:
| Trance House Techno | Heading with no punctuation (no lead-in) List items are words or phrases (not full sentences) List items don’t need indent or bullet |
| Use indent or bullet if it helps people scan |

rule_summary: Be clear by being grammatical.
rule_detail: Be clear by being grammatical

rule_summary: Keep writing simple by using plain language.
rule_detail: Keep it simple: plain language

rule_summary: Use structure to make content readable with bullet lists.
rule_detail: Use structure to make it readable: bullet lists

rule_summary: Make content accessible and inclusive.
rule_detail: Make it accessible and inclusive

rule_summary: Use the Government writing handbook as a print-first publication.
rule_detail: The Government writing handbook is a print-first publication (ISBN 978-1-7635508-9-6).

rule_summary: Use the HTML version for the same content as the print edition, but note its limitations.
rule_detail: This HTML version has the same content, but does not include an index or reflect the layout of the original.

rule_summary: Provide an accessible PDF version for download.
rule_detail: You can download an accessible version of the Government writing handbook [PDF 3.29 MB].

rule_summary: Use an Australian dictionary to check the spelling and usage of words.
rule_detail: Use an Australian dictionary to find out how to spell and use words.

rule_summary: Use Australian English when writing for government.
rule_detail: Use Australian English when you write for government.

rule_summary: Use the first headword spelling from the dictionary entry.
rule_detail: Use the spelling of the first word in the dictionary entry (the 'headword').

rule_summary: Follow dictionary guidance on hyphenation, capitalisation, plurals, and derogatory or offensive use.
rule_detail: Dictionaries also provide guidance about hyphenation, capitalisation, plurals and derogatory or offensive use.

rule_summary: Use the spelling of the first word in the dictionary entry as the headword.
rule_detail: Use the spelling of the first word in the dictionary entry (the 'headword').

rule_summary: Write dates and times consistently.
rule_detail: Write dates and times consistently.

rule_summary: Use a colon between hours and minutes in times of day.
rule_detail: Use a colon between the hours and minutes in times of day.

rule_summary: Write am and pm in lower case with a non-breaking space before them.
rule_detail: Write 'am' and 'pm' in lower case with a non-breaking space (Ctrl+Shift+Spacebar) between the time and 'am' or 'pm'.

rule_summary: Use two zeros to show the full hour if desired, but keep the style consistent.
rule_detail: You can use 2 zeros to show the full hour, but they are not essential. Be sure to follow your chosen style consistently in your document.

rule_summary: Use the 24-hour clock for certain content and when space is limited.
rule_detail: The 24-hour clock is used for certain types of content. It's also useful when space is limited. Timetables and schedules often use the 24-hour clock. The format is 'hh:mm', or 'hh:mm:ss' if you add seconds.

rule_summary: Use noon, midday or midnight instead of 12 am or 12 pm.
rule_detail: Use 'noon', 'midday' or 'midnight' instead of '12 am' or '12 pm'. This is easier to understand.

rule_summary: Write dates in the day month year format without commas.
rule_detail: Use the 'day month year' format (with no commas) when writing dates in numerals and words. Use a non-breaking space between the day and the month.

rule_summary: Use a non-breaking space between the day and the month.
rule_detail: Use a non-breaking space between the day and the month.

rule_summary: Use numeric dates only when space is limited.
rule_detail: Only use numeric dates when space is limited (such as in tables). Numeric dates can be confusing because their order and format differs between countries.

rule_summary: Separate Australian numeric dates with an unspaced forward slash in d/m/yyyy format.
rule_detail: Australian style is to separate numerals with an unspaced forward slash, using the format 'd/m/yyyy'. This format uses single digits for days and months and 4 digits for the year.

rule_summary: Use two-digit years only in the specified exception cases.
rule_detail:
There is an exception. You can use 2 digits for the year ('dd/mm/yy') when:

- writing financial data
- it's clear which century you're referring to
- users understand that the order is 'day/month/year'.

rule_summary: Write decades with an s and no apostrophe.
rule_detail: Write decades with an 's' on the end. Don't use an apostrophe to show the plural.

rule_summary: Use from ... to or between ... and instead of an en dash for spans of years.
rule_detail: Use 'from … to' or 'between … and' instead of an en dash for spans of years.

rule_summary: Use an en dash for specified date-span exceptions.
rule_detail:
There are exceptions. Use an en dash in date spans for:

- financial years
- calendar years
- titles of publications and programs
- terms of office
- lifespans (birth and death)
- content in limited space.

rule_summary: Allow either date-first or time-first order when combining dates and times, but keep the day of week adjacent to the date.
rule_detail: You can choose whether the date or the time comes first when you combine them. There is no fixed rule. But if you add the day of the week, just make sure the time doesn't come between it and the date.

rule_summary: Use standard abbreviations for days and months when space is limited.
rule_detail: You can use standard abbreviations for days and months when you have limited space. This might be in a table, social media post or display text. Don't forget to add a non-breaking space before 'am' and 'pm' and between the day and month.

rule_summary: Use lists to help users scan and understand a series of items.
rule_detail: Use lists to make it easy for users to scan and understand a series of items.

rule_summary: Use numbered lists when the order of items is important.
rule_detail: Use them when the order of list items is important.

rule_summary: Use bullet lists when the order of items is not important.
rule_detail: Use them when the order of list items isn't important.

rule_summary: Do not use and, or, semicolons or commas at the end of list items in general content.
rule_detail: Lists in general content don't need 'and', 'or', semicolons or commas at the end of list items.

rule_summary: Use sentence lists for a series of complete sentences.
rule_detail: Use sentence lists for a series of complete sentences.

rule_summary: Allow sentence lists to use a sentence lead-in with a colon.
rule_detail:
Sentence lists can have a:

- sentence lead-in with a colon

rule_summary: Allow sentence lists to use a sentence lead-in with a full stop.
rule_detail:
Sentence lists can have a:

- sentence lead-in with a full stop

rule_summary: Allow sentence lists to use a phrase lead-in with a colon.
rule_detail:
Sentence lists can have a:

- phrase lead-in with a colon

rule_summary: Allow sentence lists to use a heading with no punctuation.
rule_detail:
Sentence lists can have a:

- heading with no punctuation.

rule_summary: Follow normal sentence structure in each sentence list item.
rule_detail: Follow normal sentence structure in each list item.

rule_summary: Start each sentence list item with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.
rule_detail: Start each list item with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.

rule_summary: Align run-over lines with the text, not the bullet or number.
rule_detail: Align run-over lines with the text, not the bullet or number.

rule_summary: Avoid using multiple sentences in each bullet or numbered item.
rule_detail: Avoid using multiple sentences in each bullet or numbered item.

rule_summary: Use fragment lists for a series of incomplete sentences.
rule_detail: Use fragment lists for a series of incomplete sentences.

rule_summary: Allow fragment lists to use a sentence lead-in with a colon.
rule_detail:
Fragment lists can have a:

- sentence lead-in with a colon

rule_summary: Allow fragment lists to use a phrase lead-in with a colon.
rule_detail:
Fragment lists can have a:

- phrase lead-in with a colon.

rule_summary: Make a phrase lead-in and each fragment form a complete sentence.
rule_detail: A phrase lead-in and each fragment must make a complete sentence.

rule_summary: Keep the resulting sentence from a fragment list to no more than 25 words.
rule_detail: Keep the resulting sentence to no more than 25 words.

rule_summary: Start each fragment with a lower-case letter unless it begins with a proper noun.
rule_detail:
Fragment lists have a:

- lower-case letter for the first letter of each fragment, unless the fragment begins with a proper noun

rule_summary: Put a full stop after the last fragment only.
rule_detail:
Fragment lists have a:

- full stop for the last item only.

rule_summary: Use stand-alone lists for a series of items under a heading with no lead-in, colon or full stop.
rule_detail: Use stand-alone lists for a series of items under a heading (no lead-in, colon or full stop).

rule_summary: Allow stand-alone list items to use indents, no indents or bullets.
rule_detail:
List items can have:

- indents
- no indents
- bullets.

rule_summary: Start stand-alone list items with a capital letter.
rule_detail:
Stand-alone lists have:

- a capital letter to start list items

rule_summary: Do not use full stops after stand-alone list items.
rule_detail:
Stand-alone lists have:

- no full stops after list items.

rule_summary: Use numbered lists when the order matters.
rule_detail: Use numbered (ordered) lists when the order is important.

rule_summary: Use numbered lists for instructions, an order of events or ranked items.
rule_detail: You might use numbered lists for instructions, an order of events or when you rank items.

rule_summary: Try to use single-level lists in general content.
rule_detail: Try to use single-level lists in general content.

rule_summary: Use en dashes, not hollow bullets, for the second level of multilevel lists.
rule_detail: Use en dashes (not hollow bullets) for the second level.

rule_summary: Use the same symbol, number or letter for the same level in each multilevel list.
rule_detail: Use the same symbol, number or letter for the same level in each list.

rule_summary: Use numerals for numbers 2 and above.
rule_detail: Use numerals for '2' and above

rule_summary: Write zero and one in words.
rule_detail: Write the numbers 'zero' and 'one' in words

rule_summary: Use words for numbers below 10 in government writing that follows journalistic conventions.
rule_detail: You can use words for numbers below 10 in government writing that follows journalistic conventions (e.g. media releases).

rule_summary: Write a number in words when it starts a sentence.
rule_detail: Use words for a number that starts a sentence.

rule_summary: Use numerals 0 and 1 for units of measurement, times of day, comparisons, and number series.
rule_detail:
Write the numerals '0' and '1':

- for units of measurement
- for times of day
- to compare numbers
- in a series of numbers.

rule_summary: Use commas in numbers with four or more digits.
rule_detail: Use commas in numbers with 4 or more digits. Separate the digits into groups of 3 (working from right to left).

rule_summary: Use words for fractions when only a general idea of values is needed, for proper nouns that include a number in words, and for figures of speech.
rule_detail:
Always use words for:

- fractions when users need only a general idea of values
- proper nouns that include a number in words
- figures of speech.

rule_summary: Use numerals for large numbers when precision matters, mathematical relationships, percentages, centuries, and decimals.
rule_detail:
Always use numerals:

- for large numbers when it's important to be precise
- to show mathematical relationships
- when using the percentage symbol
- for centuries
- for decimals.

rule_summary: Use words and numerals for large rounded numbers from a million and for ordinal numbers.
rule_detail:
Use words and numerals for:

- large rounded numbers from a million
- ordinal numbers.

rule_summary: Use numerals and symbols for amounts of money unless the amount is an approximation.
rule_detail: Use numerals and symbols for amounts of money, unless it's an approximation.

rule_summary: Write in plain language to help users understand your message.
rule_detail: Write in plain language to help users understand your message.

rule_summary: Structure your content with headings, lists and paragraphs.
rule_detail: Headings, lists and paragraphs help to break up content. Most users will scan content before they read it. Structured content is easier to scan and less intimidating than long blocks of text.

rule_summary: Put the most important message first.
rule_detail: Users might not read to the bottom of your content. So, make sure the most important message is at the start.

rule_summary: Use clear, short headings and keep them under 70 characters.
rule_detail: Headings should be clear and short (no more than 70 characters, including spaces).

rule_summary: Put keywords in the first 2 or 3 words of headings.
rule_detail: Put keywords (words that people commonly associate with the topic) in the first 2 or 3 words of headings.

rule_summary: Use sentence case and minimal punctuation in headings.
rule_detail: Use sentence case and minimal punctuation.

rule_summary: Start each paragraph with a topic sentence.
rule_detail: Start each paragraph with a topic sentence that introduces the topic. Use active voice. Topic sentences help users follow your meaning as they scan the content.

rule_summary: Use active voice in topic sentences.
rule_detail: Start each paragraph with a topic sentence that introduces the topic. Use active voice. Topic sentences help users follow your meaning as they scan the content.

rule_summary: Use bullet lists to group related information.
rule_detail: Use bullet lists to group related information – this helps users scan content.

rule_summary: Use numbered lists to show sequence or rank information by importance.
rule_detail: Use numbered lists to show an order of steps or to arrange information by its importance.

rule_summary: Use everyday words that most people understand.
rule_detail: Use everyday words that most people understand. Using common, simple words makes content more accessible to people with low literacy, disability and English as a second language.

rule_summary: Include keywords in your first paragraph.
rule_detail: Include keywords in your first paragraph so users know what the content is about. To identify keywords, think about familiar words that people use when searching for your topic.

rule_summary: Choose simple words.
rule_detail: Choose words that most people understand. Most complicated words have simpler alternatives. Use a thesaurus to find simpler words that mean the same thing.

rule_summary: Avoid jargon.
rule_detail: Jargon excludes people. It is specialised language used by a specific group. It's likely to include technical terms or acronyms that people outside that group won't understand.

rule_summary: Explain technical terms when content is complicated.
rule_detail:
If your content is complicated:

- explain technical terms
- include a glossary
- provide a plain language summary
- include pictures and diagrams.

rule_summary: Include a glossary when content is complicated.
rule_detail:
If your content is complicated:

- explain technical terms
- include a glossary
- provide a plain language summary
- include pictures and diagrams.

rule_summary: Provide a plain language summary when content is complicated.
rule_detail:
If your content is complicated:

- explain technical terms
- include a glossary
- provide a plain language summary
- include pictures and diagrams.

rule_summary: Include pictures and diagrams when content is complicated.
rule_detail:
If your content is complicated:

- explain technical terms
- include a glossary
- provide a plain language summary
- include pictures and diagrams.

rule_summary: Use active voice.
rule_detail: Active voice emphasises the person or thing doing the action, which makes it easy to understand who is doing what. Passive voice emphasises the receiver of the action. Active voice is more direct and often uses fewer words than passive voice.

rule_summary: Aim for an average of 15 words per sentence.
rule_detail: Aim for an average of 15 words per sentence.

rule_summary: Keep sentences to 25 words or fewer.
rule_detail: Sentences should be no longer than 25 words.

rule_summary: Use a mix of longer and shorter sentences for readability.
rule_detail: Use a mix of longer and shorter sentences for readability.

rule_summary: Start a sentence with a conjunction when it makes the sentence shorter.
rule_detail: To make a sentence shorter, it's okay to start a sentence with a conjunction such as 'and', 'but' and 'or'. But don't overdo it.

rule_summary: Use positive sentences when asking users to do something.
rule_detail: Positive sentences are usually shorter than negative sentences. Use positive sentences when asking users to do something. People are more likely to respond to positive instructions than to negative instructions.

rule_summary: Prefer your agency's Australian dictionary and use its headword spelling.
rule_detail:
Your agency is likely to have a preferred Australian dictionary. Style Manual recommends the Australian concise Oxford dictionary or the Macquarie dictionary.

Check the meaning and spelling of words in your agency's preferred dictionary. Use the spelling of the first word in the entry (the 'headword'). The headword is the most common spelling. Using the headword helps to make spelling consistent across agency content.

rule_summary: Check the dictionary for hyphenation, capitalisation, plural forms, and derogatory or offensive use.
rule_detail: Check the dictionary for guidance on hyphenation, capitalisation, plural forms and derogatory or offensive use.

rule_summary: Minimise your use of capital letters.
rule_detail: Minimise your use of capital letters. Overusing capital letters can disrupt the flow of reading.

rule_summary: Capitalize the first word in a sentence and use lower case for all other words except proper nouns.
rule_detail: Capitalise the first word in a sentence. Use lower case for all other words, except for proper nouns. Follow the same style for headings.

rule_summary: Use lower case for generic references to organisational names, titles and programs.
rule_detail: Use lower case for generic references to organisational names, titles and programs. Using lower case in this way isn't disrespectful. 'Australian Government' is capitalised: 'the government' is not.

rule_summary: Use links only when they support a user need.
rule_detail: Only use links when they support a user need. Use descriptive links (words that describe the link destination) not 'click here'.

rule_summary: Use descriptive link text instead of 'click here'.
rule_detail: Only use links when they support a user need. Use descriptive links (words that describe the link destination) not 'click here'.

rule_summary: Put links at the end of sentences when possible.
rule_detail: Try to put links at the end of sentences.

rule_summary: Link to the landing page that hosts a file, not to the file itself.
rule_detail: Link to the landing page that hosts a file (e.g. PDF or Word document), not to the file itself.

rule_summary: Include the document title, file type, and size if you must link directly to a file.
rule_detail: If you must link to a file, include the document title (not file name), file type and size.

rule_summary: Use 'from ... to' or 'between ... and' instead of an en dash for spans of years.
rule_detail: Use 'from … to' or 'between … and' instead of an en dash for spans of years.

rule_summary: Use en dashes in date spans for specified exceptions.
rule_detail:
There are exceptions. Use an en dash in date spans for:

- financial years
- calendar years
- titles of publications and programs
- terms of office
- lifespans (birth and death)
- content in limited space.

rule_summary: Use an unspaced en dash in most instances.
rule_detail: Use an unspaced en dash in most instances.

rule_summary: Use a spaced en dash to set off non-essential information in sentences.
rule_detail:
Use a spaced en dash in sentences to set off non-essential information.

### Example

- They invited 3 employees – Walter, Yana and Aya – to the presentation.

rule_summary: Use the correct symbol for an en dash, minus symbol, or hyphen.
rule_detail:
Use the correct symbol. The table shows 3 ways to code the en dash, minus symbol and hyphen.

| – en dash | − minus symbol | ‐ hyphen | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unicode (type the character code, then press Alt x) | U+2013 | U+2212 | U+2010 |
| HTML entity | – | − | ‐ |
| Word | Ctrl+minus symbol on the number pad | Unicode or HTML entity preferred | Press the hyphen key |

rule_summary: Use an Australian dictionary to check spelling and word usage.
rule_detail: Use an Australian dictionary to find out how to spell and use words.

rule_summary: Write dates and times consistently.
rule_detail: Write dates and times consistently.

rule_summary: Use lists to help users scan and understand a series of items.
rule_detail: Use lists to make it easy for users to scan and understand a series of items.

rule_summary: Follow the rules for numbers to support accessibility and readability.
rule_detail: Follow the rules for numbers to support accessibility and readability for users.

rule_summary: Write in plain language to help users understand your message.
rule_detail: Write in plain language to help users understand your message.

rule_summary: Read the style rules for common style topics.
rule_detail: Read the style rules for common style topics.

rule_summary: Use APS Academy training to access writing and editing training for Australian Public Service employees.
rule_detail: Australian Public Service employees can access training through the Australian Public Service Academy (APS Academy).

rule_summary: Base APS Academy writing and editing training on the Style Manual content.
rule_detail: This training is based on the content in the Style Manual.

rule_summary: Treat writing as a fundamental skill required of APS employees.
rule_detail: Writing is one of the fundamental skills required of APS employees.

rule_summary: Choose APS Academy workshops if you want to improve current-level writing performance or move to a new role or level.
rule_detail:
The APS Academy offers writing skills workshops for those seeking to:

- be more effective at their current level
- transition to a new role or level.

rule_summary: Use the APS 1–4 writing course to learn plain language, accessibility, readability, active voice, punctuation and types of lists.
rule_detail: [ Essential writing for APS 1–4 levels](https://www.apsacademy.gov.au/essential-writing-aps-1-4-levels) highlights the relationship between plain language and accessibility and readability. It also covers active voice, punctuation and types of lists.

rule_summary: Use the APS 5–6 writing course to develop evidence-based argumentation and recommendations.
rule_detail: [ Essential writing for APS 5–6 levels](https://www.apsacademy.gov.au/essential-writing-aps-5-6-levels) suits all APS and executive level staff who write analytically. It focuses on how to outline an evidence‑based argument and recommend a course of action.

rule_summary: Use the executive-level writing course if you manage or coordinate writing tasks with others' input or move into a higher-level writing role.
rule_detail:
[ Essential writing for executive levels](https://www.apsacademy.gov.au/essential-writing-executive-levels) is suitable for staff who:

- manage or coordinate writing tasks with others’ input
- transfer into a role demanding higher-level writing skills.

rule_summary: Search the APS Academy Courses page for 'writing' to find more training.
rule_detail: For more information visit the APS Academy website and search for ‘writing’ on the [ Courses](https://www.apsacademy.gov.au/courses) page.

rule_summary: Treat content writers, content creators and content designers as digital professionals.
rule_detail: Content writers, content creators and content designers are digital professionals.

rule_summary: Join the Digital Profession if you work with government content and want to connect with others in the field.
rule_detail: If you work with government content, the [Digital Profession](https://www.apsprofessions.gov.au/digital-profession) is a great way to connect with others in the field.

rule_summary: Use Digital Profession membership to join communities, collaborate and attend training and events.
rule_detail: Digital Profession members can join communities specific to their skills and interests, collaborate with others and attend training and events.

rule_summary: Join the Digital Profession if you work in Australian, state or local government.
rule_detail: Membership is open to anyone working in Australian, state or local government.

rule_summary: Use these resources as companions to the Style Manual.
rule_detail: Use these resources as companions to the Style Manual. They will help you style Australian Government content consistently.

rule_summary: Learn about common style topics in the blog.
rule_detail: [Blog](/style-manual-resources/blog)Learn more about common style topics. Read about how we produce content for the Style Manual.

rule_summary: Use the quick guides to cover common style topics.
rule_detail: [Quick guides](/style-manual-resources/quick-guides)The 6 quick guides cover common style topics. View them online or download accessible versions from each page. The accessible PDFs are designed to be printed.

rule_summary: Download accessible versions of the quick guides or print the accessible PDFs.
rule_detail: [Quick guides](/style-manual-resources/quick-guides)The 6 quick guides cover common style topics. View them online or download accessible versions from each page. The accessible PDFs are designed to be printed.

rule_summary: Access training through the APS Academy if you work in the Australian Public Service.
rule_detail: [Training and professional development](/style-manual-resources/training-and-professional-development)The Style Manual team does not run training. Australian Public Service employees can access training through the Australian Public Service Academy (APS Academy). People working in Australian, state or local government can join the Digital Profession to connect with others.

rule_summary: Join the Digital Profession to connect with others if you work in Australian, state or local government.
rule_detail: [Training and professional development](/style-manual-resources/training-and-professional-development)The Style Manual team does not run training. Australian Public Service employees can access training through the Australian Public Service Academy (APS Academy). People working in Australian, state or local government can join the Digital Profession to connect with others.

rule_summary: Write in plain language to help users understand content quickly.
rule_detail: Plain language can express complex ideas. Engage people with words they can understand quickly: use the list on this page. Clarify expressions people might be unfamiliar with.

rule_summary: Use everyday words that people are familiar with.
rule_detail:
Use everyday words

Choose words that people are familiar with. Unfamiliar words make content harder to read and understand.

rule_summary: Write in plain language for accessibility and understanding.
rule_detail: Write in plain language. This helps all users and is essential for some.

rule_summary: Avoid or explain unusual words, phrases and idioms.
rule_detail: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on.

rule_summary: Expand acronyms on first use.
rule_detail: Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Avoid double negatives.
rule_detail: Avoid using double negatives.

rule_summary: Use personal pronouns such as we, you and us when they suit the voice and tone.
rule_detail:
Use ‘we’, ‘you’ and ‘us’ if you can

Use personal pronouns (like ‘we’, ‘you’, ‘us’) when it suits the voice and tone.

rule_summary: Use active voice to make responsibility clear.
rule_detail: A direct, active voice and tone helps to engage users. Active voice and tone makes it clear who must do what.

rule_summary: Avoid jargon, slang and idioms.
rule_detail:
Avoid jargon

Remove jargon, slang and idioms.

rule_summary: Use inclusive language that respects all people.
rule_detail:
Use inclusive language

People can relate to content when it uses inclusive language. Choose words that respect all people, including their rights and their heritage.

rule_summary: Match word choice to the terms people use to search for the content.
rule_detail: Find out if your word choice matches the words people will use to find the content. What is obvious to you might not be obvious to them.

rule_summary: Use user research and content testing to identify unfamiliar jargon and concepts.
rule_detail:
You can build insight through user research and content testing. For example, you can check whether:

- you are using unfamiliar jargon
- you need to highlight unfamiliar concepts and explain them.

rule_summary: Check search analytics for the terms people use to find related content.
rule_detail: Check search engine analytics for terms people are using to find related content online.

rule_summary: Use keywords discovered from search engine optimisation research.
rule_detail: You can discover useful search terms and keywords to include in search engine optimisation.

rule_summary: Choose the simplest, clearest way to say something.
rule_detail:
Choose simple words, not complicated expressions

There is usually more than one way to express something. Find the simplest, clearest option.

rule_summary: Replace longer words and phrases with simpler alternatives.
rule_detail: Replace longer words and phrases with simpler alternatives.

rule_summary: Use the simplest alternative for technical wording in the provided list.
rule_detail:
Use this table as a starting point.
