rule_summary: Keep words and phrases with special meaning to a minimum.
rule_detail:
Keep words and phrases with special meaning to a minimum

People can be unfamiliar with words you need to use, for example:

For names and terms with special meaning, follow style rules and conventions. This helps users scan content.

rule_summary: Be selective about shortened forms.
rule_detail: Be selective about shortened forms, such as abbreviations, contractions, acronyms and initialisms.

rule_summary: Use shortened forms only when they are well known or used many times.
rule_detail: Shorten only the words and phrases that are well known or used many times in your content. Shortened forms can help people read and understand content, but too many can be difficult to keep track of.

rule_summary: Spell out shortened forms the first time you use them.
rule_detail: Spell them out the first time you use them.

rule_summary: Avoid shortened forms that are used only once or twice.
rule_detail: Shortened forms can be a type of jargon that is not suitable in plain language content. Try to avoid them altogether if they are used only once or twice.

rule_summary: Use technical or specialist terms only when research shows your audience uses them.
rule_detail: You can include technical or specialist terms if your research shows your audience uses them. But start with plain language words as the default to keep the reading level accessible.

rule_summary: Explain specialist or technical terms for users.
rule_detail:
To help people understand specialist or technical content:

- explain terms – for example, use a glossary
- include a short summary without using specialist terms.

rule_summary: Reserve shortened forms for the most frequently used terms in content with many specialist terms.
rule_detail: In content with many specialist terms, reserve shortened forms for the most frequently used terms only. Spell out other terms in full.

rule_summary: Keep sentences short to improve readability and scanability.
rule_detail: Clear sentences in active voice improve readability. Keep sentences short to help people scan content.

rule_summary: Write sentences in plain language.
rule_detail: Write plain language sentences

rule_summary: Use standard English subject–verb–object order as the basis of plain language writing.
rule_detail: Standard English sentences are built on subject–verb–object order. This structure forms the basis of plain language writing.

rule_summary: Keep sentences to an average of 15 words and no more than 25 words, especially for digital content.
rule_detail: Keep sentences to an average of 15 words and no more than 25 words, especially for digital content.

rule_summary: Write in plain language for accessibility.
rule_detail: Write in plain language. This helps all users and is essential for some.

rule_summary: Avoid or explain unusual words, phrases, idioms and similar expressions.
rule_detail: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Expand all acronyms on first use.
rule_detail: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Avoid using double negatives.
rule_detail: Avoid using double negatives.

rule_summary: Use active voice rather than passive voice.
rule_detail: Use active rather than passive voice. Active voice helps users understand who is doing what. It can also help people know exactly what their responsibility is.

rule_summary: Construct sentences so they are positive rather than negative.
rule_detail: Write sentences so they are positive rather than negative.

rule_summary: Avoid double negatives.
rule_detail: Double negatives can lead to misunderstandings, so avoid them.

rule_summary: Keep only words that play a necessary role in the sentence.
rule_detail: Make each word work for its place in the sentence. Sentence structure is clearer if each word plays a necessary role. Clear sentences improve readability.

rule_summary: Keep the subject, verb and object and remove unnecessary words.
rule_detail: Keep the words that play a critical function in the sentence. Remove all the words except the subject, verb and object (if applicable).

rule_summary: Check that a sentence is grammatically correct after removing nonessential words.
rule_detail: Check if the sentence is grammatically correct when you remove the other words.

rule_summary: Leave out words that are not absolutely necessary when rebuilding a sentence.
rule_detail: Build the sentence back together, leaving out any words that aren’t absolutely necessary. Adverbs and adjectives are usually good candidates to leave out in this kind of test.

rule_summary: Check that the basic meaning remains and the result is grammatical.
rule_detail: Check if the basic meaning of the sentence remains, and if it’s grammatical. Then check if the words you’ve removed are really working to keep their place.

rule_summary: Use sentence-combination testing to produce concise and easily understood content.
rule_detail: Testing combinations as you write will also help create concise and easily understood headings, fragment lists and descriptive links.

rule_summary: Make sentence combinations support punctuation, spelling, capitalisation and formatting rules.
rule_detail: Word combinations affect punctuation, spelling, capitalisation and formatting. For example, there are rules about the use of commas between adjectives and the use of hyphens between adverbs and verbs.

rule_summary: Use plain language words and terms instead of bureaucratic language.
rule_detail: Instead of bureaucratic language, use plain language words and terms.

rule_summary: Use a verb instead of the noun related to that verb where possible.
rule_detail: For example, use a verb instead of the noun that relates to the verb. If you use the noun instead, you have to change the verb into the noun and usually add other words.

rule_summary: Use fewer than three adjectives or nouns at a time.
rule_detail: Use fewer than 3 adjectives or nouns at a time

rule_summary: Rephrase strings of adjectives or noun trains to improve understanding.
rule_detail: Phrases that combine more than 3 adjectives or nouns are difficult to understand. Rephrase sentences to break up strings of adjectives or noun trains.

rule_summary: Rephrase long adjective or noun strings as a clause.
rule_detail: You can often rephrase the string of adjectives or noun train as a clause. Follow the rule to keep sentences short and their structure simple.

rule_summary: Avoid using if and unless together in the same sentence.
rule_detail: Don’t use words such as ‘if’ and ‘unless’ in the same sentence.

rule_summary: Use other than carefully so the exception is clear.
rule_detail: When you use ‘other than’, make sure it’s clear which words are included in the exception.

rule_summary: Avoid using such ... as.
rule_detail: Don’t use the ‘such ... as’ form.

rule_summary: Use and instead of being or not being.
rule_detail: Use ‘and’ instead of ‘being’ or ‘not being’.

rule_summary: Adjust writing style to meet user needs.
rule_detail: Adjust your style to meet user needs.

rule_summary: Adapt tone and voice to engage users.
rule_detail: Adapt tone and voice to engage users, so the content can meet their needs.

rule_summary: Align tone to context.
rule_detail: Align tone to context

rule_summary: Use word choice deliberately because it affects how users respond.
rule_detail: Word choice will influence how users respond to you and your organisation. The smallest details, such as using contractions, can affect how content comes across.

rule_summary: Use the second person pronoun 'you' to make content active, direct and personal.
rule_detail: The second person (using the pronoun ‘you’) is active, direct and personal. It can be more engaging for people reading and using government content.

rule_summary: Use the first person singular 'I' only rarely, except in correspondence.
rule_detail: Using the first person singular (the pronoun ‘I’) is rarely suitable in government content, except in correspondence.

rule_summary: Choose the level of formality according to the relationship between content and user.
rule_detail: The appropriate level of formality depends on what the relationship is between content and its user.

rule_summary: Use a formal tone to create distance.
rule_detail: A formal tone creates a distance between the content’s persona and the content’s reader.

rule_summary: Use an informal tone to suggest a more casual and intimate relationship.
rule_detail: An informal tone suggests a relationship that is more casual and intimate.

rule_summary: Use a standard tone for most government content.
rule_detail: A standard tone sits between these 2. It is appropriate for most government content. It creates little distance, but not too much familiarity, into the relationship with readers.

rule_summary: Choose the standard tone for most government content because it is easiest for many people to understand.
rule_detail: Standard style is the easiest for many people to understand.

rule_summary: Recognise that formality does not affect plain language.
rule_detail: Formality does not affect [plain language](/node/55).

rule_summary: Do not use contractions in formal tone.
rule_detail:
Formal tone:

- doesn’t use
[contractions](/node/191) - is literal – words are used with their dictionary meaning
- doesn’t use metaphor, slang or idioms
- often uses the third person (he, she, they, them).

rule_summary: Write literally in formal tone, using words in their dictionary meaning.
rule_detail:
Formal tone:

- doesn’t use
[contractions](/node/191) - is literal – words are used with their dictionary meaning
- doesn’t use metaphor, slang or idioms
- often uses the third person (he, she, they, them).

rule_summary: Do not use metaphor, slang or idioms in formal tone.
rule_detail:
Formal tone:

- doesn’t use
[contractions](/node/191) - is literal – words are used with their dictionary meaning
- doesn’t use metaphor, slang or idioms
- often uses the third person (he, she, they, them).

rule_summary: Often use the third person in formal tone.
rule_detail:
Formal tone:

- doesn’t use
[contractions](/node/191) - is literal – words are used with their dictionary meaning
- doesn’t use metaphor, slang or idioms
- often uses the third person (he, she, they, them).

rule_summary: Use formal tone in legal writing, policies, reports, ministerial letters, emails and letters to people you have not yet met, and in ceremonies or to show respect to authority.
rule_detail:
Legal writing, policies, reports and ministerial letters often adopt a formal tone. You can also use it in emails and letters when you have not yet met the person you are writing to.

Formal tone is used in ceremonies and to show respect for someone in authority.

rule_summary: Use contractions in standard tone.
rule_detail:
Standard tone:

- can use contractions and
[personal pronouns](/node/131#there_are_different_kinds_of_pronouns) - doesn’t use metaphors, idioms or slang.

rule_summary: Use personal pronouns in standard tone.
rule_detail:
Standard tone:

- can use contractions and
[personal pronouns](/node/131#there_are_different_kinds_of_pronouns) - doesn’t use metaphors, idioms or slang.

rule_summary: Do not use metaphors, idioms or slang in standard tone.
rule_detail:
Standard tone:

- can use contractions and
[personal pronouns](/node/131#there_are_different_kinds_of_pronouns) - doesn’t use metaphors, idioms or slang.

rule_summary: Use informal tone in social media and blogs.
rule_detail: Informal tone is often used in [social media](/node/43) and [blogs](/node/44). Your writing might also become more informal as you get to know the people you are writing to.

rule_summary: Use contractions and personal pronouns in informal tone.
rule_detail: Informal tone uses contractions and personal pronouns.

rule_summary: Do not use slang when writing on behalf of government.
rule_detail: You should not use slang when writing on behalf of government.

rule_summary: Check your organisation's style guide for advice about voice.
rule_detail: Check your organisation’s style guide to see if it has advice about the organisation’s voice.

rule_summary: Use a basic government voice if your organisation's style guide provides no voice advice.
rule_detail:
If not, a safe place to start is with a basic government voice. It is the voice of a ‘definitive source’ and is:

- respectful
- clear and direct
- objective and impartial.

rule_summary: Use a respectful writing style that speaks to people without being inflammatory or overly familiar.
rule_detail:
A respectful writing style:

- uses
[inclusive language](/node/178) - expresses ideas in everyday words
- ‘speaks’ to people – using the pronoun ‘you’, for example
- doesn’t use inflammatory language, such as name-calling or sarcasm
- doesn’t speak down to people, but isn’t too familiar either.

rule_summary: Use inclusive language and everyday words in a respectful writing style.
rule_detail:
A respectful writing style:

- uses
[inclusive language](/node/178) - expresses ideas in everyday words
- ‘speaks’ to people – using the pronoun ‘you’, for example
- doesn’t use inflammatory language, such as name-calling or sarcasm
- doesn’t speak down to people, but isn’t too familiar either.

rule_summary: Use the pronoun 'you' when speaking to people in a respectful writing style.
rule_detail:
A respectful writing style:

- uses
[inclusive language](/node/178) - expresses ideas in everyday words
- ‘speaks’ to people – using the pronoun ‘you’, for example
- doesn’t use inflammatory language, such as name-calling or sarcasm
- doesn’t speak down to people, but isn’t too familiar either.

rule_summary: Use plain language.
rule_detail: Use plain language.

rule_summary: Write short and simple sentences in active voice.
rule_detail: Write short and simple sentences in active voice.

rule_summary: Engage people with words they can understand quickly.
rule_detail: Plain language can express complex ideas. Engage people with words they can understand quickly: use the list on this page. Clarify expressions people might be unfamiliar with.

rule_summary: Clarify expressions people might be unfamiliar with.
rule_detail: Plain language can express complex ideas. Engage people with words they can understand quickly: use the list on this page. Clarify expressions people might be unfamiliar with.

rule_summary: Keep sentences short to help people scan content.
rule_detail: Clear sentences in active voice improve readability. Keep sentences short to help people scan content.

rule_summary: Adjust your style to meet user needs.
rule_detail: Writing style is a result of voice and tone. Adjust your style to meet user needs. It influences whether and how people engage with content.

rule_summary: Ensure content meets user needs and expectations through editing and proofreading.
rule_detail: Editing and proofreading help ensure consistency so content meets user needs and expectations.

rule_summary: Make sure content is clear, accurate and consistent to meet the Digital Service Standard.
rule_detail: You must make sure content is clear, accurate and consistent to meet the Digital Service Standard:

rule_summary: Make sure content is consistent, has a clear structure and is error free to make it accessible for all users.
rule_detail: You must make sure content is consistent, has a clear structure and is error free to make it accessible for all users.

rule_summary: Use plain language.
rule_detail: Make sure content uses plain language. This helps all users and is essential for some. Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases and idioms. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Make other content elements accessible to all users.
rule_detail: Make sure other content elements, including captions, transcripts, alt text, link text, headings and instructions are accessible to all users.

rule_summary: Agree on the scope of the substantive edit before starting.
rule_detail: Before starting, agree on the scope of the substantive edit in the team.

rule_summary: Use a substantive edit to conduct a plain English review.
rule_detail: The substantive edit can: conduct a plain English review to check sentence length, replace complex words with simpler alternatives and remove jargon

rule_summary: Use a substantive edit to check the design of the content and confirm it is the best possible format.
rule_detail: The substantive edit can: check the design of the content to make sure it is the best possible format

rule_summary: Use a substantive edit to reorganise content for flow and navigation.
rule_detail: The substantive edit can: reorganise content to improve the flow of information and navigation

rule_summary: Use a substantive edit to identify gaps in the content or information that can be removed.
rule_detail: The substantive edit can: identify gaps in the content or any information that can be removed

rule_summary: Use a substantive edit to reword content for clarity, understanding, voice and tone.
rule_detail: The substantive edit can: reword content to make it easier to understand and to achieve consistent voice and tone

rule_summary: Use a substantive edit to check compliance with specific government requirements.
rule_detail: The substantive edit can: check compliance with specific government requirements.

rule_summary: Update the style sheet through a substantive edit to record decisions for copyediting.
rule_detail: The style sheet is updated through a substantive edit to record any decisions that can inform a copyedit.

rule_summary: Do not use substantive editing to write significant new content.
rule_detail: Substantive editing does not: write a significant amount of new content (but it can include advice to add more content)

rule_summary: Do not use substantive editing to substantially rewrite text to shorten it.
rule_detail: Substantive editing does not: substantially rewrite to shorten text (but it can involve advice to delete content)

rule_summary: Do not use substantive editing to choose typeface or apply formatting styles.
rule_detail: Substantive editing does not: choose the right typeface or apply formatting styles (but can include checking bolded, italicised and underlined font)

rule_summary: Do not use substantive editing to fact-check content.
rule_detail: Substantive editing does not: fact-check, such as checking names of people and places, dates, citations, quotes or links to external content.

rule_summary: Complete substantive editing before any separate rewriting or fact-checking begins.
rule_detail: An editor can rewrite or fact-check content, but these are separate tasks to substantive editing. They should happen before any editing begins.

rule_summary: Agree on the scope of the copyedit before starting.
rule_detail: Before starting, agree on the scope of the copyedit within the team.

rule_summary: Address any substantive issues identified during a copyedit.
rule_detail: An editor might identify substantive issues with the content during the copyedit. The team should decide how it will address those issues.

rule_summary: Copyedit content again after any substantive editing or rewriting that follows the copyedit.
rule_detail: If there is any more substantive editing or rewriting after the copyedit, the content will need to be copyedited again.

rule_summary: Correct language issues in line with the style sheet during copyediting.
rule_detail: During copyediting, an editor: corrects issues with language in line with the style sheet

rule_summary: Align references and citations with the agreed referencing style during copyediting.
rule_detail: During copyediting, an editor: aligns the style of references and citations with agreed referencing style

rule_summary: Comment on inconsistencies in voice and tone during copyediting.
rule_detail: During copyediting, an editor: comments on inconsistencies in voice and tone.

rule_summary: Check design, layout, function and other elements for issues or inconsistencies during copyediting.
rule_detail: A copyedit also checks for issues or inconsistencies with: design, layout and function illustrations, tables, headings, sequences, internal links and other elements.

rule_summary: Update the style sheet during a copyedit to record style decisions.
rule_detail: The style sheet is updated during a copyedit to record style decisions.

rule_summary: Do not use copyediting to restructure content except to make sentences clear and grammatically correct.
rule_detail: Copyediting does not: restructure content (other than to make sentences clear and grammatically correct)

rule_summary: Do not use copyediting to write new content or shorten text.
rule_detail: Copyediting does not: write new content or shorten text

rule_summary: Do not use copyediting to rewrite text for voice or plain English except for isolated issues.
rule_detail: Copyediting does not: rewrite text to unify voice or edit for plain English (other than to deal with isolated issues)

rule_summary: Do not use copyediting to format or design text.
rule_detail: Copyediting does not: format or design text

rule_summary: Do not use copyediting to fact-check content.
rule_detail: Copyediting does not: fact-check

rule_summary: Do not use copyediting to check external links except for a spot check when systemic issues are suspected.
rule_detail: Copyediting does not: check external links embedded in the content (other than a spot check in case there are systemic issues).

rule_summary: Design content based on the ways users find information.
rule_detail: Design content based on the ways users find information.

rule_summary: Do user research to understand how content will be found, answered, presented and phrased.
rule_detail:
Do user research so you can work out how content will:

- be found using different search strategies
- answer the questions users ask
- present the way users think it will
- use everyday language – many search queries are voice search.

rule_summary: Include the main words and phrases people search for.
rule_detail: Include the main words and phrases that people search for. This is part of [search engine optimisation (SEO)](/node/103).

rule_summary: Use clear page titles.
rule_detail: Write clear page titles. This is the first thing to appear in search results and the first words heard by screen reader users.

rule_summary: Organise content in a clear order using section headings.
rule_detail: Organise content in a clear order using section headings. Make sure all users can navigate through all content in the intended order, regardless of the technology they are using.

rule_summary: Use the same navigation elements consistently across services.
rule_detail: Use the same navigation elements consistently across services. Make sure the user can understand where they are within the website or service.

rule_summary: Write link text that makes the destination and purpose of the link clear.
rule_detail: Write link text that makes the destination and purpose of the link clear.

rule_summary: Write clear and concise headings.
rule_detail: Write clear and concise headings to help users find the information they're looking for.

rule_summary: Match keywords to the search terms people use.
rule_detail: Match keywords to the search terms people use

rule_summary: Use keywords to help people find content that meets their search intention.
rule_detail: Using keywords helps people find content that meets their search intention.

rule_summary: Help people find information and achieve what they need to do.
rule_detail: Government content should help users find information and achieve what they need to do.

rule_summary: Understand what users need to do with government and which keywords they are likely to use.
rule_detail:
To write for users and search engines, you need to understand:

- what users need to do with government
- the keywords they’re likely to use.

rule_summary: Use the information from user needs and keyword research to design content for people and search engines.
rule_detail: Use this information to design content for people and search engines. You can combine it with other techniques for [on-page optimisation](/node/71).

rule_summary: Include the keyword in the content, title, meta description and URL when it is relevant.
rule_detail: Include ‘citizen’ in the content, title, meta description and web address (URL).

rule_summary: Help users of your service find the information they need to meet the Digital Service Standard.
rule_detail: You must help the users of your service to find the information they need to meet the [Digital Service Standard](https://www.dta.gov.au/help-and-advice/digital-service-standard/digital-service-standard-criteria).

rule_summary: Write in plain English.
rule_detail: Write in plain English. This helps all users and is essential for some.

rule_summary: Avoid or explain unusual words, phrases, idioms and similar language.
rule_detail: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Expand all acronyms on their first use.
rule_detail: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Use keywords that users expect to see and search engines are likely to index.
rule_detail: Use keywords that users expect to see and are looking for, so they are indexed by search engines.

rule_summary: Find which keywords to use through keyword tools, analytics and user research.
rule_detail:
Find out which keywords to use through a keyword tool, analytics and
[user research](https://www.dta.gov.au/help-and-advice/build-and-improve-services/user-research).

rule_summary: Write using keywords and descriptive plain language.
rule_detail:
Write content using keywords and descriptive
[plain language](/node/55). [Structure content](/node/192)(including forms and online tools) so people find what they need.

rule_summary: Structure content, including forms and online tools, so people can find what they need.
rule_detail:
Write content using keywords and descriptive
[plain language](/node/55). [Structure content](/node/192)(including forms and online tools) so people find what they need.

rule_summary: Include keywords once or twice in the first paragraph when they make sense, and you can also include them in the final paragraph.
rule_detail: Include keywords once or twice, if they make sense, in the first paragraph of the content. You can also include them in this way in the final paragraph.

rule_summary: Include closely related terms and concepts to help search engines understand the page theme.
rule_detail: Include terms and concepts that are closely related to the topic you are writing about. This helps search engines understand the theme of the page.

rule_summary: Do not use too many keywords or keywords outside the content context.
rule_detail: Don’t use too many keywords or keywords that are outside the context of the content. This is known as keyword stuffing. Search engines ban or penalise this type of content.

rule_summary: Include place or group-specific details when the information relates to a specific location or audience.
rule_detail: Some information could relate to a specific place or a group of people. Make sure you include these details (for example, ‘student placements in northern NSW’).

rule_summary: Make sure people can discover information produced by Australian Government agencies.
rule_detail: People must be able to discover information produced by Australian Government agencies.

rule_summary: Make content easy for people to find using search engines.
rule_detail: Make content easy for people to find using search engines.

rule_summary: Include keywords in URLs, metadata and content.
rule_detail: Include keywords in URLs, metadata and content.

rule_summary: Create accessible links to high-quality content.
rule_detail: Create accessible links to high-quality content.

rule_summary: Focus on users first when optimising content.
rule_detail: Focus on making the page for users first, and for search engines second.

rule_summary: Use keywords, metadata and links in page content when doing on-page optimisation.
rule_detail: On-page optimisation includes using keywords, metadata and links in the page content.

rule_summary: Use optimisation techniques to help people find the content they need.
rule_detail: Help people find the content they need using optimisation techniques.

rule_summary: Tailor content to the words and topics users actually search for.
rule_detail: Write content that includes these terms and topics, and that answers the questions people are most likely to ask.

rule_summary: Help users find information they need to meet the Digital Service Standard.
rule_detail: You must help the users of your service to find the information they need to meet the Digital Service Standard.

rule_summary: Use keywords in the URL and content.
rule_detail: Use keywords in the URL and content

rule_summary: Use keywords in the web address, metadata, headings, page content, internal links, captions and alt text for images.
rule_detail:
Use keywords in the:

- web address (URL, or ‘uniform resource locator’)
- metadata
[headings](/node/51)[page content](/node/72)[internal links](/node/193)[captions and alt text for images](/node/49).

rule_summary: Put the main keywords close to the start of the URL.
rule_detail: Create URLs that contain words from the title of the page with the main keywords close to the start.

rule_summary: Keep URLs below 100 characters and make them meaningful to users.
rule_detail: The URL should be below 100 characters and make sense to the user.

rule_summary: Separate URL words with hyphens instead of spaces or underscores.
rule_detail: To separate words in the URL, use hyphens instead of spaces or underscores.

rule_summary: Write metadata that explains the page.
rule_detail: Write metadata that explains the page

rule_summary: Write page titles and meta descriptions so users can tell whether the page meets their needs.
rule_detail: Write these parts so that users can tell whether the page holds what they’re looking for.

rule_summary: Include keywords in titles.
rule_detail:
The title should:

- include keywords
- be different on each page
- be 70 characters or fewer.

rule_summary: Make each page title different.
rule_detail:
The title should:

- include keywords
- be different on each page
- be 70 characters or fewer.

rule_summary: Keep titles to 70 characters or fewer.
rule_detail:
The title should:

- include keywords
- be different on each page
- be 70 characters or fewer.

rule_summary: Write titles that are not cut off by search engines.
rule_detail: Titles that are too long will get cut off by search engines.

rule_summary: Write titles that work as headlines in search results.
rule_detail: In a search result, the title is usually the first line. It works as a headline in the search results.

rule_summary: Write clear page titles for screen reader users.
rule_detail: Write clear page titles. This is the first thing a screen reader user will hear and needs to assure them they are on the right page.

rule_summary: Ensure linking text to a page relates to the page title.
rule_detail: Ensure the linking text to this page relates to the title.

rule_summary: Write meta descriptions in plain language.
rule_detail: Describe the content in plain language. This helps users to know if it’s what they need.

rule_summary: Make meta descriptions user-focused and keyword-rich.
rule_detail: Descriptions need to be user-focused and contain keywords. They can be up to 160 characters.

rule_summary: Keep meta descriptions to 160 characters or fewer.
rule_detail: Descriptions need to be user-focused and contain keywords. They can be up to 160 characters.

rule_summary: Use useful links to high-quality content.
rule_detail: Create useful links to high-quality content

rule_summary: Link to pages that support your site’s quality and ranking.
rule_detail: The quality of the pages you link to affects the ranking of your site.

rule_summary: Use relevant keywords as anchor text.
rule_detail: Use relevant keywords as the anchor text (for example, don’t use ‘click here’ as link text).

rule_summary: Avoid using 'click here' as link text.
rule_detail: Use relevant keywords as the anchor text (for example, don’t use ‘click here’ as link text).

rule_summary: Place links to other quality sites towards the end of the content.
rule_detail: Link to content on other quality sites towards the end of the content.

rule_summary: Use responsive design methods to make sure users can read content on all devices.
rule_detail: Make sure users can read content on all devices using responsive design methods.

rule_summary: Write link text that makes the destination and purpose of the link clear.
rule_detail: Write link text that makes the destination and purpose of the link clear.

rule_summary: Use analytics as part of user research.
rule_detail: Use analytics as part of research with users.

rule_summary: Do not rely on analytics alone.
rule_detail: Don’t rely on analytics alone.

rule_summary: Write and design content so users can easily find it with search engines and voice search.
rule_detail: Metadata, keywords and page structure are important. Write and design content so users can easily find it with search engines and voice search.

rule_summary: Use algorithms to index websites, search the index, and organise results.
rule_detail:
Search engines:

- index websites (using algorithms)
- search the index
- organise the results.

rule_summary: Use keywords in titles and metadata to help algorithms index content.
rule_detail: To index the content, algorithms use [keywords in titles and metadata](/node/72). The HTML <title> element is the heading that most search engines display in search results.

rule_summary: Monitor search performance and update content to keep keywords current.
rule_detail: Algorithms change. Monitor how content is performing in search results and update it so you are always using the right keywords.

rule_summary: Understand the tools and systems used to build the service and test it end to end to meet the Digital Service Standard.
rule_detail: You must understand the tools and systems used to build the service, and you must test the service from end to end to meet the Digital Service Standard:

rule_summary: Use plain language to help people find content.
rule_detail:
In general, to help people find content:

- Use
[plain language](/node/55). - Include
[headings](/node/51). - Embed keywords in the
[metadata and content](/node/71).

rule_summary: Include headings to help people find content.
rule_detail:
In general, to help people find content:

- Use
[plain language](/node/55). - Include
[headings](/node/51). - Embed keywords in the
[metadata and content](/node/71).

rule_summary: Embed keywords in metadata and content to help people find content.
rule_detail:
In general, to help people find content:

- Use
[plain language](/node/55). - Include
[headings](/node/51). - Embed keywords in the
[metadata and content](/node/71).

rule_summary: Place a reference number after the form title so algorithms can find the form.
rule_detail: If you include a reference number, place it after the form’s title so the algorithm can find the [form](/node/177).

rule_summary: Ensure the words people expect to see are indexed by search engines.
rule_detail: Ensure that the words people expect to see and are looking for are indexed by search engines.

rule_summary: Write in plain language.
rule_detail: Write in plain language. This helps all users and is essential for some.

rule_summary: Use plain language because it helps all users and is essential for some.
rule_detail: Write in plain language. This helps all users and is essential for some.

rule_summary: Write at a lower secondary education reading level for AAA accessibility.
rule_detail: Level AAA requires a lower secondary education reading level, after removal of proper names and titles (year 7 or between 12 and 14 years old).

rule_summary: Avoid or explain unusual words, phrases, and idioms.
rule_detail: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Expand all acronyms on first use.
rule_detail: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on. Expand all acronyms on their first use.

rule_summary: Use the inverted pyramid to put the most important content at the top of the page.
rule_detail:
To put the most important content at the top of the page, use the
[inverted pyramid](/node/77).

rule_summary: Use sequential structure to lead people through a series of steps.
rule_detail:
To lead people through a series of steps, use
[sequential structure](/node/78).

rule_summary: Include keywords in headings and final paragraphs.
rule_detail: Include keywords that users relate to the topic in [headings](/node/51#use_keywords_to_start_headings) and final [paragraphs](/node/53). Algorithms look at these structural elements to assess and rank webpages.

rule_summary: Create direct content that answers users' questions for voice search.
rule_detail:
People using voice search will be able to find the content more easily if you:

- avoid words that sound similar to other words (homophones) – for example, a voice search could confuse the words ‘hear’ and ‘here’
- create direct content that answers users’ questions.

rule_summary: Avoid words that sound similar to other words in voice search.
rule_detail:
People using voice search will be able to find the content more easily if you:

- avoid words that sound similar to other words (homophones) – for example, a voice search could confuse the words ‘hear’ and ‘here’
- create direct content that answers users’ questions.

rule_summary: Design content for more than one search engine.
rule_detail: People sometimes don’t use their usual search engine when they use voice search. Design content for more than one search engine to help people find what they need.

rule_summary: Write and design content that is easy for the user to find with a search engine.
rule_detail: Write and design content that is easy for the user to find with a search engine.

rule_summary: Design content based on the ways users find information.
rule_detail: Design content based on the ways users find information.

rule_summary: Use metadata, keywords and page structure to help users find content in search engines and voice search.
rule_detail: Metadata, keywords and page structure are important. Write and design content so users can easily find it with search engines and voice search.

rule_summary: Choose keywords that reflect the core ideas and topics in your content.
rule_detail: Keywords reflect core ideas and topics in content. Choosing the right keywords will support people’s ability to find the content they need when they search for it online.

rule_summary: Include keywords in URLs, metadata and content to improve findability.
rule_detail: Make content easy for people to find using search engines. Include keywords in URLs, metadata and content. Create accessible links to high-quality content.

rule_summary: Create accessible links to high-quality content.
rule_detail: Make content easy for people to find using search engines. Include keywords in URLs, metadata and content. Create accessible links to high-quality content.

rule_summary: Use protective markings for government information and follow organisational procedures to add them.
rule_detail: Use protective markings for government information. Follow your organisation’s procedures to add them.

rule_summary: Follow your organisation’s procedures when assessing government information and applying protective markings.
rule_detail: Follow your organisation's procedures when assessing government information and applying protective markings.

rule_summary: Use all four security classification levels for government business information and services.
rule_detail: There are 4 levels of security classification – ‘Official: Sensitive’, ‘Protected’, ‘Secret’ and ‘Top Secret’.

rule_summary: Carry protective markings on all security-classified information, including emails.
rule_detail: All security-classified information, including emails, must carry protective markings.

rule_summary: Mark information metadata as well as the information itself.
rule_detail: Information metadata is also marked.

rule_summary: Mark other information as Official or Unofficial.
rule_detail: All other information is marked as ‘Official’ (a routine level of protection) or ‘Unofficial’ (information that is not part of official duties).

rule_summary: Treat Official and Unofficial as non-classification, non-mandatory markings.
rule_detail: ‘Official’ and ‘Unofficial’ are not security classifications and are not mandatory markings.

rule_summary: Include caveats and information management markers as additional protective markings.
rule_detail: Other protective markings include caveats (such as codewords and special handling instructions) and information management markers.

rule_summary: Apply caveat markings to Protected and higher classifications.
rule_detail: Caveat markings are mandatory for security classifications of Protected or higher.

rule_summary: Treat information management markers as optional.
rule_detail: Information management markers are optional.

rule_summary: Format protective markings to be clearly identifiable.
rule_detail: The Protective Security Policy Framework (PSPF) explains how protective markings should be formatted. To achieve clearly identifiable protective markings, the PSPF recommends:

rule_summary: Use capitals, bold text, large font and a distinctive colour, preferably red.
rule_detail: using capitals, bold text, large font and a distinctive colour (red preferred)

rule_summary: Place markings at the centre top and bottom of each page.
rule_detail: placing markings at the centre top and bottom of each page

rule_summary: Separate markings with a double forward slash.
rule_detail: separating markings by a double forward slash to help clearly differentiate each marking.

rule_summary: Follow PSPF requirements for government information before referring to the PSPF.
rule_detail: When you write for the Australian Government, be aware of [PSPF requirements for government information](https://www.protectivesecurity.gov.au/pspf-annual-release). Follow organisational procedures to apply security classifications and protective markings to content before referring to the PSPF.

rule_summary: Use an initial capital when writing about protective markings in general content.
rule_detail: In general content, use an initial capital unless you are reporting how the protective marking actually appears on the page.

rule_summary: Use quotation marks and preserve the original form when reproducing a marking exactly as it appears on the page.
rule_detail: In general content, use an initial capital unless you are reporting how the protective marking actually appears on the page. In that instance, write the marking as it appears and use quotation marks.

rule_summary: Create content that meets a real need.
rule_detail: Only design and write content that meets a real person’s need.

rule_summary: Find out about users and their needs through user research.
rule_detail: Find out about users and their needs through user research.

rule_summary: Understand user needs to meet the Digital Service Standard.
rule_detail: You must understand the needs of the users of your service to meet the Digital Service Standard: Criterion 1. Understand user needs.

rule_summary: Write for the user, not for an audience.
rule_detail: Writing for an audience is not the same as writing for the user.

rule_summary: Research the range of users and their contexts.
rule_detail: It’s not enough to imagine one kind of user. You need to do user research to learn about the range of users and their contexts. It's important to find out about their specific and diverse needs.

rule_summary: Include accessibility-related differences in user research.
rule_detail: A user’s needs and context may include: a primary language that is something other than English; assistive technology they use to read the content; a range of devices they use to access the content with; the availability and speed of their internet access; a need for a paper or non-digital way to access content.

rule_summary: Do user research to understand how to meet the needs of all users.
rule_detail: Do user research to help you to understand how to meet the needs of all users.

rule_summary: Include people with disability in user research.
rule_detail: Include people with disability in your user research to avoid creating any barriers for them.

rule_summary: Adjust the research approach to the context.
rule_detail: The way you research changes based on the kind of work you are doing and its context.

rule_summary: Work with a user researcher to plan the approach if possible.
rule_detail: If you can, work with a user researcher to plan the approach.

rule_summary: Avoid making assumptions about people you are writing about.
rule_detail: If you are writing about other people, make sure you are not making assumptions about them. This includes other people working in government as well as end users.

rule_summary: Take part in the user research process when creating content.
rule_detail: If you are creating content you need to be part of the user research process.

rule_summary: Observe research sessions led by an experienced user researcher if possible.
rule_detail: It is best if you can observe research sessions led by an experienced user researcher. Then help to synthesise and analyse the research.

rule_summary: Make everyone on the service team take part in research regularly.
rule_detail: In a team that is delivering a service, everyone is part of research for at least 2 hours every 6 weeks. This include writers, content designers and editors.

rule_summary: Ensure content workers participate in the discovery process.
rule_detail: People who work on content must be part of the discovery process. They need to observe research sessions and contribute their perspective in analysis. Content designers, writers and editors notice things that other people may miss. They provide a critical content lens on the work.

rule_summary: Do some desktop research if you cannot access a user researcher or users.
rule_detail: If you or your team are not able to access a user researcher or to talk to users, at least do desktop research.

rule_summary: Use desktop research to identify search keywords and user questions.
rule_detail: Desktop research includes looking at website analytics to identify search keywords and topics. It also involves exploring forums and social media to find out the questions people are asking and the words they use.

rule_summary: Be aware that search terms vary by audience and platform.
rule_detail: When you look at search data be aware that people use different words to search for and to talk about things. Search terms can also be different based on the forum and site they are using.

rule_summary: Prefer user research over no research at all.
rule_detail: Desktop research will not provide the same quality of insight as you get from talking to users. It is better to do this than no research at all.

rule_summary: Use desktop research as well as interviewing users.
rule_detail: It’s also helpful to do desktop research as well as interviewing users.

rule_summary: Review relevant existing research as part of desktop research.
rule_detail: Review existing relevant research as part of your desktop research. This includes research by other teams and academic research from outside government.

rule_summary: Account for context differences and gaps when reviewing existing research.
rule_detail: When you review existing research, be aware that the context will be different. There may also be gaps in the research.

rule_summary: Use existing research as a starting point.
rule_detail: Use existing research as a starting point. It’s not helpful to research the same thing over and over.

rule_summary: Do user research rather than market research when you have a choice.
rule_detail: If you have a choice, do user research. It can be helpful to do market research and stakeholder management as well.

rule_summary: Use qualitative and quantitative research in user research.
rule_detail: User research: uses qualitative research (feedback) and quantitative research (statistics)

rule_summary: Focus user research on why people do things and what they do.
rule_detail: User research: focuses on the ‘why’ (including people’s underlying needs, motivations and the goals they are trying to achieve) and the 'what’ (what people actually do), as well as the usability of what is being designed

rule_summary: Use small-scale, iterative techniques in user research.
rule_detail: User research: uses small-scale and often iterative techniques (for example, interviews, feedback, usability testing, sample-size testing, field studies and workshops)

rule_summary: Aim user research at understanding needs and fixing usability problems.
rule_detail: User research: aims to understand user needs and fix usability problems

rule_summary: Use user research to design accessible and usable services.
rule_detail: User research: helps to design content and services that are accessible and usable for all users

rule_summary: Use quantitative research in market research.
rule_detail: Market research: uses quantitative research (statistics)

rule_summary: Focus market research on what happens.
rule_detail: Market research: focuses on the ‘what’

rule_summary: Use market research to provide broad information.
rule_detail: Market research: provides broad information

rule_summary: Create content only when it meets a user need.
rule_detail: Only create content that meets a need. Find out about users and their needs through user research.

rule_summary: Find out about users and their needs through user research.
rule_detail: Only create content that meets a need. Find out about users and their needs through user research.

rule_summary: Use plain language.
rule_detail: Use plain language. Write short and simple sentences in active voice.

rule_summary: Write short, simple sentences in active voice.
rule_detail: Use plain language. Write short and simple sentences in active voice.

rule_summary: Write and design content so users can find it with a search engine.
rule_detail: Write and design content that is easy for the user to find with a search engine.

rule_summary: Use protective markings for government information.
rule_detail: Use protective markings for government information. Follow your organisation’s procedures to add them.

rule_summary: Follow your organisation's procedures to add protective markings.
rule_detail: Use protective markings for government information. Follow your organisation’s procedures to add them.
